projects.name: Boston Central Artery/Tunnel (Big Dig)
projects.description: The Big Dig relocated 29 miles of utility lines maintained by 31 separate companies. Unknown subsurface conditions, utility conflicts, and rework caused cost escalation from $2.8B to $14.8B.
projects.detail: The project required moving 29 miles of electric, sewer, gas, water, telephone, and other utility lines maintained by 31 separate companies, some infrastructure being 150 years old. Construction crews encountered uncharted utilities not on any plans, as well as utilities shown on drawings that were never actually installed. Flooding and damage occurred due to underground sewer pipes not present on drawings. The failure to assess unknown subsurface conditions was cited as a primary cause of overruns.

projects.name: Honolulu Skyline Rail Transit
projects.description: Hawaii's rail project is $7B+ over budget. A $400M utility relocation contract was canceled after only 8% completion; a new $496M contract was awarded. Utility work costs exceeded $700M total.
projects.detail: HART awarded Nan Inc. a $400M contract in 2018 to relocate nearly 40 miles of utility lines along the Dillingham corridor. By fall 2020, costs far exceeded estimates. HART cancelled the contract after incurring $84M, with only 50-75% of work useful. New contracts were awarded: $496.2M to Nan for 1.5 miles and $218M to Coluccio Construction, pushing total utility relocation costs past $700M. The HART board estimated final utility costs could exceed double the original estimate.

projects.name: California High-Speed Rail (Central Valley)
projects.description: 57% of 1,850 utility relocation projects remain uncompleted after 10 years. The Authority signed construction contracts before completing utility relocation agreements — the State Auditor called this the root cause of most cost overruns.
projects.detail: The Authority did not complete many critical planning tasks before beginning construction, including not sufficiently accounting for utility relocation costs. Three teams of contractors have been working on 1,850 utility relocation projects, but 57% remain uncompleted after a decade. On the CP2-3 section alone, 273 change orders totaling $800M were approved. 20% of utility relocations had not yet started by December 2023. The out-of-sequence approach meant crews repeatedly encountered unresolved utility conflicts requiring costly redesigns.

projects.name: East Side Access (Grand Central Madison)
projects.description: LIRR extension ballooned from $3.5B to $11.1B. Amtrak and MTA couldn't cooperate on track access at Sunnyside Yard, and a contractor punctured a subway tunnel during construction in 2014.
projects.detail: The deep-level cavern excavation accounted for $1.9B, almost triple its initial estimate. Delays from coordination failures between Amtrak and MTA on track access at Sunnyside Yard raised construction costs by almost $1B as of April 2018. In October 2014, a contractor accidentally punctured the subway tunnel underneath. NYC's complex and largely unmapped underground infrastructure was a significant contributor. Planning costs alone exceeded $2B.

projects.name: Maryland Purple Line Light Rail
projects.description: 16.2-mile light rail line plagued by protracted utility relocation. The original P3 contractor walked away in 2020 after $800M+ in change orders. A major Verizon facility relocation took far longer than expected.
projects.detail: Challenges included coordinating relocation of several existing services on single utility poles in a particular order, with each utility having its own relocation request process. A major Verizon-owned facility midway along the route required above-ground and underground utility relocation that took far longer than expected. As of June 2022, only 77% of utility relocations were complete. The original P3 consortium quit in 2020; Maryland paid a $250M settlement. Permitting and legal fees, originally budgeted at $6M, consumed roughly $800M.

projects.name: Second Avenue Subway (Phase 1 & 2)
projects.description: Crews repeatedly struck uncharted utilities in Manhattan's complex underground. As-built drawings were inaccurate. The lesson was so significant that Phase 2 proactively awarded a $182M utility relocation contract.
projects.detail: During Phase 1, an Arup director described conditions as 'a spaghetti of tunnels, utilities, pipes and cables — I’ve never seen anything like it.' Utility relocation took 14 months, nearly double the anticipated 8 months. These discoveries forced work stoppages, redesigns, and change orders throughout construction. Phase 2 proactively awarded a $182M utility relocation contract to C.A.C. Industries before station/tunnel construction to avoid repeating Phase 1 problems. Phase 2 budget grew from $5B (2019) to $7.7B (2023).

projects.name: San Francisco Central Subway
projects.description: 1.7-mile subway extension delayed 4 years and $375M+ over budget. Workers breached a water main (July 2014) and a natural gas pipeline (May 2015). Hard rock and utility relocations were cited as main delay causes.
projects.detail: Contractor Tutor Perini predicted a 15-month delay due to hard rock and required utility relocations. An underground river was encountered. The $840M main construction contract was already $120M over budget at award. Of 37 schedule updates submitted 2014-2017, SFMTA rejected 21. Tutor Perini received a $143M settlement. Total contract cost increases were approximately $300M. Two initial utility relocation contracts were extensive, with utilities relocated into a shared vault under sidewalks.

projects.name: I-69 Section 5 (Bloomington to Martinsville)
projects.description: P3 concessionaire failed due to delays and cost overruns, forcing the state to take over. Utility relocation in isolated areas was a significant challenge, with costs not included in earlier estimates.
projects.detail: The Indiana Finance Authority took over the Section 5 segment after the P3 with I-69 Development Partners failed. Many utilities underground needed to be moved, and the isolated location required significant effort. Costs such as construction administration, design changes, and utility relocation were not included in earlier estimates. The project cost more than doubled from $422M to $863M+.

projects.name: Hardscrabble Road Widening
projects.description: 8-mile road widening from 2 to 5 lanes delayed 6 years and $18M over budget due to inaccurate waterline relocations by City of Columbia Water.
projects.detail: The contractor said City of Columbia Water caused a delay of around 2.5 years because waterline relocations were 'inaccurate' and 'not performed to an acceptable standard.' Despite more than 1,000 days of delays, SCDOT did not assess any liquidated damages because many delays were outside the contractor's control. A state bill was introduced to help small businesses impacted by the prolonged construction.

projects.name: Juban Road Widening
projects.description: Road widening delayed 4 years because utility relocations (energy, sewer, water, fiber, cable, gas) took nearly 3 years before road work could even begin.
projects.detail: Construction crews broke ground in 2019 for utility relocation. DOTD stated that utility relocations were the source of delays, not 'lackadaisical efforts.' It took almost three years for the utilities to move their infrastructure. COVID-19 compounded the delays. By combining two originally separate project phases, DOTD cut costs by $5M.

projects.name: Miami I-395/SR-836 Signature Bridge
projects.description: FDOT cited utility relocation as one of several reasons for delays. The construction JV claims $405M in design-related overruns; FDOT acknowledged $64M+ in cost increases.
projects.detail: FDOT aimed to complete the interchange project including a 1,000-foot signature bridge by 2021. The Archer Western-De Moya JV filed lawsuits claiming HDR Engineering miscalculated wind loads and that parts of the bridge had to be demolished and rebuilt. FDOT cited weather, supply chain issues, utility relocation, and a bid protest as delay reasons. Total cost hiked from $840M to $866M officially, while the JV claims $405M in overruns.

projects.name: SR 99 Tunnel (Alaskan Way Viaduct Replacement)
projects.description: State funding didn't cover utility relocation, pushing the burden to Seattle. The TBM 'Bertha' was stuck underground for 2 years after advancing only 1/9 of the route.
projects.detail: State funding was not authorized for utility relocation costs, meaning the City of Seattle funded it separately. The tunnel boring machine Bertha broke down after advancing only one-ninth of its route and was stuck underground for two years, costing at least $60M. The state had to keep staff and consultants on longer than expected, driving $223M in cost overruns.

projects.name: Hilltop Tacoma Link Extension
projects.description: Workers found 'completely different underground conditions than what was mapped,' requiring streets to be torn up, redesigned, and torn up again. Over 100 businesses disrupted.
projects.detail: Sound Transit CEO described: 'construction workers would rip the streets up, find completely different underground conditions than what was mapped, cover the holes, re-design the project and rip up the streets again.' The agency attributed overruns to 'differing site conditions and obstructions, conflicts, and contaminated materials related to utility relocations.' A state audit blamed $100M in contract changes across Sound Transit projects on failing to locate underground utilities before construction.

projects.name: RapidRide G Line (Madison BRT)
projects.description: Unanticipated utility discoveries during construction caused redesigns and change orders. Inaccurate as-built plans prompted Metro to increase utility mapping on all subsequent projects.
projects.detail: Originally planned for 2019 opening with a $134M price tag. Unanticipated utility discoveries caused redesigns and change orders. The experience was so impactful that Metro began requiring more extensive advanced potholing at pole locations to minimize utility conflicts on future projects. After opening, the city paid $650,000 to fix a construction error where steel plates lifted buses by approximately one inch.

projects.name: RapidRide H Line (Delridge)
projects.description: Inaccurate as-built plans and underground utility documentation caused months of redesigns and change orders during 2021-2022 excavation.
projects.detail: During excavation in 2021-2022, inaccurate as-built plan sets and underground utility documentation required several months of redesigns and change orders, causing a three-month delay. A concrete workers' strike added 6 months and station design problems added 1 year. The utility challenges led King County Metro to increase investment in utility conflict mapping for subsequent projects.

projects.name: Tempe Streetcar (Valley Metro S Line)
projects.description: 3-mile streetcar accumulated $14M in change orders including hundreds of conflicts between the overhead contact system and underground/overhead utilities.
projects.detail: Construction began June 2017 with utility relocation preceding track installation. Over the 3-year construction phase, the project accumulated $14M in contract change orders, including hundreds of conflicts between the overhead contact system (OCS) and underground/overhead utilities. Arizona placed financial responsibility on Valley Metro for all third-party utility relocations, including design costs.

projects.name: Clear Path 465 (I-465/I-69 Interchange)
projects.description: Crews knew about utilities under the interstate but 'were not aware of how extensive they were,' requiring far more coordination than planned.
projects.detail: INDOT's project to improve the I-465 and I-69 interchange began in 2022 targeting 2025 completion. During construction, underground utilities beneath the interstate were far more extensive than anticipated. While their presence was known, the actual extent required significantly more coordination, pushing completion to late 2026.

projects.name: Cumberland Road Widening
projects.description: A complex network of underground/overhead utilities owned by multiple companies creates a cascading dependency — one utility cannot proceed until another finishes.
projects.detail: The project will widen Cumberland Road between 106th and 116th streets from two lanes. City officials confirmed utility relocations are the primary factor delaying the project. Water, sewer, natural gas, electric, and fiber optic cables owned by multiple companies create a cascading effect where one utility cannot proceed until another finishes. The Board of Works approved a $237,000 utility reimbursement agreement with Duke Energy.

projects.name: Route 7 Corridor Widening
projects.description: Widening 7 miles of Route 7 required coordinating utility relocations with 19 separate utility companies. The team projected a 1-year delay from utility scheduling alone.
projects.detail: The project team identified during procurement that relocation of utilities owned by 19 companies had potential for significant schedule impacts, projecting a likely one-year delay. To mitigate, utility relocations were consolidated to overlapping corridors. Coordination included Washington Gas, Verizon, Dominion Power, DC Water, and 15 others. The project reportedly finished on budget at $313.9M.

projects.name: NC 16 Widening
projects.description: NCDOT identified getting existing utilities moved and relocated as the biggest challenge on this $41M highway widening project, running about 10% behind schedule.
projects.detail: The project widened N.C. 16 from two to four lanes over an 8-mile stretch. During construction, the project ran approximately 10% behind schedule. The NCDOT project manager identified getting existing utilities moved as the biggest challenge. Slow utility relocation is a chronic problem for North Carolina DOT projects.

projects.name: SR 20 Widening (Canton to Cumming)
projects.description: GDOT widening project will cost the City of Cumming nearly $30M solely for utility relocation — a massive financial burden separate from the $146M construction budget.
projects.detail: Georgia DOT is widening 5.2 miles of SR 20 from four to six lanes. The total project estimate is $146M, but the City of Cumming faces an additional nearly $30M in utility relocation costs pushed to the local municipality. An estimated 214 parcels will be affected. This illustrates how utility relocation costs are often pushed to local governments. Clearing began August 2024.

projects.name: Durham-Orange Light Rail (Cancelled)
projects.description: After 20 years and $130M in planning, the project was killed when Duke University denied right-of-way over utility relocation and infrastructure concerns.
projects.detail: The proposed route required relocating utility infrastructure including data and water lines at Duke University, with undetermined costs. The plan called for widening Erwin Road and further burying main lines supplying all power to Duke's campus, hospital, clinics, and laboratories. GoTriangle agreed to elevate the route at $90-115M additional cost, but Duke denied access in 2019, killing the project.

projects.name: Islands Expressway Bridge Replacement
projects.description: City of Savannah utility service relocations repeatedly disrupted construction. GDOT fined the contractor $5,000/day, accumulating nearly $2M in penalties before reaching an agreement.
projects.detail: The project to replace a drawbridge with a taller crossing started in 2018 targeting 2022 completion. Utility relocation disruptions pushed the timeline repeatedly. GDOT fined contractor Prince Contracting $5,000/day, accumulating nearly $2M in penalties. Ultimately, GDOT and the contractor agreed to add time, removing penalties. Twin bridges now slated for August 2026 completion.

projects.name: I-4 Ultimate (Central Florida)
projects.description: $2.3B Interstate 4 project faced $100M in delay claims and 245-day delay from drilled shaft failures caused by unexpected subsurface conditions.
projects.detail: Florida DOT's $2.3B I-4 Ultimate project — a P3 between Skanska, John Laing, and SGL Constructors — faced claims of a 245-day delay and $100M overrun. Claims revolved around two drilled shaft failures during bridge foundation work caused by unexpected subsurface conditions. A separate 1996 Florida study found 30% of FDOT highway cases involved utility coordination problems.

projects.name: Voyager Parkway Bridge
projects.description: Utility relocation consumed $4M (a quarter of the bridge cost) and caused 4 months of delays, including waiting for Lumen Technologies to relocate fiber optic lines linked to the Air Force Academy.
projects.detail: $4M was spent on utility relocations, representing a quarter of the total bridge cost. The project was delayed 4 months after frustrating utility delays including relocating a Lumen Technologies fiber optic line linked to the Air Force Academy. The bridge was scheduled for August 2024 completion before the nearby Ford Amphitheater opening. The venue opened a month early while the bridge fell behind. Bridge finally opened late March 2025.

projects.name: 8th Street Corridor Improvements
projects.description: Crews discovered many previously unmarked underground utilities installed before modern record-keeping, delaying the water main replacement phase.
projects.detail: Crews drilling to locate utilities discovered many unmarked underground lines between Motor City Drive and the Fountain Creek bridge. Some were installed before modern record-keeping. The newly-identified lines are being recorded and incorporated into updated design plans. The water main replacement phase was pushed from winter 2025 to spring 2026.

projects.name: San Diego Mission Beach Sewer/Water Project
projects.description: Crews found 324 underground utilities where only 160 were documented — more than double. Productivity dropped 62-73%, causing 159-day delay and $1.26M settlement.
projects.detail: A massive discrepancy between documented and actual underground utilities: 324 found vs. 160 documented in city records. Crew productivity dropped from 75 feet/day to 20-50 feet/day (62-73% reduction). The 159-day delay resulted in a $1.26M settlement. This became a widely cited case study in the utility locating industry.

projects.name: Richmond Highway Project (Virginia SUE)
projects.description: SUE investment of $93,553 (156 test holes) identified 75 utility conflicts. Design changes eliminated 61, avoiding $731,425 in utility adjustments. Net savings: $637,872.
projects.detail: VDOT's consultant dug 156 test holes at potential highway-utility conflict locations. Using the SUE data, designers determined conflicts would occur at 75 of 156 sites. Design changes successfully eliminated 61 of 75 conflicts, avoiding $731,425 in utility adjustments. The $93,553 cost of test holes resulted in net savings of $637,872 — a 7:1 ROI. This became a key FHWA case study for SUE value.

projects.name: Maryland Highway Realignment (SUE Case)
projects.description: SUE investment of $56,000 reduced utility impacts from 5,000 feet to 400 feet per utility, saving $1,340,000 — a 24:1 return on investment.
projects.detail: On a highway project involving realignment and widening from 2 to 6 lanes, SUE mapping of underground utilities enabled MSHA to redesign hydraulics to minimize conflicts. Instead of impacting 5,000 feet of each utility line, conflicts were reduced to 400 feet each — a 92% reduction. The $56,000 SUE cost saved $1,340,000, representing $23.93 returned for every $1 spent.

projects.name: Columbus Ohio 138 kV Underground Line
projects.description: SUE investment under $100,000 resulted in $400K lower bids and zero change orders, zero relocations, zero damages, zero contractor claims.
projects.detail: For a 2km underground 138 kV electric line installation, SUE costing less than $100,000 mapped all existing subsurface utilities. The accurate data enabled precise planning: $400,000 reduction in contractor bids (bidders priced with confidence rather than padding for unknowns). Completed with no change orders, no relocations, no damages, no claims — an exceptional outcome for urban underground construction.
projects.budget: <$100K SUE investment → $400K in lower bids + zero claims
projects.timeline: Completed on schedule with zero delays

projects.name: NC 168 Water Line Project
projects.description: 40 vacuum excavation test holes costing less than $10,000 saved $500,000 by confirming 21,280 ft of PVC water line could remain in place instead of being relocated.
projects.detail: Along 18 miles of NC 168, NCDOT used vacuum excavation to locate PVC water lines undetectable by conventional electromagnetic methods. 40 test holes costing less than $10,000 confirmed that 21,280 feet (over 4 miles) of water line could remain in place rather than being relocated. Without SUE, the entire length would have been assumed to conflict, requiring unnecessary $500,000 relocation. ROI: ~$50 per dollar spent.

projects.name: Merrimack Valley Gas Disaster Road Reconstruction
projects.description: Gas over-pressurization caused fires/explosions in 40+ homes, killing one. 50 miles of roads dug up for gas main replacement, requiring $80M in road reconstruction.
projects.detail: On September 13, 2018, over-pressurization of Columbia Gas lines caused fires and explosions in over 40 homes, killing one person and forcing 30,000 to evacuate. Columbia Gas replaced 43.5 miles of gas lines, 5,086 service lines, and 8,570 meters. 50 miles of roadways were dug up. Columbia Gas entered an $80M settlement for road/sidewalk restoration. Lawrence received $31.9M. Columbia Gas was also fined $53M federally and reached a $56M state deal.
projects.budget: $80M road restoration settlement + $53M federal fine + $56M state
projects.timeline: Road restoration planned in four phases beginning 2019

projects.name: 1998 St. Cloud Downtown Gas Explosion
projects.description: Fiber optic crew punctured underground gas pipe, causing explosion that killed 4 people, injured 11, and destroyed 5 downtown buildings.
projects.detail: On December 11, 1998, Cable Constructors Inc. employees punctured a one-inch underground gas pipe while installing a utility pole support anchor. Officials tried to secure the area for 90 minutes until gas built up in a basement was ignited by a water heater pilot light. The explosion destroyed five downtown buildings. The NTSB faulted Cable Constructors' safety practices and the fire department's gas leak response.

projects.name: Matthews Gas Line Explosion
projects.description: Duke Energy subcontractor drilling for utility poles struck an 8-inch gas main, igniting a massive fireball that burned for over an hour and damaged 2 homes (May 2026).
projects.detail: Pike Electric crews contracting with Duke Energy struck an 8-inch natural gas main while drilling for a utility pole just before noon on May 13, 2026. Flames shot into the air and burned for over an hour. Firefighters intentionally let the gas-fed fire burn until utility crews could safely shut off supply. Two homes heavily damaged. NC811 data shows Mecklenburg County recorded more than 500 excavation-related utility strikes in just one quarter — the second-highest total in NC.
projects.budget: 2 homes heavily damaged; project costs not disclosed
projects.timeline: Project halted; 500+ utility strikes per quarter in county

projects.name: Imperial Home Explosion (AT&T Fiber)
projects.description: AT&T fiber subcontractor struck Spire gas line due to inaccurate underground utility markings, destroying one home and damaging two others (March 2026).
projects.detail: A subcontractor for AT&T struck a natural gas line during fiber optic installation. AT&T stated the damage was 'the result of inaccurate markings of underground utilities.' The Spire gas line status read 'Not complete — in progress — trouble locating.' Gas accumulated in a residence for 80 minutes before exploding. A family with four young children escaped. The home was destroyed and two neighbors' homes damaged.
projects.timeline: March 3, 2026 — caused by inaccurate utility markings

projects.name: Providence North Main & Meeting Streets
projects.description: Two Providence streets ripped up by Rhode Island Energy just one month after being freshly paved in summer 2022. City council voted to stop issuing permits to the utility.
projects.detail: North Main Street and Meeting Street were resurfaced summer 2022. Weeks after completion, RI Energy crews returned to tear up both streets for utility connections. The Providence City Council voted for a resolution asking DPW to stop issuing permits to RI Energy, with a councilman stating the utility had 'failed to return our roads to preconstruction condition time and time again.'
projects.timeline: Paved summer 2022 → dug up ~1 month later

projects.name: Boston North End Salem Street
projects.description: Fresh pavement on Salem Street promptly dug up by NStar (now Eversource) for underground electrical work (2014). Led to Boston implementing the COBUCS utility coordination system.
projects.detail: In June 2014, Salem Street in Boston's North End received fresh pavement. The new surface didn't last long before NStar dug a hole for underground electrical wires. This chronic problem of utility companies failing to coordinate with paving schedules led Boston to implement the COBUCS (City of Boston Utility Coordination Software) system requiring every utility to complete work and sign off on each block before paving.

projects.name: Cleveland Circle, Boston
projects.description: MBTA and Boston planned road fixes during a May 2026 C-Line shutdown, but National Grid was set to dig up the same streets shortly after for gas main replacement.
projects.detail: MBTA and Boston planned to use a May 2026 C-Line shutdown to fix dangerous potholes at Cleveland Circle. However, National Grid was set to dig up the same streets to replace gas mains under all roads and trolley tracks. Road repairs from the MBTA shutdown would be destroyed by subsequent utility work. Discussed at an April 2026 meeting with residents.
projects.budget: Road repair investment about to be wasted
projects.timeline: May 2026 road repairs pre-empted by National Grid plans

projects.name: San Francisco Utility Cut Pavement Degradation
projects.description: Landmark city study found utility cuts reduce pavement life by 20% to 56%. San Francisco enacted a 3-year moratorium and street damage restoration fees of $1.00-$3.50/sq ft.
projects.detail: SF's landmark study confirmed utility cuts reduce estimated pavement life by 20-56%, increasing roughness in both immediate and surrounding areas. In response, SF enacted fees from $1.00/sq ft for 15-20 year old streets to $3.50/sq ft for streets less than 5 years old. A 3-year moratorium on excavation in newly surfaced streets was established. SF publicly tracks moratorium streets through its open data portal.
projects.budget: Millions in premature repair costs city-wide
projects.timeline: Ongoing: pavement life reduced from 15-20 years to as low as 7-12 years

projects.name: Los Angeles Utility Cut Pavement Damage
projects.description: Utility cuts reduced arterial street life from 25 to 16.5 years (34%) and local streets from 34.5 to 28.5 years. LA's SDRF ordinance generates $51M+/year in restoration fees.
projects.detail: LA research found utility cuts reduced average pavement life from 25 to 16.5 years for arterials and 34.5 to 28.5 years for local streets. The SDRF ordinance charges $8.24/sq ft on residential and $19.44/sq ft on major streets (including 5-foot buffer around excavations). In FY 2024-25, the SDRF generated approximately $51.3M. The Annual Resurfacing Program is submitted to over 200 utility companies for clearances before paving.
projects.budget: SDRF generates $51.3M/year; pavement damage costs millions more

projects.name: Austin Utility Cut Pavement Damage
projects.description: Study found utility cuts reduce pavement life by 17.5% (longitudinal) to 33.4% (transverse). Austin implemented a 5-year residential / 7-year arterial moratorium.
projects.detail: Austin's study found pavement life reduced 17.5% on streets with longitudinal cuts and 33.36% with transverse/combination cuts. Austin implemented a Protected Streets program: 5-year moratorium on residential and 7-year on collector/arterial streets. Streets with an RCI above 7 have strict guidelines for cut justification and restoration. A street damage recovery fee covers the lost pavement life.
projects.budget: Street damage recovery fees for lost pavement life
projects.timeline: Pavement life reduced 17-33% by utility cuts

projects.name: Kansas City Telecom Utility Cut Damage
projects.description: Telecom industry construction devastated city streets in the late 1990s-2000s. A 2001 ordinance with pavement degradation fees generated $1.2M in its first year.
projects.detail: Kansas City was overwhelmed by street destruction from the telecommunications industry's rapid expansion in the late 1990s-2000, which required extensive excavation. In February 2001, the city passed an ordinance with pavement degradation fees and restoration requirements. By June 2002, it had generated $1.2M dedicated to road improvements. Fees are higher for recently constructed streets, creating an incentive to avoid cutting new pavement.
projects.budget: $1.2M/year in fees collected; millions in underlying damage

projects.name: San Diego Moratorium Audit (18% Violation Rate)
projects.description: A 2010 audit found that 18% of sampled streets resurfaced in FY2009 were excavated during the 3-year moratorium period despite the city's prohibition.
projects.detail: San Diego's Municipal Code prohibits excavations into streets that received asphalt overlay for 3 years and slurry seal for 1 year. A November 2010 City Auditor audit found about 18% of sampled streets resurfaced in FY2009 were excavated during the moratorium period. While all cases were for allowed reasons, the high rate demonstrates the persistent challenge of protecting pavement investments from utility work.
projects.budget: Pavement investment degraded despite moratorium protections

projects.name: LA Metro Regional Connector
projects.description: 1.9-mile underground light rail connector in downtown LA where century-old unmapped utilities forced extensive redesign and relocation, adding $400M and 3 years to the project.
projects.detail: The Regional Connector Transit Corridor linked the A Line, E Line, and added three underground stations in downtown Los Angeles. During construction, crews discovered that many utilities under downtown LA were neither in the location nor condition specified by utility records, requiring a complete re-design and replacement of much of the underground infrastructure. Preliminary studies failed to identify numerous early-history utility connections and 19th-century water and electric infrastructure. The project's original $1.4 billion baseline grew to $1.8 billion by completion, and the opening was delayed from 2020 to June 16, 2023.

projects.name: LA Metro D Line (Purple Line) Extension
projects.description: 3.9-mile subway extension along Wilshire Boulevard where advance utility relocations at multiple stations and difficult tunneling conditions drove cumulative cost overruns exceeding $700M.
projects.detail: Section 1 of the D Line Extension runs 3.9 miles from Wilshire/Western to Wilshire/La Cienega. Advance utility relocation contracts were required at Wilshire/La Brea and Wilshire/La Cienega stations, involving relocation of Beverly Hills water, storm drain, and sewer utilities. The Metro board approved successive cost overruns: $200M (August 2020), $150M (May 2021), $225M (May 2024), and $154M, bringing total Section 1 costs from $2.8 billion to $3.51 billion. The first phase opened in March 2026, years behind the original schedule.

projects.name: I-205 Abernethy Bridge Project
projects.description: Oregon's largest construction project saw costs triple from $250M to $815M due to soil stabilization, underground obstructions, utility relocations, and engineering surprises after construction began.
projects.detail: ODOT's project to widen and seismically strengthen the I-205 Abernethy Bridge was estimated at $250 million in 2018. When bids opened in 2022, costs doubled to $495 million. Once construction began, costs escalated further to $662M and then $815M due to additional soil stabilization work, unexpected concrete pier strengthening, excavation obstructions, supply chain issues, and utility relocations. The project is now more than 200 days behind its October 2026 target, with the contractor estimating January 2028 completion.

projects.name: I-5 Rose Quarter Improvement Project
projects.description: Portland highway project ballooned from $450M to over $2B, with $67.5M obligated for utility relocations as part of early construction phases, while facing a $1.5B funding gap.
projects.detail: The I-5 Rose Quarter Improvement Project was approved by the Oregon legislature in 2017 at an estimated cost of $450 million. The cost estimate has since grown to $1.96-2.08 billion. Of the federal funding granted, $67.5 million for design and utility relocation has been obligated. Phase 1A covering stormwater improvements, bridge preservation, and seismic upgrades began in summer 2025. However, the project faces a more than $1.5 billion financial hole after the federal government pulled back a grant and a state transportation package failed.
projects.timeline: Original construction start ~2020 → Phase 1A started 2025, full completion TBD

projects.name: Interstate Bridge Replacement Program
projects.description: The I-5 Columbia River bridge replacement project doubled from $6B to $14.4B, with utility relocation a significant scope item, as construction costs nationwide increased 70% between 2020 and 2024.
projects.detail: The Interstate Bridge Replacement Program to replace the aging I-5 bridge over the Columbia River between Portland and Vancouver saw its cost estimate soar approximately 140% from a 2022 estimate of $6 billion to a new target of $14.4 billion (range: $13.5B-$15.2B). The program includes right-of-way acquisition and utility relocation as budgeted components. A combination of project delays, rising materials and labor costs, tariffs, and the scope of extending light rail from North Portland to downtown Vancouver drove the increases.
projects.timeline: Construction start repeatedly delayed, completion TBD

projects.name: Sound Transit Lynnwood Link Extension
projects.description: 8.5-mile light rail extension requiring extensive utility relocations across four municipal jurisdictions experienced $500M in cost overruns from scope creep, land costs, and construction inflation.
projects.detail: Sound Transit's Lynnwood Link Extension, an 8.5-mile light rail line from Northgate to Lynnwood, was originally budgeted at $2.4 billion with a late 2023 opening. In August 2017, Sound Transit announced $500 million in cost overruns and a six-month delay. Cost increases included enlarged station designs ($150-190M), higher land costs due to 44% inflation and 190 additional parcels ($100M), and construction market increases ($140-190M). The project spanned four municipal jurisdictions and required extensive utility relocations. The line ultimately opened August 30, 2024, with a final cost approaching $3.2 billion.

projects.name: Sound Transit Federal Way Link Extension
projects.location: Angle Lake / Kent / Federal Way, WA
projects.description: 7.8-mile light rail extension hit $460M in overruns from construction inflation, land costs, unstable soils requiring redesign, and a 140-day concrete truck driver strike.
projects.detail: The Federal Way Link Extension saw its estimated cost revised from $2.09 billion to $2.55 billion in July 2018, due to land acquisition costs and limited contractor availability. During construction, unstable soils in a wetland along I-5 required a 500-foot elevated span redesign costing about $72 million. A 140-day concrete truck driver strike further delayed the project. Originally planned for 2024, the extension opened December 6, 2025.

projects.name: Tucson Downtown Links
projects.description: Voter-approved $76M road improvement became a $110M+ project after telecom utility relocation near Union Pacific railroad tracks caused multiple delays and increased costs.
projects.detail: Tucson's Downtown Links project was sold to voters in 2006 as a $76 million multimodal corridor connecting Barraza Aviation Parkway to St. Mary's Road. Telecom utility relocation near the railroad tracks, combined with prolonged difficulties coordinating with Union Pacific on tunnel design, caused multiple delays and cost increases. Crews waited for relocation of fiber-optic utilities within UPRR's right-of-way. The project is now $34 million over budget, pushing past $110 million, and targeted for completion in early 2026.

projects.name: Phoenix South Central Light Rail Extension
projects.description: 5.5-mile light rail extension delayed 2 years from 2023 to 2025 due to unanticipated utility relocations, COVID-19, and a ballot initiative, while replacing 30+ miles of underground infrastructure.
projects.detail: Valley Metro's $1.34 billion South Central Extension added 5.5 miles of light rail to south Phoenix. Construction began in 2019 with an expected 2023 completion. A combination of COVID-19 pandemic impacts, unanticipated utility relocations, and a ballot initiative from project opponents delayed the opening by two years. The extension replaced more than 30 miles of underground utility infrastructure. The project finally opened June 7, 2025. While it remained on budget, the two-year delay significantly impacted South Central Phoenix businesses, with many shutting their doors permanently.

projects.name: Albuquerque Rapid Transit (ART)
projects.description: BRT system on Central Avenue required $4.2M-$30M in water line relocations, then faced 2-year delay after stations had to be rebuilt for ADA violations and defective electric buses were returned.
projects.detail: The Albuquerque Rapid Transit project built bus rapid transit along Central Avenue (Route 66). The Water Utility Authority relocated water lines in five sections so they would not be underneath ART stations, with costs ranging from $4.2 million to $30 million. Many of the water pipes were over 50 years old. The $119 million project faced over two years of delay. The contractor had to rebuild several stations due to inconsistent platform heights, ADA violations, and intersection geometry issues. Additionally, 15 defective electric buses from BYD were returned and replaced with $7.5M in diesel buses. Regular service finally began November 30, 2019, with a final cost of $133.6 million.

projects.name: Denver Central 70 (I-70) Project
projects.description: The $1.2B I-70 reconstruction required 468 utility relocations and faced $100-150M in overruns from railroad design conflicts after the contractor built above the water table to avoid utility complications.
projects.detail: The Central 70 Project reconstructed 10 miles of Interstate 70 through north Denver. The project required 468 utility relocations. While the utility relocations themselves were managed with zero claims, the contractor elected to build above a specific level to avoid complications from the water table and underground utilities. This forced the design around existing railroads, but Union Pacific rejected the design, requiring costly modifications. The railroad design conflict added an estimated $100-150 million in extra costs and a 10-month delay.
projects.timeline: September 2022 → mid-2023 (delivered early on revised schedule)

projects.name: Colorado Springs Fiber Network Line Strikes
projects.description: Municipal fiber network installation resulted in 766 utility line strikes in one year, $500K in fines, a $5.35M lawsuit settlement, and 450+ neighborhood outages.
projects.detail: Colorado Springs Utilities' $203 million fiber network expansion experienced severe underground utility damage. Contractors hit neighborhood service lines 766 times in one year, with 56 strikes having high probability of injuring someone. The damage caused more than 450 neighborhood outages. Fines of $500,000 were assessed. Colorado Springs Utilities paid $5.35 million to settle a lawsuit with contractor ADB Companies, who alleged that Utilities delayed locating underground facilities — at one point being late to respond to 80% of utility location requests. The utility also adopted stop-work authority for unsafe digging practices.
projects.timeline: Ongoing through 2029, delayed by lawsuits and enforcement actions

projects.name: BART Silicon Valley Phase II Extension
projects.description: Six-mile BART extension to downtown San Jose grew from $4.7B (2014) to $12.75B, with utility relocation part of $25M early construction phase, and an 18-month delay to find a new tunnel contractor.
projects.detail: VTA's BART Silicon Valley Phase II Extension, a six-mile underground extension bringing BART to downtown San Jose and Santa Clara with four new stations, has experienced dramatic cost escalation. In 2014, the project was estimated at $4.7 billion with a 2036 opening. By 2024, the estimate had grown to $12.75 billion with a 2037 opening target. VTA won a $5.1 billion federal grant in August 2024 but still faces a roughly $700 million shortfall. Utility relocation is part of the $25 million early-stage construction.

projects.name: Sound Transit East Link (2 Line)
projects.description: 14-mile light rail extension across Lake Washington delayed 3 years when contractors had to rebuild 4 miles of flawed concrete track supports, with utility relocation saving $75M through alignment change.
projects.detail: Sound Transit's 2 Line, a 14-mile light rail extension from downtown Seattle to Redmond across a floating bridge, was to begin service by July 2023. Contractors discovered they had to reinforce or rebuild 4 miles of flawed concrete track supports, causing a delay of a year or more. The project ultimately opened March 28, 2026, about three years late. In South Bellevue, a realignment was adopted specifically to reduce utility relocation costs, achieving $75 million in savings. A total of 170 businesses in Bellevue and Redmond were relocated.

projects.name: Denver RTD FasTracks Program
projects.description: Voter-approved $4.7B transit expansion has spent $5.5B with 75% complete and still needs $1.6B more, as escalating construction costs and utility coordination challenges left four corridors unfinished.
projects.detail: Denver's FasTracks program was approved by voters in 2004 at $4.7 billion to build rail transit corridors across the metro area. RTD has expended more than $5.5 billion and completed approximately 75% of the program. RTD estimates it still needs $1.6 billion to complete four unfinished corridors by 2034. Challenges include very low sales tax revenue growth, escalating construction costs, raw materials inflation, and labor market challenges. The G Line commuter rail to Wheat Ridge was notably delayed from October 2016 to April 2019 due to automated crossing gate timing issues.

projects.name: Picture Main Street Reconstruction
projects.description: Eversource Energy installed gas lines that did not align with city-approved design plans, forcing the city to dig 20 test pits to locate misplaced utilities and delaying bidding by at least 10 months.
projects.detail: Northampton's Picture Main Street project aimed to widen sidewalks, add protected bike lanes, and modernize century-old infrastructure beneath Main Street. In late 2024, the city discovered that Eversource had installed new gas lines in positions that conflicted with planned traffic signal foundations. The city spent approximately $50,000 excavating over 20 test pits. Design revisions were required, pushing the bidding timeline from August 2026 to at least June 2027. The project cost estimate climbed from $26.3 million to $43.3 million by May 2026.

projects.name: Oxbo Road Realignment Project
projects.description: An independent investigation found 'extreme mismanagement' including no utility relocation plan and no project manager, causing Georgia Power pole relocations to stall the road project for years.
projects.detail: Roswell's Oxbo Road connector project was originally estimated at $7 million in 2016. The road closed in early 2020 for construction, but work halted in early 2021 after costs ballooned. An investigation found the city had no project manager, no utility relocation plan, and failed to follow state law for property acquisition. Georgia Power had difficulty acquiring easements for relocating approximately 25 utility poles. Costs soared to $18.4 million by 2023. The road finally reopened in June 2023 after being closed for over three years.

projects.name: Keene Downtown Infrastructure Project
projects.description: Bids to replace 100+ year-old water, sewer, and gas utilities beneath downtown came in at $28M-$31M against a $19M budget, forcing the city to cut scope, rebid, and reallocate road maintenance funds.
projects.detail: Keene's downtown underground infrastructure includes pipes over 120 years old. The city set a $19 million budget for comprehensive replacement, but the first round of bids came in at approximately $28 million and $30.8 million. Contractors cited the difficulty of maintaining production rates in the tight downtown area. The city cut scope items worth $1.6 million, reallocated $2.74 million from road preservation funds, and rebid. The project was delayed by over a year through multiple rounds of bidding.

projects.name: James Avenue Reconstruction
projects.description: Utility leaks, utility conflicts, and field changes added 47 working days to the project, with an additional 40 days lost to weather, pushing the $3.66M road project well past its deadline.
projects.detail: The James Avenue Reconstruction Project was part of the Better Streets Waco initiative. The $3.66 million project aimed to improve roadways, sidewalks, and underground utilities. During construction, crews encountered utility leaks and underground utility conflicts that required field changes. A total of 87 working days were added — 47 due to utility leaks, conflicts, and field changes, and 40 due to weather. The project was only 75% complete when city officials addressed the delays publicly.

projects.name: Downtown Pullman Reconstruction
projects.description: Crews encountered over 525 tons of contaminated soil from a former gas station site and faced supply chain delays for traffic signals, pushing a 4-month project into a second year.
projects.detail: Pullman's downtown reconstruction began in April 2024 with an expected 4-month timeline and approximately $12 million budget. Crews rebuilding Main Street and underground utilities discovered petroleum-contaminated soil from a former Chevron gas station, requiring removal and proper disposal of more than 525 tons of contaminated material. Supply chain challenges prevented receiving stoplights on schedule. The project ran roughly $350,000 overbudget and extended more than 6 months beyond its original timeline.

projects.name: Ringgold Road Multimodal Corridor
projects.description: Unexpected underground utility conflicts and deteriorated stormwater infrastructure were discovered during construction of a multimodal path, delaying the project and increasing costs.
projects.detail: The first phase of a 1.2-mile, $8.6 million multimodal construction project along Ringgold Road encountered unexpected issues with underground utilities and deterioration of stormwater and sewer structures once excavation began. The project was only 35% complete when the utility surprises were discovered. Stormwater work represents about half the project cost. The utility conflicts slowed work significantly, and the full cost impact was still being assessed.
projects.timeline: Summer 2022 start → Delayed (Phase 1 incomplete as of Jan 2023)

projects.name: Kinsey Court Water Main Replacement
projects.description: A water main upgrade on a dead-end street was stalled for months by a fiber optic vault conflict and failed pressure testing, requiring reassignment to a new project team.
projects.detail: The Kinsey Court water main replacement project in Buckhead's Peachtree Hills neighborhood began in May after residents lost water pressure. The project required upgrading from a 2-inch to a 6-inch line. The initial project team encountered several utility conflicts including a fiber optic vault that interfered with the planned route. After initial pipe replacement, the system failed pressure testing, requiring additional rework. The original project team was eventually replaced. The project was completed in December 2025 after five months of construction.
projects.timeline: May 2025 → Dec 2025 (5+ months for a routine replacement)

projects.name: Warren Subdivision Water Main Replacement
projects.delayAbs: Missed Dec 1, 2025 deadline; work paused until spring
projects.description: A water main replacement project missed its December 1 deadline by months because the city was dependent on a local utility provider to relocate gas main infrastructure.
projects.detail: Residents of a Warren subdivision received a notice around August 9 that water main work on Arsenal Avenue would be completed by December 1, weather permitting. By November the deadline had slipped due to 'unforeseen circumstances.' City Engineer Tina Gapshes said the 21-inch storm sewer along Arsenal from Stanley to 12 Mile had deteriorated and needed replacement, and several gas leads were found to be too shallow. The city said it was dependent on a local utility provider to relocate gas main infrastructure, which was outside its control. The contractor planned to stop for winter and return in the spring.
projects.timeline: Aug 2025 start → Dec 1, 2025 deadline missed; resuming spring 2026

projects.name: Warner Avenue Widening Project
projects.description: A street widening project first approved in 2015 has been delayed for over a decade by Southern California Edison and communication companies' slow utility undergrounding work.
projects.detail: Santa Ana's Warner Avenue widening project, designed to expand the roadway from 2 to 3 lanes in each direction, was first approved around 2015. The project has been plagued by delays from multiple sources: Southern California Edison and communication companies were slow to complete utility undergrounding work; the city deemed one contractor 'terrible' and entered litigation. City officials cited utility pole delays specifically as a major impediment. The project remains partially under construction over a decade after initial approval.

projects.name: Carroll Road Reconstruction
projects.description: Underground utilities found in conflict with storm sewer construction forced a change order for lost production time and extended the project completion by 9 months.
projects.detail: The Carroll Road reconstruction project encountered utilities in conflict with planned storm sewer work within the construction limits. Contractor Fleming Excavating submitted a $9,001 change order for loss of production and time due to the utility conflicts. A separate change order extended the project completion date from August 13 to May 31, 2025. Both change orders required unanimous approval from the Huntertown Town Council before being submitted to INDOT for final approval.

projects.name: North High Street Reconstruction
projects.description: A complete street reconstruction was delayed for years while the city waited for the Morgantown Utility Board and WVU to finish replacing water/sewer lines and rebuilding an underground steam tunnel.
projects.detail: Morgantown's North High Street required complete reconstruction. However, the project was delayed for years because multiple underground utility projects had to be completed first. The Morgantown Utility Board needed to replace water and sewer lines, and WVU contractors needed to rebuild an underground steam tunnel. City officials described the situation as 'kicking it down the road' as each utility entity slowly completed their work. The road deteriorated significantly during the wait. The City Council finally approved reconstruction contracts in late November 2025.

projects.name: Green Bag Road Improvement Project
projects.description: Utility relocation work and eminent domain proceedings for 15 parcels still in court have delayed a major road reconstruction project with planned roundabouts.
projects.detail: The Green Bag Road Improvement Project involves major reconstruction including new roundabouts. Contractors were still relocating utility lines as a prerequisite to the main reconstruction. The utility relocation caused significant traffic disruptions, and temporary materials failed under traffic volume. Property acquisition has been a major obstacle — approximately half the needed parcels are tied up in court, including eminent domain proceedings for 15 parcels. Only 12 of the needed parcels have been acquired. The DOH described the project schedule as being 'at the mercy of the court.'
projects.timeline: Utility relocation ongoing as of Apr 2026

projects.name: NYC DDC Capital Construction Projects (Audit)
projects.description: A NYC Comptroller audit found that 64% of 5,128 city capital projects were delayed at least 3 months, with utility relocation identified as a common source of delays and cost overruns.
projects.detail: The NYC Comptroller's audit of the Department of Design and Construction found systemic problems. Of 5,128 projects analyzed, 64% were delayed at least three months and nearly half were three or more years behind schedule. Over 50% exceeded initial budgets, with planned spending $54.5 billion more than initially projected. DDC officials stated that utility relocation is a common source of delays and cost overruns, noting the agency has no control over private utility companies. One audited project found NYPD electrical boxes not identified in design ($700K relocation cost), a 48-inch sewer connection misaligned by seven feet ($541K), and $1.6 million in unplanned traffic control costs.

projects.name: Gowanus Canal CSO Retention Tanks
projects.description: Design disagreements between NYC and EPA over underground sewer overflow tank construction at a Superfund site caused a 1,300%+ cost increase and 6.5-year delay.
projects.detail: The Gowanus Canal Superfund cleanup required construction of two combined sewer overflow retention tanks. EPA's 2013 Record of Decision set the original timeline and cost estimate. Disagreements between New York City and EPA Region 2 led to substantial delays — the city repeatedly delayed between 2014 and 2023, citing design discrepancies and budget issues, and at one point proposed replacing the two tanks with a 16-million-gallon tunnel. The project fell approximately 6.5 years behind schedule, with costs escalating over 1,300% before a $329 million contract was finally awarded for the first tank.

projects.name: Honolulu Auloa Road Repaving Waste
projects.description: City spent nearly $250,000 to repave Auloa Road in July 2022, only for the Board of Water Supply to rip it up months later for a $15M water main replacement, due to complete lack of inter-agency coordination.
projects.detail: The City and County of Honolulu spent nearly a quarter-million dollars resurfacing a two-mile stretch of Auloa Road in July 2022. Months later, the Board of Water Supply began tearing up the freshly paved road to replace half-century-old 16-inch water mains, a $15 million project that had been seven years in the making. Despite all that planning, word of the water main work apparently never reached city hall. About a third of a mile of brand-new asphalt was destroyed. The incident became a textbook example of failed coordination between city departments.

projects.name: Spokane Cheney-Spokane Road Dig-Up
projects.description: The City of Spokane repaved Cheney-Spokane Road in summer 2024, then weeks later crews dug up the freshly repaved road to replace a water transmission main, frustrating area business owners.
projects.detail: In summer 2024, the City of Spokane completed a full strip-and-repave of Cheney-Spokane Road. Just weeks later, construction crews returned to dig up the newly repaved road for the Marshall Road Water Transmission Main project, a $10 million infrastructure upgrade. Although the city said the water main replacement was planned and that delaying it would have left the street unpaved longer, the optics infuriated business owners who had already endured months of construction disruption.
projects.budget: Repaving cost unknown; $10M water main project

projects.name: Connecticut Eversource Fake Paving Moratorium
projects.description: Eversource paid $3.6M in total penalties after using fictitious 'paving moratoriums' as high-pressure sales tactics to rush homeowners into natural gas conversions in towns where no such moratoriums existed.
projects.detail: Connecticut's Attorney General and the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority investigated Eversource after the utility sent deceptive notices to homeowners claiming that local 'paving moratoriums' would prevent them from getting natural gas hookups for years if they did not act immediately. The investigation identified multiple Connecticut towns where these notices were sent but no such paving moratoriums existed. Eversource paid a $1.8 million civil penalty imposed by PURA, then agreed to an additional $1.8 million settlement with the AG's office.

projects.name: Baltimore Hopkins Duct Bank Excavation
projects.description: Baltimore's Board of Estimates approved Johns Hopkins University's plan to excavate streets in the Remington neighborhood for underground duct banks, despite the streets having been repaved within the prior month.
projects.detail: In April 2026, Baltimore's Board of Estimates approved Johns Hopkins University's plan to install underground duct banks along Howard Street, Wyman Park Parkway, 23rd Street, and 29th Street in the Remington neighborhood, despite opposition from City Council members and more than 30 written public comments. The streets targeted for excavation had been repaved within the prior month. The duct bank project was needed to supply power to Hopkins' Homewood campus and its under-construction Data Science and AI Institute. Construction was set to continue in phases through January 2027.
projects.budget: Unknown repaving cost; multi-million-dollar duct bank project
projects.timeline: Streets repaved March-April 2026; excavation approved April 2026

projects.name: Baltimore BGE Transmission Line Dispute
projects.description: BGE's proposed underground transmission line through historic Baltimore neighborhoods saw costs quadruple from $100M to $400M, prompting the Maryland Senate President to introduce oversight legislation.
projects.detail: Baltimore Gas and Electric proposed a major underground transmission line project that would tear up streets in the historic Otterbein and Ridgely's Delight neighborhoods. Residents pushed back, citing disruption of dense residential blocks and elimination of street parking. The project's cost escalated from $100 million to $400 million. Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson introduced legislation requiring utilities to provide further justification for need, cost, and route selection. BGE announced it was 'temporarily pausing' the project in March 2026 amid political and community opposition.

projects.name: St. Louis South Grand Gas Main Replacement
projects.description: Spire tore up streets to replace century-old cast iron gas mains, sometimes hitting freshly paved roads with emergency leak repairs, prompting monthly utility coordination meetings.
projects.detail: Spire Energy undertook a sweeping infrastructure overhaul along South Grand Boulevard in St. Louis, replacing aging cast iron and steel gas mains, some nearly 100 years old. Emergency leaks sometimes cropped up on streets that had just been freshly paved, causing public frustration. The experience prompted a significant change: Spire became one of the city's most engaged utility partners, hosting monthly coordination meetings that changed how St. Louis approaches paving decisions. City officials now say they never pave a street without running it by Spire first.

projects.name: Clifton NJ Half-Paved Streets (PSE&G)
projects.description: More than 40 roads in Clifton were left half-paved after PSE&G gas line upgrades that began in April 2016, because PSE&G historically only repaved the trenched areas.
projects.detail: In April 2016, PSE&G began a gas line upgrade project in Clifton, NJ. According to CBS New York, PSE&G historically only refilled the trenches and paved over the areas that were excavated, and its plan included curb-to-curb paving only on roads that had received upgrades over the last seven years. As of June 2017 more than 40 Clifton roads were left half-paved. Mayor James Anzaldi said the city planned to repave the roads at a cost of $2 million, but that may not happen until spring 2018.
projects.timeline: Gas upgrades began April 2016 → full curb-to-curb repaving of remaining roads possibly not until spring 2018

projects.name: Brick NJ Mantoloking Road Utility Markings
projects.description: New Jersey Natural Gas began digging small test pits to map gas lines on Mantoloking Road about two months after Ocean County finished repaving it, angering residents who feared the new surface would be damaged.
projects.detail: Ocean County's Roads Department repaved Mantoloking Road in Brick in September 2018, a $765,817.67 project using 8,000 tons of asphalt. About two months later, flags and markings appeared as New Jersey Natural Gas crews mapped existing gas lines with small excavations. NJNG said the work was part of a longer-term project to locate and map existing facilities for future system improvement projects. Residents expressed frustration on social media that the new paving could be damaged so soon. County Roads Director Thomas Curcio said the county had repeatedly postponed the paving and 'just couldn't put it off anymore.'

projects.name: Cleveland Opportunity Corridor
projects.description: A $331M boulevard connecting I-490 to University Circle experienced utility relocation delays and a grade design change that added $4.6M and six months to the schedule.
projects.detail: The Cleveland Opportunity Corridor is a five-lane, three-mile boulevard connecting I-490 to the University Circle neighborhood. During construction, unforeseen utility relocation delays impacted the project schedule and had to be mitigated by rephasing work. Additionally, ODOT requested a grade change where I-490/Opportunity Boulevard passes under E. 55th Street for safety reasons, adding approximately six months of work and $4.6 million. The opening of I-490 between I-77 and E. 55th Street was delayed from spring 2021 to November 1, 2021.

projects.name: Cincinnati Streetcar (Cincinnati Bell Connector)
projects.description: Duke Energy's $37.8M utility relocation estimate far exceeded city projections, creating an impasse over cost responsibility that delayed construction and pushed the streetcar $20M over its original $128M budget.
projects.detail: The Cincinnati Streetcar project faced a major dispute between the City of Cincinnati and Duke Energy over who should pay to relocate gas and electric lines within three feet of the streetcar tracks. Duke Energy produced a $37.76 million estimate for utility relocation, approximately $16 million higher than the city's projections. Civil construction bids also came in significantly higher than anticipated, creating a budget gap exceeding $20 million. The project cost grew from $128 million to $148 million. The streetcar ultimately opened on September 9, 2016.

projects.name: Cincinnati Western Hills Viaduct Replacement
projects.description: Cost estimates nearly doubled from $398M to $785.6M as design advanced, driven significantly by the 3-4 year process of relocating a Duke Energy substation and transmission line.
projects.detail: The City of Cincinnati and Hamilton County are jointly replacing the aging Western Hills Viaduct with a new cable-stayed bridge. As design advanced from 10% to 30% completion, the cost estimate nearly doubled from $398 million (2022) to $785.6 million (2025). A major driver is the relocation of a Duke Energy substation and transmission line, a process taking three to four years. Duke began building the replacement Camp Washington substation in 2024. Other significant cost risks include railroad track relocation and environmental remediation. A total funding gap of approximately $294 million remains.
projects.timeline: Construction start 2022, originally ~2028 → now extending well beyond

projects.name: Youngstown Realty Building Gas Explosion
projects.description: A scrap removal crew cut into an active Enbridge gas line mislabeled as abandoned, causing an explosion that killed one Chase Bank employee, injured seven, and required full demolition of the Realty Building.
projects.detail: On May 27, 2024, a scrap removal crew in the basement of the Realty Building in downtown Youngstown cut into what they believed was an abandoned gas service line. However, the line was active — Enbridge Gas Ohio had a 2015 work order to shut it down, but the NTSB found no paperwork confirming deactivation. Six minutes after the cut, the building exploded, killing Akil Drake, a 27-year-old Chase Bank employee, and injuring seven others. The NTSB determined the gas line had been incorrectly marked as abandoned in Enbridge's system despite still carrying natural gas.

projects.name: I-490 / Elgin O'Hare Western Access Utility Lawsuit
projects.description: Contractor Judlau sued the Illinois Tollway for $29.4M after discovering the agency had not secured easements or completed utility relocation before awarding contracts, causing 777-day and 514-day delays.
projects.detail: Judlau Contracting filed a March 2026 lawsuit against the Illinois Tollway, claiming $29.4 million in damages from the I-490 corridor project. Judlau held contracts to build a Union Pacific Railroad bridge ($21M+) and a retaining wall ($37.8M). The Tollway's stated 13-month timeline for the bridge 'turned out to be wildly untrue' when Judlau discovered the agency had neither received permission to access UP property nor conducted utility relocation. It took 777 days before bridge work could start. The retaining wall contract suffered 514 lost days because the Tollway had not secured right-of-way easements.
projects.timeline: Contracts awarded → 777 days and 514 days of delay

projects.name: Route 47 Widening
projects.description: IDOT's Route 47 widening was delayed one full year after bids came in $9M over estimates, largely due to utility relocation costs ballooning from $13.2M to $25.1M for the city's share.
projects.detail: The Illinois Department of Transportation's Route 47 widening project in Woodstock was originally expected to begin in spring 2025, but was delayed a full year after construction bids came in approximately $9 million higher than engineer estimates. The city's share of expenses increased from $16 million to $25.1 million, with utility relocation costs representing the bulk of the increase. To offset costs, Woodstock secured $15.65 million in outside funding including $3.15 million in federal Community Project Funding and a $10 million state grant. Construction finally began April 2026.
projects.timeline: Spring 2025 start planned → Spring 2026 actual start; completion 2028

projects.name: IndyGo Blue Line BRT
projects.description: Indianapolis's Blue Line BRT project ballooned from $220M to $520M — mostly due to sewer connection costs — before being redesigned down to $378M, with a two-year schedule delay.
projects.detail: IndyGo's Blue Line bus rapid transit project along Washington Street was initially projected to cost $220 million in 2019. By 2022, costs had ballooned to $520 million, primarily because stormwater drainage improvements and sewer connections to Citizens Energy Group's system proved far more expensive than anticipated. Drainage work increased from 30% to 42% of the total project cost. Hundreds of underground utility conflicts were expected. IndyGo redesigned the project, cutting costs to $378 million, and broke ground in March 2025. The 24-mile route is now expected to open in 2028.

projects.name: I-94 East-West Corridor Expansion
projects.description: Utility negotiations drove up the cost of Milwaukee's I-94 East-West expansion by approximately $150 million, pushing the project to $1.65 billion and requiring a seven-year construction window.
projects.detail: The Wisconsin Department of Transportation's I-94 East-West project covers approximately 3.5 miles of interstate in Milwaukee County, expanding from six to eight lanes. A Transportation Projects Commission report revealed that utility negotiations had increased the anticipated cost by about $150 million, bringing the total to $1.65 billion. The project had previously been abandoned entirely for lack of funds before being revived. Construction began in late 2025 with utility relocation as the first phase, expected to take seven years through 2032.

projects.name: Milwaukee Hop Streetcar
projects.description: Milwaukee's Hop streetcar was delayed approximately three years by a legal and legislative battle over $55-70M in utility relocation costs, forcing a route redesign to reduce the expense.
projects.detail: Milwaukee's Hop streetcar project was approved in 2011 but immediately ran into a protracted dispute over utility relocation costs. We Energies and AT&T estimated collective relocation costs in excess of $60 million. The city intended to make utilities bear these costs, but the Wisconsin Legislature inserted language making it unlawful for municipalities to require utilities to pay for streetcar-related relocations. One alderman estimated the project could have opened three years earlier without the utility dispute. In February 2016, the route was redesigned to reduce utility relocation costs. The streetcar opened November 2, 2018, at a total cost of $128 million.
projects.timeline: Approved 2011 → opened Nov 2018 (~3 years of utility delays)

projects.name: METRO Green Line Extension (Southwest LRT)
projects.description: The SWLRT project more than doubled in cost from $1.3B to $2.86B, with nearly 1,400 utility relocations, tunnel complications in watery soil, and freight rail conflicts causing massive delays.
projects.detail: The Metropolitan Council's METRO Green Line Extension is a 14.5-mile light rail corridor connecting Minneapolis and Eden Prairie. Originally estimated at $1.3 billion in 2013 with a 2023 opening, it ballooned to $2.86 billion with a 2027 completion target. Nearly 1,400 utilities required relocation. The biggest cost driver was the Kenilworth tunnel, complicated by rocky, watery soil and proximity to a condominium building, requiring expensive secant wall piling that added $38.9 million. A state legislative audit found the Metropolitan Council obligated funds it did not have and solicited bids with incomplete specifications.

projects.name: Omaha Streetcar
projects.description: The Omaha Streetcar project is two years behind schedule primarily due to Metropolitan Utilities District gas and water line work that ballooned from $10.6M to $46.5M.
projects.detail: Omaha's 3.2-mile streetcar project was originally budgeted at $306 million with a late-2026 completion target. The Metropolitan Utilities District initially estimated gas and water line replacement at $10.6 million, but costs exploded to $46.5 million as MUD demanded replacement of pipes further from the rails than originally agreed. City officials blame MUD for nearly two years of delay. The total project cost rose to $421 million by mid-2025 and $459 million including corridor-wide costs. Nearby businesses doubt they will survive to see the streetcar open, now expected in 2028.

projects.name: Oklahoma City Pipeline Strike (NW 178th St)
projects.description: A road construction excavator struck a 16-inch crude oil pipeline, creating an oil geyser that spewed 88,200 gallons, contaminating stormwater drains and requiring extensive soil remediation.
projects.detail: On September 25, 2023, an excavation operator working on a new road for a residential development struck a 16-inch Energy Transfer LP crude oil pipeline near NW 178th Street and North Portland Avenue. Oil spewed approximately 30 feet into the air, and approximately 2,100 barrels (88,200 gallons) of crude oil leaked before the pipe was sealed. Some oil seeped into stormwater drains, requiring flushing and extensive soil recovery. Energy Transfer's subsidiary Sunoco was previously fined a record $1 million by Oklahoma regulators for a separate 2018 crude oil spill.

projects.name: Flint Lead Service Line Replacement
projects.description: Flint's $97M court-ordered lead service line replacement, due by 2020, was still unfinished in 2024, requiring an estimated $4.75M in state funds to finish yard, sidewalk and driveway restoration.
projects.detail: A 2017 federal court settlement provided $97 million to replace lead and galvanized service lines in Flint by 2020. The work was dogged by repeated delays and the city was held in contempt by the judge. By May 2024 roughly 31,500 homes had been addressed but about 1,900 still awaited yard and sidewalk repairs, and Flint's fund had only about $1 million left. The state agreed to provide an estimated $4.75 million to complete restoration, with completion proposed for August 2025.
projects.timeline: 2017 settlement, 2020 deadline → state proposed Aug 2025 completion

projects.name: Foxconn / Wisconn Valley Infrastructure
projects.description: Wisconsin spent $1.2B+ on highway widening, water mains, sewer systems, and underground transmission lines for Foxconn's promised factory — infrastructure that became largely stranded when the factory was dramatically scaled back.
projects.detail: In anticipation of Foxconn's promised $10 billion manufacturing campus, state and local officials spent over $1.2 billion on infrastructure including $252 million to widen I-94, $117 million for transmission lines and substations (including an underground 138-kV line), $7 million for water main construction, and 16.5 miles of local road work. The infrastructure buildout required extensive utility coordination. When Foxconn dramatically scaled back its plans — never building the promised LCD manufacturing plant — much of this infrastructure became stranded assets, making it one of the largest utility-infrastructure coordination debacles in Midwest history.
projects.budget: $1.2B+ in public infrastructure (highway, water, sewer, electrical)
projects.timeline: Infrastructure construction 2018-2020; Foxconn factory never built as planned

projects.name: Van Ness Bus Rapid Transit (BRT)
projects.description: 1.96-mile BRT line delayed 3 years and $184M over original estimates due to unmapped century-old water and sewer lines under Van Ness Avenue that had to be relocated curbside.
projects.detail: The Van Ness Improvement Project was planned at $162.7M when rated by the FTA in 2014, but total cost reached $346M by opening in April 2022. A 2021 Civil Grand Jury report found SFMTA failed to account for location and maintenance of underground utility lines; 19th-century water and sewer mains buried under the center of Van Ness had to be relocated to the curbside. In 2018, an additional five-month delay was caused by unexpected abandoned utilities including dot-com era fiber optic cables and original California Street Cable Railroad tracks.

projects.name: OC Streetcar (Santa Ana)
projects.description: 4.15-mile streetcar line nearly doubled from $289M to $579M+ and is 5+ years late, driven by discovery of unmapped old utilities, contaminated soil, and Native American remains.
projects.detail: When first presented to the federal government, the OC Streetcar was expected to cost $289M with a 2021 opening. Latest cost estimate of $579M may still be revised upward. Lead contractor Walsh Construction sued OCTA alleging the agency failed to properly plan, citing incomplete design and differing conditions. A mediation resulted in OCTA agreeing to pay Walsh nearly $50M in settlement. The project is now targeting a 2026 opening.

projects.name: SFMTA King Substation Improvement
projects.description: Muni electrical upgrade near Oracle Park spiraled from $11.3M to $15M+ and was delayed 2.5+ years as PG&E took over a year to review footage and another year to power on a temporary substation.
projects.detail: The King Substation Improvement Project was originally budgeted at $11.3M with a June 2020 completion. PG&E coordination failures caused costs to balloon to over $15M and the completion date to slip to January 2023. PG&E took 10 months to review boring footage and another year to power on the temporary substation. The contractor had to suspend construction while meeting PG&E demands.

projects.name: Twin Peaks Tunnel Trackway Improvement
projects.description: The $52M tunnel project was completed in January 2019 but had to be partially redone at tens of millions after contaminated ballast and hazardous material issues were discovered underground.
projects.detail: A City Controller audit found SFMTA failed to communicate the need to test for and remove hazardous material, leading to $523K in change orders. When faced with contaminated ballast, the decision was made to reuse it rather than replace it, but the contractor did not properly wash the material. Two years later, Muni was forced to redo the project at tens of millions to fix track instability at the Eureka curve.

projects.name: Pure Water San Diego (SDG&E Utility Conflict)
projects.description: San Diego's $5B+ water recycling project faced $130M in cost increases including a lawsuit against SDG&E over $98.8M in utility relocation costs and a $20M pump station flooding miscalculation.
projects.detail: SDG&E refused to relocate its underground gas and power lines unless the city fronted the money. The city advanced $35.6M and then sued SDG&E in 2019. SDG&E estimated total relocation costs at $98.8M. Separately, the Morena Boulevard pump station flooded repeatedly due to miscalculation of underground water levels, requiring a $20M secant wall. The project faces a federal deadline to complete by early 2027.
projects.budget: Phase 1 original estimate → $130M+ over across multiple components
projects.timeline: Original schedule → 2+ year delay; federal deadline 2027

projects.name: Calaveras Dam Replacement Project
projects.description: Dam replacement nearly doubled from $416M to $820M+ and was delayed 4 years after excavation revealed two ancient buried landslides requiring complete redesign.
projects.detail: The SFPUC Calaveras Dam Replacement began in 2011. During excavation, crews discovered two ancient buried landslides requiring 3.5 million additional cubic yards of excavation. The spillway had to be relocated and bedrock backfilled with 18,570 cubic yards of concrete. Budget rose from $416M to $718M, then $810M, and ultimately exceeded $820M.

projects.name: HSR Fresno Section Utility Relocations
