projects.description: Utility relocation costs for the 29-mile Fresno section of California High-Speed Rail exploded from $69M to $396M — a 474% increase — after discovering previously undetected underground utilities.
projects.detail: The original plan had AT&T and PG&E moving their own equipment, but once work began, the utility companies said they could not complete the work before the deadline. Contractor Tutor Perini took over at increased cost. Workers discovered previously undetected utilities that needed relocation. The original number of linear feet requiring relocation was underestimated, as was the cost per linear foot.
projects.timeline: Original utility relocation schedule not met; ongoing

projects.name: San Francisco Richmond District Gas Explosion
projects.description: A fiber optic installation crew for Verizon struck a PG&E gas main on Geary Boulevard in 2019, causing a massive explosion that destroyed five buildings and caused $10M+ in damage.
projects.detail: On February 6, 2019, a crew installing fiber optic cable for Verizon ruptured a PG&E 2-inch natural gas main at Geary and Parker streets. The subcontractor, Kilford Engineering, was later cited as not having a proper license. The explosion caused a three-alarm fire, damaging or destroying five buildings including a popular restaurant. Over 100 people were displaced.

projects.name: LAX Sepulveda Blvd Gas/Water Main Strike
projects.description: An LADOT crew struck both a 6-inch gas main and water main on Sepulveda Blvd near LAX in May 2026, forcing major road closures that severely disrupted Memorial Day holiday travel.
projects.detail: On May 20, 2026, an LADOT crew performing utility work struck a 6-inch steel gas main and water main at approximately 9:10 p.m. Northbound lanes of Sepulveda Boulevard at Imperial Highway and east/westbound lanes of 96th Street were closed. The road closures severely impacted Memorial Day holiday travel to and from LAX, one of the nation's busiest airports.

projects.name: East Los Angeles Oil Pipeline Rupture (Fiber Drilling)
projects.description: A telecom drilling crew struck a 16-inch crude oil pipeline in East LA in May 2026, spilling 2,400 gallons of crude oil into streets, storm drains, and the LA River, oiling nearly 80 birds.
projects.detail: On May 22, 2026, a telecommunications crew drilling a 6-inch fiber optic line struck a 16-inch underground crude oil pipeline. Oil spilled at approximately 5 gallons per second before the pipeline was shut off, with 2,400 gallons released entering the roadway, storm drain system, and LA River. LA County declared a local disaster. The drilling company had been previously accused of puncturing another pipeline.
projects.budget: N/A (damage event; cleanup costs to be determined)

projects.name: VTA Eastridge to BART Regional Connector
projects.description: The 2.4-mile light rail extension received a $437M construction bid — $122M (39%) over VTA's $315M estimate — while $30M was spent on utility relocation including a power transmission line and 24-inch water main.
projects.detail: The $437M joint bid from MCM Construction and RailWorks came in $122M over VTA's $315M estimate. Prior to the construction contract, VTA spent approximately $30M over three years acquiring property and relocating major utilities including a power transmission line and a 24-inch water main. Total project cost from start to finish is expected to be $653M.

projects.name: Sacramento Downtown Riverfront Streetcar
projects.description: Construction bids in 2019 came in $76M over estimates, forcing a complete redesign to a shorter 1.5-mile route that reduced utility relocation impacts.
projects.detail: The Sacramento Downtown Riverfront Streetcar initially planned a longer route requiring extensive utility relocations. In 2019, the lowest construction bid came in at $184M — $76M higher than the anticipated $108M. The sticker shock forced a complete redesign into a shorter 1.5-mile route that explicitly avoided as many utility relocations and traffic impacts as the original plan.

projects.name: SFMTA 5 Fulton Outer Route Fast Track
projects.description: SFMTA's bus transit enhancement project was delayed 1.7 years due to poor communication with the Public Works department, as documented in a 2021 City Controller audit.
projects.detail: A February 2021 San Francisco City Controller audit found this project was delayed 1.7 years and incurred $23,000 in change order costs due to poor communication between SFMTA and Public Works. The audit was part of a broader review of four SFMTA capital projects that found the agency cost the city millions through communication failures and insufficient collaboration with other agencies.

projects.name: Denver 16th Street Mall Reconstruction
projects.description: Discovery of unmapped 1880s brick-lined sewer and complex layered utilities beneath 13 blocks forced redesign and delayed the $149M mall rebuild by a full year.
projects.detail: In July 2023, crews discovered an active 1880s brick-lined sewer along with centuries-old water lines, steam lines, storm and sanitary lines, electrical infrastructure, gas networks, and over a dozen telecom lines. The complex underground utilities required redesign in the first four blocks, pushing the originally planned 2024 completion to fall 2025. Final cost reached $176.7M.

projects.name: Seattle Elliott Bay Seawall Replacement
projects.description: Replacing 75 years of underground utilities along the central waterfront required temporary utility bridges over excavation pits, contributing to a $71M budget overrun.
projects.detail: The project was originally budgeted at $339.2M. Crews found that many existing utilities were unavoidable and needed temporary relocation. The project built several utility bridges to allow temporary connections to span excavation pits. Combined with unexpected soil conditions requiring a costly soil freeze wall, the budget ballooned to $410.2M. Construction completed in 2017, more than a year late.

projects.name: SR 520 Portage Bay Bridge & Roanoke Lid
projects.description: Bids came in 70% above the $800M engineer estimate, driven in part by extensive utility relocation scope including sewer outflow protection and duct bank relocation.
projects.detail: WSDOT received two bids in summer 2023 — Skanska at $1.37B and Kiewit at nearly $1.7B — both vastly exceeding the $800M estimate. The scope includes protecting sewer outflow, relocating a lumen duct bank, replacing trolley poles, and stormwater conveyance. The contract was awarded to Skanska at approximately $1.4B with construction through 2031.

projects.name: North Spokane Corridor (US 395)
projects.description: WSDOT's 10.5-mile freeway through urban Spokane required a $276M legislative appropriation with unknown utility conflicts in built urban environments cited as a key risk.
projects.detail: After completing roughly $650M in construction and $345M in right-of-way purchases, WSDOT's cost validation identified significant escalation. The Legislature provided an additional $276M. WSDOT highlighted risks including unknown utility conflicts in built urban environments. Specific utility relocation projects are underway including the NSC Trent Interchange Utilities Project ($1.54M) to relocate aging cast iron water mains.

projects.name: Reno Spaghetti Bowl Xpress (SBX) Phase 1
projects.description: NDOT's Spaghetti Bowl Phase 1 came in 10% over its $165M estimate after initial bids were rejected, with utility relocation as a key scope element.
projects.detail: NDOT opened competitive bidding in spring 2020, but all three bids came in non-responsive or too expensive. NDOT accepted an unsolicited proposal from Ames Construction and Q&D Construction in September 2020 at approximately $181.5M. The overall Spaghetti Bowl reconstruction is a $1.5+ billion multi-decade program.

projects.name: Henderson Interchange (I-11/I-215)
projects.description: Bids far exceeded estimates, forcing NDOT to scrap design-build procurement and switch to phased design-bid-build, with utility relocations ongoing during the restructuring.
projects.detail: Originally estimated at $350-$400M, the budget ballooned to $495-$520M. NDOT Director stated bids came in considerably higher than expected and the department would continue to work on utility relocations. NDOT canceled design-build procurement and transitioned to phased design-bid-build, pushing construction start from fall 2023 to late 2027 or early 2028.

projects.name: CDOT I-70B / US 6 Improvements (Clifton)
projects.description: CDOT's US 6 project in Clifton was delayed when crews hit poor soils and challenging subsurface conditions, forcing redesign of underground utilities.
projects.detail: The project began in fall 2022 to add roundabouts, new concrete pavement, underground electrical infrastructure, stormwater systems, and sidewalk improvements. CDOT Region 3 stated they ran into very poor soils requiring redesign and additional work. The project was completed in October 2025.

projects.name: Portland SE 82nd Avenue Gas Main Rupture
projects.description: An ODOT contractor boring under SE 82nd Avenue struck a 4-inch NW Natural gas main, causing a 5.5-hour gas leak, mass evacuation, and requiring overnight intersection dig-up.
projects.detail: During an ODOT construction project, a crew boring under the pavement struck a 4-inch natural gas line at SE 82nd Avenue and SE Washington Street. Businesses and civilians within a one-block radius were evacuated. NW Natural crews had to dig into 82nd Avenue on both sides to place temporary shut-off valves. The leak continued for nearly 5.5 hours. The intersection was shut down for approximately 14 hours.

projects.name: Seattle South Juneau Street Gas Main Strike
projects.description: Construction workers hit a 2-inch gas main near S Juneau Street, forcing evacuation of nearly a dozen homes on December 27, 2023.
projects.detail: On December 27, 2023, Seattle firefighters evacuated nearly a dozen homes near South Juneau Street and 48th Avenue South after construction workers hit a 2-inch gas main. The incident forced road closures and disrupted the neighborhood. Puget Sound Energy crews responded to secure the line.

projects.name: Seattle Columbia City Gas Leak (MLK Jr Way)
projects.description: A gas line was struck near a building under construction in Columbia City, disrupting Link light rail service and forcing evacuations of nearby buildings.
projects.detail: In April 2026, a leaking 2-inch natural gas line was found near a building under construction on the 5000 block of MLK Jr Way South. Firefighters evacuated nearby buildings while PSE secured the leak. The incident disrupted Sound Transit Link light rail between Mount Baker and Rainier Beach stations, requiring shuttle buses.

projects.name: Boise State Street Reconstruction
projects.description: An unexpected Idaho Power vault sitting higher than planned in the 8th Street intersection prevented paving and forced ACHD to extend the road closure through November 2024.
projects.detail: ACHD's original plan was to get 8th Street open in July, but crews discovered an Idaho Power vault at the State and 8th Street intersection that sat higher than expected, preventing paving. The issue forced ACHD to keep 8th Street closed through November, extending closure by approximately 4 months. Business owners expressed significant frustration.

projects.name: WSDOT Fish Passage Barrier Removal Program
projects.description: WSDOT's court-mandated culvert replacement program ballooned from $1.88B to $7.8B, with utility franchise agreements requiring relocation of water, sewer, and electrical assets at each site.
projects.detail: A federal court order requires Washington state to remove fish passage barriers under state highways. The original cost estimate was $1.88B; it has since quadrupled to $7.8B. Each barrier removal averages $20M, with some costing up to $100M due to the need to purchase property and relocate utilities. The Legislature's proposed $5B funding plan appeared dead as of April 2025.

projects.name: CDOT I-25 North Express Lanes
projects.description: CDOT expanded project scope to avoid relocating utilities multiple times within a five-year period, adding 2 years to the timeline.
projects.detail: CDOT discovered that building the bridge at a temporary location would require expensive utility relocations, and those same utilities would have to be relocated again within five years for the permanent interchange. CDOT elected to build on permanent alignment to avoid double-moving utilities but this required a more ambitious scope, adding approximately 2 years.

projects.name: DART Silver Line (Cotton Belt) Regional Rail
projects.description: The 26-mile DART Silver Line faced $83M in cost overruns and $150K/day in delay costs, driven by utility relocation coordination failures across seven cities.
projects.detail: Engineers developed relocation plans for 43 water lines and 22 wastewater lines spanning seven cities. DART warned that $83M in overruns could be deducted from $111M in sales tax revenue. The overruns included $50M in delay costs and $33M in betterments. Some design reviews took far longer than the required 10-day timeframe. The line opened in late 2025, three years late.

projects.name: I-44/US-75 Interchange Reconstruction (Tulsa)
projects.description: Dubbed 'Oklahoma's Stonehenge,' this interchange project stalled for over a year mid-construction awaiting utility relocation completion and additional funding.
projects.detail: The $153M first phase left only concrete structural components visible — earning the nickname 'Traffic Henge.' The project entered a yearlong holding pattern while ODOT awaited additional funding and completion of utility relocation. The Oklahoma Traffic Commission later approved a $252M contract — the largest highway contract in state history.

projects.name: NM 68/US 64 Roadway Reconstruction (Taos)
projects.description: Taos's $21.9M road reconstruction was delayed 3 years because the Town of Taos did not provide accurate utility maps, leading to repeated discovery of unmapped underground lines.
projects.detail: The primary reason for delays was that the Town of Taos did not provide accurate utilities maps. Crews continually discovered unmapped underground utilities including water, electrical, internet, and gas lines. In June 2023, crews cut a fiber line causing a 48-hour internet and cell phone outage across Taos County.

projects.name: Guadalupe Street Road Reconstruction (Santa Fe)
projects.description: Santa Fe's $10.3M Guadalupe Street reconstruction discovered a gas main only 6 inches below the asphalt, forcing unplanned relocation of two major gas mains.
projects.detail: On May 30, 2025, a gas main was discovered only 6 inches under the existing asphalt at the intersection of Johnson and Guadalupe Streets. City code requires gas mains to be 3 feet below pavement. Contractors had previously discovered leaking gas valves and water mains that required repair.
projects.timeline: Ongoing, multiple schedule revisions due to utility discoveries

projects.name: Floresville Gas Main Explosion (Fiber Installation)
projects.description: A fiber optic contractor struck an underground gas main in Floresville, causing an explosion that leveled one home and damaged 13 others, with $517K in property damage.
projects.detail: On July 16, 2024, 4C Unlimited, installing conduit for Rise Broadband, struck a gas main. The investigation revealed a series of oversights. One home was leveled and 13 others damaged. Total property damage was $517,016. The utility was fined $27,500. Two days later, the same crew ruptured a second gas line in the same town.

projects.name: Saginaw Gas Pipeline Strike
projects.description: A construction crew struck a gas pipeline in Saginaw, forcing neighborhood evacuation. One-third of excavators in DFW pipeline strikes had not contacted 811 before digging.
projects.detail: On February 6, 2025, a construction crew struck a natural gas pipeline near Knowles Drive and Normandy Lane. This is part of a larger pattern: more than 4,800 excavation-related pipeline strikes were reported across Texas in 2026, with over 1,000 in the DFW region. Roughly one-third of excavators had not contacted the 811 One-Call system before digging.

projects.name: Katy (Cinco Ranch) Fiber Optic Water Line Damage
projects.description: Ezee Fiber contractors broke 16 water lines in six months during fiber optic installation in Katy, prompting a city-wide moratorium and a $70K lawsuit from a local MUD.
projects.detail: Contractors working for Ezee Fiber broke 16 water lines in six months. The Katy City Council unanimously voted to pass a 120-day moratorium on all fiber-optic installation. A Katy-area MUD sued Ezee Fiber for $70,000 in damages. The moratorium required future companies to coordinate with the city for proper water line marking.

projects.name: 19th Street Reconstruction (Lubbock)
projects.description: TxDOT's $25M+ Lubbock 19th Street reconstruction was delayed a year after crews discovered unmarked, decades-old underground utilities not shown on city maps.
projects.detail: TxDOT stated: 'The contractor ran into a lot of unmarked utilities that really slowed the process down.' The city's maps were not accurate because many utilities were placed before mapping began. When a utility was found, TxDOT had to contact the City of Lubbock to determine if it was abandoned or still in use.

projects.name: I-610/I-69 Interchange Reconstruction (Houston)
projects.description: TxDOT's $259M Houston interchange project encountered numerous unknown underground utilities requiring bridge redesigns, column relocations, and construction workarounds.
projects.detail: Crews repeatedly discovered underground utilities not shown on plans — sanitary sewer lines, fiber optic cables, storm sewers, waterlines, communication cables, steel casings, and buried concrete foundations. Local governments had installed utilities before construction began without notifying the designer. Bridge designers had to modify cap lengths so support columns would avoid underground conflicts.

projects.name: Houston METRORail Purple Line (Southeast)
projects.description: Houston's Purple Line light rail cost $822M vs. the $591M estimate — 39% over budget — with underground utility coordination and soil contamination among key challenges.
projects.detail: Originally estimated at $591M in 2008, the project cost $822M — a 39% overrun. Environmental analyses showed soil contamination from underground storage tanks in industrial areas would make an underpass too costly, requiring a design change to an overpass. The line was expected to open in 2013 but did not open until May 2015. Actual weekday ridership of 5,230 is less than 20% of projections.

projects.name: Houston METRORail Green Line (East End)
projects.description: Houston's Green Line took 8 years instead of the planned 3, with underground utility coordination and soil contamination from buried storage tanks forcing costly design changes.
projects.detail: Environmental analyses revealed soil contamination from underground storage tanks in the East End's industrial areas, making the originally planned underpass too costly. This forced a redesign to an overpass solution. The extended construction was crippling for businesses along Harrisburg Boulevard. Full service was not achieved until January 2017.

projects.name: Post Oak Boulevard BRT (Houston)
projects.description: Houston Uptown's $192M Post Oak BRT project went $31M over budget, with most work involving rebuilding 60-year-old underground utility systems.
projects.detail: Most of the construction work involved rebuilding the 60-year-old utility systems beneath the boulevard, including CenterPoint Energy and AT&T infrastructure. Utility relocation by CenterPoint, AT&T, and other contractors was subject to ongoing schedule changes based on weather conditions and utility conflicts. The line opened August 23, 2020.

projects.name: Waller Creek Tunnel (Flood Control)
projects.description: Austin's Waller Creek flood tunnel ballooned from a $25M voter-approved project to over $160M, with underground engineering surprises and a Capitol view corridor conflict.
projects.detail: In 1998, voters approved $25M. Engineering studies revealed the project would cost far more. Construction began in 2011 but halted in 2014 when the inlet facility blocked a legally protected view of the Capitol. The city demanded $22M back from the contractor, citing defective construction including substandard concrete and missing structural rebar. Total costs exceeded $160M — nearly seven times the original price tag.

projects.name: Austin Project Connect Light Rail
projects.description: Austin's Project Connect light rail doubled from $5.8B to $10.3B, with the downtown tunnel doubling from $2B to $4.1B after planners discovered it needed to go deeper to avoid utilities and flood zones.
projects.detail: Approved by voters in 2020 at $5.8B, costs ballooned to $10.3B by April 2022. The downtown tunnel was the primary cost driver, doubling from $2B to $4.1B after planners discovered it would need to plunge deeper underground due to FEMA flood zones and the need to move utilities. The tunnel was ultimately stripped from the plan. The pared-down $7.1B version includes 9.8 miles of light rail but no tunnel.

projects.name: Tucson Broadway Boulevard Widening
projects.description: Tucson's $72M Broadway widening was delayed three times in two years after crews discovered three miles of underground storm drains requiring replacement before repaving.
projects.detail: The biggest challenge was the discovery that approximately three miles of underground storm drain piping had to be completely replaced before any repaving could begin. Combined with pandemic-era asphalt shortages and staffing issues, the underground piping work became the primary schedule driver. Construction had already cost more than $23M when delays were reported.
projects.timeline: Delayed 3 times, 6+ months behind original schedule

projects.name: El Paso Adabel Drive Water Main Failures
projects.description: A water main on Adabel Drive broke six times in under a month, repeatedly destroying freshly repaired pavement and creating sinkholes just feet from homes.
projects.detail: The water main broke on January 30, February 8, 9, 13, 14, and 25, 2026 — six failures in less than a month. Each repair involved repaving the road, only for it to be torn up again by the next break. Residents noted 'Crews paved the road all perfect and nice, and then it broke again.' El Paso Water attributed failures to aging infrastructure with an average pipe age of about 45 years.
projects.timeline: January 30 - February 25, 2026 (6 breaks in under 1 month)

projects.name: Carolina Crossroads (Malfunction Junction) Phase 3
projects.description: The $2.1B I-20/I-26/I-126 interchange overhaul had its $1.1B Phase 3 broken into five subphases after underground utility risks left the project too exposed for potentially large change orders.
projects.detail: SCDOT's project director stated that risks in underground utility locations left Phase 3 too exposed for potentially large change orders. Agency leadership canceled the original Phase 3 procurement in October 2023 and broke it into five smaller subphases. Phase 3A specifically covers utility and frontage road relocation around the I-20/I-26 intersection.
projects.timeline: Original single-phase → split and extended to late 2030s

projects.name: I-85 Widening (Spartanburg County)
projects.description: 29-mile I-85 widening from Spartanburg to the NC border was delayed 2+ years with a 5% budget increase driven primarily by state-mandated water and sewer utility relocation work.
projects.detail: A change in South Carolina law required SCDOT to assist with wet utilities if local entities are unable to do so for financial and technical reasons, adding both time and cost. Utility relocation delays, right-of-way and railroad challenges contributed to the overruns. The utility work was identified as the main culprit in driving up costs by 5 percent on the $480M construction budget.

projects.name: Woodruff Road Congestion Relief Bypass
projects.description: The Woodruff Road bypass in Greenville saw costs more than double from $121M to $277M, with the first construction phase dedicated entirely to utility relocation taking 18-24 months.
projects.detail: In 2017 the estimated price was $121M; by 2025 it had climbed to $277M. The first phase of construction will consist entirely of site work, demolition, and utility relocation, taking 18 months to two years before actual road construction begins. The massive cost increase will likely delay other road projects across the Upstate region.

projects.name: Capital Boulevard Freeway Conversion (Raleigh)
projects.description: Costs ballooned from $465M to $1.34B and completion slipped from 2021 to 2031, with utility relocation cited alongside land acquisition as key drivers.
projects.detail: NCDOT cited unforeseen challenges in land acquisition, utility relocation, and the sheer scale of the work as key delay factors. Rising construction costs, inflation, and labor shortages compounded the problem. A tolling study was conducted to determine whether toll revenue could speed up the timeline.

projects.name: NC 51 Widening (Matthews)
projects.description: NCDOT's NC 51 widening in Matthews saw costs explode from $4M to $42.5M — a 963% increase — driven by revised estimates for right-of-way, utility relocations, and construction.
projects.detail: Since last summer, the state revised more than 1,000 separate estimates for right-of-way, utility, and construction costs across more than 450 transportation projects. The project involves widening approximately one mile of NC 51 from four to six lanes. It is currently funded but on hold, with construction tentatively scheduled for 2029.

projects.name: I-95 Widening (Lumberton)
projects.description: The $432M I-95 widening through Lumberton was delayed at least one year beyond 2026 due to significant issues relocating natural gas and power utility lines.
projects.detail: NCDOT cited unforeseen issues involving railroad right-of-way, land acquisition, and delays relocating power and natural gas lines. NCDOT approved a $7.4M cost escalation in 2023 to assist all companies working on the project. The widening also includes bridge replacements and grade elevation for flood resilience.

projects.name: Richmond Highway Corridor Improvements (Route 1)
projects.description: The $1B+ Richmond Highway widening and BRT project faced a potential $264M cost increase and 2-year delay from utility undergrounding requirements, threatening federal funding.
projects.detail: VDOT's $372M widening contract included $15M for moving utilities. However, proposals to underground overhead utilities would add at least $264M and push completion to 2031. County officials warned the delay could jeopardize FTA funding. Dominion Energy estimated undergrounding at around $60M, but total project impact was far greater when accounting for cascading schedule effects.

projects.name: Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel Expansion
projects.description: Virginia's largest highway project ($3.9B) fell 18 months behind schedule due to unforeseen cost and schedule impacts, requiring $53M in supplemental state contingency funds.
projects.detail: The state agreed to provide an additional $53M in supplemental contingency and set a $373M cap on construction cost increases through a First Amendment executed in February 2024. The tunnel boring machine 'Mary' completed excavation in early 2026, with full completion now expected Spring 2027.

projects.name: I-10 Widening (Baton Rouge)
projects.description: The I-10 widening through Baton Rouge was delayed 3 years to 2031 after construction approach changes to maintain traffic lanes during utility and infrastructure work.
projects.detail: The initial plan called for maintaining two lanes each direction during construction, but concerns over congestion led to maintaining three lanes, significantly extending the timeline. The construction of an additional lane on the westbound flyover at the I-10/I-110 interchange will cost an estimated $50M. DOTD's internal review found the department too often allows construction to go past deadline and over budget.

projects.name: New Orleans JIRR Road Reconstruction Program
projects.description: New Orleans' FEMA-funded road reconstruction quietly blew a $123M hole in city finances due to spiraling costs from underground sewer and water utility work.
projects.detail: The program involves coordinating with the Sewerage & Water Board to replace underground water and sewer lines as part of road reconstruction across 6,000 blocks. The program ran up a $123M deficit before officials realized they were draining the general fund, forcing the state legislature to approve a $125M short-term loan to avoid missing payroll.
projects.budget: $1.7B FEMA program → $123M budget hole from utility cost overruns

projects.name: I-16/I-75 Interchange Reconstruction (Macon)
projects.delayAbs: No final completion date (6+ years in)
projects.description: GDOT's $500M I-16/I-75 interchange reconstruction in Macon has no estimated completion date after 6+ years, with sewer force main relocation required as a critical early phase.
projects.detail: After six years of construction, GDOT stated there is no final completion date. A critical early component was the I-16/I-75 Phase 6 Sanitary Sewer Force Main project to increase flow capacity. The complex interchange reconstruction requires coordinating multiple construction phases with ongoing utility relocations in one of Georgia's busiest traffic corridors.
projects.timeline: June 2017 start → no final completion date

projects.name: Atlanta BeltLine Southside Trail (Segments 4+5)
projects.description: Underground utility conflicts at United Avenue repeatedly derailed completion targets for the BeltLine's Southside Trail, pushing opening back roughly a year.
projects.detail: Unexpected underground utility conflicts at United Avenue wiped out the BeltLine's completion goals repeatedly — pushing from spring to summer 2025, then fall 2025, then early 2026. Environmental remediation work compounded the delays. The trail section was critical for creating a continuous 17-mile BeltLine loop.

projects.name: Downtown Atlanta Gas Line Strike (State Capitol)
projects.description: A contractor struck a 6-inch gas main at Piedmont Ave and MLK Drive in November 2024, forcing evacuation of the Georgia State Capitol and closure of a MARTA station.
projects.detail: On November 6, 2024, a contractor doing construction work struck a 6-inch gas main approximately five feet underground near the Georgia State Capitol. The fire department warned the leak had potential to lead to an explosion. The leak was contained by 4 p.m., with full repairs completed that evening.

projects.name: North Avondale Road Gas Strike (Avondale Estates)
projects.description: Contractors on an $8.5M complete street project struck a gas line, forcing evacuation of five businesses and closure of a major road in both directions.
projects.detail: On October 3, 2024, a crew working on the $8.5M U.S. 278 complete street project struck a gas line, forcing closure of North Avondale Road in both directions. DeKalb County Fire Rescue evacuated five businesses. The leak was capped and the road reopened around 5 p.m. that same day.

projects.name: Nashville Paramount Tower Gas Strike
projects.description: A construction crew at the Paramount Tower luxury condo site struck a gas line on June 3, 2026, forcing evacuation of the downtown YMCA and closure of Church Street.
projects.detail: On June 3, 2026, a crew working on the Paramount Tower building site struck a gas line. The downtown YMCA was evacuated and a section of Church Street was closed. Spire estimated repairs would take 4-5 hours. No injuries were reported.

projects.name: Highway 501 Realignment (Myrtle Beach)
projects.description: The $14M Highway 501 realignment required replacing old sewer and water lines and moving utility lines underground, with delays from an upsized stormwater drainage pipe.
projects.detail: Crews fell about three weeks behind schedule partly because the city installed a larger stormwater drainage pipe than originally planned. The project is part of a broader $33M utility underground conversion program that has buried overhead lines along 60 blocks of Ocean Boulevard and 25 blocks of Kings Highway.

projects.name: Myrtle Beach Underground Utility Conversion Program
projects.description: Myrtle Beach has spent $33M+ retrofitting overhead utilities underground across major corridors, requiring repeated excavation of previously paved roads at ~$1M per mile.
projects.detail: The program has converted utilities along 60 blocks of Ocean Boulevard, 25 blocks of Kings Highway, 10 blocks around HGTC's campus, and other corridors. Each conversion requires excavating the roadway and then repaving — effectively digging up roads that had been previously paved. The 20+ year program continues at approximately $1M per mile.

projects.name: I-10 Mobile River Bridge and Bayway
projects.description: Alabama's $3.7B I-10 bridge and bayway project saw costs climb from $2.7B amid repeated delays, with the timeline described as indefinite.
projects.detail: Costs have escalated from $2.7B to $3.5B and then to $3.7B after a contractor shakeup. ALDOT officials stated the timeline is indefinite because inflation and rising interest rates made the project unfeasible without additional federal aid. The project must navigate above two aging tunnels beneath Mobile Bay.

projects.name: Sheboygan County TC Energy Pipeline Rupture
projects.description: Excavation crew struck a 10-inch TC Energy gas main while installing cable, triggering a massive explosion that injured 4 workers, damaged 2 homes, and forced evacuation of 60 homes.
projects.detail: On November 14, 2025, an excavation crew working on cable installation struck a highly pressurized 10-inch natural gas main. Four workers were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. Two houses were rendered uninhabitable. Approximately 60 homes within a mile-wide area were evacuated.
projects.budget: Two homes rendered uninhabitable; property damage to surrounding structures
projects.timeline: November 14, 2025; evacuations lifted same evening for most residents

projects.name: Newark Magazine Street Gas Explosion
projects.description: A construction crew doing water line work on Magazine Street struck a gas line after reportedly being incorrectly told it was shut off, triggering an explosion that tore the facade off a home and injured four people.
projects.detail: On March 14, 2026, around 12:20 p.m., a construction crew working on a water line at 86 Magazine Street in Newark struck a gas line. According to a Newark official quoted by NJ.com, the workers tapped the line after being incorrectly told it was shut off. The explosion blew the front facade off a home and shattered nearby windows. Four people were hurt, including two teenagers, and all were expected to recover. PSE&G crews repaired the line and the Red Cross assisted displaced families.

projects.name: Wappingers Falls Gas Line Rupture and Building Collapse
projects.description: An excavator ruptured a gas line during routine maintenance, causing an explosion that collapsed four homes, injured 15 people including 5 first responders.
projects.detail: On November 2, 2023, a gas line was ruptured by an excavator during routine maintenance work. The explosion caused a multi-family building to collapse. Fifteen people were injured including five first responders, with a majority in critical condition. Four homes collapsed. Police Commissioner stated there was no criminal intent.
projects.budget: Four homes destroyed; multi-family building collapsed

projects.name: Haymarket Virginia Home Explosion
projects.description: A private contractor replacing a water line struck a gas line, and despite evacuations and utility response, the home exploded roughly an hour later, destroying everything two families owned.
projects.detail: On October 16, 2024, a contractor replacing a water line struck and ruptured an underground gas line. Fire crews evacuated the home and neighbors. Washington Gas arrived about an hour later, but at 5:36 p.m. the home exploded. Two couples and their young children lost everything. The families' pets are believed to have died.
projects.budget: Home completely destroyed; total loss for two families
projects.timeline: October 16, 2024; home exploded approximately 80 minutes after gas line strike

projects.name: Logan Utah Fiber Optic Cable Mass Cut
projects.description: A construction company boring into a road severed 1,300 fiber optic cables, causing a two-day internet blackout that knocked out government offices, schools, and a major food facility.
projects.detail: On August 21, 2023, a construction company bored into the road and cut through approximately 1,300 communication cables. The fiber cut caused a large-scale broadband outage affecting thousands across Cache County. County government offices, major employer JBS Foods, and nearly half of the school district's 25 schools lost internet. Crews spliced all cables within 28 hours.
projects.budget: Extensive economic disruption to businesses, schools, and government services

projects.name: Louisiana-Mississippi 911 System Fiber Cut
projects.description: Severed AT&T fiber optic cables knocked out 911 emergency calling systems across two states for several hours, disabling roughly 80 emergency systems in Mississippi alone.
projects.detail: On September 25, 2025, damage to AT&T fiber optic cables caused widespread 911 outages across Louisiana and Mississippi. The outages impacted Louisiana's three largest cities and roughly 80 emergency systems in Mississippi. AT&T restored services before 6 p.m. local time. Public safety leaders called for additional path diversity for 911 traffic.
projects.budget: No direct property damage; severe public safety risk
projects.timeline: September 25, 2025; services restored within approximately 4 hours

projects.name: Virginia Voter Registration System Fiber Cut
projects.description: A county contractor installing a sewer cut an unmarked Verizon fiber optic cable, shutting down Virginia's online voter registration system for hours on the final day to register.
projects.detail: On October 13, 2020, a county contractor working on sewer installation severed a Verizon fiber optic cable that was not properly marked. The cut temporarily shut down Virginia's online voter registration system on the last day of registration. The ACLU filed a lawsuit to extend the deadline.
projects.budget: No direct property damage; major disruption to democratic process

projects.name: Chesterfield Township Mobile Home Gas Explosion
projects.description: Crews excavating in a Chesterfield Township mobile home community struck a SEMCO gas line, causing an explosion that destroyed a home and killed the family's dog.
projects.detail: Around 10:50 a.m. on May 26, 2023, crews excavating on Jamestown Drive in the Carriage Way Mobile Home Community struck a gas line, causing an explosion. The mobile home was destroyed and nearby homes were evacuated. The family was not home, but their 2-year-old dog was killed. SEMCO Gas responded to shut down the line.

projects.name: Huntsville Alabama Home Explosion (Comcast Contractor)
projects.description: An independent contractor working for Comcast struck a gas pipe, causing a leak that ignited before utility response, destroying a home where a family of seven barely escaped.
projects.detail: On March 11, 2023, a Comcast contractor struck an underground gas pipe. The family of seven smelled gas and evacuated. Before a Huntsville Utilities worker could take action, something sparked an explosion and the house went up in flames. The home's roof was completely destroyed and the house declared a total loss.

projects.name: Lexington Missouri Fatal Gas Explosion (Fiber Installation)
projects.description: A fiber optic drilling subcontractor struck an unmarked gas main that Liberty Utilities had certified as properly marked, causing an explosion that killed a 5-year-old boy.
projects.detail: On April 9, 2025, a drilling subcontractor installing fiber optic line drilled into an unmarked section of a capped underground gas main. Liberty Utilities had told the excavator all pipelines were properly marked, but markings were inaccurate due to a mapping error. Gas leaked for over three hours before igniting. Five-year-old Alistair Lamb was killed; his father and sister were critically injured. Liberty Utilities was ordered to pay the maximum civil penalty of $30,000.
projects.budget: $30,000 maximum civil penalty; home destroyed; two homes damaged

projects.name: Wooster Ohio Mobile Home Explosion (Fiber Installation)
projects.description: Contractors installing fiber optic cables at a mobile home park struck a 4-inch Enbridge gas line, causing an explosion that flattened a mobile home.
projects.detail: On May 7, 2025, a contractor installing fiber optic cables struck a 4-inch Enbridge gas line at Shelmar Mobile Home Park. The explosion completely flattened a mobile home. The home was unoccupied and no injuries were reported. Multiple state and local investigations were opened.
projects.budget: Mobile home completely destroyed; total loss

projects.name: Girard Ohio House Explosion (Lumos Fiber)
projects.description: A gas explosion destroyed a home and injured a firefighter and police officer after Lumos Networks was laying fiber optic lines nearby. The city imposed a ban on all fiber optic digging.
projects.detail: On April 30, 2026, a natural gas explosion knocked a two-story house off its foundation. Lumos Networks had been installing fiber optic lines along adjacent Gordon Street. One firefighter and a police officer were hospitalized but released. The house was subsequently demolished. The gas outage affected 47 homes. The city imposed a ban on fiber optic companies digging in Girard.
projects.budget: Home destroyed and demolished; 47 homes affected
projects.timeline: April 30, 2026; citywide fiber dig ban imposed

projects.name: Dacono Colorado Mobile Home Explosion (Fiber Boring)
projects.description: A contractor boring underground fiber optic lines punctured a gas line. An hour later the accumulated gas ignited, destroying a mobile home.
projects.detail: On December 2, 2025, a contractor struck a gas line. Responders found only a light odor of gas. Approximately one hour later, gas that had migrated through gravel bedding of nearby water lines emerged under a mobile home and was ignited by an unknown source. The mobile home was deemed a complete loss. No injuries.

projects.name: Naugatuck Connecticut Electrocution (Mismarked Power Line)
projects.description: An excavator bucket severed an underground power line marked nearly 8 feet from its actual location, electrocuting a construction worker who suffered permanent injuries. Jury awarded $2M.
projects.detail: On June 18, 2019, an excavator bucket severed an underground primary power line while a worker was in a 3-foot-deep trench. The power line was located 7 feet 8 inches from its marked position. The worker suffered nerve and muscle damage and now walks with a cane. A jury awarded $2,000,000 in damages, finding him 0% responsible.

projects.name: Kingsbridge Bronx Water Main Strike
projects.description: A subcontractor struck a 24-inch water main during excavation for a housing project, sending millions of gallons into a construction site and threatening a 300-foot tower crane, forcing closure of the Major Deegan Expressway.
projects.detail: On June 25, 2025, a private subcontractor struck a 24-inch water distribution main during excavation for an apartment building. Millions of gallons gushed into the site, threatening a 300-foot-tall tower crane. The FDNY ordered evacuations and closure of the Major Deegan Expressway (I-87) for several hours. An engineer used a drone to inspect the crane and deemed it safe. The Department of Buildings issued a partial stop work order.
projects.budget: Major Deegan Expressway closure; stop work order

projects.name: Swatara Township Chambers Hill Road (PA)
projects.description: UGI utility company tore up Chambers Hill Road just weeks after PennDOT finished repaving it, despite being told to coordinate its gas pipe work before paving was completed.
projects.detail: PennDOT completed paving as part of a $38.5M Route 322 intersection improvement project. Just weeks later, UGI dug up sections to move and upgrade gas pipes. PennDOT stated it had approved UGI's permit with the explicit condition that work be coordinated with the paving project, but UGI failed to coordinate. UGI stated it would cover all costs to restore the road.
projects.budget: Part of $38.5M Route 322 project; UGI covering road restoration
projects.timeline: PennDOT paved 2023 → UGI dug up weeks later in 2023

projects.name: Memphis Philadelphia Street MLGW (TN)
projects.description: Memphis Light Gas and Water tore up a freshly paved street in the Cooper-Young neighborhood just hours after new asphalt was laid.
projects.detail: In July 2019, MLGW crews began drilling into Philadelphia Street just hours after fresh pavement was laid. The city's public works director said there appeared to be 'some sort of confusion between the two departments.' The incident highlighted a fundamental coordination failure between two city agencies.
projects.budget: Part of federally mandated SARP sewer program
projects.timeline: Paved July 2019 → Torn up hours later same day

projects.name: Birmingham Phelan Park Streets (AL)
projects.description: Utility crews tore up freshly paved streets and sidewalks in Birmingham's Phelan Park neighborhood just months after a major city repaving effort.
projects.detail: In April 2025, streets paved just months earlier were being torn up by utility crews. Sidewalks were destroyed and filled with gravel that sank during rain, creating hazardous holes. Residents with electric wheelchairs were forced into the road. The city had approved $13M in street resurfacing contracts and $15M in FY2025 paving budget.
projects.budget: $13M in council-approved resurfacing; $15M FY2025 paving budget
projects.timeline: Paved late 2024/early 2025 → Torn up by April 2025

projects.name: Elmira East Water Street (NY)
projects.description: Motorists enjoyed smooth pavement on East Water Street in Elmira for less than three days before utility crews tore it up again for pipe replacement.
projects.detail: In September 2024, parts of East Water Street were paved before underground pipe replacement was finished, because the contractor had many more projects scheduled and was unsure it could return before asphalt plants closed for winter. The road was torn up again three days later on September 16.
projects.timeline: Paved mid-September 2024 → Torn up 3 days later

projects.name: Kansas City Linwood Blvd Spire Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Spire Energy dug a trench through recently repaved Linwood Boulevard, violating new road construction regulations and prompting the city to freeze all Spire work permits.
projects.detail: Kansas City had invested nearly $40M in street preservation and completed curb-to-curb resurfacing of Linwood Boulevard. Weeks later, Spire ripped up the freshly paved road and laid a concrete patch in the middle of an asphalt road. Officials called it 'blatant disregard of our new street excavation rules.' The city froze all new Spire work permits until damage on Linwood, Gillham Road, 27th Street, and 31st Street was addressed.
projects.budget: Part of $40M city street preservation program
projects.timeline: Linwood repaved 2022 → Spire dug trench weeks later

projects.name: Pittsfield Valentine Rd & East St (MA)
projects.delayAbs: Days to weeks between paving and destruction
projects.description: Two freshly resurfaced roads in Pittsfield were torn up within days — Valentine Road for a water line and East Street for a gas line — prompting residents to ask if the five-year moratorium had been rescinded.
projects.detail: Valentine Road was resurfaced then promptly excavated for a new water line. East Street was resurfaced and torn up within days for a gas line installation by Berkshire Gas. A frustrated resident questioned whether Pittsfield's five-year moratorium had been rescinded. A $13M state reconstruction of East Street was also planned.
projects.budget: $13M state reconstruction of East Street planned
projects.timeline: Both resurfaced 2025 → Dug up days/weeks later

projects.name: San Diego Juan Street Old Town Moratorium Violation
projects.description: A two-year, $8M Juan Street project — touted as a model of the city's 'One Dig' philosophy — had sections torn up again shortly after completion for additional utility work.
projects.detail: In August 2014, Mayor Faulconer lauded the project as a perfect example of the city's One Dig philosophy. However, by April 2017, a construction crew came back and tore up the recently paved street for additional utility pipe work. Frustrated residents questioned why all pipes couldn't be replaced before repaving.
projects.timeline: Construction 2014-2017 → Sections torn up again April 2017

projects.name: Bethesda Bradley Blvd Water Main Burst
projects.description: A 20-inch water main burst on Bradley Boulevard in Bethesda just months after the road had been repaved, flooding the street and requiring major road reconstruction.
projects.detail: On May 19, 2026, a 20-inch water main burst on Bradley Boulevard. Residents reported the section had been repaved within the last few months. The pipe had been installed in 2018, making its failure unusual. WSSC Water repaired the main and undertook extensive road restoration work.
projects.budget: WSSC Water covering repair and road restoration costs
projects.timeline: Road repaved early 2026 → Water main burst May 19, 2026

projects.name: Plymouth Water Street Sewer (MA)
projects.delayAbs: Road dug up 3 times in 2 years
projects.description: Water Street in Plymouth was dug up three times in two years for a sewer interceptor project that ballooned from $4.5M to $6.5M after groundwater problems and pipe settlement.
projects.detail: Work began in December 2022 with planned completion by June 2023. Groundwater problems, shifting soil, and damage forced a shutdown for engineering evaluation. The street was repaved and reopened, then dug up again when a section of new sewer pipe dropped five inches below specification. The town and contractor settled on a $2M increase.
projects.timeline: Construction began Dec 2022 → Third dig-up Dec 2024 → May extend to June 2026

projects.name: Nashville Clarksville Pike AT&T Delay
projects.delayAbs: 12-month delay due to AT&T utility conflicts
projects.description: TDOT's Clarksville Pike widening was delayed a full year beyond its scheduled completion primarily due to AT&T communication line conflicts discovered underground.
projects.detail: The project was originally scheduled for spring 2023 completion but was delayed to spring 2024. TDOT identified AT&T communications lines as the primary source of utility problems, with crews repeatedly finding unexpected communication lines underground. The project experienced four major utility conflicts involving water, gas, and communication lines.
projects.budget: TDOT road widening project (cost not publicly stated)
projects.timeline: Construction Sept 2019 → Original spring 2023 → Delayed to spring 2024

projects.name: Toms River Utility Road Damage Ordinance (NJ)
projects.description: Repeated utility cuts into recently paved roads in Toms River prompted a proposed ordinance requiring curb-to-curb repaving of roads under five years old and a moratorium on excavating newly paved streets.
projects.detail: In November 2024, Mayor Dan Rodrick championed a Toms River ordinance in response to frequent and often poorly executed utility road repairs. Under the proposal, a utility that cuts into a road less than five years old must pay for full curb-to-curb reconstruction rather than patching. The ordinance also includes a street excavation moratorium limiting how soon after paving utilities can dig. The ordinance was at first reading in November 2024.
projects.timeline: Ongoing incidents through 2024 → Ordinance introduced November 2024

projects.name: Cincinnati Citywide Utility Cut Damage Study
projects.delayAbs: One-third of street service life lost
projects.description: A 2011 consulting study found Cincinnati lost one-third of the service life of its streets due to repeated utility construction cuts, costing millions in premature repair.
projects.detail: A 2011 Envista report found Cincinnati lost approximately one-third of its streets' service life from repeated utility cuts. Burlington, Vermont was spending $500K annually on unnecessary patching, and Kansas City suffered $4M in damages from cuts to streets resurfaced within three years. Cincinnati modified its repaving decisions to consider other agencies' projects.
projects.budget: Millions in premature repairs; Burlington VT: $500K/year; KC, MO: $4M in 3-year damage

projects.name: Jane Byrne Interchange Reconstruction (Chicago)
projects.description: Reconstruction of Chicago's busiest interchange ballooned from $535M to $806M and took 4 years longer than planned, partly due to abandoned water tunnels that turned out to be active.
projects.detail: The Jane Byrne Interchange reconstruction began in 2013 with a $535M budget and 2018 completion target. Complications included unstable soil, abandoned water tunnels that turned out to be active, lengthy utility relocations, and COVID-19. IDOT officials specifically pegged delays on the need to wait for utilities to be relocated. Final cost reached $806.4M and the project reopened December 16, 2022.

projects.name: Peoples Gas System Modernization Program (Chicago)
projects.description: Peoples Gas pipe replacement program has ballooned from $2B to nearly $11B, is a decade behind schedule, and has torn up Chicago streets for years.
projects.detail: When the program began in 2011, it was estimated to cost less than $2B to replace more than 2,000 miles of aging gas mains by 2030. By 2023, projections had soared to nearly $11B with only 38% completed. The Illinois Commerce Commission paused the program in late 2023. Chicago enforces a 5-year moratorium for resurfaced streets, but the ongoing work has repeatedly required excavation of recently restored roads. The Citizens Utility Board called it a boondoggle.

projects.name: CTA Red Line Extension (South Side Chicago)
projects.description: Chicago's 5.6-mile Red Line Extension saw costs jump from $3.6B to $5.75B, with extensive utility relocation work underway through 2027 before track construction can begin.
projects.detail: The CTA underestimated soft costs like engineering and project management — budgeting $280M that ballooned to $1.24B. Demolition and utility relocations are ongoing through 2027. Track and station construction is scheduled 2026 through 2029 with completion targeted for 2030. The project broke ground in April 2026 after securing a $2B federal Full Funding Grant Agreement.

projects.name: Akron Waterways Renewed! Consent Decree Sewer Program
projects.description: Akron's EPA-mandated sewer overhaul grew from $870M to over $1.2B, with the Ohio Canal Interceptor Tunnel missing its deadline by 290 days, resulting in $1.2M in EPA penalties.
projects.detail: Since 2014, Akron has been under one of the strictest federal consent decrees requiring a complete sewer overflow overhaul. The cost grew from $870M to over $1.2B. The OCIT tunnel missed its deadline by 290 days, discharging hundreds of millions of gallons of untreated sewage. A federal judge denied Akron's appeal, forcing an additional $209M treatment facility and an immediate 23% increase in water/sewer bills.
projects.timeline: Completion by 2028 per consent decree → multiple milestones missed

projects.name: I-39/I-90 Expansion (Madison to Illinois Line)
projects.description: The I-39/I-90 corridor expansion was originally estimated at $715M but came in at more than $1.2B, part of a pattern where 19 major Wisconsin road projects doubled from $772M to $1.5B.
projects.detail: The Badger Institute documented this as part of a systemic problem: 19 major Wisconsin road projects from 2006 to 2015 totaled approximately $1.5B, roughly twice the original $772M in combined estimates. Wisconsin passed Act 46 in 2023 creating a process for WisDOT to compensate contractors delayed by unmarked utilities.

projects.name: US-40/K-10 Diverging Diamond Interchange (Lawrence)
projects.description: KDOT's $14M interchange project was delayed 8+ months when unexpected utility relocation setbacks forced postponement of the major road closure.
projects.detail: A complete 100-day closure of US-40 originally scheduled for July 2023 was postponed to spring 2024 due to 'unexpected utility relocation setbacks.' The delay caused months of additional traffic disruption. The project was completed in September 2024.
projects.timeline: Summer 2023 start → Feb 2024 start; completion late 2024

projects.name: O'Fallon Gateway Fiber House Explosion (MO)
projects.description: A Gateway Fiber subcontractor struck a gas line while boring fiber optic cable in O'Fallon, MO, triggering an explosion that destroyed one home and damaged roughly 40 others.
projects.detail: On March 1, 2022, a subcontractor using directional boring equipment struck a Spire natural gas line. The blast destroyed one home and damaged approximately 40 surrounding homes. The city imposed a two-week drilling moratorium and passed Ordinance No. 6909 enacting stringent excavation standards. The City Council voted 9-0 requesting the Missouri Attorney General enforce underground utility marking laws.
projects.timeline: Fiber installation halted; two-week moratorium imposed

projects.name: Independence Google Fiber Gas Explosion (MO)
projects.description: A Google Fiber crew struck a gas line causing a house explosion, and two days later another Google Fiber strike in Parkville forced more evacuations.
projects.detail: On August 26, 2024, a Google Fiber crew accidentally struck a gas line. Leaking gas migrated into a nearby unoccupied home and ignited. Just two days later, another Google Fiber crew hit a gas line in Parkville approximately 20 miles away. A third similar incident occurred in Shawnee, Kansas. Telecommunications-related construction was the leading cause of gas line hits nationally in 2022-2023.

projects.name: AT&T Fiber South St. Louis County Gas Line Strikes
projects.description: An AT&T Fiber subcontractor struck three gas lines, two power lines, and knocked out telecom service multiple times on a single street, leading the county to suspend AT&T's permit.
projects.detail: In 2022, subcontractor Olam Communications struck three gas lines on one street, two power lines, and knocked out telecom service multiple times. St. Louis County suspended AT&T's excavation permit. AT&T's permit had expired the same day the gas main was struck. The Common Ground Alliance reported fiber construction was responsible for one in four utility strikes nationally.
projects.timeline: AT&T permit suspended; project halted pending safety review

projects.name: AT&T Kansas Utility Locate Failures (KCC Fine)
projects.description: The Kansas Corporation Commission fined AT&T $60,000 for 60 documented failures to mark underground lines within the required two-day window for excavators.
projects.detail: In April 2025, the KCC issued AT&T a $60,000 civil penalty for failing to mark buried infrastructure within two days of requests. The KCC's chief engineer stated that AT&T apparently made a decision to save money by not completing requests promptly. The fine was $1,000 per violation.

projects.name: KC Streetcar Riverfront Extension
projects.description: The KC Streetcar Riverfront Extension cost surged 203% from $20.2M to $61.1M, driven by scope additions and utility relocation work.
projects.detail: The original 2021 estimate was just $20.2M. Cost increases were driven by extending the project 0.15 miles closer to the KC Current stadium, building double tracks, larger-than-anticipated costs on the Grand Viaduct, and significant utility relocation work. Utility relocations involved coordinating approximately 20 private utilities through an online portal with GIS-based mapping. The extension opened May 18, 2026.

projects.name: Minneapolis 50th & Penn Water Main Break
projects.description: A water main burst at 50th and Penn in Minneapolis flooded businesses for six blocks with water that froze in single-digit temps. Three businesses permanently closed; the city denied all damage claims.
projects.detail: On February 13, 2025, a water main burst sending water flowing six blocks until crews shut it off. In single-digit temperatures, water quickly froze. Three businesses permanently closed: Terzo Italian restaurant (water reached the ceiling of the basement), Paperback Exchange bookstore (roughly 100,000 books ruined), and Sparrow Cafe. The City denied all damage claims citing municipal immunity.

projects.name: Washtenaw County Ellsworth Road Gas Line Strike
projects.description: A third-party contractor struck a DTE underground gas line during construction, causing a high-pressure gas release mistaken for an explosion that damaged several cars.
projects.detail: On February 12, 2026, a third-party contractor struck an underground gas line near Ellsworth Road and State Street. The high-pressure release sent mud and debris flying, producing a loud noise initially mistaken for an explosion. The incident caused property damage to several cars but no injuries.
projects.timeline: Intersection closed during emergency response and repairs

projects.name: Bronx Van Cortlandt Park Water Main Strike (School/Housing Site)
projects.description: A private contractor building a school and housing complex struck a 24-inch water main in June 2025, flooding the site, threatening a 300-foot crane, and shutting down the Major Deegan Expressway.
projects.detail: On June 25, 2025, Metropolitan Water and Sewer, a private contractor working on a new public school and housing complex at Van Cortlandt Park South and Broadway in the Bronx, struck a 24-inch water distribution main. Millions of gallons gushed into the construction site, threatening the stability of a 300-foot tower crane. The Major Deegan Expressway was closed in both directions from West 230th Street to Van Cortlandt Park South. Nearby buildings were evacuated. An engineer used a drone and transit device to assess the crane before it was deemed stable three hours later. A partial stop-work order was issued for the construction site. The incident highlighted the risks of inadequate utility mapping at active construction zones.

projects.name: I-295/I-76/Route 42 Direct Connection (South Jersey)
projects.description: Utility problems, right-of-way acquisition, and design revisions extended this $900M+ interchange project from a 2022 target to 2028.
projects.detail: The Direct Connection project to untangle one of New Jersey's most congested interchanges where I-295, I-76, and Route 42 meet began construction in 2013 with an estimated budget of $900 million and a 2022 completion target. Utility relocation problems, combined with right-of-way acquisition difficulties and design revisions to the pier system for a new ramp, pushed the completion date to 2028. A retaining wall collapse in March 2021 added further delay. The project has been compared to Boston's Big Dig for its prolonged timeline and escalating costs.

projects.name: DC H Street / Benning Road Streetcar
projects.description: The 2.2-mile DC streetcar cost nearly $200M and opened three years late, largely due to Pepco utility relocation complications. It was shut down in March 2026.
projects.detail: The DC Streetcar on H Street NE was originally budgeted around $50 million with a planned 2013 opening. Underground utility work, particularly coordination with Pepco for electrical relocations, caused repeated construction halts. The project ultimately cost Washington taxpayers nearly $200 million and didn't open until February 2016 -- more than three years late. Plagued by cost overruns, unreliable service running in mixed traffic, and higher-than-expected maintenance costs, the system was shut down on March 31, 2026, after only 10 years of operation, and replaced by an electric bus system.

projects.name: Brooklyn Flushing Avenue Greenway (Utility Interference Delays)
projects.description: A protected bike lane project along Flushing Avenue near the Brooklyn Navy Yard was delayed over five years by repeated utility interference discovered during construction.
projects.detail: Brooklyn Community Board 2 endorsed the plan for a two-way protected bike lane on Flushing Avenue in 2013, with construction scheduled to begin in 2014. However, DDC's contractor did not begin work until fall 2017 -- three years behind schedule -- and the project dragged on through 2019 due to repeated utility interference underground. The DDC's own Strategic Blueprint acknowledges that street reconstruction projects are typically delayed 3 to 9 months because of interference with existing utilities, but the Flushing Avenue project exceeded even that range. The project was consistently featured on Streetsblog's annual lists of 'DDC projects taking forever to build,' highlighting how NYC's unmapped underground utility infrastructure creates chronic delays for surface improvements.

projects.name: Union City NJ Mislabeled Gas Line Strike
projects.description: Veolia Water contractors performing routine water main repair struck a mislabeled 20-inch PSE&G gas line in July 2024, forcing evacuation of 700 people and two schools.
projects.detail: On July 11, 2024, around 9:30 a.m., a Veolia crew performing water main work at Summit Avenue and 26th Street in Union City struck a 20-inch gas main, spraying gas and water into the air. Veolia officials said the gas line was mismarked by PSE&G; PSE&G declined to comment on specifics while the matter was investigated. About 700 people were evacuated from 10 buildings, and Union City High School and Robert Waters Elementary were dismissed early. PSE&G crews plugged the leak before noon, and no injuries were reported.

projects.name: Baltimore Consent Decree Sewer System Overhaul
projects.description: Baltimore's EPA consent decree to end sewer overflows, originally due by 2016, was extended to 2030 and the city now seeks a further 16-year delay to 2046, with $674M in additional construction costs.
projects.detail: Baltimore entered into a consent decree with the EPA in 2002 to end raw sewage overflows into local streams and the harbor. The original deadline was 2016, which was extended to 2030. Now the city's Department of Public Works is seeking another 16-year extension to 2046, citing the need for 26 additional construction projects to improve hydraulic capacity at an estimated cost of $674 million. Underground utility conflicts have complicated the sewer improvement work: in one project, AECOM allegedly failed to account for bedrock near sewer pipes under Chinquapin Run and undercounted trees, causing the city to overspend by nearly $14 million on a two-mile stretch alone. Sewage rates jumped 18% in 2025 -- the highest increase in history.

projects.name: Monroe CT Pepper Street Reconstruction
projects.description: An $8 million road reconstruction was delayed over a year because utility companies did not begin relocating gas and water pipes until after construction had already started.
projects.detail: The roughly $8 million Pepper Street Improvements and Multi-use Trail project in Monroe, Connecticut began in June 2020 with an expected two-year timeline. Contractors were repeatedly delayed by utility line conflicts involving gas and water pipes owned by utility companies that did not start relocation work until after the road construction had already begun. The contractor submitted $445,078 in reserved claims for unanticipated conditions attributable to utility conflicts with the design, including $232,000 in utility relocation costs plus escalation costs for fuel, labor, materials, and vendor services. The project caused persistent traffic jams on this heavily traveled commuter route.

projects.name: PA PUC Statewide Utility Line Strike Enforcement (2024-2025)
projects.description: Pennsylvania's Damage Prevention Committee levied $163,550 in penalties and 84 mandatory training orders against 120 excavators and utility owners in a single month for underground utility strikes.
projects.detail: The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission's Damage Prevention Committee, created through Act 50 of 2017, regularly reviews alleged violations of the One Call Law involving underground utility line strikes during construction. In February 2025 alone, the committee levied $163,550 in penalties and ordered 84 mandatory training requirements against 120 excavators, facility owners, and project owners for utility strikes across the state. Repeat offenses included failure to respond to emergency and routine 8-1-1 locate requests. Comcast was fined $2,000 for a third offense in Lebanon County, and Verizon was fined $2,500 for a subsequent emergency response violation. Act 127 of 2024 reauthorized and expanded the Commission's enforcement authority.

projects.name: Selinsgrove PA UGI Gas Main Moratorium Dispute
projects.description: UGI Utilities requested a moratorium waiver to replace a 1950s-era gas main under 18th Street -- paved just one year earlier -- but Selinsgrove Borough Council blocked the request.
projects.detail: UGI Utilities sought to replace a 2-inch gas main dating back to the 1950s along a 650-foot section of 18th Street in Selinsgrove Borough, between Hower Street and University Avenue. The problem: the borough had paved 18th Street just one year prior, and borough code imposes a five-year moratorium on non-emergency street cutting on newly paved pavement. UGI requested the council waive the moratorium, but the Selinsgrove Borough Council declined, upholding the moratorium protection. The standoff illustrates the tension between aging utility infrastructure needing replacement and municipalities trying to protect their road investment, and the cost of failing to coordinate utility work before repaving.

projects.name: NJ Route 3 Passaic River Bridge Replacement (Rutherford/Lyndhurst)
projects.description: Contractors replacing the Route 3 bridge over the Passaic River near MetLife Stadium said they were delayed by underground and overhead utility relocations, threatening completion before the 2014 Super Bowl.
projects.detail: NJDOT's project replaced the moveable Route 3 bridge over the Passaic River with a fixed span and added shoulders and auxiliary lanes in Rutherford, Lyndhurst and Clifton. In September 2012, contractors said they were being delayed by moving underground and overhead utilities, and the projected cost had risen to $156 million from $149 million at contract award in 2010. The state transportation commissioner would not promise the job would be finished by the February 2014 Super Bowl. In March 2013, NJDOT told the Assembly Transportation Committee that utility relocations had caused more than a nine-month delay on Route 3 over the Passaic River.

projects.name: NJ Route 18 Extension (Piscataway) Utility Stall
projects.description: The NJDOT cited a three-year construction stall on the Route 18 extension in Piscataway caused by utility companies failing to relocate infrastructure on schedule.
projects.detail: At a March 2013 hearing of the New Jersey Assembly Transportation Committee, NJDOT Assistant Commissioner Anthony Attanasio told lawmakers that road projects are routinely held up by utilities delayed in relocating wires or pipes. The department cited a three-year stall of the Route 18 extension in Piscataway as an example. Lawmakers were reviewing legislation to penalize utilities that miss agreed relocation deadlines, which supporters said could save taxpayers tens of millions of dollars each year. The New Jersey Utilities Association opposed the bill.

projects.name: Tonnelle Avenue Widening (North Bergen NJ)
projects.description: Construction on the Tonnelle Avenue (US Routes 1 & 9) widening in North Bergen halted several times while utility companies failed to meet relocation schedules.
projects.detail: Construction on the Tonnelle Avenue (US Routes 1 & 9) widening in North Bergen had to halt several times to accommodate the relocation of utility infrastructure. State Senator Nicholas Sacco, chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, cited these delays when introducing a bill requiring utilities and NJDOT to jointly plan relocations and holding utilities liable for cost overruns when they miss the relocation schedule.

projects.name: NYC DDC Section U Infrastructure Projects (Citywide Utility Delays)
projects.description: A DDC analysis found that older 'Section U' infrastructure projects averaged $5.8M in additional utility-driven costs per project -- nearly 300% more delay than the newer Joint Bidding model.
projects.detail: New York City's Department of Design and Construction published a comprehensive 2024 Utility Coordination Report analyzing 20 years of data on its Joint Bidding program versus the older Section U model. Under Section U, city contractors had to open streets and negotiate directly with private utility companies (Con Edison, National Grid, Verizon) to move and protect their lines -- a time-consuming process that left streets open and neighborhoods disrupted. The analysis found Section U projects averaged $5.8 million in additional utility-driven costs per project, while Joint Bidding projects averaged only $1.5 million. The average utility-related delay for Section U projects exceeded Joint Bidding delays by nearly 300%. The Joint Bidding model saves the city over $107 million per year.

projects.name: NYC East Side Coastal Resiliency Project (Phase 2 Utility Conflicts)
projects.description: The $1.45 billion East Side Coastal Resiliency project was delayed to end of 2027 due to unforeseen underground construction debris and extensive utility conflicts requiring alternate engineering.
projects.detail: New York City's East Side Coastal Resiliency project -- the largest urban climate adaptation project in the country -- was originally estimated at $770 million before the design was overhauled, pushing the budget to $1.45 billion. Phase 2, which involves complete reconstruction of East River Park and a new 8-foot flood wall, encountered unforeseen underground conditions including large amounts of historic construction and demolition debris and extensive utility conflicts that required mitigation and alternate engineering approaches. The DDC acknowledged that 'interference with existing underground utilities that are sometimes unknown or poorly mapped is the largest driver of DDC infrastructure project delays.' Completion was pushed from end of 2026 to end of 2027.

projects.name: Stamford CT Lakeside Drive Bridge Replacement
projects.description: A $3.9M bridge replacement project expected to take 8 months was delayed a full year due to complications relocating utility lines running above and below the bridge.
projects.detail: The $3.9 million Lakeside Drive bridge replacement in Stamford, Connecticut began in April 2023 and was originally expected to take eight months. However, the contractor encountered complications stemming from weather, river diversion, and complexities associated with relocating utility lines running both above and below the bridge. The completion date was pushed to November 2024 -- a full year behind schedule. The project was funded 80% by federal funds with the remainder from the state. Stamford had five road bridges rated 'poor' by CTDOT, and the delays on Lakeside Drive frustrated residents who relied on the route.

projects.name: NJ Turnpike Interchange 6-9 Widening (Pipeline Relocation)
projects.description: The $2.7 billion NJ Turnpike widening required $200 million just to relocate 12 miles of three private fuel and petroleum pipelines running through the project corridor.
projects.detail: The New Jersey Turnpike Authority's $2.7 billion Interchange 6 to 9 Widening Program expanded a 35-mile section of the Turnpike to 12 lanes, building 60 new bridge structures and modifying 36 others. The work included relocating 12 miles of three fuel and petroleum pipelines owned by private companies, at a cost of $200 million. The program was scheduled for completion in 2014.

projects.name: Fetters Mill Road Bridge (PECO Gas Delay)
projects.description: The Fetters Mill Road bridge rehabilitation over Pennypack Creek was delayed by unanticipated PECO Gas main relocation work, pushing completion to November 2026.
projects.detail: The rehabilitation of the Fetters Mill Road bridge over Pennypack Creek between Lower Moreland Township and Bryn Athyn in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania was delayed due to unanticipated complications with PECO Gas main relocation. The project scope includes temporary trail relocation, utility relocations, removal and rehabilitation of the historic truss, replacement of bridge abutments, scour protection, new steel floor beams and stringers, a new fiber-reinforced polymer bridge deck, and roadway approach reconstruction. The PECO Gas main had to be relocated before the Support of Excavation system could be installed around the existing bridge abutments. The delay pushed the expected completion to November 2026.

projects.name: DC Streetcar Suspended Streets Moratorium System
projects.description: Washington DC enforces a 5-year excavation suspension on recently restored or repaved roads, but emergency waivers and utility non-compliance remain persistent problems.
projects.detail: The District Department of Transportation (DDOT) maintains a 'Suspended Streets' list -- roads that have recently been restored or repaved and are suspended from excavation for five subsequent years unless DDOT issues a waiver. Despite this policy, utility companies have repeatedly sought emergency waivers or conducted excavation work that damages recently improved road surfaces. The system is designed to protect the city's investment in road infrastructure, but coordination failures between DDOT's paving schedule and utility companies' maintenance and upgrade plans mean that streets frequently end up on the suspended list without utility companies having completed their planned underground work first, forcing costly moratorium exceptions.

projects.name: Corridor H (Wardensville to Virginia Line) (WV)
projects.description: Utility relocation and property acquisition costs pushed the Corridor H highway segment over the $500M federal threshold, triggering a 'major project' reclassification that delayed construction by over a year.
projects.detail: The Corridor H segment from Wardensville to the Virginia state line in West Virginia was budgeted at $475 million for construction alone. When preconstruction activities including design, right-of-way acquisition, and utility relocation were added, the total exceeded the $500 million threshold that triggers Federal Highway Administration 'major project' designation.
