This reclassification imposed additional federal oversight requirements, reviews, and reporting that delayed the project by over a year. Corridor H has been on the books since 1964 and is now expected to be completed in 2034 -- 70 years after first being proposed. The Parsons to Davis section alone is estimated at $800 million for just 9.2 miles.

projects.name: NYC 3D Underground (3DU) Mapping Crisis Response
projects.description: NYC launched a $10 million initiative to create the nation's first shared 3D underground utility map after unforeseen utility conflicts chronically delayed capital projects and inflated costs.
projects.detail: In November 2025, New York City announced the 3D Underground (3DU) initiative -- a $10 million program funded by HUD disaster recovery grants -- to create a secure, shared 3D model of all subterranean infrastructure including water and sewer lines, gas mains, electric and telecom conduits, fiber networks, and subsurface geology. The program was a direct response to chronic capital project delays and cost overruns caused by unmapped 'utility spaghetti' beneath city streets. Workers routinely encountered unknown pipes, cables, and conduits during construction, forcing project redesigns, crew standdowns, and costly mitigation. Con Edison, National Grid, Verizon, and city agencies will share data on the platform, which is expected to launch in early 2028 and could shave days or weeks off construction schedules.

projects.name: Morgantown WV Van Voorhis Road Sewer/Water Relocation
projects.description: DOH's Van Voorhis Road widening required $624K in Morgantown Utility Board contracts for sewer and waterline relocation before highway construction could begin.
projects.detail: The West Virginia Division of Highways' Van Voorhis Road project between the W.Va. 705 intersection and West Run Road involves lane widening, an additional southbound lane, shoulder paving, sidewalks, curbs, gutters, retaining walls, and drainage upgrades. Before highway construction could begin, the Morgantown Utility Board had to complete sewer and waterline relocation, awarding two contracts totaling $624,160: $522,610 to Green River Group for 1,100 feet of 8-inch sewer line and 1,690 feet of 6-inch water line, and $101,550 to Snider & Son for 400 feet of 8-inch water line via directional drill plus 60 feet of 36-inch steel casing. The utility relocation required complete road closures in July 2024.

projects.name: DC Potomac Interceptor Sewer Repair Delay
projects.description: Eight years of coordination delays between DC Water and the National Park Service on sewer pipe repairs culminated in a catastrophic 200-million-gallon sewage spill into the Potomac River in January 2026.
projects.detail: DC Water identified the need to repair the aging Potomac Interceptor sewer line as early as 2018, but a prolonged environmental review process with the National Park Service -- which controls the federal land the pipe runs through -- delayed construction for eight years. The agency had planned to reinforce the section in 2019 but repeatedly pushed back the timeline as federal officials studied potential environmental impacts, including risks to a blue wildflower and an endangered bat species. In January 2026, the pipe ruptured, spilling more than 200 million gallons of untreated sewage into the Potomac River. Repair costs are now estimated at $425 million for near-term work, with long-term costs expected to reach $600 million. The DOJ and Maryland have sued DC Water over the catastrophic spill.

projects.name: Silver Line Phase 2 Dulles Metro Extension (Virginia/DC)
projects.description: The $3 billion Silver Line Phase 2 extension to Dulles Airport opened four years late in November 2022, with utility relocation among the factors that delayed earlier phases.
projects.detail: The Silver Line Phase 2 extension from Tysons Corner to Dulles Airport and beyond was scheduled to open in 2018 but did not begin passenger service until November 15, 2022 -- four years late. During eight years of construction, the $3 billion project recorded multiple cost overruns, with the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority increasing the budget by $250 million to pay contractors for delays. Utility relocation was specifically cited as responsible for some unfinished work on Phase 1, and similar underground coordination challenges affected Phase 2. The project was further plagued by criminal charges against contractors who falsified records to hide faulty concrete panels -- more than 1,700 defective panels were used in station construction.

projects.name: NJ Route 9 Intersection Widening (Lakewood/Toms River)
projects.description: A $48.5M Route 9 widening project that NJDOT initially promised would take 2-3 years has extended to a potential 5-year timeline, with utility relocation as a primary cause.
projects.detail: NJDOT's $48.5 million Route 9 project resurfaces about seven miles between Indian Head Road in Toms River and 2nd Street in Lakewood, widening eight signalized intersections, adding two signals and adding left-turn lanes at seven unsignalized intersections. Construction began in September 2022 with water main relocation, and NJDOT scheduled completion for Summer 2025. By July 2024, FAA News reported that DOT officials, who had promised completion in 2-3 years, conceded in court filings that the project may take 5 years. NJDOT said most overhead utility wires had been relocated but watermain, sewage, telecommunication and overhead electric/cable relocations were still ongoing; DOT declined to explain the timeline extension.
projects.timeline: Sept 2022 start → Summer 2025 scheduled → may take 5 years (2024)

projects.name: CTfastrak Bus Rapid Transit (Hartford-New Britain)
projects.description: The CTfastrak busway required extensive utility relocations along a shared right-of-way with Amtrak, contributing to a total project cost of $567 million for the 9.4-mile system.
projects.detail: The CTfastrak bus rapid transit system, connecting Hartford and New Britain along a dedicated 9.4-mile guideway, faced significant utility relocation challenges during its three-year construction phase beginning in May 2012. The shared right-of-way with Amtrak required coordination of utility relocations, installation of traffic signals at intersections, and provisions for adaptive signal controls. Engineering efforts included relocating gas, water, electric, and telecom lines that crisscrossed the abandoned railroad corridor being converted to a busway. Despite these challenges, the core construction concluded ahead of schedule, opening March 28, 2015. However, the total project cost escalated to $567 million, reflecting the cumulative impact of utility coordination, infrastructure upgrades, and contingency measures.

projects.name: PGW Cast Iron Gas Main Replacement Program (Philadelphia)
projects.description: Philadelphia Gas Works is replacing 950+ miles of pre-WWII gas mains at 30 miles/year, requiring extensive road closures and utility coordination with the Philadelphia Water Department.
projects.detail: The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission approved Philadelphia Gas Works' accelerated replacement of more than 950 miles of gas mains installed before World War II. PGW replaces approximately 30 miles of gas mains annually, requiring temporary road closures in work zones across the city. A 2019 fatal gas explosion prompted a PUC settlement in January 2025 requiring PGW to bolster collaboration with the Philadelphia Water Department, other city officials, and owners of underground facilities. The massive scale of the replacement program -- affecting neighborhoods like West Oak Lane and requiring PennDOT road closure permits -- creates ongoing conflicts with the city's road paving schedule and other underground utility work. Coordination between PGW, Philadelphia Water, PECO, and telecom companies remains a persistent challenge.

projects.name: SR 9/Main Street Widening (Alpharetta)
projects.description: GDOT's $50 million road widening project delayed two years by utility relocation failures and design changes from new development along the corridor.
projects.detail: The Georgia Department of Transportation's project to widen SR 9/Main Street from Upper Hembree Road to Windward Parkway in Alpharetta began in April 2021 with an original completion date of Spring 2024. However, delayed utility relocations and unanticipated right-of-way and design changes caused by numerous new residential developments pushed completion to Spring 2026. As of September 2025, delayed utility relocations were still ongoing in critical areas throughout the project. The $50 million project adds two vehicle lanes, bike lanes, on-street parking, upgraded drainage, and pedestrian lighting along approximately 3.6 miles of roadway.

projects.name: Brookhaven Google Fiber Gas Main Strike
projects.description: Google Fiber crews struck a gas main near Montgomery Elementary School, triggering a school lockdown and citywide stop-work order affecting 10,000+ properties.
projects.detail: On December 13, 2024, crews installing Google Fiber in Brookhaven struck a gas main on Ashford Dunwoody Road near Montgomery Elementary School, putting the school on lockdown as emergency responders rushed to the scene. The City of Brookhaven issued a citywide stop-work order the following day, halting all Google Fiber installation across the city. Nearly 100 residents had already filed complaints about Google Fiber's underground installation work, which impacts more than 10,000 residential properties. The incident was part of a pattern of disruptions caused by fiber installation across the community, with about 30% of the installation completed at the time of the stoppage.

projects.name: Campbellton Road Fiber Gas Line Strike (Po Freddie's BBQ)
projects.description: Fiber installation contractor ruptured a 6-inch gas line on Campbellton Road, causing an explosion that destroyed a 50-year-old BBQ restaurant and forced evacuation of seven buildings.
projects.detail: In March 2024, an outside contractor damaged a 6-inch natural gas line while installing underground fiber cables in the Campbellton Road area of southwest Atlanta. The resulting gas leak led to an explosion and fire that destroyed Po Freddie's BBQ, a restaurant that had been in operation for nearly 50 years. The gas leak prompted evacuations of seven nearby buildings, including an apartment complex, and shut down Campbellton Road for days. Atlanta Gas Light confirmed the contractor was responsible for the damage. Fortunately no injuries were reported, but the longtime business was completely destroyed.

projects.name: Sylvan Road Underground Gas Explosion
projects.description: A contractor hit a 4-inch gas main while working on traffic signals, causing underground flames to erupt through the pavement and engulf a car on Sylvan Road.
projects.detail: On September 20, 2023, a contractor working on traffic and street signal lights damaged a 4-inch plastic natural gas main at 2049 Sylvan Road SW in Atlanta. The ruptured gas line ignited underground, with flames erupting through the pavement along the road, engulfing a parked car and forcing a nearby daycare to evacuate. Atlanta Fire and Rescue spent about two hours extinguishing the underground fire. Sylvan Road was closed for the remainder of the day while Atlanta Gas Light repaired the damaged gas line, reopening the following day around noon.

projects.name: Morgan Road-Lakeshore Parkway Extension (Jefferson County, AL)
projects.description: ALDOT's $19 million Morgan Road extension requires extensive utility relocation of water lines, power poles, and drainage systems before road widening can proceed.
projects.detail: The Alabama Department of Transportation's $19 million project to redesign Morgan Road and connect it to Lakeshore Parkway at SR-150 in Jefferson County requires workers to first clear land and relocate utilities such as water lines, power poles, and drainage systems before road widening of SR 150 from Morgan Road to Shannon Road can proceed. The project, a partnership between Jefferson County and ALDOT, began in December 2025 with completion expected by the end of 2026, though the overall project may continue through 2027. The extension creates a more efficient route between Interstate 459 and Interstate 65 to address rapid commercial, industrial, and residential growth that has increased traffic beyond what the current road system can handle.

projects.name: Ogeechee Road Widening (Savannah)
projects.description: GDOT's Ogeechee Road widening in Savannah requires extensive underground utility work and bridge demolition, with completion pushed to 2027.
projects.detail: The Georgia Department of Transportation is widening Ogeechee Road from Victory Drive to Tremont Road in Savannah, a corridor carrying over 18,100 vehicles daily as of 2023. The project includes significant utility relocation work underground and under bridges, road widening and paving operations, bridge demolition, and new bridge construction over the CSX Railroad. Utility work is needed from Liberty Parkway to Horizon Parkway before widening can proceed. The project's completion is estimated for spring or summer 2027, reflecting the complexity of coordinating utility relocations with active bridge and road construction in a congested urban corridor.

projects.name: SR 56 Widening (Waynesboro/Mike Padgett Highway)
projects.description: The $29 million SR 56 widening project experienced unexpected utility relocation difficulties and workforce disruptions that delayed construction.
projects.detail: The Georgia Department of Transportation's SR 56/Mike Padgett Highway widening and reconstruction project beginning at Bennock Mill Road and extending to Old Waynesboro Road experienced delays due to unexpected difficulties with utility relocation, disruptions to the construction workforce, and considerable weather delays. The City of Waynesboro was required to relocate and install ductile iron water lines as part of the project requirements. The $29 million project, which began construction in late 2013, has seen its timeline extended well beyond original estimates as crews navigate underground infrastructure conflicts in the corridor.

projects.name: Longwood Fiber Optic Water Main Strikes
projects.description: Fiber optic installation by WOW! and other providers caused over a dozen utility strikes in Longwood, including three significant water main breaks that disrupted neighborhoods.
projects.detail: The city of Longwood, Florida experienced a growing number of underground utility strikes tied to fiber optic installation work in 2026, with more than a dozen incidents reported, three of which were considered significant. Subcontractors working for WideOpenWest (WOW!) caused major disruptions in neighborhoods, tearing apart residential lawns and striking cable and sewer lines while preparing to run underground fiber conduit. On Bearss Circle, crews struck the water main three times. Recorded utility depths often did not match actual depths, complicating construction even when contractors drilled where directed. WOW! eventually dropped its subcontractor and promised new oversight protocols. The city began budgeting for biannual testing of roughly 20,000 water valves in response.

projects.name: DeLand Fiber Optic Water Main Strikes
projects.description: Fiber optic boring crews breached a major water main in DeLand, creating a 20-foot-wide, 7-foot-deep crater and triggering boil water advisories.
projects.detail: On April 13, 2026, a contractor boring underground for MasTec Inc. to install fiber optic cable breached a large water main under the intersection of West Euclid Avenue and State Road 15A in DeLand, Florida. The break triggered a powerful release of water that created a crater roughly 20 feet wide and up to 7 feet deep, closing the road and cutting off water service to southwest DeLand customers. A boil water advisory was issued for the affected area. This was part of a broader pattern: three companies (T-Mobile/Tillman Fiber, Wire 3, and AT&T) were simultaneously laying fiber optic cable underground as part of a state-led broadband expansion project, and DeLand commissioners noted multiple water main breaks in a single day caused by fiber installers.

projects.name: Century Highway 29 Utility Relocation Overrun
projects.description: The Town of Century's utility relocation costs for FDOT's Highway 29 project more than doubled from $265,000 to $555,000 after unmapped water pipes were discovered.
projects.detail: A $4.7 million Florida Department of Transportation safety project to resurface Highway 29 between Henry and Cottage streets required the Town of Century to relocate its water, sewer, and natural gas lines at its own expense. Initially estimated at $264,773 in August 2022, the total ballooned to $554,964 as the project progressed -- more than double the original estimate. The cost increase was driven in part by the discovery of an unmapped Town of Century water pipe that required additional relocation work. The small town was forced to authorize a 15-year promissory note with FDOT for the full amount, a significant financial burden for a municipality that acknowledged it did not have the funds available.

projects.name: Fort Lauderdale Effluent Forcemain Directional Boring Strike
projects.description: A subcontractor performing directional boring to relocate fiber optic line drilled through a 54-inch effluent forcemain without notifying the city or prime contractor.
projects.detail: On September 30, 2024, a subcontractor working on the City of Fort Lauderdale's Redundant Effluent Forcemain Project unintentionally drilled through the existing 54-inch effluent forcemain while performing directional boring to relocate a fiber optic line. The forcemain transmits fully treated effluent from the George T. Lohmeyer wastewater treatment facility to the injection wellfield. Critically, the subcontractor did not notify either the City or the general contractor of its plans to drill in that location. The contractor accepted full responsibility for all costs and expenses related to the incident, which required emergency repairs to a major piece of the city's wastewater infrastructure.

projects.name: I-95/I-295 Interchange Reconstruction (Jacksonville)
projects.description: The $177 million I-95/I-295 interchange reconstruction in North Jacksonville was supposed to finish in 2020 but won't be completed until 2026 due to cascading coordination failures.
projects.detail: The $176.8 million reconstruction project on the Interstate 95 and I-295 interchange in North Jacksonville started in 2016 to improve traffic flow, safety, and capacity. Originally planned for completion in 2020, the project has been delayed repeatedly and won't be done until 2026. Delays stem from multiple coordination challenges including CSX railroad requirements, workforce development issues, washouts, drainage problems that forced design changes to the interchange plan, and complications from supply chain hold-ups during the COVID-19 pandemic. The project's contractor, Archer Western, faced particular challenges working over and around the railroad corridor.

projects.name: N. Highland Lake Road Modernization (Flat Rock)
projects.description: NCDOT's road modernization project ballooned from $2.6 million to nearly $10 million after discovering an unmapped sewer line requiring complete redesign.
projects.detail: NCDOT's modernization project for 1.1 miles of North Highland Lake Road in Flat Rock started with an estimated cost of $2.6 million. After construction began in April 2023, the project was plagued by utility issues: material supply delays added 177 days, and then crews discovered a main sewer line that was not on existing plans, requiring a complete construction revision and redesign of the water and sewer infrastructure. Field conditions varied significantly from the engineering plans. The current estimated cost has soared to $9.97 million -- a 281% increase -- with $1.6 million for utility relocation and right-of-way and $6.7 million for construction. A local dermatologist was forced to close their practice due to prolonged road closures.

projects.name: Fayetteville Road Widening (Lumberton)
projects.description: NCDOT's $39 million Fayetteville Road widening project has experienced over 18 months of utility relocation work before road construction could begin.
projects.detail: The North Carolina Department of Transportation awarded a $39 million contract for the Fayetteville Road widening project in Lumberton, with construction expected to continue through 2030. Utility relocation work along the corridor has been underway for close to a year and a half, with lane closures required to facilitate the extensive underground infrastructure moves before road widening can commence. The project is part of a broader NCDOT challenge: the state has revised more than 1,000 separate estimates for right-of-way, utility, and construction costs in more than 450 transportation projects, with costs in some cases more than doubling from initial projections due to inflation.

projects.name: Lumos Fiber Columbia Utility Strikes
projects.description: Lumos Fiber's underground installation caused dozens of gas and water line strikes across Columbia, prompting fire department stop-work orders and city bans.
projects.detail: Lumos Fiber's underground fiber installation in Columbia, South Carolina triggered an unprecedented series of utility strikes in 2024-2025. The company hit at least two 6-inch water mains, caused half a dozen gas leaks requiring neighborhood evacuations in Elmwood Park, created a large sinkhole in the Murraywood subdivision, and broke five water mains in the Sandhills neighborhood. The Columbia-Richland Fire Department issued a stop-work order on November 14, 2024, with Fire Chief Aubrey Jenkins stating the department had never experienced a situation in which one company caused so many leaks in such a short time frame. Lexington County also issued a stop-work order after repeated water line strikes. Despite the bans, Lumos later resumed work in other areas and continued to cause utility damage.

projects.name: Kinetic Fiber Lexington Gas Line Strikes
projects.description: Kinetic Fiber Internet subcontractors struck multiple Dominion Energy gas lines in Lexington, causing a shelter-in-place order and prompting a citywide stop-work order.
projects.detail: On April 23, 2026, the Town of Lexington issued a stop-work order to Kinetic Fiber Internet after one of its subcontractors struck a city gas line while placing new fiber optic internet line underground. The incident followed a 2-inch gas main break in the Woodcreek neighborhood, which prompted a shelter-in-place for nearby residents and an emergency response along Ridgecreek Drive. The mayor noted that Kinetic Fiber has a history of violations in Lexington, including multiple prior Dominion Energy gas line strikes. The stop-work order remains in place pending a meeting between the Town of Lexington, Dominion Energy, and Lexington County Fire Service to address the recurring safety issues.

projects.name: Google Fiber S&N Communications Utility Damage (Georgia)
projects.description: Google Fiber contractor S&N Communications ruptured underground utility lines 36 times, triggering a Georgia Public Service Commission investigation and potential fines up to $10,000 per violation.
projects.detail: The Georgia Public Service Commission launched an investigation into S&N Communications, a contractor hired by Google Fiber to install underground fiber optic cables across the Atlanta metropolitan area. The contractor reported 36 incidents of damaging underground utility lines since July of the investigation year. The commission considered fines of up to $10,000 per violation for the repeated utility strikes. The incidents highlighted systemic failures in underground utility location and coordination during the rapid expansion of fiber broadband infrastructure across Georgia's suburban communities. The pattern of damage raised concerns about contractor oversight and the adequacy of existing utility mapping in fast-growing metro Atlanta corridors.

projects.name: Nashville 5-Year Paving Moratorium Program
projects.description: Nashville enacted a 5-year paving moratorium in 2022 after systematic utility cuts were destroying newly resurfaced roads across the city.
projects.detail: In June 2022, the Nashville Department of Transportation and Multimodal Infrastructure established a 5-year new pavement excavation moratorium on newly paved streets in direct response to the increase in pavement surface damage from utility companies' development and construction work throughout the city. Spot pavement cuts had damaged many roads, especially streets recently resurfaced as part of NDOT's paving program. The moratorium was established to minimize pavement degradation, increase the overall network condition rating, and maintain structural integrity of the city's road investments. Contractors performing utility or development work in the public right-of-way must obtain permits, and damage to pavement caused by permitted work is the contractor's responsibility to restore to Metro specifications.

projects.name: I-640 Reconstruction (Knoxville)
projects.description: The $21 million I-640 reconstruction project in Knoxville was delayed nine months due to added bridge repair work and coordination challenges with railroad infrastructure.
projects.detail: The I-640 reconstruction project in Knoxville, which started in July 2022, faced a nine-month delay when TDOT pushed the estimated completion date from late 2023 to August 31, 2024. The delay was caused by additional bridge repair work discovered during construction and winter weather constraints that limited the working season. Phase 2 of the reconstruction between I-275 and I-40 in northeast Knoxville required particular coordination with railroad infrastructure, as bridges over Rutledge Pike needed extensive coordination with the railroad and its consultants due to proximity to the Interstate 40 interchange. Rogers Group, the contractor, had to navigate complex scheduling around active rail operations while managing the expanded scope of bridge repairs.

projects.name: I-24/I-75 Interchange Reconstruction (Chattanooga)
projects.description: The $328 million I-24/I-75 interchange project in Chattanooga used design-build delivery combining utility relocation and construction, but still faced coordination challenges.
projects.detail: The two-phase I-24/I-75 split project in Chattanooga cost $328 million and used a design-build delivery method that combined regulatory permit approvals, utility relocation, and construction into a single contract. Despite this integrated approach, the project pushed past its completion timeline to spring 2026. Tennessee transportation officials cited challenges with the construction of a railroad overpass on the I-75 segment as a primary reason for delays, alongside the inherent complexities of coordinating numerous subcontractors and navigating environmental regulations. A ribbon-cutting ceremony was held in April 2026, marking the completion of one of the state's largest recent infrastructure investments.

projects.name: Sullivan Road Widening (Central, LA)
projects.description: Louisiana DOTD's Sullivan Road widening was crippled by utility companies failing to relocate water, gas, and electric lines on time, forcing removal of a planned roundabout to avoid four more years of delay.
projects.detail: The Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development began widening a mile-long stretch of Sullivan Road between Wax Road and Hooper Road from one lane to two lanes in each direction. The project was plagued by multiple coordination failures: utility companies did not relocate water, gas, and electric lines on time, meaning other contractors couldn't proceed with their work. Crews also found unexpected bad soil conditions and drainage issues. Multiple scope changes compounded the delays. DOTD ultimately removed a planned roundabout from the design because additional utility lines would need to be moved, which would have added up to four more years of delay. Crews went home in November, halting work entirely, and the project was eventually restructured as an East Baton Rouge Green Light Plan initiative.
projects.timeline: Started March 2022 (significant delays; roundabout deferred indefinitely)

projects.name: La. 98 Acadia Parish Utility Relocation Delay
projects.description: DOTD's $1.8 million construction project on La. 98 in Acadia Parish was rescheduled multiple times as utility relocation work extended past projected timelines.
projects.detail: A $1.8 million Louisiana Department of Transportation and Development construction project on LA 98 (West Jeff Davis Avenue) in Acadia Parish was repeatedly delayed by utility relocation issues. The project, involving grading, base course, milling, asphalt concrete overlay, and drainage structures, was originally scheduled to start on October 2, 2023, but was rescheduled to October 16 due to utility relocation delays. The eastbound lane had intermittent closures beginning September 12 for utility relocation work, with closures extended through November 10. The delays disrupted traffic patterns and local business access along the corridor between LA 35 and N Eastern Street.

projects.name: New Orleans Sewerage & Water Board Power Complex
projects.description: The New Orleans Sewerage & Water Board's $2 billion water system action plan reveals massive coordination failures between road construction and underground utility infrastructure across the city.
projects.detail: In March 2026, the New Orleans Sewerage & Water Board released a $2 billion water system action plan after the system became increasingly disrupted by pipe breaks, unfinished construction, and boil water advisories. The plan identified eight urgent risk transmission mains requiring about $27.5 million, of which only $10 million was currently available. The city demanded $87.5 million in repayment from the S&WB for roadwork the city had fronted on the utility's behalf, creating a financial crisis that threatened ongoing infrastructure projects. The S&WB's power complex construction was also delayed, compounding the agency's inability to maintain water pressure across the system while road construction projects simultaneously required utility relocations.

projects.name: Springdale Northern Bypass Phase 2 (Highway 612)
projects.description: ArDOT's $181 million Springdale Northern Bypass was delayed 13 months after complicated utility relocations by three separate utility companies created scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The Arkansas Department of Transportation changed the estimated completion date for phase two of the Springdale Northern Bypass from July 2026 to August 2027 -- a 13-month delay. The nearly 7-mile Highway 612 segment extends from U.S. Highway 412 to Arkansas Highway 112 in Tontitown. ArDOT communications division head Dave Parker confirmed that complicated utility relocations contributed to the delay, with Springdale Water Utilities, Black Hills Energy, and Ozarks Electric Cooperative Corp. each having infrastructure that needed to be moved. Columbia, Missouri-based contractor Emery Sapp & Sons was selected for the $180.78 million project, which started construction in spring 2024. ArDOT received a $24.46 million federal grant to help fund the phase.

projects.name: Biloxi Infrastructure Repair Program (Post-Katrina)
projects.description: Biloxi's $366 million post-Katrina infrastructure repair program faces a $111 million FEMA funding gap after the agency admitted it omitted key cost factors from its original estimate.
projects.detail: The City of Biloxi's infrastructure repair program, valued at $366 million, replaces water, sewer, and drainage lines across the city's aging systems. As of October 2025, over $318 million of work had been completed, but the city filed a second appeal with FEMA requesting an additional $111,159,912 in funding. FEMA acknowledged that costs for general conditions, contingencies, change orders, cost escalation, contractor overhead and profit, permitting, and other soft cost factors were 'inadvertently omitted from FEMA's original estimate.' Inflationary pressures further increased costs across all construction-related materials including fuel, labor, PVC pipe, concrete, and asphalt. The Mississippi congressional delegation backed Biloxi's funding request, with two remaining construction projects scheduled for completion by December 2025 and two more expected to be bid-ready by Q2 2026.
projects.timeline: Started July 2022 (West Biloxi phase); ongoing through 2026+

projects.name: West Alabama Corridor Project (Highway 43)
projects.description: ALDOT's planned 75-mile Highway 43 improvement ballooned from $800 million to potentially $1.1 billion, stalling $112 million in other road projects statewide.
projects.detail: The Alabama Department of Transportation presented a $74.9 million design-build contract for the initial stages of the West Alabama Corridor project, a proposed 75-mile, four-lane highway from Thomasville to Tuscaloosa along Alabama Highway 43. The overall project's estimated cost grew from roughly $800 million to potentially $1.1 billion -- a $300 million increase. State Senator Chris Elliott publicly expressed concern that 'this administration has a habit of getting started on a project that then goes wildly above budget.' The dispute over funding has stalled $112 million in other ALDOT projects across the state, as the use of federal funds on the West Alabama project means less money available for other improvements. The project also triggered 2026 legislation (HB 542) to authorize utility relocation reimbursements for large utilities affected by ALDOT road projects.

projects.name: Brent Spence Bridge Corridor Utility Relocations (Covington)
projects.description: The $4.39 billion Brent Spence Bridge Corridor project requires extensive utility relocation, stormwater separation, and sewer reconstruction in Covington before major bridge construction can begin.
projects.detail: The Brent Spence Bridge Corridor Project, a $4.39 billion infrastructure initiative jointly funded by Ohio, Kentucky, and federal sources spanning eight critical miles of I-71 and I-75, requires extensive early utility work before the new companion bridge can be built. On the Kentucky side in Covington, crews are performing utility relocation work, stormwater and sewer system separation projects in coordination with the city and Sanitation District No. 1 of Northern Kentucky. Sewer line and water line reconstruction on 3rd Street in Covington is underway, along with building demolitions and tree clearing. Utility relocation is expected to finish by late 2025, with major bridge construction beginning in 2026 and the new bridge opening targeted for 2031. The project has been discussed for decades and represents the region's most significant infrastructure investment since completion.
projects.timeline: Utility relocation through late 2025; bridge construction 2026-2031

projects.name: Charlotte Water Infrastructure Failures
projects.description: Charlotte's aging underground water infrastructure, with some cast iron pipes from the 1920s still in use, caused 35 water main breaks in a single day and construction crews discovering unmapped leaks under I-85.
projects.detail: Charlotte's aging underground water infrastructure has created cascading problems for road construction and daily operations. Some cast iron pipes from the 1920s and 1930s are still in use throughout the system. In February 2026, 35 water main breaks occurred between 8 a.m. Tuesday and 8 a.m. Wednesday following a historic snowstorm, flooding West Morehead Street and forcing road closures. In fall 2024, crews installing a new pipe under Interstate 85 discovered excessive water entering tunneling pits; investigations revealed two underground leaks and cracked asphalt, requiring at least a month of overnight I-85 lane closures for repairs. Charlotte Water crews were more than a week slower to fix leaks in 2025 compared to the prior year, while service requests increased by over 30%, highlighting the growing gap between infrastructure decay and repair capacity.

projects.name: Lexington County Lumos Fiber Sinkhole (Murraywood)
projects.description: Lumos Fiber subcontractors struck a water main in the Murraywood subdivision, creating a large sinkhole and triggering a Lexington County stop-work order banning fiber work countywide.
projects.detail: On September 11, 2024, subcontractors working for Lumos Fiber struck a water main line while doing underground work in the Murraywood subdivision of Irmo in Lexington County, creating a large sinkhole. The Lexington County Public Works Department determined it was 'of the best interest to cease work immediately in Lexington County due to the damages done' and issued a stop-work order halting all Lumos fiber installation countywide. The company had already been banned from working in the City of Columbia after causing half a dozen gas leaks and multiple water main breaks across the city. The repeated strikes highlighted a pattern of inadequate underground utility locating practices by fiber installation contractors in the rapidly growing Midlands region of South Carolina.

projects.name: Troy John R Road Gas Main Strike (Kroger Construction)
projects.description: Contractors building a Kroger gas station in Troy struck a Consumers Energy gas main, closing John R Road in both directions between Big Beaver and Maple roads for overnight repairs.
projects.detail: On October 28, 2025, a crew working at the site of a new Kroger gas station in Troy struck a natural gas main, closing John R Road in both directions between Big Beaver and Maple roads. Consumers Energy responded and crews worked through the night on repairs. By the next morning one lane was reopened in each direction. No injuries or evacuations were reported.

projects.name: Google Fiber Gas Line Strikes (Parkville/Shawnee, KS-MO)
projects.description: Three gas line strikes by Google Fiber contractors occurred across the Kansas-Missouri state line within 24 hours in August 2024, including one that caused a house explosion in Independence.
projects.detail: In August 2024, a cluster of gas line strikes by Google Fiber installation contractors occurred across the Kansas City metropolitan area. A gas line was hit in a Parkville, Missouri neighborhood while crews installed fiber, and nearly 24 hours earlier, part of a home exploded in Independence, Missouri after a Google Fiber contractor struck a gas line. Across the state line, another natural gas line was struck by a contractor in Shawnee, Kansas. Investigation found that the Google Fiber installer had contacted Missouri 811 before digging and there were no issues with the ticketing or notifications, but something went wrong during the construction process related to locating. The incidents fueled concerns about fiber installation safety across the metro area.

projects.name: UW-Madison East Campus Utility Project Unmapped Pipe Discovery
projects.description: The UW-Madison East Campus Utility Project was delayed after crews discovered unmapped underground pipes dating to 1892 that had no accurate plans, forcing a redesign of the excavation approach.
projects.detail: Construction crews working on the UW-Madison East Campus Utility Project since late May encountered a major setback due to numerous unforeseen conflicts with underground utility pipes that had been buried for over a century. Project manager Rob Kennedy of Facilities Planning and Management noted the older pipes 'were not expected to be there' and that some of the university's pipes are so old that accurate plans or mapping to indicate their locations simply did not exist. Crews were digging near an 1892 water main that bursts easily if uncovered, requiring extreme caution. The work was not completed by the target date of August 24, and contractors worked at full speed to finish before September 7, the day after Labor Day, to minimize impact on the academic calendar.

projects.name: Camby Indiana Home Explosion (Cable Boring Gas Line Strike)
projects.description: A cable company installer bored through an underground Vectren gas line in Camby, causing a house explosion that destroyed a two-story home and killed two family dogs.
projects.detail: An installer for a cable company bored through an underground Vectren natural gas line while working at a residence in the Heartland Crossing community of Camby, Indiana. The resulting gas buildup caused an explosion and fire that destroyed the two-story house and left neighboring homes uninhabitable. The family's two dogs were killed. The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission's Pipeline Safety Division investigation also revealed that Vectren had failed to timely locate its gas lines in at least 148 instances in 2016 and 162 instances in 2017, indicating a systemic failure to mark lines within the legally required two-day window. The IURC found the gas company bore responsibility for failing to properly mark infrastructure before excavation.

projects.name: Springfield Rail Improvements Water Main Relocation
projects.description: The Springfield Rail Improvements Project required $10.2 million in water main relocations and faced over a year of delay after being denied $138 million in federal funding.
projects.detail: The Springfield Rail Improvements Project, which relocates all passenger and freight rail traffic from the Third Street corridor to Tenth Street, required extensive utility relocations including a $4.8 million relocation of 2,000 feet of 24-inch water main on North Grand Avenue. Total City Water Light and Power investment for water infrastructure relocations and upgrades reached $10.2 million. The U.S. Department of Transportation denied a critical $138 million grant request needed to complete final portions of the project, delaying the originally-planned 2025 completion by more than a year. The multi-year project also required closure of Reservoir Street between 9th and 11th Streets for utility work.

projects.name: Dayton I-75 Reconstruction Unexpected Underground Discovery
projects.description: ODOT's $103 million I-75 reconstruction in Dayton was delayed a full year after discovering unexpected deep pavement and decades of buried repairs beneath the roadway.
projects.detail: The Ohio Department of Transportation's $103 million I-75 reconstruction north and south of downtown Dayton hit a significant setback when crews discovered multiple areas where the pavement thickness was deeper than anticipated, requiring substantial additional work. This marked the first time this section had been rebuilt to the base since its original installation in the late 1950s, and decades of projects and buried repairs under the roadway needed to be removed before constructing a new road. ODOT pushed the completion date from summer 2026 to summer 2027, as much of the additional work could not be performed during winter months. The project began in spring 2023 and involves full interstate reconstruction across multiple phases.

projects.name: MetroNet Fiber Gas Line Strikes (Fishers/Carmel, IN)
projects.description: MetroNet's fiber optic installation caused 20 gas line damage incidents in Fishers and Carmel, prompting an IURC investigation that found the company responsible for half the strikes.
projects.detail: The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission launched an investigation after 20 reports of damage to natural gas lines in Fishers and Carmel caused by MetroNet's fiber optic installation subcontractors. The IURC found MetroNet responsible for 10 of the 20 incidents, while Vectren (the gas line operator) was faulted in 6 cases for failing to properly mark gas lines. All six MetroNet subcontractors under investigation were from out of state, and only one had legally registered to do business in Indiana. Four subcontractors received warning letters and mandatory training, while International Inc. Corporation was assessed $13,500 in civil penalties. Vectren also received $6,000 in penalties. The investigation was referred to the Indiana Attorney General for further review of contractor registration violations.

projects.name: Melvindale Gas Main Rupture (Greenfield Road)
projects.description: A contractor performing underground work struck a DTE gas main in Melvindale, forcing road closures and business evacuations for up to four days while crews struggled to shut off the gas.
projects.detail: On January 12, 2024, a contractor performing underground work struck a gas main on Greenfield Road in Melvindale, Michigan. Police closed Greenfield Road between Allen Road and Schaefer Highway, and businesses in the area were evacuated as a precaution. DTE Energy crews had difficulty shutting off the gas main, with Mayor Nicole Shkira indicating DTE might not be able to turn off the gas until early the following Monday or Tuesday, potentially leaving the area disrupted for days. The incident disrupted traffic and commerce along one of Melvindale's major commercial corridors and highlighted the risks of construction activity near aging gas infrastructure.

projects.name: Alpena 2nd Avenue Road Reconstruction Gas Line Strike
projects.description: Construction crews on the $3.3 million 2nd Avenue road reconstruction in Alpena ruptured a large gas line during their first week of work, forcing evacuations and bridge closure.
projects.detail: During the first week of Alpena's nearly $3.3 million 2nd Avenue reconstruction, which replaces water and sewer infrastructure and rebuilds the street from Fletcher Street to Hueber Street, a miss dig by the construction company ruptured a three-to-four-inch gas line near 2nd Avenue and Fletcher Street. The fire department removed people near the site and the 2nd Avenue Bridge was closed during the response. DTE Energy crews capped the leak.
projects.timeline: Construction began late April 2024; incident first week (May 1, 2024)

projects.name: Sebring Fiber Optic Gas Line Double Strike
projects.description: Fiber optic installation crews in Sebring struck two gas lines simultaneously, forcing the evacuation of nearly two blocks of homes as a thunderstorm threatened to ignite the leaked gas.
projects.detail: In Sebring, Ohio, a contractor installing fiber optic cable struck a gas line in an alley, resulting in two separate leaks that could be seen, heard, and smelled by residents. Nearly two blocks along Oregon Street between 12th and 15th Streets were evacuated as a precaution. The situation was complicated by an approaching thunderstorm with lightning that threatened to ignite the escaped gas. All of Sebring lost power after the storm moved through. Incoming city manager Chris Frazer described it as 'just a freak accident where a contractor was digging, and they hit a gas line in one of the alleys.' There were no injuries reported.

projects.name: Leetonia OmniFiber Gas Line Strike and Evacuation
projects.description: OmniFiber contractors struck a Columbia Gas line in Leetonia, forcing a 500-foot-radius evacuation as gas backed up into the sewer system and cutting service to 250 customers.
projects.detail: Third-party contractors installing fiber optic internet for OmniFiber in Leetonia, Ohio struck a Columbia Gas line near the intersection of Lisbon and Somer Streets. The gas leak was severe enough to back up into the sewer system, prompting firefighters to evacuate homes within a 500-foot radius. Columbia Gas crews sealed the leak by 8 p.m. that evening, but approximately 250 customers lost gas service. Before residents could return, firefighters checked 32 homes on Somer Street to ensure indoor gas levels were at zero. As of the following afternoon, 70 customers—mostly in neighboring Washingtonville—still lacked service. The assistant fire chief described it as 'worst scenario with best outcome.'

projects.name: Columbus North Market Gas Line Strike Evacuation
projects.description: A construction crew struck a gas line near Columbus' North Market, forcing the evacuation of 800-1,000 people from the market and nearby businesses.
projects.detail: In April 2026, a construction crew working near the Merchant Tower building at the intersection of Park and Vine streets in downtown Columbus struck a Columbia Gas line, triggering a major emergency response. The Columbus Division of Fire evacuated between 800 and 1,000 people from the nearby North Market and surrounding businesses. The leak was contained about an hour later, but North Market remained closed for the rest of the day while Columbia Gas and AEP Ohio worked repairs. The incident disrupted one of downtown Columbus' busiest commercial areas and highlighted the risks of construction activity in dense urban environments with complex underground utility networks.

projects.name: MUD Florence Water Plant Pipeline Rupture (Omaha)
projects.description: A Hawkins Construction excavator ruptured a pressurized water pipeline at Omaha's Florence Water Treatment Plant, releasing 14 million gallons of water and prompting a $5 million+ lawsuit.
projects.detail: On July 25, 2023, a Hawkins Construction excavator performing a capital improvement project at the Metropolitan Utilities District's Florence Water Treatment Plant struck a pressurized water pipeline, causing a catastrophic rupture. Over 14 million gallons of water were released in just two hours, damaging MUD's facility and equipment and forcing a full plant shutdown. MUD filed a lawsuit in Douglas County District Court alleging Hawkins Construction failed to take required steps to ensure its excavation would not damage the pipe. The utility sought more than $5 million in damages. The case proceeded to arguments over the legal doctrine of res ipsa loquitur—whether the rupture itself proved negligence.

projects.name: Plainfield Township DTE Gas Line Rupture (Grand Rapids Area)
projects.description: A third-party construction crew ruptured a DTE Energy gas line on Plainfield Avenue, forcing half-mile-radius evacuations including homes, businesses, and a library branch.
projects.detail: On September 16, 2025, around 8:20 a.m., a third-party construction crew struck a DTE Energy gas line under a service drive across from 5 Mile Road off Plainfield Avenue in Plainfield Township, Kent County. Businesses and homes within about a half-mile were evacuated, including the Kent District Library's Plainfield Township branch, and Northview High School and North Oakview Elementary sheltered in place. DTE sealed the leak and Plainfield Avenue reopened after several hours. No injuries were reported.

projects.name: Escanaba Gas Line Damage (North Lincoln Road)
projects.description: A third-party construction crew damaged a DTE natural gas service line in Escanaba, closing a portion of North Lincoln Road near two gas stations.
projects.detail: On the evening of May 16, 2023, a third-party construction crew damaged a DTE natural gas service line in Escanaba, causing a leak that temporarily closed a portion of North Lincoln Road near the Marathon and Holiday gas stations. DTE crews responded, and one home was temporarily without natural gas service.

projects.name: Geneva East State Street Utility Relocation Bottleneck
projects.description: Five utility companies must sequentially relocate underground infrastructure on East State Street before IDOT road construction can begin, creating a 6-8 month pre-construction bottleneck.
projects.detail: The Illinois Department of Transportation's East State Street (Route 38) reconstruction in Geneva required five utility companies—Verizon, AT&T, Comcast, Nicor Gas, and Metronet—to relocate their underground infrastructure before road construction could begin. AT&T started relocation in August 2025, with Verizon and Nicor Gas following in September. Comcast and Metronet still needed to perform similar work. The sequential nature of utility relocations created a 6-to-8-month bottleneck, potentially longer, pushing the full road reconstruction to Spring 2026 at the earliest with completion in late 2027. The project encompasses roadway widening, bike lanes, traffic signal upgrades, new lighting, and water main and storm drainage improvements.

projects.name: Sellersburg Fiber Installation Utility Line Strikes (IN)
projects.description: Fiber optic installation by Lumos/T-Mobile contractors in Sellersburg repeatedly struck gas and water lines, cutting service to 200 customers and forcing traffic diversions on State Road 60.
projects.detail: Contractors installing fiber optic lines for T-Mobile and Lumos in Sellersburg, Indiana's Yorktown Park subdivision caused repeated utility line strikes that angered residents. In one incident, crews hit a main gas line while digging, causing a gas leak that shut off service for approximately 200 customers and forced traffic on State Road 60 to be diverted. Residents reported that 'every time Lumos or T-Mobile fiber comes into a neighborhood, gas lines get cut, water lines get cut.' The repeated strikes tore up lawns and created muddy conditions throughout the subdivision. Residents were advised to file complaints through Access Indiana regarding the pattern of utility damage.

projects.name: Iowa City Court Street Reconstruction Utility Conflicts
projects.description: Private utility conflicts on the $10 million Court Street reconstruction in Iowa City prevented completion to Wales Street, pushing the project into the 2026 construction season.
projects.detail: Iowa City's nearly $10 million Court Street reconstruction project, running from Muscatine Avenue to South First Avenue, encountered private utility conflicts that disrupted the planned construction schedule. The conflicts prevented crews from completing work to Wales Street as originally planned, with paving and utility installations reaching only through Seventh Avenue. The remaining work was rescheduled for the 2026 construction season, adding a full year to the project timeline. Crews had to complete a joint utility trench and underground private utility lines, coordinating work among multiple providers. City officials noted construction was expected to reach South Seventh Avenue by end of 2025 season, weather permitting.

projects.name: Wichita 143rd Street East KDOT Coordination Overrun
projects.description: The sole bid for Wichita's 143rd Street East project came in at $14.2 million—$5.8 million over the engineer's estimate—because coordination complexity with KDOT's East Kellogg Project deterred all other bidders.
projects.detail: Wichita's 143rd Street East project from Kellogg to Harry Street received only one bid at $14.2 million, approximately $5.8 million over the engineer's estimate of $8.4 million and $3.92 million over the council-approved budget of $8.97 million. The primary deterrent to bidding, according to contractors who declined, was the coordination complexity with KDOT's concurrent East Kellogg Expansion Project. Mayor Wu pulled the item citing concerns about both the cost overrun and single-bidder situation. When asked about delaying the project, contractors said they still would not bid due to ongoing KDOT coordination concerns. The Wichita City Council ultimately approved the project in March 2026 with Wildcat Construction Co. as contractor.

projects.name: Brent Spence Bridge Corridor Utility Relocations
projects.description: The $4 billion Brent Spence Bridge Corridor project requires extensive utility relocations on both the Ohio and Kentucky sides, with utility work among the first major construction activities.
projects.detail: The Brent Spence Bridge Corridor Project, connecting Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky with a companion bridge alongside the existing structure, carries a total estimated cost of $4.05 billion. Utility relocation is among the earliest and most complex construction activities, with work on the Kentucky side involving coordination with the city of Covington and Sanitation District No. 1 of Northern Kentucky for stormwater and sewer system separation. On the Ohio side, significant utility relocation is required through dense urban infrastructure. Utility relocation was targeted for completion by late 2025, but the phased approach means coordination between utilities, ODOT, KYTC, and multiple municipalities will continue through the project's duration, with the companion bridge expected to open in 2031 and approach work completed by 2033.

projects.name: Columbus I-70/I-71 Downtown Ramp Up Utility Conflicts
projects.description: The I-70/I-71 Downtown Ramp Up in Columbus expanded from a planned completion in the mid-2020s to the 2030s, with utility conflicts among the underground challenges encountered during the $1.4 billion reconstruction.
projects.detail: The Downtown Ramp Up is a series of projects to reconstruct Interstates 70/71 through downtown Columbus, addressing safety and congestion problems. Construction began in 2010 with an expected completion well before 2030 and a total budget of $1.4 billion. The project has since extended into the 2030s due to the complexity of widening and reconstructing the roadway, replacing bridges, and rebuilding ramps through downtown's dense underground infrastructure. A single phase from Spring 2022 to Fall 2026 alone cost $280 million. Multiple construction closures have been postponed due to complications including utility relocations, weather delays, and the discovery of subsurface conditions requiring additional work.

projects.name: Peoples Gas Chicago Neighborhood Road Destruction
projects.description: Peoples Gas pipe replacement crews left open trenches, metal plates, and gaping holes across Chicago streets and sidewalks, repeatedly cutting into recently paved roads with minimal coordination.
projects.detail: Peoples Gas's $11 billion System Modernization Program has caused widespread pavement destruction across Chicago neighborhoods as crews replace aging cast iron gas pipes. Residents reported crews showing up for a few hours each day, breaking holes in roads, and covering them with metal plates that created hazardous driving conditions. Streets became completely impassable during busy hours without proper road closures, forcing drivers to back up onto adjacent avenues. The ICC found that open trenches, exposed pipes, and gaping holes in streets and sidewalks were scattered across neighborhoods when the program was paused in November 2023. Nearly $47 million of paused work involved completing pipeline replacement where open trenches and exposed pipes remained unfinished. The pattern of road damage without adequate restoration constituted ongoing violations of pavement integrity standards across the city.

projects.name: Kansas City Infrastructure Bond Program Failures
projects.description: Kansas City council members called the city's $800 million infrastructure bond program 'an absolute failure,' with funds being spent at an unsustainable rate that would exhaust the 20-year program in 15 years.
projects.detail: Kansas City councilmembers blasted the city's infrastructure improvement program as 'an absolute failure,' citing wasted millions and poor coordination between utility companies and road projects. Voters approved $800 million in general obligation bonds in 2017 to be spread over two decades for infrastructure repairs, but the city council distributed funds at a rate that would exhaust the program in approximately 15 years. The city's Utility Liaison Coordination Committee holds monthly meetings with utility companies to discuss active and future work, and the annual Street Preservation list is shared in early spring, yet coordination failures continued. When conflicts between utility work and road resurfacing could not be resolved, Public Works typically delayed street resurfacing to avoid utility cuts on freshly resurfaced roads, further pushing back needed repairs.

projects.name: Fairdale Indiana Fiber Optic Gas Main Strike
projects.description: Fiber optic installation crews struck a six-inch main gas line in a Fairdale neighborhood, part of a pattern of gas line damage by a company already hit with stop-work orders in Indiana.
projects.detail: In Fairdale, Indiana, crews installing fiber optic cable hit a six-inch main gas line in a neighborhood near Piroutette Avenue at Sissone Drive. The incident was linked to a fiber optic company that had already been hit with stop-work orders in Indiana due to repeated utility damage. The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission investigated, noting that thousands of gas lines are damaged every year in Indiana during construction activity. The incident highlighted the recurring conflict between the rapid expansion of fiber optic networks and the safety of existing underground gas infrastructure, particularly when out-of-state contractors unfamiliar with local utility layouts perform the installation work.

projects.name: East Kellogg Expansion Utility Coordination Impact (Wichita)
projects.description: KDOT's $288 million East Kellogg expansion project in Wichita requires extensive utility relocation across 26 bridges and 32 retaining walls, creating coordination complexity that deterred contractors from bidding on adjacent projects.
projects.detail: The Kansas Department of Transportation awarded its largest-ever single contract at $287.97 million to rebuild U.S. Highway 54/Kellogg Avenue and Kansas Highway 96 in east Wichita. The massive project includes 26 bridge replacements, 32 new retaining walls, and two-lane frontage roads. The project's extensive utility relocation requirements created such coordination complexity that contractors refused to bid on adjacent local road projects, including Wichita's 143rd Street East project, citing the impossibility of managing work alongside the massive KDOT undertaking. Businesses along the corridor expressed concerns about surviving years of construction disruption. The project began in March 2026 and represents a cornerstone of the state's IKE transportation investment program.

projects.name: South Alamo Street Reconstruction (San Antonio)
projects.description: The 2017 bond-funded rebuild of South Alamo Street from Market Street to East César E. Chávez Boulevard climbed from a $36.6M estimate at its 2021 start to about $48M amid a City–SAWS dispute over century-old water and sewer mains.
projects.detail: Voters approved South Alamo Street improvements in the 2017 bond program at an estimated $9 million; by the time work started in 2021 the estimate was $36.6 million, and about $48 million had been spent by mid-2025. In 2024 the City and the San Antonio Water System deadlocked over who would pay to replace century-old water and sewer mains slated for replacement during the project. The two signed a new agreement in January 2025 governing how they work together on joint construction. In June 2025 City Council unanimously amended Sundt Construction's $50 million contract by $7.6 million, with completion expected in spring 2026.

projects.name: Zona Cultural District Road Reconstruction (San Antonio)
projects.description: Road reconstruction on Commerce, San Saba and Santa Rosa streets in San Antonio's Zona Cultural district was delayed by unforeseen utility conflicts and archaeological constraints, requiring a $2.7M contract amendment.
projects.detail: Work on the Zona Cultural streets (Commerce, San Saba and Santa Rosa) began in January 2022 under a $37.7 million contract with Sundt Construction. The City said the project was delayed by unforeseen utility conflicts, and added archaeological constraints also changed the scope. In June 2025 City Council added $2.7 million to the contract, alongside $7.6 million for the adjacent South Alamo Street project. Completion was then expected in fall 2025.

projects.name: West Side Military Drive Road Project (San Antonio)
projects.description: A $9.3M Military Drive road project on San Antonio's far west side ran about a year behind schedule and roughly $640K–$660K over budget, mainly because SAWS and CPS Energy changed their utility scopes, plus the discovery of caves.
projects.detail: The Military Drive project near the Villages of West Creek neighborhood, overseen by Bexar County and the Alamo Regional Mobility Authority, began in November 2022 with completion promised by March 2024; by April 2025 the target had moved to late May 2025. Officials said the main delay was utility challenges, with SAWS and CPS Energy returning to the Alamo RMA board with changes in their scope. The unexpected utility work cost an additional $640,000 on top of the $9.3 million project, to be paid by SAWS and CPS Energy. Crews also uncovered caves that required environmental reviews and tests to ensure sinkholes would not form beneath the roadway. A 52-year-old worker was fatally struck by a steel pipe on the site in 2023, prompting an OSHA investigation.
projects.timeline: November 2022 start → March 2024 planned → late May 2025 expected

projects.name: Sandman Hotel Gas Line Explosion (Fort Worth)
projects.description: A construction contractor struck a gas line during basement restaurant work at the historic W.T. Waggoner Building in downtown Fort Worth, causing a massive explosion that injured 21 people and shattered windows seven blocks away.
projects.detail: On January 8, 2024, a construction contractor struck a gas line while working on a basement-level restaurant at the Sandman Signature Fort Worth Downtown Hotel, housed in the historic 20-story W.T. Waggoner Building at 810 Houston Street. The resulting explosion blew out the two bottom floors of the building, injured 21 people (one critically, two seriously), and shattered windows up to seven blocks away. Debris including drywall, wood, insulation, glass, and metal was scattered hundreds of feet. The hotel had only opened in March 2023 after a major renovation. The ATF and Fort Worth Fire Department investigated the incident.

projects.name: Old Jacksonville Highway Widening (Tyler/Bullard)
projects.overbudgetAbs: $10.2 million paid for 41 days of work
projects.description: A $225 million TxDOT highway widening project in East Texas was paralyzed by utility relocation delays involving nine utility companies, costing taxpayers $4,500 per day while the contractor sat idle.
projects.detail: TxDOT's project to widen and reconstruct Old Jacksonville Highway from Loop 323 south to FM 2813 in Bullard, originally budgeted at approximately $225 million, has been devastated by utility coordination failures. Nine utility companies needed to relocate infrastructure out of the right-of-way, but the work stalled as companies waited on each other to complete sequential relocations. Contractor Longview Bridge & Road worked only 41 days since July 2023 yet was paid $10.2 million by TxDOT, including 'project overhead' at $4,542.08 per day. The contractor was also the victim of a ransomware attack that held all project and accounting files hostage. The project's start date has been pushed back to 2030, and local businesses like Bernards have closed, blaming TxDOT for the delays and roadblocks that drove away customers.

projects.name: Katy Fiber Optic Water Line Moratorium
projects.description: Sixteen water line ruptures in six months by fiber optic installers forced Katy, Texas to impose a 120-day moratorium on underground fiber construction, with one utility district suing for $70,000 in damages.
projects.detail: Between October 2024 and March 2025, fiber optic installation companies caused 16 separate incidents involving city water lines in Katy, Texas. The damage was so severe that the Katy City Council unanimously voted to implement a 120-day moratorium on below-ground fiber-optic installation projects. West Harris County Municipal Utility District No. 2 filed a lawsuit against Ezee Fiber Texas for $70,000 after the company allegedly bored through water mains on July 15 and July 17, forcing 1,150 homes to lose water access and prompting a boil water notice. The city lacked an ordinance regulating fiber installation, allowing companies to excavate in residential easements without proper knowledge of underground water line locations. Ezee Fiber also broke a water line serving Exley Elementary School.

projects.name: Spicewood Springs Road Widening Water Main Strike (Austin)
projects.description: A contractor widening Spicewood Springs Road struck a 48-inch water main, launching a geyser 50 feet over treetops and draining 16 million gallons of treated water into a ravine, killing 100 fish.
projects.detail: On September 23, 2024, a contractor working on the $34.18 million Spicewood Springs Road widening project struck a 48-inch water main pipeline near Loop 360 in northwest Austin. The break launched a geyser 50 feet over treetops that sprayed for approximately 45 minutes before crews could shut off the water. More than 16 million gallons of treated water drained into a ravine, and around 100 dead fish were discovered in the aftermath. Road closures remained in effect for days as Austin Water worked on repairs, which took five days to complete. The project, funded by the 2016 mobility bond, aims to widen the two-lane road to four lanes with pedestrian improvements and upgraded water systems. Construction, which broke ground in December 2023, is now expected to continue into 2026.

projects.name: Houston I-45 NHHIP Utility Coordination (Segments 3B)
projects.description: TxDOT's $7.9 billion North Houston Highway Improvement Project faces massive utility relocation requirements as it sinks I-69 into a trench and reconstructs I-45, with weather and utility coordination influencing construction sequencing.
projects.detail: The North Houston Highway Improvement Project (NHHIP) is TxDOT's $7.9 billion redesign of I-45 in three segments from US 59 to Beltway 8 North. The project requires extensive utility relocation as it sinks the existing I-69 elevated freeway into a depressed trench through Midtown. Segment 3B-1, budgeted at $121 million, began construction in January 2025, with Segment 3B-2 starting in January 2026. TxDOT acknowledges that weather, utility relocations, material availability, and coordination with adjacent work can all influence the order of construction activities. The Houston utility relocation ordinance program adds another layer of coordination, requiring the city and TxDOT to work together on relocating utilities within public rights-of-way. The project's sheer scale and urban density make utility coordination one of its most significant ongoing risks.

projects.name: Waxahachie Saddlebrook Estates Gas Explosion (Fiber Installation)
projects.description: A fiber optic contractor struck an Atmos Energy gas line in Waxahachie's Saddlebrook Estates subdivision, leading to a home explosion that destroyed four homes, damaged seven others, and severely burned two residents.
projects.detail: On September 21, 2015, Circle L Construction, a subcontractor laying fiber optic lines for AT&T in Waxahachie's Saddlebrook Estates subdivision, struck an Atmos Energy gas line. Gas service to the neighborhood was disrupted for four days before Adele Chavez and her brother Jamie Rodriguez were severely burned when their home on Arabian Road exploded after Chavez turned on her stove. Four homes were total losses and seven others were significantly damaged. Twenty Waxahachie homeowners filed a lawsuit against Atmos Energy, alleging the utility failed to act on reports of the severed gas line. The Texas Railroad Commission, Waxahachie Fire Marshal, and Atmos Energy all investigated. A settlement was eventually reached with AT&T and Circle L Construction.

projects.name: Arlington Collins Street Gas Line Explosion (Near AT&T Stadium)
projects.description: A construction crew drilling at a site near AT&T Stadium in Arlington hit a gas line, causing an explosion and fire that forced the closure of Collins Street and required emergency gas line shutdown.
projects.detail: A construction crew drilling at a site in the 800 block of North Collins Street in Arlington, just across from AT&T Stadium where the Dallas Cowboys play, struck a gas line causing an explosion and fire. The equipment operator smelled gas and ran away from the truck moments before the explosion. Collins Street was closed from Division Street to Randol Mill Road as natural gas crews dug several hundred feet from the cut gas line to locate a cutoff valve. No injuries were reported, but the incident highlighted the risks of construction excavation near major gas infrastructure in a densely developed entertainment district.

projects.name: El Paso Coronado Hills AT&T Fiber Utility Damage
projects.description: AT&T fiber optic installation in El Paso's Coronado Hills neighborhood damaged virtually every utility in the area -- water, sewage, electric, gas, and cable TV systems -- causing prolonged disruption.
projects.detail: AT&T fiber optics installation crews working on Somerset Drive in El Paso's Coronado Hills neighborhood caused extensive damage to virtually every type of underground utility during installation work beginning in November 2017. Water lines, sewage pipes, electric lines, gas lines, and existing cable TV systems were all damaged. In one case, a subcontractor's fiber optic installation pierced through a sewer pipe, causing blockages and forcing a homeowner to hire a lawyer to obtain reimbursement from AT&T. Multiple residents reported ongoing property damage and utility service disruptions. AT&T stated its goal was to minimize impact on residents, and in some cases reimbursed affected families, but the damage pattern revealed a systemic failure to properly locate and avoid existing underground utilities.

projects.name: FM 2100 Widening (North Harris County)
projects.description: TxDOT assessed $758,870 in liquidated damages on the FM 2100 widening project in North Harris County due to construction delays, then credited $310,800 back to the contractor citing utility relocation issues.
projects.detail: The FM 2100 widening project in North Harris County experienced significant construction delays tied to utility relocation coordination failures. TxDOT assessed $758,870 in liquidated damages against the contractor for the delays, but subsequently credited $310,800 back after the contractor argued delays were beyond their control due to utility line relocation issues. This project was cited in a broader KHOU investigation revealing that TxDOT statewide assessed $88 million in liquidated damages over three years but credited $39 million (44%) back to contractors, often because utility relocation problems were the root cause of delays.

projects.name: FM 1960 Widening (Lake Houston Area)
projects.description: TxDOT's $128 million FM 1960 widening project in the Lake Houston area was delayed by utility relocation challenges and contaminated soil discovery, pushing completion well beyond the original schedule.
projects.detail: TxDOT's two-segment Farm-to-Market 1960 widening project in the Lake Houston area, budgeted at $128 million, was significantly delayed by utility relocation challenges and discovery of contaminated soil. The project to widen the roadway from 4 to 6 lanes with a new overpass bridge faced sequential utility coordination problems. Construction that was originally set to begin in late 2021 was pushed to late 2022 in the Willowbrook area segment alone. The project was still nearing completion as of April 2026, years behind the original timeline. The delays impacted commuters along one of Houston's most heavily traveled corridors.

projects.name: Houston Downtown Water Main Strike (Fannin & Franklin)
projects.description: A contractor hit a 12-inch water main in downtown Houston, flooding the intersection of Fannin and Franklin streets for hours and threatening water service to the Harris County Jail.
projects.detail: On December 2, 2024, a construction contractor struck and seriously damaged a 12-inch water main in downtown Houston, flooding the intersection of Fannin and Franklin streets for several hours. The leak, which started around midday, was not fully repaired until late that night. Houston Public Works had to reroute water lines to ensure the Harris County Jail maintained water service during the repairs. While no buildings or vehicles flooded, the incident disrupted downtown traffic and operations for an extended period. The strike highlighted the risks of construction excavation in Houston's dense downtown utility corridor.

projects.name: Norman Indian Hills Turnpike Water Well Relocation (OK)
projects.description: The Oklahoma Turnpike Authority's Indian Hills roadway project required relocating four city water wells and 20,000 linear feet of water lines, costing $8.9 million and delaying council approval amid community opposition.
projects.detail: The Oklahoma Turnpike Authority's east-west connector through Norman required relocating four of the city's groundwater wells and approximately 20,000 linear feet of water lines between 48th Avenue NW and 24th Avenue NW. Under the utility-relocation agreement, the OTA committed $8.9 million for well relocation while Norman would spend $1.9 million for water line relocation. The total project package of $31.4 million from OTA and $4.9 million from the city included widening 36th Avenue NW and stormwater drainage. The Norman City Council delayed the vote for two weeks amid community opposition over flooding concerns, environmental impacts, and drinking water contamination fears before voting 7-2 to approve in March 2026.

projects.name: Spectrum Fiber Property Damage (Round Rock/Leander)
projects.description: Spectrum fiber optic installation crews in Williamson County damaged sewer lines, sprinkler systems, and gas lines across Round Rock and Leander neighborhoods, with one home flooded with sewage.
projects.detail: In 2023-2024, Spectrum crews installing fiber optic lines in Williamson County caused widespread property damage across Round Rock and Leander neighborhoods. In the Parkside at Mayfield Ranch community, contractors using ditch witch equipment hit a sewer line, flooding the first floor of one home with sewage water. Homeowner Ryan Ford in Leander reported repeated sprinkler line breaks beginning in December 2023. In another incident, Spectrum damaged a gas line in the public right of way, and the crew immediately called 911. Despite residents' complaints, the city said it only permits work within an easement and does not have authority to take action against a utility provider for damage. Spectrum maintained it had the required city and county permits for all work.

projects.name: US-87/FM-41 Bridge Project (South Lubbock County)
projects.description: A $21.6 million TxDOT bridge project south of Lubbock stalled for years after the original contractor was declared in default, with utility coordination issues and design errors contributing to the collapse.
projects.detail: TxDOT's $21.6 million project to reconstruct the U.S. Highway 87 and Farm-to-Market Road 41 intersection south of Lubbock, including a new bridge, entrance and exit ramps, and safety lighting, was thrown into chaos when contractor Allen Butler Construction abruptly stopped work in December 2022. The contractor was declared in default in July 2023, blaming significant rainfall, flooding, and multiple design errors. The project sat idle for years while a replacement contractor was found.
