TxDOT awarded a new contract to Webber Construction LLC, with construction restarting in April 2026 and a new completion date of late 2027 -- three years past the original October 2024 target. Local business Bernards permanently closed, blaming the project delays.

projects.name: TxDOT Statewide Utility Delay Liquidated Damages
projects.overbudgetAbs: $88 million in liquidated damages assessed (44% credited back)
projects.description: A KHOU investigation found TxDOT assessed $88 million in liquidated damages over three years but credited $39 million (44%) back to contractors, largely because utility relocation failures caused the delays.
projects.detail: An investigation by KHOU revealed that the Texas Department of Transportation assessed $88 million in liquidated damages against contractors statewide over a three-year period for road construction delays. However, TxDOT credited $39 million -- 44% of the total -- back to contractors who disputed the penalties. Contractors routinely argued that delays were beyond their control due to utility line relocation failures and poor coordination between utility companies and TxDOT. Notable examples included FM 2100 in North Harris County ($758,870 assessed, $310,800 credited back) and State Loop 494 in Montgomery County ($475,450 assessed, $470,310 credited back -- nearly the full amount). The pattern revealed systemic utility coordination failures costing Texas taxpayers tens of millions.

projects.name: Google Fiber Austin Utility Damage Campaign
projects.description: Google Fiber installation in Austin generated 254 complaints in one year, including broken gas and water lines and a major flood caused when contractors blocked storm drains, resulting in $760,000 in damages.
projects.detail: Google Fiber's network installation across Austin generated 254 complaints in 2015 alone, including reports of broken gas and water lines, landscape and property damage, and construction materials obstructing sidewalks. In one notable incident, contractors laying fiber cables blocked off storm drains during an October flood event, resulting in an estimated $760,000 in damages to surrounding properties. The city struggled to regulate the rapid installation pace as Google Fiber contractors operated across multiple neighborhoods simultaneously. The damage pattern underscored the risks of large-scale underground utility installation without adequate coordination with existing infrastructure.

projects.name: Oklahoma City MAPS 4 Construction Cost Escalation
projects.description: Oklahoma City padded MAPS 4 budgets with additional contingency as construction costs climbed, forcing planners to break large utility-heavy projects into smaller bid packages to attract contractors.
projects.detail: Oklahoma City's MAPS 4 capital improvement program, which includes a multipurpose stadium, mental health crisis center, and Family Justice Center, has faced rising costs forcing the city to add contingency to project budgets. Program managers and local outlets pointed to pandemic-era inflation and a tight subcontractor market as recurring headwinds. Planners adjusted construction phasing and bid packaging, breaking big jobs into smaller pieces to widen the bidder pool and avoid getting stuck in repeat bid cycles. Underground utility work in downtown and Midtown areas has added complexity to projects with aging infrastructure. City materials show roughly $44.6 million set aside for Mental Health and about $42 million for the Family Justice Center, with contingency additions across the board.

projects.name: Improve Our Tulsa Street Program Utility Delays
projects.description: Tulsa's $79.7 million Improve Our Tulsa bond program suffered widespread delays across multiple street projects due to utility relocation taking up to 18 months per project.
projects.detail: The City of Tulsa's Improve Our Tulsa capital improvement program, including a $79.7 million bond for street projects, has experienced widespread delays driven by utility relocation challenges. City staff briefed the Budget and Special Projects Committee in April 2025 that utility relocations were causing long delays across many street and infrastructure projects. Some projects required utility relocation taking up to 18 months depending on the scope of relocations needed and the workload of utility companies. Inflation and supply chain issues compounded the delays, making every line item in the bond program more expensive. The city acknowledged that projects are scheduled based on multiple factors including utility coordination, and that some cannot advertise for bids until right-of-way acquisition and utility relocations are completed.
projects.timeline: Ongoing; delays of up to 18 months per project

projects.name: ODOT Green Country Highway Projects Cost Escalation
projects.description: Rising costs and utility relocation challenges delayed multiple ODOT highway projects across Green Country (northeast Oklahoma), forcing project reprioritization and timeline extensions.
projects.detail: The Oklahoma Department of Transportation delayed multiple highway projects across Green Country -- the northeast Oklahoma region centered on Tulsa -- due to rising construction costs and utility relocation challenges. The delays affected projects in the $670 million eight-year Tulsa County construction work plan. Utility relocation work, which is often a prerequisite before road construction can begin, added time and cost pressure to already strained budgets. ODOT acknowledged that everything in their bond programs had become more expensive, with utility relocation being a recurring bottleneck that pushed project timelines beyond original estimates.

projects.name: 30 Crossing I-30 Corridor (Little Rock)
projects.description: Arkansas's largest-ever highway project to widen I-30 through Little Rock ballooned from $650 million to nearly $1 billion, with an unexpected sewer line location forcing the first-ever use of foam glass aggregate backfill.
projects.detail: The 30 Crossing project to widen 7.3 miles of I-30 through Little Rock and North Little Rock was ARDOT's first billion-dollar project and first design-build project. Originally estimated at $650 million, costs ballooned to nearly $1 billion. During construction, an existing sanitary sewer line was discovered running under a proposed embankment at the I-30/I-40 interchange. The project team was concerned the embankment could settle onto the utility, requiring an innovative solution: the contractor used ultra-lightweight foam glass aggregate as backfill material over the sanitary line to minimize load -- the first time ARDOT had ever employed this technique. Phase 1 wrapped up in late 2024 with a $634 million price tag for the 6.7-mile stretch from I-530 in Little Rock to I-40 in North Little Rock.

projects.name: Highway 112 Widening Utility Relocation (Fayetteville to Bentonville)
projects.overbudgetAbs: $200 million in utility/ROW costs on top of $500M construction
projects.description: The $500 million Arkansas Highway 112 widening between Fayetteville and Bentonville requires $200 million in additional utility relocation and right-of-way costs, with the first segment alone needing $11.6 million in water/sewer relocation.
projects.detail: ARDOT's project to widen Arkansas Highway 112 from two to four lanes over 18 miles between Fayetteville and Bentonville carries an estimated construction cost of $500 million. However, when right-of-way acquisition and utility relocation are included, the total rises to $700 million -- an additional $200 million (40%) for utility-related work. The first segment alone costs $43.94 million, with $11.6 million designated for relocating city water and sewer infrastructure. Newly constructed and relocated utilities include approximately 5,100 linear feet of 8-inch and smaller water/sewer mains, 8,700 linear feet of 12-inch waterlines, and 2,900 linear feet of 36-inch waterline. Construction on the first segment began in late 2025 and is expected to take approximately 21 months.

projects.name: Highway 5 Widening (Saline County)
projects.description: ARDOT's $22.5 million Highway 5 widening in Saline County was delayed several months past its completion date due to utility relocation red tape that an official called 'the red tape of any project.'
projects.detail: ARDOT's $22.5 million project to widen Highway 5 in Saline County, awarded to Kiewit Infrastructure South, experienced delays driven by utility relocation challenges. Construction started on March 5, 2024, and the project was originally estimated for completion by February 2025. However, utility work pushed the timeline out several months. An ARDOT official acknowledged the delays, saying: 'It's no one's fault, but the utilities part. It's kind of the red tape of any project, and that's what we're running into here.' The project was expected to be substantially complete by mid-December 2024 if weather cooperated. Local businesses along Highway 5 in the Benton-Bryant corridor felt significant impact from the prolonged construction.

projects.name: Cantrell Road (Highway 10) Widening (Little Rock)
projects.description: The $81 million Cantrell Road widening project in Little Rock required extensive underground utility location work beginning in 2018, with additional phases now adding $30 million more.
projects.detail: ARDOT's $81 million project to widen Cantrell Road (AR Highway 10) between Pleasant Ridge Road and Pleasant Valley Drive in Little Rock required utility location work beginning in September 2018 -- excavating small holes to determine accurate locations of existing underground utility lines for surveying and mapping in the final design. The utility locating and design phase contributed to the project not beginning construction until well after the initial planning phase. The project was eventually completed in 2023, but ARDOT has since announced an additional $30 million phase of Cantrell Road widening set to begin in 2026. Concerns have been raised about the expansion eroding the historic Black Pankey community neighborhood.
projects.timeline: Design from 2018; construction completed 2023; Phase 2 begins 2026

projects.name: I-25 Improvements (Las Cruces to Raton, NM)
projects.description: New Mexico DOT's I-25 improvement projects face utility relocation challenges as state law requires disputes over relocation costs not delay work, yet coordination with multiple utility owners routinely extends timelines.
projects.detail: New Mexico DOT's program of I-25 improvements along the state's primary north-south corridor faces recurring utility relocation challenges. State administrative code requires that utility relocations on interstate highway projects be coordinated between NMDOT and utility owners, with disputes over costs resolved without delaying construction. However, in practice, coordination with multiple utility companies along the heavily developed I-25 corridor through Albuquerque routinely extends project timelines. The Gibson Boulevard interchange reconstruction off I-25 in Albuquerque, projected at $150 million, exemplifies the complexity of working around dense underground utility networks in urban highway reconstruction. New Mexico's broader infrastructure challenge is underscored by nearly $6 billion in unspent infrastructure funds, with projects facing 'no activity, no or minimal reporting, significant challenges or delays.'

projects.name: DFW Region Pipeline Strike Epidemic (2026)
projects.description: Over 1,000 excavation-related pipeline strikes were reported in the Dallas-Fort Worth region in early 2026 alone, with one-third of excavators failing to call 811 before digging, contributing to the deadly Dallas apartment explosion.
projects.detail: More than 4,800 excavation-related pipeline strikes were reported across Texas in 2026, with over 1,000 occurring in the Dallas-Fort Worth region alone (Dallas, Tarrant, Collin, and Denton counties). Railroad Commission data showed roughly one-third of excavators involved in reported pipeline strikes had not contacted the 811 notification system before digging. The crisis was underscored by the May 28, 2026 Dallas apartment explosion that killed three people after engineering firm ECS struck a gas line during soil testing for new construction. Contributing factors included aging infrastructure, incomplete mapping records, difficulty locating non-metallic pipelines, and inaccurate utility markings that failed to identify smaller service lines or indicate correct pipe depth.

projects.name: Corpus Christi Bond 2024 Road/Utility Program
projects.description: Corpus Christi's $700 million bond program for 69 road projects found that underground utility replacement was as costly as the surface road work itself, extending timelines on projects like McArdle and Everhart Roads.
projects.detail: Corpus Christi's 2024 bond program authorized $700 million for 69 road construction projects, but the city's Engineering Director acknowledged a major complication: underground utility replacement was typically as expensive as the surface road improvements. On the McArdle Road and Everhart Road projects, the city chose not to leave underground utilities that were 'fully depreciated or undersized,' meaning each road project became a dual road-and-utility reconstruction. Everhart Road work is not expected to be completed until the end of 2025 or early 2026, with frustrated residents reporting prolonged detours. The program revealed that Corpus Christi's aging underground infrastructure effectively doubles the cost and timeline of any road improvement project.

projects.name: AT&T Fiber Denton County Neighborhood Lawsuit (Wynnwood Haven)
projects.description: Dozens of Denton County residents sued AT&T after fiber optic installation beginning in 2021 destroyed roads, drainage systems, and water infrastructure in the Wynnwood Haven Estates community.
projects.detail: Approximately three dozen residents of Wynnwood Haven Estates, an unincorporated community on a peninsula in Lewisville Lake in Denton County, sued AT&T over extensive damage from fiber optic cable installation that began in 2021. The narrow-streeted neighborhood suffered road damage, compromised drainage flow from fill dirt left by contractors, water leaks from damaged well-based water utility infrastructure, and persistent puddling from blocked drainage ditches. The community, which relies on a small well-based water utility, lacks funds to repair the leaks residents claim AT&T caused. The lawsuit seeks repair costs plus additional damages as an example. The case highlights how fiber installation in older, unincorporated communities with limited infrastructure records can cause cascading utility damage.

projects.name: Houston Street Cut Ordinance Enforcement
projects.description: Houston's Street Cut Ordinance requires special permitting for excavations in roads less than five years old, but enforcement gaps allow utility companies to degrade newly paved streets with inadequate restoration.
projects.detail: Houston's Street Cut Ordinance regulates how excavations are performed and restored within the city's right-of-way, with enhanced requirements for excavations in public ways less than five years old. Utility companies must submit drawings, specifications, and a Certificate of Restoration, with permit suspension as the penalty for violations. However, the system faces enforcement challenges: utility companies with standing permits can perform work with minimal oversight, and the 14-calendar-day window from first pavement break to total completion is frequently exceeded. Failed inspections and missing Certificates of Restoration are ongoing problems, degrading the condition of streets the city has invested millions to repave. The Houston mobility permits presentation to City Council highlighted the gap between the ordinance's intent and actual utility company compliance.

projects.name: HART Dillingham Boulevard Utility Relocation (Honolulu Rail)
projects.description: Utility relocation failures along Dillingham Boulevard became a central driver of the Honolulu rail project's cost explosion from $5.1 billion to $12.4 billion, with a single $497 million utility relocation contract awarded after a previous $400 million contract was canceled at 8% completion.
projects.detail: The Honolulu Authority for Rapid Transportation awarded a $497 million contract to Nan Inc. to relocate water, sewer, power, and telecommunications utilities along Dillingham Boulevard, a prerequisite for rail guideway construction. This came after a previous $400 million utility relocation contract with the same firm was canceled, but not before Nan was paid roughly $100 million to complete only about 8% of the work. HART's Dillingham utility relocation has been called the most painful piece of the rail project, snarling urban traffic and costing hundreds of millions. The difference between the lowest and highest bids for the utility work was $400 million, reflecting deep uncertainty about the scope of underground infrastructure. The utility failures contributed to the project's overall cost ballooning from $5.1 billion to $12.4 billion and its completion date sliding from 2020 to 2031.

projects.name: HART Airport Guideway STG Utility Lawsuit (Honolulu Rail)
projects.description: Shimmick/Traylor/Granite sued HART for $99 million over utility relocation failures on the Airport Guideway segment, alleging HART claimed designs were 90% complete when they were far from it. HART settled for $60 million.
projects.detail: The Shimmick/Traylor/Granite (STG) joint venture, holding an $875 million contract to build four stations and 5.2 miles of elevated track from Aloha Stadium to Middle Street, filed a $99 million lawsuit against HART over utility relocation delays. STG alleged that HART had assured bidders the utility relocation designs were 90% complete, but the authority then took over one year to provide data needed to finish utility designs. When STG presented evidence of the problems and their impact on the construction schedule, HART took three more years to negotiate and execute change orders. Contractors were forced to absorb the cost of utility-related delays without compensation. HART settled for approximately $60 million in December 2023, acknowledging long-standing utility relocation problems near Honolulu airport.

projects.name: Hitachi Rail $324M Lawsuit Against HART (Honolulu Rail)
projects.description: Hitachi Rail filed a $324 million lawsuit against HART, alleging that mismanagement of contractor coordination and utility relocation led to countless delays and significantly increased costs on the Honolulu Skyline project.
projects.detail: Hitachi Rail Honolulu Joint Venture (HRH) filed a $324 million lawsuit against HART in December 2024, claiming that mismanagement of the Skyline project by the defendants 'has led to countless delays and other errors resulting in significantly increased costs for HRH.' The lawsuit alleges HART failed to coordinate the numerous contractors involved in the project, a task vital to the delivery system HART chose. This followed the earlier STG lawsuit settlement of $60 million and came as HART struggled with utility relocation along Dillingham Boulevard. The pattern of contractor lawsuits highlighted systemic failures in utility coordination that rippled across multiple project segments.

projects.name: I-10 Broadway Curve Improvement Project (Phoenix)
projects.description: ADOT's largest urban freeway reconstruction tracked over 1,500 potential utility conflicts with 30+ utility companies and coordinated 70+ relocation plans, finishing at $832 million versus a $615 million contract.
projects.detail: The I-10 Broadway Curve Improvement Project was ADOT's largest-ever urban freeway reconstruction, expanding capacity on 11 miles of Interstate 10 in the Phoenix area. One of the design team's biggest challenges was tracking over 1,500 potential utility conflicts with more than 30 different utility companies and coordinating over 70 sets of relocation plans. The original contract was $615 million, but the total project cost reached $832 million including utility relocations, right-of-way acquisition, and ITS signal upgrades. Salt River flooding caused a four-month delay, and state-imposed limits on road closures during weekends and holidays further extended the timeline. After four years of construction, the project was completed in May 2025.

projects.name: ADOT I-17 Flex Lane Project
projects.description: The 23-mile I-17 flex lane project north of Phoenix went $76 million over the $446 million bid price to $522 million, with redesign of 21 concrete box culverts and bridge abutments adding to costs alongside preconstruction utility work.
projects.detail: The Arizona Department of Transportation's 23-mile project to add flex lanes on I-17 north of Phoenix exceeded its original $446 million bid by more than $76 million, reaching $522 million. ADOT cited three contributors: $45 million from federal environmental requirement changes by the Army Corps of Engineers and EPA that altered waterway definitions and fill material rules, $27 million for design and capacity changes to 21 concrete box culverts, and $4.2 million for bridge abutment redesign. Preconstruction work including utility relocation was underway simultaneously on related Phoenix-area freeway projects, adding complexity to the already challenging desert corridor construction. Despite the cost overruns, the project remained on its original 2025 completion schedule.

projects.name: Tucson Grant Road Improvement Project (Phases 3-4)
projects.description: The $64 million Grant Road widening requires relocating miles of aging sewer, water, and storm drain utilities underground before road construction can proceed, with the sewer phase alone taking months and water line work expected to last over a year.
projects.detail: The Tucson Grant Road Improvement Project, a multi-decade effort to widen this major corridor, entered its most complex phase with the $64 million Phases 3 and 4 stretching from Sparkman Boulevard to Swan Road. Because of the density of surrounding development combined with the age of utility infrastructure, preliminary work was extensive, including acquisition of numerous properties and relocation of miles of above- and below-ground utilities. Underground sewer lines were moved first, taking until at least June, followed by water line rerouting under Grant Road expected to take at least a year. Underground stormwater drainage systems also required relocation. The project will expand the roadway to six lanes with buffered bike lanes and improved sidewalks, with completion expected by October 2026. Future Phases 5 and 6 starting in 2029 will require another year of utility relocation before road construction can begin.

projects.name: Gypsum Colorado Comcast Fiber Gas Explosion
projects.description: Underground boring for Comcast's fiber optic network struck a gas line in Gypsum, causing a fatal home explosion and forcing evacuation of the Chatfield Corners neighborhood. A prior gas strike had occurred on the same project months earlier.
projects.detail: A Comcast fiber optic installation project in Gypsum, Colorado became deadly when contracting company SNEFCO struck a gas line while boring underground trenches. The resulting gas leak caused a home on Cottonwood Pass Road to explode, killing one person and forcing the evacuation of the entire Chatfield Corners neighborhood. Electric service was cut to the subdivision since gas may have leaked into service vaults and conduit containing power lines. This was not an isolated incident: a family in an adjacent neighborhood had been evacuated in July when the same contracting company hit a gas line during fiber installation. Following the fatal explosion, the towns of Gypsum and Eagle halted all underground boring work associated with Comcast's fiber optic installation indefinitely.

projects.name: Colorado Springs Austin Bluffs Parkway Utility Relocation
projects.description: Crews discovered an unexpected, unmarked utility line during electric infrastructure relocation on Austin Bluffs Parkway, requiring four months of additional work to identify the line and reroute existing infrastructure around it.
projects.detail: The Austin Bluffs Parkway utility relocation project in Colorado Springs, part of the Central Bluffs Substation infrastructure work, was delayed four months when crews discovered an unexpected unmarked utility line that had to be identified and required other existing lines to be relocated around it. The same type of unmarked utility discovery had previously delayed the Voyager Parkway bridge project and slowed progress on the Coral Bluffs substation work. A subsequent phase in early 2026 was delayed again after additional preparation and inspection work was needed, with lane closures pushed back by over a month. Colorado Springs Utilities began rolling lane closures for electric infrastructure relocations with work expected through June 2026.

projects.name: Colorado Springs Galley Road Bridge Replacement
projects.description: The $8 million Galley Road bridge replacement was delayed over a year when fiber optic line relocation took 12 months instead of the expected 3-4 months, compounded by unexpected utility line discoveries and water main work.
projects.detail: The $8 million Galley Road bridge replacement project in east Colorado Springs experienced over a year of delays primarily driven by utility relocation complications. Relocation of sensitive fiber optic lines took a full year instead of the expected three to four months, while crews also encountered difficulty relocating telecommunications cables and discovered unexpected utility lines. Concurrent Colorado Springs Utilities water main upgrades at the Wooten Road intersection added further traffic impacts, reducing westbound traffic and closing eastbound lanes. Neighbors and drivers expressed frustration at the series of overlapping projects along the Galley Road corridor, with the bridge replacement and utility work stretching well beyond original timelines.

projects.name: Colorado Springs Utilities Fiber Network Contractor Settlement
projects.description: After its fiber contractor ADB Companies caused widespread utility damage and fell behind schedule, Colorado Springs Utilities canceled the contract and paid $5.35 million to settle a resulting $61 million lawsuit.
projects.detail: Colorado Springs Utilities' $600 million citywide fiber network project faced major setbacks when contractor ADB Companies LLC fell behind schedule in 2023 and 2024 during broadband installation. CSU canceled ADB's contract, prompting the contractor to file a lawsuit seeking at least $61 million in damages. After 16 months of litigation, CSU agreed to a $5.35 million settlement, with the majority reflecting payments previously withheld for completed work and planned project shutdown costs. The City Council approved the settlement in March 2026. CSU then hired three new fiber installation contractors to get back on track, employing a combination of strategic ramp-up and expanded resources to meet its broadband deployment goals.

projects.name: Black Forest Road Corridor Widening (Colorado Springs)
projects.description: Mountain View Electric and Colorado Springs Utilities needed additional months to complete underground infrastructure work, extending road closures through May 2023 and pushing the $32 million widening project past its original schedule.
projects.detail: The $32 million Black Forest Road widening project, expanding the road to a four-lane principal arterial from Woodmen Road to Research Parkway with new bridges over Cottonwood Creek, was delayed by underground utility coordination issues. Construction began in April 2022, but road closures had to be extended through May 2023 to allow Mountain View Electric and Colorado Springs Utilities to complete essential work on their respective underground utility infrastructure. The Vollmer Road section was particularly affected, requiring sequential utility work followed by roadway reconstruction. Rainy weather further slowed progress, though drier conditions later helped crews catch up. The project was expected to finish by October 2024, about six months behind the original schedule.

projects.name: Powers Boulevard Extension Utility Delay (Colorado Springs)
projects.description: The Powers Boulevard extension bridge was delayed four months by the slow relocation of a utility line linked to the Air Force Academy, alongside weather impacts and construction complications.
projects.detail: The Powers Boulevard Extension project, connecting Highway 83 to Voyager Parkway in north Colorado Springs, experienced a four-month bridge construction delay caused by the need to relocate a utility line linked to the U.S. Air Force Academy. The utility relocation proved more time-consuming than anticipated, compounding weather-related delays. The overall Powers Boulevard Extension project started in 2019 and will likely not be finished until 2030 at the earliest, spanning the construction of bridges and utility line relocations across multiple segments. The remaining phase involves extending Powers two miles through the Flying Horse subdivision, with workers building bridges while simultaneously relocating additional utility lines.

projects.name: University of Wyoming Dormitory Construction Gas Line Strike (Laramie)
projects.description: An excavator working on the $264 million UW residence hall construction project struck a 2-inch gas service line, forcing evacuation of four campus buildings including both dormitories under construction, fraternity houses, and the College of Business.
projects.detail: On October 9, 2024, an excavator working on the University of Wyoming's $264 million residence hall construction project struck a 2-inch gas service line in the middle of an intersection on campus, causing natural gas to leak at a significant rate. The Laramie Fire Department's Engine 4 arrived at 11:16 a.m. and evacuated structures on both sides of 15th Street, including both dormitory buildings under construction, two fraternity homes, the UW Lab School, UW Operations/Service Building, UW College of Business, and McWhinnie Hall. Black Hills Energy responded and arrived by 11:45 a.m., remotely exposing the line by 12:50 p.m. and stopping gas flow by 12:57 p.m. No injuries or fire resulted. The $264 million residence hall project, managed by JE Dunn Construction, was already facing challenges including 49 days of crane shutdowns due to Laramie's high winds and a shortage of skilled subcontractors in Wyoming.

projects.name: Salt Lake City 300 West Reconstruction
projects.description: Coordination with third-party fiber and cable providers, aging city utility lines requiring extra repairs, and scheduling conflicts pushed the 300 West reconstruction eight months past its November 2022 target.
projects.detail: Salt Lake City's 300 West reconstruction project missed its originally anticipated November 2022 completion date by approximately eight months, not finishing until mid-2023. A major contributing factor was poor coordination with third-party utilities: fiber and cable providers needed additional time to make updates, and aging city utility lines required extra repairs that were not anticipated in the original project scope. The project was also impacted by a concrete shortage that reduced pour capacity by 80%, region-wide post-pandemic labor shortages, and materials delays. Despite the schedule overruns, the project was reported to remain within its original budget. The completion in July 2023 was described as collectively producing sighs of relief from Salt Lakers.

projects.name: Bangerter Highway Interchanges (Jordan Valley Aqueduct)
projects.description: UDOT's $525 million Bangerter Highway interchange project required sequencing construction around the relocation of a 66-inch aqueduct serving half a million people, forcing the 4700 South interchange to be built first.
projects.detail: Utah DOT's $525 million project to build four new interchanges on Bangerter Highway required careful sequencing around a critical utility conflict: a 66-inch cement-lined steel aqueduct (the Jordan Valley Aqueduct) that supplies water to half a million people near the 4700 South intersection. Due to the budgeting and relocation complexity of the JVA, the 4700 South interchange had to begin construction before the other three intersections at a cost of $114 million, while the remaining three projects carried a combined $217 million construction budget. Utility corridors were evaluated early to determine the optimal relocation path to minimize impacts and keep the project moving. The project was targeted for completion in fall 2025.

projects.name: West Davis Corridor SR-177 Extension (Utility Relocations)
projects.description: UDOT's $225 million West Davis Corridor extension requires more than 25 third-party utility relocations including water districts, irrigation companies, and power infrastructure before highway construction can proceed.
projects.detail: The $225 million extension of SR-177 as part of the West Davis Corridor project requires more than 25 third-party utility relocations before the bulk of highway construction can begin. Crews from Hooper Water Improvement District, Davis and Weber Counties Canal Company, Hooper Irrigation Company, and Rocky Mountain Power must all move infrastructure out of the new highway's path. Preliminary utility relocation began in advance of full construction anticipated for summer 2026, with the project scheduled for completion in 2028. The corridor connects Farmington to West Point and will add a 16-mile highway through rapidly developing areas of Davis County where the density of agricultural water infrastructure adds complexity to utility coordination.

projects.name: Ketchum Main Street Reconstruction (Idaho)
projects.description: Ketchum's Main Street reconstruction discovered the geotechnical subsurface survey was incorrect, requiring foundation replacement before paving, while waterline work closed entire blocks and contractor/material shortages compounded delays.
projects.detail: The Ketchum Main Street reconstruction project in Idaho's Sun Valley resort area experienced multiple delays stemming from underground utility and subsurface complications. In mid-July 2024, it was determined that the Idaho Transportation Department's original geotechnical survey of Main Street's subsurface was not correct, and the road foundation would need to be replaced before paving could proceed. The city's waterline project required full lane closures from 2nd Street to 4th Street, proceeding one block at a time. The City's original request for bids attracted no interested contractors, immediately delaying the project. When a contractor was finally selected, they had trouble securing subcontractors and equipment for electrical and curb work, while shortages of materials such as signal mast arms and controller boxes caused further setbacks.

projects.name: Boise Downtown Utility-Driven Road Closure Cascade
projects.description: Multiple simultaneous utility and road construction projects from ACHD, the city, and urban renewal converged in downtown Boise, creating months-long road closures as underground utility connections for new development ripped up streets.
projects.detail: Downtown Boise experienced a cascade of overlapping road closures in 2024-2025 as an accumulation of construction projects from the Ada County Highway District, the city of Boise, and Boise's urban renewal agency all converged at once. Significant development happening downtown required connection to underground utilities, meaning construction crews repeatedly ripped up and repaved roads for sewer, water, and utility access. State Street required extensive underground work due to utility lines, stormwater pipes, fiber cables, and underground tunnels connecting State of Idaho buildings. Some roads were fully or partially closed for months, including Grove Street during hotel and apartment construction. Businesses reported revenue losses due to reduced parking and difficult road navigation. An ACHD spokesperson acknowledged the frustration, noting that multiple agencies had independent timelines that unfortunately overlapped.

projects.name: Boise Cloverdale Road Gas Line Installation Delay
projects.description: Intermountain Gas's Cloverdale Road gas line installation in southwest Boise was delayed well past its 2023 completion target when crews hit bedrock, contributing to cascading road construction delays in the area.
projects.detail: In southwest Boise, Intermountain Gas Company's gas line installation project on Cloverdale Road was scheduled for completion in early 2023 but ran significantly behind when crews encountered bedrock underground. The delay cascaded into other planned road construction projects in the area, as multiple agencies including ACHD, the City of Boise, and private developers all had overlapping construction timelines in southwest Boise. The area was experiencing rapid growth, and the accumulation of delayed utility projects and road construction from several agencies created significant traffic disruption and frustration for businesses and residents, with some roads fully or partially closed for months longer than planned.

projects.name: Idaho State University Steam Tunnel Water Main Strike
projects.description: Construction crews working on a steam tunnel replacement project at Idaho State University struck a critical water main, forcing emergency shutoffs to multiple campus buildings and disrupting university operations.
projects.detail: On July 1, 2024, construction personnel working on a deferred maintenance steam tunnel replacement project at Idaho State University in Pocatello hit a critical water main line. The strike required an emergency water shut-off affecting multiple buildings including Lillibridge Engineering, Physical Science, Chemistry, Business Administration, Frazier Hall, and Liberal Arts buildings. The contractor, Engineered Structures Inc. of Boise, had been trenching for new power conduits so that high voltage lines inside existing tunnels could be removed to enhance worker safety. The water main break disrupted university operations for the remainder of the day as site personnel and Facilities Services worked with the City of Pocatello to assess and address the damage.

projects.name: Las Vegas Boulevard North Improvement (Underground Surprises)
projects.description: The city's biggest-ever public works project encountered numerous underground surprises including abandoned sewer lines at unexpected elevations, forgotten utility installations, and paved-over 1950s infrastructure.
projects.detail: The Las Vegas Boulevard North improvement project, a three-year effort to improve 2.5 miles of Las Vegas Boulevard north of the famous Strip, was the city of Las Vegas's biggest-ever public works project and a lesson in underground utility discovery. Crews encountered abandoned sewer lines at unexpected elevations, forgotten utility installations, old traffic signals, and a long-paved-over concrete section of old U.S. Highway 91. Many of these relics dated to the 1950s when the city had a population of about 50,000 and underground mapping was not a priority. During one weekend marathon to install new storm drains, crews hit a sewer line at an unexpected elevation and had to make an on-the-spot decision to temporarily plug and cut through the sewer line, allowing storm drain construction to proceed with sewer repairs scheduled later.

projects.name: Reimagine Boulder Highway (Henderson, NV)
projects.description: The $172 million Boulder Highway revamp grew to $184 million after requiring relocation of all conflicting water, electric, gas, and internet lines to prevent future service disruptions along the 7.5-mile corridor.
projects.detail: Henderson's Reimagine Boulder Highway project, a 7.5-mile transformation of one of Southern Nevada's busiest corridors, grew from $172 million to $184 million during construction. The project required relocating all water and utility lines that conflicted with the new design, including electric, gas, and internet infrastructure, specifically to prevent future service disruptions. Key utility relocations were completed as a prerequisite before road reconstruction could proceed. The project reduces traffic lanes from six to four, adds wider sidewalks and elevated bike lanes, and creates a center-run bus rapid transit system. As of 2026, approximately 400 new streetlights were installed, and the project passed its halfway mark with completion expected by 2027.

projects.name: Las Vegas Boulevard Waterline/Road Improvement (Strip Phases)
projects.description: A multi-year, $60 million phased waterline replacement and road improvement project on the Las Vegas Strip requires midnight-to-morning construction and coordination between Clark County, the Water District, and dozens of casinos.
projects.detail: Clark County's Las Vegas Boulevard Improvement Project is a multi-phase effort spanning the length of the famous Las Vegas Strip from Sahara Avenue to the 215 Beltway. Each phase includes waterline replacement by the Las Vegas Valley Water District, roadway repaving, traffic signal modifications, lighting and power upgrades, and pedestrian bollard installation. The latest $60 million phase between Tropicana and Russell Road began in June 2025, with construction restricted to overnight hours (midnight to 9 a.m.) to minimize impacts on the tourism corridor. Coordinating between Clark County, the Water District, communications utilities, and dozens of adjacent casino properties adds significant complexity, with utility adjustments and potholing required before each road segment can be repaved.

projects.name: Reno Virginia Street BRT Extension
projects.description: The Virginia Street BRT Extension project in downtown Reno grew from $80.8 million to $98.5 million after design refinements, with $6 million dedicated to utility relocation and storm drain improvements involving AT&T, NV Energy, and Truckee Meadows Water Authority.
projects.detail: The Regional Transportation Commission's Virginia Street Bus RAPID Transit Extension in downtown Reno saw its project cost increase from $80.78 million to $98.48 million, a 22% increase resulting from design refinements. A significant component was the $6 million allocated for utility relocation and storm drain improvements, requiring coordination with AT&T, NV Energy, and Truckee Meadows Water Authority. The project involved putting above-ground utilities underground and performing much-needed utility infrastructure upgrades along Virginia Street. The federal government provided $40.4 million through the Capital Investment Grant program. Construction began with utility work as the first phase, upgrading aging underground infrastructure before the above-ground BRT features could be built.

projects.name: Cheyenne Wyoming Road Utility Construction Season (2026)
projects.description: Cheyenne's 2026 construction season kicked off with multiple simultaneous water main rehabilitation and sewer manhole replacement projects requiring full road closures, illustrating the competing schedules of utility and road agencies.
projects.detail: The City of Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities launched its 2026 construction season with multiple simultaneous utility projects requiring full road closures across the city. A water main rehabilitation project on E. 20th Street between Logan Avenue and E. 21st Street required full road closure from late March through mid-April, with an additional manhole replacement project at the intersection of Dell Range Boulevard and Grandview Avenue running concurrently to improve sewer service reliability. Weather conditions and material availability threatened to extend both timelines. The simultaneous launches illustrated the challenge facing Wyoming's capital city in coordinating utility infrastructure upgrades with road maintenance, with officials unable to stagger the projects to minimize combined disruption.

projects.name: WYDOT 11-Project Delay ($436M Redirected to Maintenance)
projects.description: Wyoming DOT delayed 11 construction projects and redirected $436 million to road maintenance, reflecting 15 years of 'preservation only mode' that deferred infrastructure and utility coordination investments.
projects.detail: The Wyoming Department of Transportation delayed 11 planned construction projects and redirected $436 million to road maintenance, reflecting a systemic infrastructure coordination crisis. WYDOT Director Darren Westby confirmed the agency faces an unfunded need of approximately $500 million annually, with $300 million specifically for road construction. The state has been stuck in 'preservation only mode' for the last 15 years, tabling capacity-expanding projects including passing lanes, parking areas, and the utility coordination work that accompanies new construction. The $436 million redirection meant that planned road projects where utility relocations had already been coordinated were shelved, potentially requiring re-coordination with utility providers if and when the projects are eventually funded.

projects.name: Billings Bypass (Montana's Largest MDT Project)
projects.description: Montana DOT's most expensive project at $136 million, the six-phase Billings Bypass required extensive utility coordination across the Yellowstone River Bridge, railroad overpass, and multiple road segments through 2028.
projects.detail: The $136 million Billings Bypass is the Montana Department of Transportation's most expensive project to date, a six-phase effort linking Billings Heights to Interstate 90 in Lockwood. The project required coordination across multiple complex segments including the Yellowstone River Bridge, a railroad overpass, and the planned Johnson Lane Interchange. Two of six phases are complete and open to the public, with the bypass tentatively scheduled for full completion in 2028. The scale of the project through varied terrain and across critical infrastructure corridors including the Yellowstone River required careful utility coordination with multiple providers. As Montana's largest MDT project, it has tested the state's capacity for coordinating utility relocations across a multi-year, multi-phase construction effort.

projects.name: Pasadena Raymond Avenue Undergrounding Project
projects.description: A $36 million utility undergrounding project on Raymond Avenue has been in planning for over 20 years and suffered a recent delay when the City Council rejected construction bids in March 2025.
projects.detail: The Pasadena Raymond Avenue Undergrounding Project aims to bury two miles of overhead power lines from Maple Street to the northern city boundary. Part of a citywide program begun in 1968, the project has faced decades of coordination challenges. In March 2025, the City Council rejected construction bids, pushing the timeline back approximately 12 weeks. With $25.8 million budgeted for fiscal year 2026 alone and a total cost of $36 million, the project also includes street paving, lighting, sidewalk improvements, and street trees. The broader Pasadena undergrounding program is projected to cost $2 billion and take over 500 years at the current pace of 0.5 to 0.7 miles per year.

projects.name: NE Portland Gas Line Strike (Morris Street)
projects.description: A construction crew drilling underground struck a gas line on NE Morris Street in August 2025, causing gas to vent through the soil toward neighboring homes and triggering an emergency response.
projects.detail: On August 25, 2025, a construction crew operating an underground drill struck a gas line at 11400 NE Morris Street in Portland. Portland Fire & Rescue responded around 11:40 a.m. after gas began pushing up through the soil on top of the line and migrating toward neighboring homes. Crews monitored nearby structures to prevent gas infiltration. NW Natural arrived around noon to manage the leak. The incident disrupted construction operations and required an extended emergency response to secure the area.

projects.name: Redmond ADA Curb Ramp Gas Line Strike (Highway 126)
projects.description: An ODOT contractor building ADA-compliant curb ramps struck a 2-inch natural gas line in November 2025, shutting down Highway 126 and forcing traffic detours for hours.
projects.detail: On November 24, 2025, a contractor working on an ODOT ADA curb ramp project in Redmond hit a two-inch Cascade Natural Gas steel pipe near SW Highland Avenue (Oregon Highway 126) and 11th Street. The gas leak forced closure of Highway 126 and surrounding roads for several hours. ODOT set up detour routes while Cascade Natural Gas crews worked to stop the leak and repair the line. The curb ramp project was part of a larger effort to bring state highways in Redmond and Prineville into ADA compliance, scheduled to run from May 2025 through September 2026.

projects.name: Long Beach Colorado Lagoon Open Channel Project
projects.description: Crews discovered 25 unmapped utility lines and asbestos-containing materials during excavation, forcing repeated work stoppages and pushing the $32 million project at least $4 million over budget.
projects.detail: The Long Beach Colorado Lagoon Open Channel Project, which began creating a 12-foot-deep tidal channel between the 18-acre lagoon and Alamitos Bay, was originally scheduled to finish in March 2024. However, crews kept running into old, unmapped utilities and asbestos-containing materials while digging for a sewer siphon and bridge foundations, forcing repeated work stoppages and safety checks. A total of 25 unmapped utility lines were discovered. The city has spent at least $1.5 million on asbestos surveying and abatement alone. The project has gone at least $4 million over its original $32 million budget, with road closures around the lagoon frustrating residents into 2026.

projects.name: Portland Utility Street Cut Damage Crisis
projects.description: Utility companies including Comcast, NW Natural, and Portland General Electric cut into Portland streets so frequently that the city doubled restoration fees to $13.84/sq ft to recover $22 million annually in road damage costs.
projects.detail: Portland's Bureau of Transportation identified that utility companies including Comcast, NW Natural, and Portland General Electric were causing extensive pavement damage through street cuts for wire, pipe, and cable installations. The damage contributed to a $6 billion backlog of needed road, sidewalk, and infrastructure upgrades. In April 2026, City Council voted to nearly double utility cut restoration fees from $7.22 to $13.84 per square foot, projected to generate an additional $22 million annually. Portland also established a 5-year moratorium on cuts to newly paved streets, requiring expanded pavement restoration beyond the trench limits when moratorium streets are cut.

projects.name: Pasadena Citywide Undergrounding Program
projects.description: Pasadena's utility undergrounding program, begun in 1968, has completed only 46 miles at a pace of 0.5-0.7 miles per year, with a projected $2 billion total cost and estimated 500+ years to completion.
projects.detail: Pasadena's Underground Utility Program, started in 1968 to beautify the city and reduce electrical outages, has become a cautionary example of utility coordination challenges at scale. After nearly six decades, only about 46 miles have been completed at a pace of 0.5 to 0.7 miles per year. Category 1, covering 50 miles of civic areas and high-concentration power line streets, will take another 100 years. Category 2, covering 79 miles of residential streets and alleys, would take an additional 400 years. The total projected cost is approximately $2 billion, funded through a tax on electric bills ranging from 1.21% to 4.34%. The program fund currently holds about $38 million.

projects.name: I-405 Renton to Bellevue Widening (Washington)
projects.description: The I-405 Renton to Bellevue widening project faces an 18-month delay to summer 2027, with the contractor missing key milestones and WSDOT taking them to court over cost disputes.
projects.detail: The I-405 Renton to Bellevue Widening and Express Toll Lanes Project, originally expected to be ready by end of 2025, has been delayed to summer 2027. WSDOT blames the contractor for not meeting key milestones, while the contractor seeks additional millions to complete the work. The project adds one new lane in each direction to create a dual express toll lane system between SR 167 in Renton and NE 6th Street in Bellevue. Multiple factors contributed to delays including pandemic impacts, a concrete workers' strike, and weather, compounded by utility coordination challenges inherent in widening an active freeway corridor. The original bid was $705 million, with litigation ongoing between WSDOT and the contractor.
projects.timeline: Originally end of 2025, delayed to summer 2027

projects.name: RapidRide J Line Utility Work (Seattle Eastlake)
projects.description: The $156 million RapidRide J Line required $28 million in water main replacements along Eastlake Avenue, with 9,000 feet of pipe, 27 hydrants, and 174 service transfers coordinated between SDOT and Seattle Public Utilities.
projects.detail: Seattle's RapidRide J Line, running from the University District to South Lake Union via Eastlake, required massive utility coordination before transit improvements could proceed. Seattle Public Utilities invested $28 million to install over 9,000 feet of upgraded water main, 27 new fire hydrants, and relocated 11 water meters while transferring 174 service connections to nearby businesses and homes. SDOT applied lessons from previous RapidRide projects, conducting extensive advanced potholing at pole locations to minimize utility conflicts and avoid delays with long lead-time materials. Planning began in 2014 with service expected to launch in 2027, a 13-year timeline from conception to completion.

projects.name: San Francisco Fiber Optic Gas Explosion (Verizon/MasTec)
projects.description: A MasTec subcontractor installing Verizon fiber optic cable ruptured a PG&E gas line, causing an explosion that damaged or destroyed five buildings including a popular restaurant.
projects.detail: On February 6, 2019, an excavator operated by a subcontractor for MasTec, which was hired by Verizon to install fiber optic cables in San Francisco, struck a Pacific Gas & Electric gas distribution branch connection. The resulting gas release ignited and caused an explosion that damaged or destroyed five buildings, including a popular restaurant. The NTSB investigated the incident and determined the fiber-optic installation crew had ruptured the gas line during trench excavation. No injuries were reported, but the property damage was extensive and the incident highlighted the dangers of inadequate utility coordination during telecom infrastructure buildout.

projects.name: Los Angeles Street Damage Restoration Fee Shortfall
projects.description: A City Controller audit found that Los Angeles missed collecting $191 million in Street Damage Restoration Fees from utility companies cutting into city streets, while nearly one-fourth of LA streets received failing grades.
projects.detail: City Controller Ron Galperin's audit revealed that Los Angeles failed to collect $191 million in opportunity costs from Street Damage Restoration Fees owed by utility companies that cut into city streets. The fee had not been updated since 2006, and the city was vastly undercharging utilities for street repairs. Research found that utility cuts reduced average pavement life from 25 to 16.5 years for arterial streets and from 34.5 to 28.5 years for local streets. Nearly one-fourth of LA city streets received failing grades in pavement condition. The City Council approved updated fees of $8.24 per square foot for residential streets and $19.44 for major streets, projected to deliver over $100 million per year for repairs.

projects.name: Auburn Washington Gas Line Break (15th Street NW)
projects.description: A construction crew broke a gas line near 15th Street NW in Auburn in May 2024, forcing evacuation of nearby businesses and road closures until Puget Sound Energy completed repairs.
projects.detail: On May 2, 2024, a construction crew caused a natural gas leak near the 1600 block of 15th Street Northwest in Auburn, Washington. Firefighters from South King Fire and Rescue and Renton Regional Fire Authority responded, evacuating nearby businesses and closing surrounding roads as a safety precaution. Puget Sound Energy crews were called to shut off the gas and repair the damaged stem line. The incident disrupted business operations in the area and required a multi-agency emergency response to secure the site before normal activities could resume.

projects.name: Seattle Fremont Gas Line Rupture (Phinney Avenue)
projects.description: A two-inch gas line ruptured near Phinney Ave N and N 36th Street in Seattle's Fremont neighborhood in May 2025, forcing evacuation of a three-block radius and closing multiple streets.
projects.detail: On May 16, 2025, a two-inch gas line ruptured near Phinney Ave N and N 36th Street in Seattle's Fremont neighborhood. Authorities evacuated all buildings within a three-block radius from Phinney Ave N to Francis Ave N as a precaution against explosion and fire risks. N 36th Street was blocked between Dayton Ave N and Greenwood Ave N. No injuries were reported. By approximately 12:30 p.m. the leak had been contained, and Puget Sound Energy took over the investigation from Seattle Fire Department. The cause was under investigation by PSE.

projects.name: Outer Powell Transportation Safety Project (Portland)
projects.description: The $145 million Outer Powell safety project on US-26 requires extensive utility pole relocation and underground utility coordination across a 5-year construction period through a densely built urban corridor.
projects.detail: The Outer Powell Transportation Safety Project on US-26 (SE Powell Boulevard) between Interstate 205 and the Portland/Gresham city limits has a total estimated cost of $145 million for design, right-of-way, and construction. Phase 2 construction began in spring 2025 and is anticipated to last five years. The project requires extensive utility pole relocation, tree trimming and removal, selective building demolition, and sign removal to accommodate roadway improvements. Ongoing utility relocation activities highlight the complexity of reconstructing a major urban arterial where underground and overhead utilities must be moved in sequence before road improvements can proceed.

projects.name: Cornelius Pass Road/Willamette Water Supply Pipeline (Washington County, OR)
projects.description: Simultaneous construction of the Cornelius Pass Road improvements and a major Willamette Water Supply drinking water pipeline created two years of overlapping road closures and construction coordination challenges.
projects.detail: Washington County's Cornelius Pass Road improvement project between TV Highway and Frances Street had to be coordinated simultaneously with installation of a major Willamette Water Supply drinking water pipeline in the same corridor. The overlapping construction required careful sequencing of road work and pipeline installation, creating extended road closures and traffic disruptions from March 2022 through March 2024. The dual-project coordination challenge exemplifies how conflicting utility and road project schedules can compound delays and extend the impact on communities when multiple agencies build in the same right-of-way without unified scheduling.

projects.name: 2016 Portland NW Natural Gas Explosion (Loy Clark Pipeline)
projects.description: A Loy Clark Pipeline contractor's excavator hit and dislodged an NW Natural gas pipeline in Portland in 2016, causing an explosion that the Oregon PUC attributed to inadequate contractor notification.
projects.detail: In 2016, a Loy Clark Pipeline contractor's excavator struck and dislodged a natural gas pipeline owned by NW Natural in Portland, Oregon. The resulting gas release triggered an explosion. The Oregon Public Utility Commission investigated the incident and determined that inadequate contractor notification was the root cause. The contractor had failed to properly coordinate with NW Natural before excavating near the gas infrastructure. The incident resulted in an Oregon PUC enforcement action and highlighted the critical importance of one-call systems and proper utility locate procedures before any excavation work in urban areas with dense underground infrastructure.

projects.name: San Jose Excavation Moratorium Utility Cut Policy
projects.description: San Jose enacted a two-year moratorium on utility street cuts after resurfacing projects, but ongoing violations by utility companies continue to degrade newly paved roads across the city.
projects.detail: The City of San Jose established a policy prohibiting digging in streets for construction or utility work for two years after a resurfacing project, intended to protect the city's investment in road maintenance. Despite this moratorium, utility companies continue to need access to underground infrastructure within newly paved corridors, creating ongoing tension between road preservation and utility service needs. San Jose faces a significant infrastructure backlog partly driven by insufficient developer fees and the cumulative effect of utility cuts that reduce pavement lifespan. The challenge reflects a broader pattern across California cities struggling to coordinate utility work schedules with pavement maintenance programs.

projects.name: Ojai Five-Year Street Pavement Moratorium Program
projects.description: The City of Ojai established a five-year moratorium list to combat pavement degradation from utility cuts, covering all resurfacing types after utility companies repeatedly dug up recently improved streets.
projects.detail: The City of Ojai established a comprehensive five-year street pavement moratorium program to better manage the pavement degradation caused by utility cuts. The moratorium covers all pavement resurfacing including slurry seals, cape seals, and asphalt pavement overlays. Any utility company or entity seeking to excavate within a public street within five years of resurfacing must obtain special waivers and meet enhanced restoration requirements. The program was enacted after the city found that utility cuts were significantly shortening the useful life of recently resurfaced streets, effectively wasting public investment in road maintenance. No entity is exempt from the requirements, including utility companies, state agencies, and federal agencies.

projects.name: Sun Prairie Downtown Gas Explosion (Verizon Fiber)
projects.description: A Verizon subcontractor mismarked a gas line while installing fiber optic cable, triggering an explosion that killed a firefighter and destroyed six downtown businesses.
projects.detail: On July 10, 2018, subcontractor VC Tech, hired by Bear Communications to install fiber optic lines for Verizon Wireless, struck a gas main at the intersection of Bristol and Main streets in downtown Sun Prairie. A USIC locator had mismarked the gas line by 25 feet. The resulting explosion killed Fire Captain Cory Barr, injured firefighter Ryan Welch, displaced dozens of families, and destroyed five buildings. The contractor was fined $25,000 for failing to call 811 before digging. The city sued six firms over the damage, and a $41.4 million redevelopment project at the blast site was approved in 2024, including a hotel and apartment complex. The Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation contributed $250,000 for redevelopment.

projects.name: Austin Google Fiber Gas Line & Property Damage (TX)
projects.description: Google Fiber contractors in Austin ruptured gas lines forcing neighborhood evacuations, broke sprinkler systems, and generated 60 formal complaints in 2020 alone.
projects.detail: During Google Fiber's expansion across Austin, contractors caused repeated property damage and utility strikes in residential neighborhoods. In one incident, crews ruptured a gas line forcing an entire neighborhood to evacuate until repairs were complete. The City of Austin's 311 system received 60 complaints regarding Google Fiber in 2020 alone, ranging from broken gas and water lines to construction materials obstructing sidewalks. One homeowner's sprinkler system was broken during installation, costing $900 to repair, while another resident saw two large stepping stones damaged during a gas line repair, costing over $700. Residents reported that Google Fiber contractors dug on their property without permission and initially denied reimbursement claims for damages. Hundreds of complaints were ultimately filed with the city.

projects.name: Gypsum Fatal Home Explosion (Comcast/SEFNCO Fiber)
projects.description: A Comcast subcontractor boring for fiber optic cable ruptured a gas line in a residential neighborhood, causing a fatal home explosion that killed a mother of two.
projects.detail: On September 17, 2020, Tactical Drilling (subcontracted by SEFNCO Communications for Comcast's fiber optic project) ruptured a two-inch gas line while boring underground in the Chatfield Corners neighborhood of Gypsum. The gas leak was reported at 9:30 a.m. but the home of Patricia Ruiz Roe, 49, exploded at 12:35 p.m., killing her. The entire Chatfield Corners neighborhood was evacuated for two days. This was not an isolated incident -- a family in an adjacent neighborhood had been evacuated in July 2020 when SEFNCO hit a gas line there. The towns of Gypsum and Eagle halted all underground boring work for Comcast's fiber installation indefinitely. SEFNCO later made a donation to the community but faced significant scrutiny over safety practices.

projects.name: Frisco AT&T Fiber Gas Line Ruptures (27 Strikes)
projects.description: AT&T fiber optic installation crews ruptured 20 of 27 gas lines cut in Frisco in a single year, forcing repeated evacuations and two stop-work orders from the city.
projects.detail: During AT&T's aggressive fiber optic rollout in Frisco, Texas, 27 natural gas lines were cut in the city in a single year, with 20 of them attributed to AT&T's fiber installation project. AT&T's fast-paced installation schedule overwhelmed line locators who could not keep up with locate requests. Residents were repeatedly forced to evacuate their homes after gas line ruptures. The city issued a stop-work order for the project twice. AT&T eventually agreed to slow down its fiber installation pace to allow proper utility locating. The incidents highlighted the dangers of prioritizing speed over safety in fiber deployment.

projects.name: Brookhaven Google Fiber Stop-Work Order (GA)
projects.description: Google Fiber crews struck a gas main near an elementary school, forcing a lockdown and prompting a citywide stop-work order after nearly 100 resident complaints.
projects.detail: On December 13, 2024, a Google Fiber crew installing cable on Ashford Dunwoody Road struck a gas main near Montgomery Elementary School in Brookhaven, Georgia, forcing school officials to put the school on lockdown as firefighters responded. The following day, city officials issued a citywide stop-work order for Google Fiber. This came nearly two weeks after a November 21 water line break on Loraine Street during Google Fiber work. Nearly 100 residents filed complaints about Google Fiber in 2024, reporting broken sidewalks, burst water mains, and destroyed landscaping. The stop-work order required Google Fiber to demonstrate improved safety procedures before resuming work.

projects.name: Google Fiber Atlanta Utility Line Damage (S&N Communications)
projects.description: Google Fiber's subcontractor S&N Communications damaged utility lines 36 times in metro Atlanta, causing at least one line break per day and a 67% statewide increase in gas line damage.
projects.detail: The Georgia Public Service Commission investigated S&N Communications, the contractor installing Google Fiber in metro Atlanta, after the company reported 36 incidents of damaging utility lines. The Atlanta Fire Department stated that Google Fiber contractors were causing at least one line break per day. Under the Georgia Utility Facility Protection Act, excavators can be fined $10,000 per incident, potentially exposing S&N to over $360,000 in fines. Atlanta Gas Light reported a 67% increase in natural gas line damage across the state caused by third parties, and a 21% increase in locate requests -- both attributed largely to the fiber construction boom. The PSC considered fining Google Fiber directly for the damage caused by its contractors.

projects.name: Charlotte Fiber Broadband Utility Damage ($1.5M)
projects.description: Google Fiber and AT&T fiber crews caused 955 utility damage incidents in Charlotte over four years, with the city charging companies over $1.5 million for water and sewer line repairs.
projects.detail: Between July 2014 and April 2018, the city of Charlotte documented 955 fiber-related utility damage incidents -- 675 attributed to AT&T subcontractors and 257 to Google Fiber subcontractors. The city charged companies more than $1.5 million total for damage repairs. The three largest bills were for water line strikes: $203,000 on Tuckaseegee Road (where a Google Fiber subcontractor bored into a concrete water main, taking it out of service for two weeks), $54,000 on Richland Drive, and $53,000 on English Saddle Lane. In August 2016, a Google Fiber contractor drilled through a two-foot water main in southeast Charlotte, forcing evacuations in Cotswold and Oakhurst neighborhoods and causing school bus reroutes on Monroe Road.

projects.name: Platte City Fiber Gas Line Strike & School Evacuation (MO)
projects.description: United Fiber crews struck two gas lines while boring underground for fiber installation, forcing the evacuation of two schools and prompting the city to pause the project.
projects.detail: On August 29, 2025, contractors working for United Fiber struck two natural gas lines while boring underground in Platte City, Missouri. The strikes forced the evacuation of Siegrist Elementary School and Platte County High School, with students relocated to other facilities. Liberty Utilities responded to a damaged gas line on Thomas Drive and a service line on Bent Oak Court. City officials compared the incident to the fatal Lexington, Missouri explosion, noting it 'could have been like Lexington.' The city administrator said it was unclear whether crews were boring in the wrong location or if utility markings were incorrect. Platte City paused the fiber project pending a full safety review.

projects.name: Sebring Ohio Fiber Gas Line Double Strike
projects.description: Fiber optic installation crews hit two gas lines in Sebring, causing visible and audible leaks that forced the evacuation of 20 homes as a severe thunderstorm approached.
projects.detail: A crew installing fiber optic cable in Sebring, Ohio struck two gas lines, resulting in leaks that could be seen, heard, and smelled. Emergency officials ordered the evacuation of 20 homes between Pennsylvania and Oregon Avenues, between 13th and 14th streets. The situation became extremely dangerous when a strong thunderstorm with high lightning activity approached the area, creating the risk of igniting the escaping gas. Officials described it as 'the perfect storm of events all happening at the same exact time.' The danger was compounded when all of Sebring lost power after the storm moved through. No injuries were reported, but the incident highlighted the compounding risks of gas leaks during fiber construction.

projects.name: Algona Ezee Fiber Gas Line Ruptures (WA)
projects.description: The City of Algona suspended Ezee Fiber's installation after a second gas line rupture, following a previous neighborhood evacuation in nearby Des Moines caused by the same company.
projects.detail: In March 2025, the City of Algona suspended Ezee Fiber's fiber optic cable installation for four days after the company ruptured a second gas line in the area. This came after Ezee Fiber crews had already hit a gas line in neighboring Des Moines the previous month, prompting a neighborhood evacuation. The Algona mayor warned that if crews hit another gas line, he would suspend work again permanently. Ezee Fiber apologized for the 'accidental construction strikes' and said it had taken steps to increase oversight of construction teams. The Better Business Bureau in Texas had previously stripped Ezee Fiber of its BBB accreditation following unresolved damage complaints.

projects.name: Lexington SC Ripple Fiber Gas Line Strikes (Woodcreek)
projects.description: Ripple Fiber hit three Dominion Energy gas lines in under two weeks in Lexington's Woodcreek neighborhood, forcing evacuations and triggering a stop-work order.
projects.detail: In January 2025, Ripple Fiber struck three Dominion Energy gas lines in less than two weeks in the Woodcreek neighborhood of Lexington, South Carolina, forcing residents to evacuate. The Town of Lexington issued a stop-work order. The order was lifted in March 2025 after Ripple Fiber CEO Greg Wilson committed to improving safety protocols and working more closely with utility providers. However, this was just the beginning of Lexington's fiber troubles -- Kinetic Fiber later struck gas lines in the same Woodcreek neighborhood in April 2026, and Lumos Fiber had struck a water main in the Murraywood subdivision in September 2024. Lexington has now issued stop-work orders to three different fiber companies.

projects.name: Lexington SC Kinetic Fiber Gas Main Break (Woodcreek)
projects.description: Kinetic Fiber struck a 2-inch Dominion Energy gas main in Lexington, forcing a shelter-in-place order and becoming the third fiber company to receive a stop-work order in the town.
projects.detail: On April 23, 2026, Kinetic Fiber damaged a 2-inch Dominion Energy gas main in the Woodcreek neighborhood of Lexington, South Carolina, forcing residents to shelter-in-place. The Town of Lexington issued a stop-work order -- the third such order issued to a fiber company in recent years. The mayor noted Kinetic Fiber had a history of violations in the town. The stop-work order remained in place pending a meeting between the Town, Dominion Energy, and Lexington County Fire Service. This incident occurred in the same neighborhood where Ripple Fiber had struck three gas lines in January 2025, highlighting a systemic coordination failure between fiber installers and existing utility infrastructure.

projects.name: Lumos Fiber Murraywood Sinkhole (Lexington County, SC)
projects.description: Lumos Fiber subcontractors struck a water main while installing fiber in the Murraywood subdivision, creating a large sinkhole and leaving homes without water for hours.
projects.detail: On September 11, 2024, subcontractors working for Lumos Fiber (owned by T-Mobile) struck a water main line while installing fiber optic cable in the Murraywood subdivision of Lexington County, South Carolina. The break created a large sinkhole that made the street impassable and left several homes without water for hours. Lumos blamed the incident on 'inaccurate utility locates' and paused construction. Lexington County's Public Works Department ordered an immediate cessation of all Lumos work in the county, requiring a corrective action plan before resuming. Water issues persisted in the neighborhood months later, with residents reporting continued problems through February 2025.

projects.name: Floyd County IN Lumos Fiber Stop-Work Order
projects.description: Floyd County Commissioners twice ordered Lumos Fiber to stop all work after repeated gas and water line strikes across Clark and Floyd counties affected 80,000 planned homes.
projects.detail: Lumos Fiber of Indiana had planned to build 1,200 miles of fiber lines to reach 81,000 homes across Clark and Floyd counties. However, since work began, multiple neighborhoods reported property damage, unfilled holes, and cut utility lines. Lumos crews hit a water main in New Albany on June 27, 2025, leaving about 70 residents without water for six hours. On July 2, Lumos crews struck a six-inch gas main in Fairdale, Kentucky while working in the area. Floyd County Commissioners issued a stop-work order on June 30, the second such order they had issued to Lumos. The New Albany Township Fire Protection District raised public safety concerns, and the county required Lumos to present an improved operations plan before allowing supervised resumption of work.

projects.name: Sellersburg IN T-Mobile/Lumos Fiber Utility Strikes
projects.description: Fiber installation contractors for T-Mobile/Lumos hit gas and water lines repeatedly in Sellersburg neighborhoods, including two water line breaks in a single day.
projects.detail: In December 2024 and January 2025, contractors installing fiber optic lines for T-Mobile (via Lumos Fiber) in Sellersburg, Indiana struck multiple utility lines in residential neighborhoods. On December 23, crews hit a water line and then hit another water line the same day, flooding part of the street. Lumos also caused a gas leak by striking a main gas line while digging, shutting off service for approximately 200 customers. Residents expressed serious safety concerns, with one neighbor saying she feared her home would explode. The incidents were part of a broader pattern that led Floyd County to halt fiber optic work and ultimately resulted in a judge issuing an immediate stop-work order.

projects.name: Clinton LA Gas Line Rupture (Fiber Drilling)
projects.description: A fiber optic drilling crew punctured a gas line 13 feet deep in Clinton, cutting gas service to 300 families and requiring manual relighting of pilot lights across town.
projects.detail: In December 2025, a company performing fiber optic drilling in Clinton, Louisiana accidentally punctured a natural gas line buried 13 feet underground. The damage was so severe that gas to the entire town had to be blocked, and all meters to residences and businesses were shut off, affecting approximately 300 families. Once the line was repaired, every home without automatic ignition systems needed their pilot light manually relit by utility workers -- a process that took hours. Officials noted that the incident revealed a greater systemic issue: Louisiana does not have many of its utility lines clearly mapped, making fiber construction especially hazardous.

projects.name: Albuquerque Fiber Construction Moratorium (Ezee/Vexus/Gigapower)
projects.description: Albuquerque issued stop-work orders to three fiber companies and enacted a citywide construction moratorium after gas line strikes, flooding, and over $100,000 in damage to a single home.
projects.detail: In 2024-2025, Albuquerque became a cautionary tale for fiber broadband construction. Gigapower received a stop-work order in December 2024, Vexus Fiber in March 2025, and Ezee Fiber in May 2025. Mayor Tim Keller accused the companies of running 'roughshod' over neighborhoods. Residents reported flooding, ruptured gas lines, cut water lines, open holes left improperly covered, and destroyed yards.
