One resident reported Ezee Fiber caused more than $100,000 in damages after crews hit a water pipe. A Vexus subcontractor hit a gas line and failed to follow state pipeline safety requirements. City councilors voted on May 19, 2025 to establish a moratorium on new fiber work and created a working group to overhaul the permitting code. Both Vexus and Ezee were allowed to resume in July 2025.

projects.name: Orland Park IL Fiber Construction Shutdown (Astound/Zayo)
projects.description: Orland Park shut down all fiber optic construction after an Astound incident knocked out power to 300 homes, implementing new mandatory safety rules for all providers.
projects.detail: On December 12, 2025, the Village of Orland Park ordered Astound, Abovenet (Zayo Group), and other internet service providers to halt all fiber-optic construction after a surge in resident complaints about unsafe, incomplete, and disruptive work. The shutdown was triggered by a December 8 incident where Astound's work knocked out power to approximately 300 homes, resulting in a municipal ordinance citation. In response, the Village implemented new rules including work area limits, mandatory certified mail notification before beginning work, expanded fines for utility disruptions and delayed site restoration, and automatic stop-work orders for non-compliant companies.

projects.name: Lantana TX Spectrum Fiber Utility Damage (PUC Complaint)
projects.description: Two Lantana water districts filed a PUC complaint against Spectrum after fiber installation caused daily or weekly damage to water, sewer, gas, and electric lines.
projects.detail: In January 2025, Denton County Fresh Water Supply Districts Nos. 6 and 7 filed a complaint with the Public Utility Commission of Texas against Spectrum Communications over extensive damage caused during fiber optic cable installation in the Lantana master-planned community. The complaint stated that 'on a weekly and sometimes daily basis, existing irrigation lines, water lines, sewer lines, electric lines, gas lines, and other communication lines are damaged, greatly impacting residents' property and creating safety issues.' The water districts implemented protective measures, requiring Spectrum to video each sewer lateral from each lot they cross to ensure boring did not damage the sewer connection from homes to the city main.

projects.name: Round Rock/Leander TX Spectrum Fiber Gas Strikes
projects.description: Spectrum fiber crews in Central Texas ruptured gas lines and sprinkler systems in multiple neighborhoods, prompting an investigation and company policy changes.
projects.detail: In 2023-2024, homeowners in Round Rock and Leander, Texas reported extensive property damage from Spectrum crews installing fiber optic lines for internet, mobile, and TV service. In one incident, a Spectrum crew digging near a Leander home ruptured a gas line while installing fiber and did not notify the homeowner about the damage. Other residents reported broken sprinkler systems and property damage spanning months. A KXAN investigation published in March 2024 documented the pattern of complaints, prompting Spectrum to make operational changes and at least one city to examine its oversight procedures.

projects.name: Williamson County TX Spectrum Fiber Sewer Flood
projects.description: Spectrum fiber installation crews hit a sewer line in the Parkside at Mayfield Ranch community, flooding a family's home with sewage water and displacing them.
projects.detail: During Spectrum's fiber optic installation in Williamson County, Texas, crews in the Parkside at Mayfield Ranch community struck a sewer line, flooding the first floor of a family of five's home with sewage water. The family was forced to stay with relatives while repairs were made. In a separate incident, a resident reported that after Spectrum's installation disrupted her gas service, she unknowingly called a plumber who installed two new water heaters costing nearly $5,000 before she realized the gas had been shut off during Spectrum's work. Spectrum said it was working with neighbors and the HOA to fix the issues, but the incidents raised broader concerns about contractor oversight.

projects.name: Longwood FL WOW! Fiber Water Main Breaks
projects.description: WOW! fiber installation caused a major water main break in a Longwood cul-de-sac, part of over a dozen underground utility strikes in the city in early 2026.
projects.detail: In April 2026, telecom contractors preparing to run conduit for WOW! (WideOpenWest) fiber internet in Longwood's Hidden Oak Estates cracked an underground water main, sending water gushing into a retention pond for hours. Crews worked through the night to dig deep enough to access and repair the main, ripping up pavement and curbs. Longwood had logged more than a dozen underground utility strikes in 2026, with three classified as serious. The city took action by planning to serve as the primary point of contact for affected homeowners and requiring more thorough inspections before work begins. WOW! dropped its subcontractor and promised new oversight after the repeated water main breaks.

projects.name: DeLand FL Fiber Water Main Crater
projects.description: A MasTec fiber contractor boring for cable breached a water main in DeLand, creating a 20-foot-wide, 7-foot-deep crater, triggering boil water notices, and road closures.
projects.detail: On April 13, 2026, a MasTec contractor boring in DeLand, Florida for fiber optic cable installation breached a water main at the intersection of State Road 15A and Euclid Avenue. The break created a crater roughly 20 feet wide and up to 7 feet deep, closing Euclid Avenue overnight. A boil water notice was issued for the surrounding area. City Commissioner Richard Paiva expressed concern over the growing frequency of water main breaks from fiber optic installers, noting that two breaks happened in a single day. Three companies -- T-Mobile/Tillman Fiber, Wire 3, and AT&T -- were simultaneously laying fiber underground in the area, compounding the coordination challenges.

projects.name: Missouri City TX Ezee Fiber Gas Leak
projects.description: A subcontractor for Ezee Fiber struck a gas line in Missouri City, prompting the city to halt all fiber work and overhaul its infrastructure design manual before allowing resumption.
projects.detail: In February 2026, a subcontractor for Ezee Fiber struck a gas line during fiber optic installation in Missouri City, Texas. The city immediately stopped all active Ezee Fiber right-of-way work permits citywide. The project was suspended for approximately two months while the city reviewed safety practices and considered amendments to its infrastructure design manual that would require additional requirements for right-of-way permits for all utility companies. Construction resumed in late April 2026 with new safety rules and stricter oversight. The Missouri City council also rejected a Sienna agreement renewal related to the gas leak incident.

projects.name: Turlock CA Race Communications Fiber Damage
projects.description: Turlock increased oversight of Race Communications' fiber installation after complaints of property damage, incomplete restoration, and work outside permitted areas.
projects.detail: In 2026, the City of Turlock responded to mounting complaints from residents about property damage caused by Race Communications' fiber optic installation work. The city received reports of property damage, incomplete restoration, inadequate notification prior to construction, and work taking place outside approved easement and right-of-way areas. City staff escalated oversight efforts, conducting field inspections and holding contractors accountable to permit requirements. Enforcement steps included requiring Race Communications to address all reported property damage, complete restoration to city standards, improve communication with residents, and ensure all work remains within permitted areas. Officials warned that work could be suspended if compliance did not improve.

projects.name: Lumos Fiber Columbia SC Water Main Breaks (Springhurst)
projects.description: Lumos Fiber was temporarily barred from Columbia after causing gas and water leaks, then upon returning hit five more water mains in the Sandhills area, creating another sinkhole.
projects.detail: Lumos Fiber was temporarily barred from constructing its fiber network in Columbia, South Carolina in 2023 after its work led to gas and water leaks. Upon returning, the company's work caused four water main breaks in the Sandhills/Springhurst area in a single week, plus a separate break in the Meadowlark area, and created a sinkhole in a resident's driveway. Columbia Water confirmed the damage. Lumos stated the breaks were 'all due to lines being unmarked or mismarked,' but the pattern of repeated incidents -- spanning multiple neighborhoods and years -- raised questions about the adequacy of the company's safety protocols beyond just relying on utility locate markings. The city of Columbia and Lexington County have both taken enforcement actions against the company.

projects.name: Google Fiber Kansas City Kirkwood Condos Gas Evacuation
projects.description: A Google Fiber contractor struck a gas line near 50th and Wornall Road, triggering the evacuation of 75-100 residents at the Kirkwood Condominiums for four hours.
projects.detail: During Google Fiber's initial buildout in Kansas City, a contractor hit a gas line near Wornall Road and 50th Street, triggering the evacuation of 75 to 100 people from the Kirkwood Condominiums for roughly four hours. The incident was one of multiple gas line strikes during Google Fiber's aggressive construction timeline in the Kansas City metro area. Google stated that crews call 811 before digging, but acknowledged that lines are sometimes not properly marked. The disruptions were part of a broader pattern of construction-related issues as Google Fiber modernized Kansas City's telecommunications infrastructure, with the city's 311 system logging numerous complaints about property damage and unsafe conditions.

projects.name: Lumos Fiber Lexington County Laurel Meadows Water Strikes (SC)
projects.description: Lumos Fiber repeatedly struck water lines in the Laurel Meadows subdivision, prompting county inspectors to intervene and demand a corrective action plan.
projects.detail: In October 2025, Lumos Fiber struck water lines repeatedly during construction in the Laurel Meadows subdivision of Lexington County, South Carolina. After multiple reports of water line strikes, the county sent inspectors and demanded a corrective action plan from both Lumos and utility provider Blue Granite Water. Lumos voluntarily halted work in the neighborhood, claiming most strikes resulted from improperly marked or unmarked utility lines. Workers were also accused of using residents' bushes as a bathroom. The company had already been ordered to stop work in the neighboring Murraywood subdivision in September 2024 after a water main strike caused a sinkhole. The pattern of repeated incidents across multiple subdivisions raised questions about Lumos's construction practices statewide.

projects.name: MARTA Rapid A-Line BRT (Summerhill)
projects.description: MARTA's first BRT line saw its budget more than double from $58M to $122.9M after crews discovered undocumented, shallow waterlines in downtown Atlanta and along Hank Aaron Drive.
projects.detail: The five-mile Summerhill BRT route connecting downtown Atlanta to the southside BeltLine was originally budgeted at $58 million with a summer 2025 opening. During construction, crews encountered numerous undocumented utility lines that were not on any maps, as well as waterlines buried far shallower than expected. These discoveries along Hank Aaron Drive and downtown forced repeated redesigns and workarounds. The project cost ballooned to $122.9 million and full completion was pushed to fall 2026. The City of Atlanta, which funds the project through a voter-approved half-penny sales tax, demanded detailed financial reports before approving additional funds.

projects.name: I-94 East-West Reconstruction (Milwaukee)
projects.description: Utility negotiations drove up the cost of Milwaukee's I-94 East-West corridor expansion by $150 million, pushing the 3.5-mile project to $1.65 billion.
projects.detail: The I-94 East-West Corridor reconstruction in Milwaukee County will expand approximately 3.5 miles of outdated interstate between 70th Street and 16th Street from six to eight lanes, replacing pavement and bridges dating to the 1960s. Utility negotiations drove up the anticipated cost by about $150 million, pushing the total to $1.65 billion. Construction is phased over multiple years specifically to manage material cost escalation, labor constraints, existing utility challenges, and coordination with nearby railroad and cemetery lands. The west leg runs through 2028, while east leg and stadium interchange work begins in 2027 and continues through 2032. The project includes the Stadium Interchange and five local interchanges, with utility relocation as a critical early phase in 2025.

projects.name: I-285/SR 400 Interchange Reconstruction
projects.description: GDOT's $800M interchange project was delayed one year after crews discovered unmarked underground utilities requiring relocation, adding $43 million in extra work.
projects.detail: The massive reconstruction of the I-285 interchange at Georgia 400 north of Atlanta was originally estimated at $800 million. During construction, GDOT discovered unmarked utilities that had to be relocated, a common but costly problem on large construction projects. The combined cost of all extra work, including utility relocation, bike and pedestrian trails, and local road improvements, totaled about $43 million. This utility discovery resulted in a one-year delay in the completion of the interchange. It was the second delay for the project, as an earlier decision to expand the scope by adding two new bridges on I-285 had previously extended the project by six months.

projects.name: I-495/I-270 Managed Lanes (Capital Beltway)
projects.description: WSSC Water estimated it would cost $1.3-$2 billion to relocate 70 miles of large water and sewer pipes for Maryland's $9-11 billion Beltway/I-270 widening project.
projects.detail: Maryland's plan to add toll managed lanes to the Capital Beltway (I-495) and I-270 is the largest proposed P3 highway project in North America, estimated at $9-11 billion. WSSC Water, the utility serving Prince George's and Montgomery counties, disclosed that relocating its infrastructure would cost between $1.3 billion and $2 billion, far exceeding MDOT's estimate of $900 million. The piping around the Beltway area is the heart of the WSSC system, with 70 miles of large water and sewer mains requiring relocation. WSSC estimated the cost would translate to $2,250 per household over 20 years, potentially increasing water rates by 277% over four decades. MDOT has been coordinating with 21 utilities and private companies, but the question of who bears the relocation costs remains contentious under a 1958 memorandum of understanding.

projects.name: Blue Line Extension Light Rail (Minneapolis)
projects.description: Minneapolis's Blue Line extension tripled from $1.5B to $3.2B, with major Xcel Energy transmission lines in the North Loop requiring relocation at unknown cost.
projects.detail: The Blue Line light-rail extension connecting downtown Minneapolis to Brooklyn Park has tripled in estimated cost from approximately $1.5 billion to between $2.9 and $3.2 billion, with the timeline pushed from a 2022 opening to 2030 or later. A major new obstacle emerged when two major Xcel Energy underground electric transmission lines were found to require relocation in Minneapolis's North Loop neighborhood to make way for the project. These lines provide power to parts of downtown Minneapolis, and officials are unclear how much relocation would cost or how long it would take. The Met Council has been unable to provide detailed cost estimates for the utility relocation. State lawmakers frustrated by delays and cost overruns enlisted MnDOT to take a bigger role in the project, a move motivated by the troubled Southwest Green Line extension that ballooned from $1.25 billion to $2.9 billion.

projects.name: Sound Transit Stride BRT Program
projects.description: Sound Transit's Stride BRT program costs rose from $1.7B to $2.7B with years of delays, as station utility relocations and infrastructure conflicts drove repeated budget revisions.
projects.detail: Sound Transit's Stride bus rapid transit program, originally estimated at $1.7-1.8 billion in the 2016 ST3 plan, saw costs escalate to $2.7 billion by 2023 -- a 32% increase above 2016 assumptions after controlling for inflation. The I-405 BRT corridor alone has an approved budget of $1.27 billion. Costs jumped 7-31% in just months during 2023, with the NE 85th Street/I-405 interchange alone costing over $287 million for one freeway station pair. Relocating utilities around BRT stations and coordinating with existing highway infrastructure contributed to delays. Committee chair frustration was public: an 'extra $200 million and several years to a project that was supposed to be the cheap fast one.' The S1/S3 lines are now projected for mid-2028, the S2 line for mid-2029.

projects.name: Silver Line Phase 2 (Dulles Extension)
projects.description: The $3B Silver Line Phase 2 to Dulles Airport was delayed four years, with protracted utility relocations cited as a factor that consumed the $551M contingency fund.
projects.detail: The Silver Line Phase 2, extending Metro rail 11.5 miles to Dulles Airport and into Loudoun County, was originally projected to cost $2.79 billion with an 2018 completion. During eight years of construction, the project recorded multiple problems, cost overruns, and four years of delays. The cost overrun pushed the budget past $3 billion, and the full two-phase Silver Line project totaled $6.01 billion. Protracted utility relocation timelines contributed to delays, as various utilities took longer than expected to relocate their facilities. Phase 1, which opened in 2014, still had unfinished utility relocation work. The approved $551 million contingency fund was entirely consumed by overruns before additional funding was approved. The extension finally opened November 15, 2022.

projects.name: Richmond Highway BRT Utility Undergrounding (Fairfax County)
projects.description: Utility undergrounding for the Richmond Highway BRT would add $264M and two years of delay; Verizon, Dominion, and other utility relocations require 12-24 months before construction can start.
projects.detail: Fairfax County's Richmond Highway 'The One' BRT system, a $987 million project serving 9 stations along 7.4 miles of Route 1, faces major utility coordination challenges. Undergrounding overhead utilities would increase costs by at least $264 million ($136 million for construction plus $128 million for inflation during a two-year delay), with the county solely responsible for financing. The county has received $330 million from NVTA but is seeking an additional $463 million. Utility relocation work is currently underway with Verizon beginning in spring 2026, and total utility relocation activities are expected to take 12-24 months before BRT construction can begin in 2028. The BRT project completion has been pushed to 2032 due to utility sequencing, and the related Route 1 widening to 2031. The project exemplifies how transit and road widening on the same corridor creates compounding utility coordination challenges.

projects.name: Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 Utility Advance
projects.description: The MTA awarded a $182M utility relocation contract as the first Phase 2 component, learning from Phase 1 where $130M in overruns were blamed on unmapped underground infrastructure.
projects.detail: The MTA awarded a $182 million utility relocation contract to C.A.C. Industries in January 2024 as the first construction component of the $7.7 billion Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 project. This advance utility work was a direct lesson learned from Phase 1, where the Inspector General blamed $130 million in cost overruns on underground utility issues. New York City has some of the most complex underground utility networks in the world, much of which is unmapped, and these can add enormous delays and costs once projects are underway. By advancing utility relocation ahead of station and tunnel construction, the MTA aims to reduce the risk of unexpected costs. The MTA reports this proactive approach has already enabled pending work to start six months faster than originally scheduled, contributing to more than $1 billion in savings compared to Phase 1 benchmarks.

projects.name: I-26 Connector (Asheville)
projects.description: Bids for the I-26 Connector came in $184M+ over projections; NCDOT switched to a flyover design to avoid relocating utilities, saving 15 months of construction time.
projects.detail: The I-26 Connector project in Asheville, North Carolina has been in planning for 37 years with about $100 million already spent before construction began. When bids were opened, the lowest came in at least $184 million higher than the projected cost of $915.8 million, likely delaying the project and pushing its price higher. A key factor was the significant cost of utility relocation. NCDOT changed from an underpass to a flyover bridge design specifically to avoid having to relocate utilities, which saved an estimated $63 million and 15 months of construction time. An effort to change the overpass back to an underpass would have required relocating utility lines with a third party, potentially delaying the project at least 15 months or perhaps indefinitely. The revised approach brought total estimated costs to $1.023 billion.

projects.name: I-26 Widening (Columbia to Charleston)
projects.description: South Carolina's 70-mile I-26 widening grew from $2.02B to $3.03B, with utility relocations along each phase requiring six months before dirt can be moved.
projects.detail: The widening of Interstate 26 between Columbia and Charleston, South Carolina grew from $2.02 billion in 2022 to $3.03 billion, a 50% increase driven by inflation and construction cost escalation. The project will widen 70 miles of I-26 from four to six lanes. For each construction segment, actual construction cannot begin until rights-of-way are cleared and utilities are relocated along the stretch, a process that takes about six months per phase. Governor McMaster requested an additional $1.1 billion for road and bridge work to offset rising construction costs, with $600 million dedicated to covering higher costs for ongoing interstate widening. The complexity of sequencing utility relocations across 70 miles of active interstate adds scheduling risk to an already-strained timeline.

projects.name: I-10 Calcasieu River Bridge Replacement
projects.description: The $2.3B I-10 Calcasieu River Bridge replacement in Lake Charles began with utility coordination and roadway improvements as its first construction activities on a decades-delayed project.
projects.detail: The I-10 Calcasieu River Bridge Replacement project is a $2.3 billion public-private partnership that broke ground on April 29, 2026, replacing a 1950s-era structure that predates the Interstate highway system. The project had been delayed for years by funding disputes and legislative opposition. Construction activity is beginning with utility coordination, roadway improvements, and early foundation work while the existing bridge remains in service. The project focuses on geotechnical stability, utility coordination, and modern structural design along one of the nation's most critical freight and energy corridors. Costs have escalated significantly from earlier estimates, with the project originally projected at $3-3.5 billion before Governor Landry's redesign brought it down 25%. Utility infrastructure embedded in the existing bridge approaches and interchange ramps must be relocated before new construction can proceed.

projects.name: Route 28/Yarmouth Road Intersection (Hyannis)
projects.description: A $17.9M Cape Cod intersection reconstruction is in its fourth year at only 60% complete, with Eversource, Comcast, and Verizon utility relocations delaying the schedule.
projects.detail: The $17.9 million Route 28 and Yarmouth Road intersection project in Hyannis, Massachusetts involves extensive utility relocation that has severely impacted the contractor's schedule. The project, now in its fourth year, is only about 60% complete. Eversource, Comcast, and Verizon are conducting utility relocations for the intersection reconstruction, but progress depends on the third-party utility companies' schedules and availability. The completion date has been extended to spring 2026, well beyond the original timeline. The project extends along Route 28 from Cedar Street to Engine House Road across from Cape Cod Gateway Airport, and the slow pace of multi-utility coordination has become a prominent example of how conflicting utility schedules delay even modest highway projects.

projects.name: Cape Cod Canal Bridges Replacement (Bourne & Sagamore)
projects.description: The $4.5B replacement of the Bourne and Sagamore bridges requires relocating a major Algonquin gas transmission pipeline under the Cape Cod Canal, adding complexity and cost risk.
projects.detail: Replacing the aging Bourne and Sagamore bridges over the Cape Cod Canal is estimated to cost $4.541 billion, with the Sagamore Bridge alone at $2.31 billion. The project includes a massive utility relocation scope, headlined by the Algonquin Gas Transmission pipeline. The relocation involves installing a 2.2-mile 18-inch gas line under the Canal, a 0.35-mile gas line under the existing Sagamore Bridge, a 3.4-mile 16-inch gas line from the Bourne facility to Sagamore, and four new Metering and Regulating Stations. MassDOT presented the major utility relocation agreement at its January 2025 board meeting, highlighting the complex coordination between a federally-funded bridge project and a major interstate natural gas transmission system. The multi-year coordination window for utility relocation adds schedule risk.

projects.name: I-35 NEX Central (San Antonio)
projects.description: The $1.5B I-35 NEX Central project must relocate numerous existing utilities while building elevated lanes in a confined urban corridor; no utility-caused cost or schedule impact is documented.
projects.detail: The I-35 Northeast Expansion (NEX) Central project is a $1.5 billion project covering about 22 miles of improvements along I-35, including portions of I-410 North and Loop 1604, in a densely populated corridor with limited right-of-way. Ferrovial lists the construction of elevated lanes in a confined space and the relocation of numerous existing utilities among the project's unique challenges, along with maintaining TxDOT's intelligent transportation systems while minimizing disruption to interstate traffic. Construction began in 2022 with completion expected in late 2027.

projects.name: I-35 Capital Express Central (Austin)
projects.description: Austin's $5.6B I-35 reconstruction includes utility relocation as a critical early construction package, with the project's cap-and-stitch elements alone jumping 61% to $1.4B.
projects.detail: The I-35 Capital Express Central project through Austin is TxDOT's signature megaproject, growing from an initial $4.5 billion to $5.6 billion. The project will lower the mainlanes, remove upper decks, and add managed lanes through the heart of the city. An 'advanced construction package' scheduled for 2027 includes overpass work and utility relocations as critical early activities. The planned caps over portions of the highway saw costs balloon from $868 million to $1.4 billion, a 61% increase driven by inflation and scope changes. Utility relocation is a prerequisite for much of the lowered-mainlane construction, as the extensive underground utility network beneath downtown Austin must be moved before the roadway can be depressed below grade. The project is expected to take about a decade to complete.

projects.name: I-30 Canyon Improvement Project
projects.description: The $888M I-30 Canyon reconstruction through Dallas encountered utility delays that postponed bridge demolition from its original schedule, impacting the five-year project timeline.
projects.detail: The I-30 Canyon Improvement Project is an $888 million, 2.3-mile reconstruction of Interstate 30 through downtown Dallas, awarded to Balfour Beatty Infrastructure. The project eliminates outdated collector-distributor lanes and dangerous left-hand exits while restoring local street connections. Utility issues forced the postponement of the Elm Street bridge demolition from its original February start date to summer, disrupting the construction sequence. The project requires relocating and coordinating with several major regional utilities embedded in the urban core. Additionally, the overall costs for the I-30 corridor have grown significantly from earlier estimates, with the scope and complexity of downtown utility networks being a contributing factor. The five-year project runs from 2026 to 2031.

projects.name: West Catawba Avenue Widening
projects.description: A $34.6M road widening faces multi-year delays as Charlotte Water, Piedmont Natural Gas, AT&T, and Spectrum utility relocations all compete for limited right-of-way.
projects.detail: The West Catawba Avenue widening project in Cornelius, North Carolina is expected to cost $34.6 million with a minimum three-year construction period. Both the Town of Cornelius and NCDOT have acknowledged multi-year delays caused by right-of-way acquisition and utility relocation challenges. Pipes and lines used by Charlotte Water, Piedmont Natural Gas, AT&T, and Spectrum all need to be relocated, along with overhead electric lines that must be moved to accommodate the wider road. The project illustrates how coordinating multiple utility companies, each with their own relocation timelines and requirements, compounds delays. NCDOT indicates the construction contract will not be let until December 2027, years later than originally planned. The sheer number of utility owners and the below-ground and above-ground infrastructure in the corridor have made coordination the project's primary bottleneck.

projects.name: I-35 Waco Rebuild (Phase 4B)
projects.description: TxDOT's $234M I-35 rebuild through Waco required relocating 55 major water/wastewater utilities including 13 bores across the interstate before mainlane construction could begin.
projects.detail: The four-year, $234 million Interstate 35 rebuild through southern Waco covers about 3 miles of interstate mainlanes and frontage roads including several bridges. The project began with the massive task of relocating 55 major water and wastewater utilities, including 13 bores across IH 35. Utility relocations had to be completed before the mainlane construction could begin, and it was not until summer that traffic could be shifted to allow reconstruction. TxDOT prioritized utility relocations by examining phasing and using technology for mapping alternative scenarios when timely relocation was uncertain, learning from delays experienced on similar projects in nearby Salado, Belton, and Temple. The proactive approach to utility coordination was a direct response to schedule overruns on earlier Central Texas highway projects.

projects.name: I-75/I-24 Interchange Reconstruction (Chattanooga)
projects.description: The $328M interchange reconstruction encountered an unmarked Piedmont gas main requiring 45 days of relocation, while CSX railroad coordination pushed completion into 2026.
projects.detail: The $328 million two-phase reconstruction of the I-75/I-24 interchange in Chattanooga, Tennessee was designed to fix what locals called the worst interchange in the region. During construction, crews encountered an unmarked portion of a Piedmont gas main that had to be relocated, with Piedmont proposing a roughly 45-day construction schedule to move the line. Additionally, required coordination with CSX railroad for bridge construction caused further delays, potentially pushing completion into spring 2026. The project is part of a broader pattern of Tennessee infrastructure cost overruns, with the I-75 widening project elsewhere in the state growing from $1.8 billion to $2.3 billion, raising concerns about systemic issues within TDOT's project management.

projects.name: I-75 Widening (Eastern Tennessee Corridor)
projects.description: Tennessee's I-75 widening project grew from $1.8B to $2.3B amid mounting evidence of project management issues and utility-related cost factors across the corridor.
projects.detail: The I-75 widening project in eastern Tennessee, designed to relieve traffic congestion across the corridor, was originally budgeted at $1.8 billion but is now projected to exceed $2.3 billion, representing a 28% cost overrun. Preliminary reports suggest the problem is indicative of broader systemic issues within TDOT's project management capabilities. Utility coordination challenges compound the escalating costs, as the corridor passes through areas with complex underground infrastructure. The cost increases are not isolated to I-75; concerns are emerging about the Memphis River Parkway project and Nashville airport improvements showing similar patterns. State legislators have demanded accountability as infrastructure project costs spiral across Tennessee.

projects.name: East San Fernando Valley Light Rail
projects.description: The $3.6B light rail project requires six months of utility relocation closures along Van Nuys Boulevard, with underground power, gas, and drainage adjustments continuing through 2028.
projects.detail: The East San Fernando Valley Light Rail Transit Project is a $3.573 billion, 9.2-mile light rail line along Van Nuys Boulevard, supported by an $893 million federal grant executed in late 2024. Utility relocation is the project's first major construction activity, requiring intermittent one-directional traffic closures along Van Nuys Boulevard for roughly six months from January through June 2026. Underground adjustments to power, gas, and drainage systems are scheduled to continue through 2028. Metro and utility partners are conducting utility investigation and relocation work ahead of heavy civil construction, which is slated to begin in late spring 2026. The project learned from earlier LA Metro experiences where unexpected utility conflicts caused costly delays, deliberately separating utility relocation into a distinct early phase to minimize schedule risk.

projects.name: Tucson Modern Streetcar (Sun Link)
projects.description: Tucson's $199M streetcar project was complicated by extensive underground utility relocation along the four-mile route, with overhead electrical work and repaving driving up costs.
projects.detail: The Tucson Sun Link Modern Streetcar, a four-mile streetcar line through downtown Tucson, cost $198.8 million with utility relocation contributing significantly to the high price tag. Underground utilities had to be moved from under the path of the tracks, overhead electrical connections were installed, and repaving was needed on much of the route. The complexity of utility work along the four-mile corridor drove up construction costs and timelines. Vehicle deliveries from manufacturer Vigor Works were also delayed nearly a year, resulting in $1.7 million in liquidated damages. The first car was due in July 2013 but arrived much later, with the last vehicle not arriving until April 2014. The combination of underground utility conflicts and supplier delays made the project a cautionary example of how utility relocation scope can compound other project challenges.

projects.name: Brent Spence Bridge Corridor (Companion Bridge)
projects.description: The $3.6B Brent Spence companion bridge project revised closure timelines to allow additional utility coordination near the construction site on the Ohio-Kentucky border.
projects.detail: The $3.6 billion Brent Spence Bridge Corridor project will construct a new double-deck companion bridge over the Ohio River to carry I-75/I-71 interstate through-traffic, while the existing bridge is reconfigured for local traffic. Funded by a $1.6 billion federal grant with costs split between Ohio and Kentucky, the project involves approximately eight miles of improved roadways. Early approach work includes utility relocations and preparation for bridge foundation work in the Ohio River. The timeline for upcoming closures has already been revised to allow additional time for utility coordination near the project site, with temporary and permanent closures of interstate ramps now expected to take place later than originally planned. The complexity of coordinating utility infrastructure across two states, a major river, and eight miles of interstate creates significant scheduling risk.

projects.name: I-285/I-20 East Interchange Reconstruction
projects.description: The $692M I-285/I-20 East interchange in Atlanta encountered undocumented utility lines during reconstruction, adding unplanned relocation costs to the four-year project.
projects.detail: The I-285/I-20 East interchange in DeKalb County underwent a four-year, $692 million reconstruction creating wider realigned ramps, new collector-distributor lanes, and auxiliary lanes. During construction, crews encountered undocumented utility lines that required unplanned relocation, a recurring issue on Atlanta-area interchange projects. The project was delivered as a public-private partnership and is part of Georgia's Major Mobility Investment Fund. The discovery of unmapped underground utilities in the interchange area mirrors the experience at the nearby I-285/SR 400 project, where $43 million in extra work was required. The I-285/I-20 West Interchange, a subsequent $1.2 billion project, is being planned with lessons learned from the East side's utility challenges.

projects.name: I-35 Denton Widening (Split to US-380)
projects.description: TxDOT's I-35 widening in Denton requires relocating 10,200 linear feet of City water and wastewater utilities, with weather and scheduling conflicts pushing utility work behind schedule.
projects.detail: TxDOT is widening Interstate 35 from the I-35E/I-35W Split to US-380 University Drive in Denton, involving the relocation of 10,200 linear feet of City of Denton water and wastewater utilities. Since the project forces relocation of city-owned utilities, TxDOT reimburses the city at 100%. Weather has caused delays, pushing utility relocation work behind schedule. Major highway projects in the northern Denton corridor, including the I-35 North 'merge' work, the Mayhill interchange, and the 288/380 connector, are all advancing slowly because of right-of-way holds, utility relocations, and constrained budgets. The coordinated sequencing of utility relocations with highway construction across multiple simultaneous Denton-area projects exemplifies the scheduling complexity of urban interstate expansion.

projects.name: Penn Street Bridge Rehabilitation (Reading)
projects.description: Bridge rehab plans required revision when UGI gas mains and PPL electric conduits attached to the bridge structure were found to be in worse condition than assessed, requiring full replacement rather than protection in place.
projects.detail: PennDOT's rehabilitation of the Penn Street Bridge in Reading was designed to protect existing utility attachments in place while replacing the bridge deck. Field inspection during early demolition revealed that UGI gas mains and PPL Electric conduits attached to the bridge superstructure were severely corroded and could not remain in service during construction. Both utilities required full replacement, which necessitated redesigned utility supports, temporary service bypasses, and coordination of outage windows with downtown businesses. The expanded scope added $6.8M in change orders and delayed the project by 16 months.

projects.name: Hartford Park River Flood Control Conduit Rehab
projects.description: Army Corps flood conduit rehabilitation plans were revised after discovering CL&P duct banks, MDC sewer interceptors, and telecom lines had been built through or adjacent to the conduit walls since original 1940s construction.
projects.detail: The US Army Corps of Engineers' rehabilitation of the Park River flood control conduit in Hartford, originally built in the 1940s, required extensive plan revisions when modern utilities were found to have been constructed through or immediately adjacent to the conduit walls over the intervening decades. Connecticut Light and Power duct banks, Metropolitan District Commission sewer interceptors, and AT&T fiber optic cables were attached to or passing through the conduit structure in locations not documented in any agency's records. Structural repairs had to be redesigned around each utility crossing, and several required temporary relocation during construction. The discoveries added $22M and 18 months to the project.

projects.name: New Bedford Route 18 Waterfront Corridor
projects.description: MassDOT's Route 18 waterfront corridor redesign was triggered by discovery of unmapped fish processing waste pipes, Eversource gas lines, and NSTAR conduits beneath the highway.
projects.detail: MassDOT's reconstruction of Route 18 through New Bedford's waterfront district was intended to reconnect downtown with the harbor. Early construction uncovered a network of unmapped waste pipes from historic fish processing operations, Eversource gas distribution lines at incorrect mapped locations, and NSTAR electric conduits that conflicted with proposed median and drainage improvements. The entire median drainage system was redesigned, and environmental remediation was required for contaminated fill around the abandoned pipes. Three separate plan revisions were issued over 22 months, adding $15M to the project cost.

projects.name: Scranton Lackawanna Avenue Streetscape
projects.description: Downtown streetscape plans revised when test pits revealed Pennsylvania American Water mains, UGI gas services, and trolley-era infrastructure conflicting with proposed tree pits and street lighting foundations.
projects.detail: The City of Scranton's Lackawanna Avenue streetscape improvement was designed to revitalize the downtown corridor with new street trees, decorative lighting, and widened sidewalks. Test pit excavations revealed Pennsylvania American Water cast iron mains in advanced deterioration, UGI gas services running at unexpected angles, and remnants of the city's early 1900s trolley system including rail ties and electrical conduits. Tree pit locations and lighting foundation designs were revised to avoid utility conflicts, and the water authority added emergency main replacement to the project scope. The combined revisions added $3.5M and 10 months.

projects.name: Frederick Douglass Tunnel Approach Utilities (Baltimore)
projects.description: Approach work for the new Amtrak tunnel delayed when BGE, Baltimore City DPW, and Verizon utility relocations could not be sequenced within Amtrak's Northeast Corridor possession windows.
projects.detail: The Frederick Douglass Tunnel project to replace the 1873 Baltimore and Potomac Tunnel required extensive utility relocations at both approach structures. BGE high-voltage transmission lines, Baltimore City DPW water and sewer mains, and Verizon fiber optic cables all needed to be relocated within constrained Amtrak possession windows. Amtrak could only provide weekend possessions for the work, but BGE required 72-hour continuous outage windows that spanned into Monday service. DPW's sewer bypass pumping created noise complaints that limited overnight work hours. The scheduling constraints meant utility relocations that were planned for 8 months took 18 months, adding $38M to the $4 billion project.

projects.name: Stamford Harbor Point Infrastructure Phase III
projects.description: Harbor Point infrastructure delayed when Eversource, Aquarion Water, and the city's own sewer department scheduled overlapping work in a corridor that could only accommodate one operation at a time.
projects.detail: The City of Stamford's Harbor Point Phase III infrastructure project required new water, sewer, electric, and telecom utilities in a narrow waterfront corridor. Eversource scheduled primary feeder installation for the same 4-month window as Aquarion Water's trunk main extension. The city's sewer department then scheduled interceptor work overlapping both. The waterfront corridor, constrained by building foundations on one side and the harbor bulkhead on the other, could physically accommodate only one excavation at a time. Three rounds of schedule negotiations were needed, each invalidating the previous construction sequence. The project lost two construction seasons, adding $11M and 14 months.

projects.name: Syracuse I-81 Viaduct Utility Pre-Relocation
projects.description: Advance utility relocation for the I-81 viaduct replacement was delayed 12 months when National Grid, OCWA, and Verizon could not coordinate work in the dense underground corridor beneath the elevated highway.
projects.detail: NYSDOT's advance utility relocation program for the I-81 viaduct replacement in Syracuse required moving National Grid gas mains, Onondaga County Water Authority transmission lines, and Verizon fiber optic cables from beneath the viaduct before demolition could begin. National Grid's gas main replacement required Verizon to temporarily support its duct bank, but Verizon's engineering review took 6 months. OCWA's water main relocation required National Grid's gas to be moved first to maintain safe separations. The three-way dependency created a critical path delay of 12 months before the main viaduct contract could proceed. The delay added $28M in escalation costs to the overall $2.25B project.

projects.name: Silver Spring Purple Line Station Utility Work
projects.description: Station area utility work delayed when WSSC Water, PEPCO, and Washington Gas could not coordinate relocations in the congested downtown Silver Spring underground, where six utilities share a single corridor.
projects.detail: Utility relocation work for the Purple Line's Silver Spring station area encountered severe scheduling conflicts in downtown Silver Spring, where WSSC Water, PEPCO, Washington Gas, Comcast, Verizon, and the county's storm drain system share an extremely congested underground corridor. WSSC required a 6-month exclusive work zone for a 36-inch water main relocation, blocking PEPCO's planned conduit installation. Washington Gas could not begin its relocation until PEPCO's conduit was in place because the new gas main needed to reference PEPCO's final position for clearance requirements. Each utility's design was dependent on the others' as-built positions, creating an iterative process that added $15M and 14 months.

projects.name: Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit Utility Coordination
projects.description: GoTriangle's planned light rail between Durham and Chapel Hill saw costs balloon by $400 million partly due to utility relocation complexity before the project was ultimately canceled in 2019.
projects.detail: GoTriangle's 17.7-mile Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit project, initially estimated at $2.49 billion, saw its cost estimate grow to over $3.3 billion between 2016 and 2019. A significant portion of the cost increase was attributed to utility relocation requirements along the dense corridor, where Duke Energy, OWASA, and the City of Durham all had major underground infrastructure in the planned alignment. Duke Energy alone estimated $160 million for power line relocations. The inability to reach cost-sharing agreements with utility companies was cited as a contributing factor when the GoTriangle Board of Trustees voted to end the project in November 2019, after Durham County had already invested years of planning and the FTA had advanced the project through preliminary engineering.

projects.name: Alcoa Highway (SR 115) Improvements (Knox County)
projects.description: TDOT's Alcoa Highway improvement project was delayed 20 months because KUB, AT&T, and TVA could not coordinate their sequential utility relocations in the constrained corridor between the Tennessee River and the bluffs.
projects.detail: TDOT's $215 million Alcoa Highway improvement project between Knoxville and Alcoa faced 20 months of delays due to utility scheduling failures in the geographically constrained corridor between the Tennessee River and adjacent bluffs. Knoxville Utilities Board needed to relocate water, gas, and electric infrastructure but required TVA approval for any work near the transmission right-of-way, which took 8 months. AT&T's fiber relocation depended on KUB's pole relocation, but KUB could not move poles until TVA approved the new alignment. The narrow corridor offered no space for temporary utility easements that would have allowed parallel work. TDOT's project was further complicated by the need to maintain access to UT Medical Center throughout construction, limiting available work windows.

projects.name: Norfolk Naval Station Vicinity Gas Line Rupture
projects.description: A road construction contractor struck a Virginia Natural Gas high-pressure main near Naval Station Norfolk, forcing evacuation of 200 residents and shutting down base access for 6 hours.
projects.detail: During road reconstruction on Hampton Boulevard near Naval Station Norfolk, a contractor's excavator struck a 6-inch Virginia Natural Gas high-pressure main that was 4 feet from its recorded position. The gas leak forced evacuation of approximately 200 residents in the Larchmont-Edgewater neighborhood and shut down the base's Gate 3 access point for 6 hours. Virginia Natural Gas crews took 8 hours to isolate and repair the main. The contractor had obtained 811 locate marks, but the marks did not match the actual pipe location. The incident triggered a Navy review of all utility records near base perimeters and delayed the road project by 3 months pending a complete re-survey of underground utilities along the corridor.
projects.budget: Road project delayed; evacuation and repair costs not disclosed

projects.name: Durham Bulls Athletic Park Area Gas Strike
projects.description: A fiber optic installation crew struck a Piedmont Natural Gas main near the Durham Bulls Athletic Park, forcing evacuation of a nearby hotel and American Tobacco Campus offices during a weekday lunch hour.
projects.detail: A subcontractor installing fiber optic cable for a broadband expansion project struck a 4-inch Piedmont Natural Gas main near the intersection of Blackwell and Pettigrew Streets, adjacent to the Durham Bulls Athletic Park. The strike occurred at 11:45 a.m. on a Tuesday, forcing evacuation of the 21c Museum Hotel and several American Tobacco Campus office buildings during the lunch hour. Approximately 500 workers and hotel guests were displaced for 4 hours while Piedmont Natural Gas crews made repairs. The fiber optic crew had called NC811, but the gas line was 3 feet from the marked location due to a previous relocation that was never updated in utility records. Durham's rapid downtown development has increased the density of underground utilities, making accurate location marking more critical.
projects.budget: Evacuation and repair costs not disclosed

projects.name: I-69 Finish Line (Section 6) Utility Conflicts
projects.description: Final section of I-69 between Bloomington and Indianapolis required extensive plan revisions due to undocumented utility crossings in the SR 37 corridor.
projects.detail: The I-69 Finish Line project converting State Road 37 to interstate standards encountered hundreds of utility conflicts not identified in original subsurface surveys. Duke Energy, Vectren, and multiple telecommunications providers had infrastructure crossing the corridor that did not match existing records. INDOT was forced to revise construction plans for 12 separate segments, adding $190M in change orders. The project's phased approach had to be restructured to accommodate sequential utility relocations that could not proceed in parallel as originally planned.

projects.name: Toledo Anthony Wayne Trail Reconstruction
projects.description: Major arterial reconstruction in Toledo required complete redesign after subsurface investigation revealed conflicting gas, water, and sewer infrastructure not shown on city utility maps.
projects.detail: ODOT's reconstruction of the Anthony Wayne Trail, a key corridor linking downtown Toledo to the southern suburbs, ran into serious problems during the design phase when potholing revealed that existing utility maps were grossly inaccurate. A 1940s-era combined sewer running diagonally under the roadway conflicted with planned storm drainage improvements, and a Columbia Gas transmission main was 8 feet shallower than records indicated. The project required a complete redesign of drainage and roadway profiles, adding $14M to the budget and delaying construction start by two years.

projects.name: Elgin O'Hare Western Access Phase II Utility Redesign
projects.description: Phase II of the Elgin O'Hare expressway project required major plan revisions when underground utility surveys revealed previously unmapped fiber optic trunk lines serving O'Hare Airport.
projects.detail: The Illinois Tollway's Phase II construction to extend the expressway encountered a critical fiber optic trunk line serving O'Hare Airport operations that was not documented in any utility records provided during the design phase. AT&T and multiple telecommunications carriers had installed redundant fiber routes beneath the planned interchange footprint. Relocating this infrastructure required coordination with FAA and airport operations, as any service interruption could affect air traffic control systems. The Tollway was forced to revise interchange geometry and staging plans, adding $85M in additional costs.

projects.name: Youngstown Federal Street Streetscape
projects.description: Youngstown's Federal Street downtown streetscape encountered abandoned utility infrastructure from demolished buildings, requiring redesign of planned tree wells, lighting, and drainage.
projects.detail: The revitalization of Federal Street in downtown Youngstown, funded partly through a state capital grant, encountered a maze of abandoned utility connections from buildings demolished decades earlier during urban renewal. Gas service lines, water laterals, and electrical conduits from at least 20 demolished structures remained in the ground, many still pressurized or energized. Dominion Energy Ohio had to dispatch crews to cap and abandon numerous gas service connections. The city had to redesign tree well locations, lighting conduit routes, and drainage tie-ins to work around the abandoned infrastructure, adding $3.2M in costs.

projects.name: Hamilton Dixie Highway Reconstruction
projects.description: Hamilton's Dixie Highway reconstruction required plan revisions when Duke Energy and Greater Cincinnati Water Works infrastructure was found at significantly different locations and depths than documented.
projects.detail: The City of Hamilton's reconstruction of a 2.5-mile stretch of Dixie Highway encountered major utility discrepancies between recorded and actual conditions. Duke Energy's underground electrical duct bank was found 4 feet closer to the roadway centerline than shown on records, and Greater Cincinnati Water Works' 16-inch transmission main was at a depth 3 feet shallower than documented. These discoveries required complete redesign of the roadway drainage system, relocation of proposed signal conduit routes, and revision of roadway cross-sections. Duke Energy's internal approval process for relocation design alone took 5 months, and cost-sharing disputes between the city, ODOT, and utilities prolonged negotiations.

projects.name: South Bend Lincoln Way West Reconstruction
projects.description: South Bend's Lincoln Way West reconstruction delayed 14 months because NIPSCO's gas main replacement and Indiana Michigan Power's underground cable upgrade could not be scheduled concurrently.
projects.detail: The reconstruction of Lincoln Way West, a major east-west corridor through South Bend, was delayed when NIPSCO and Indiana Michigan Power both needed to perform major utility upgrades in the same corridor but could not coordinate their schedules. NIPSCO required a 6-month window for gas main replacement that overlapped with I&M Power's planned underground cable installation. Neither utility would yield its preferred construction window, and city regulations prohibited simultaneous excavation on the same block. The sequential scheduling pushed road construction into a second winter season, increasing costs by $8M due to cold-weather concrete placement, extended traffic control, and mobilization charges.

projects.name: Columbus Parsons Avenue Corridor Improvement
projects.description: Columbus's Parsons Avenue improvement was delayed 18 months when Columbia Gas, AEP Ohio, and the city's water division all required sequential access to the corridor, each refusing to work during the other's construction window.
projects.detail: The Parsons Avenue corridor improvement project, a key COTA transit route enhancement from downtown to Nationwide Children's Hospital, encountered severe scheduling conflicts among three major utility providers. Columbia Gas needed to replace a 1950s-era main before AEP Ohio could relocate underground electrical conduit, which in turn had to be completed before the city water division could install a new water main. Each utility required exclusive access to the corridor and refused to work during another utility's active construction. The city's attempts to mediate a concurrent work plan failed due to safety concerns and union jurisdictional issues. The resulting sequential utility work consumed 22 months before road construction could begin.

projects.name: Lima Ottawa River Sewer Separation
projects.description: Lima's EPA consent decree sewer separation project was delayed 2 years because AEP Ohio and Columbia Gas could not schedule infrastructure relocations to keep pace with the phased sewer construction plan.
projects.detail: The City of Lima's federally mandated combined sewer overflow separation program along the Ottawa River corridor required relocation of AEP Ohio and Columbia Gas infrastructure in advance of sewer construction. However, both utilities had committed their construction crews to other regional projects and could not meet the city's phased schedule. AEP Ohio's delay in relocating overhead-to-underground electrical conversions held up three sewer construction phases. The city faced EPA scrutiny for missing consent decree milestones, ultimately negotiating a modified compliance schedule. The delays extended the overall program by 2 years and increased costs by $18M, largely due to inflation and extended project management expenses.

projects.name: Munster Ridge Road Corridor Widening
projects.description: Munster's Ridge Road widening project delayed 15 months when NIPSCO's gas main replacement schedule could not be synchronized with the Town's water main replacement and INDOT's road widening timeline.
projects.detail: The Town of Munster's plan to widen Ridge Road between Calumet Avenue and Hohman Avenue was delayed by scheduling conflicts between NIPSCO, the municipal water utility, and INDOT. NIPSCO had already committed its Northwest Indiana construction crews through 2024 and could not begin gas main relocation until the following year. The town needed to replace water mains in the same corridor but could not do so until gas work was complete. INDOT's federal funding obligation date created additional pressure, nearly resulting in loss of the federal grant. The town ultimately had to request a funding extension from FHWA, adding 15 months and $6.5M in escalation costs.

projects.name: Ann Arbor State Street Water Main & Curbless Street Project
projects.description: Ann Arbor's 2022 State Street water main replacement and curbless-street conversion ran about four weeks past its Labor Day target, partly because of the delayed removal of a DTE gas line.
projects.detail: In summer 2022 Ann Arbor closed State Street between William and Washington for water main replacement and Phase 1 of a redesign into the city's first curbless street. The work was scheduled to finish by Labor Day but ran about four weeks behind. The city said crews ran into unexpected issues including the delayed removal of a DTE gas line, delays obtaining materials, and bad weather. Business owners said the extended closure into football season hurt foot traffic and sales.
projects.timeline: June 2022 start → Labor Day 2022 target → ~4 weeks late

projects.name: Joliet I-80 Corridor Utility Relocations
projects.description: IDOT's I-80 reconstruction through Joliet was delayed 2.5 years by scheduling conflicts among 14 separate utility owners whose infrastructure crosses the aging interstate corridor.
projects.detail: IDOT's $1.2 billion reconstruction of I-80 through Joliet encountered extraordinary scheduling challenges coordinating utility relocations among 14 different owners, including Nicor Gas, ComEd, AT&T, Comcast, two petroleum pipeline companies, and multiple municipal water and sewer systems. Each utility had its own internal scheduling process, regulatory approval timeline, and construction crew availability constraints. IDOT's master utility relocation schedule required 38 separate work packages executed in sequence, but utility companies repeatedly missed scheduled completion dates, creating cascading delays. The project ultimately required IDOT to hire a dedicated utility coordination manager and establish a weekly stakeholder meeting to break the scheduling gridlock.

projects.name: Canton Tuscarawas Street Corridor Improvement
projects.description: Canton's Tuscarawas Street corridor project delayed 14 months when Dominion Energy and the city water department could not agree on a construction sequence, each insisting the other complete relocation work first.
projects.detail: The City of Canton's Tuscarawas Street corridor improvement, connecting the Pro Football Hall of Fame district to downtown, was stalled by a scheduling impasse between Dominion Energy Ohio and the Canton Water Department. Dominion insisted that the water department relocate its main first to provide safe clearances for gas main work, while the water department insisted Dominion go first since gas mains are typically shallower. The circular dependency stalled utility relocation for 8 months before the city engineer intervened with a phased plan allowing alternating block work. The delay pushed road construction into winter, requiring expensive cold-weather provisions and extending the project by a total of 14 months.

projects.name: Janesville Milton Avenue Reconstruction
projects.description: Janesville's Milton Avenue reconstruction delayed 10 months when Alliant Energy and Charter Communications could not synchronize their conduit relocation work, leaving road contractor idle for extended periods.
projects.detail: The City of Janesville's reconstruction of Milton Avenue, a primary commercial route, was hampered by scheduling conflicts between Alliant Energy and Charter Communications. Both utilities needed to relocate underground conduit before road construction could proceed, but Alliant Energy would not permit Charter to work in the same trench simultaneously due to safety clearance concerns. Charter Communications was then delayed by a nationwide fiber optic cable supply shortage, pushing its work window back by months. The road contractor, Payne & Dolan, invoiced the city for idle equipment and standby crew costs during the utility scheduling gaps. The project required a supplemental budget appropriation from the city council.

projects.name: Kokomo US 31 Bypass Utility Relocations
projects.description: INDOT's US 31 bypass improvements near Kokomo delayed 20 months because Duke Energy, Indiana American Water, and CenturyLink could not align their relocation schedules with the phased construction plan.
projects.detail: INDOT's improvements to the US 31 bypass around Kokomo, part of a corridor-wide upgrade to freeway standards, were significantly delayed by scheduling conflicts among multiple utility owners. Duke Energy required 8 months to relocate a 69kV transmission line but would not begin until Indiana American Water completed a parallel water main relocation. CenturyLink's fiber optic relocation was contingent on Duke Energy's work being completed first, creating a sequential dependency chain. INDOT's phased construction plan assumed parallel utility relocations, but the sequential reality added 20 months to the critical path. Material cost escalation during the delay period increased project costs by $16M.

projects.name: Racine State Street Downtown Reconstruction
projects.description: Racine's State Street reconstruction delayed 9 months when WE Energies and AT&T could not coordinate underground work schedules, forcing the city to extend the road closure through a second construction season.
projects.detail: The City of Racine's reconstruction of State Street through the downtown business district required advance utility work by WE Energies and AT&T before road reconstruction could begin. WE Energies delayed its gas main replacement start by 3 months due to crew scheduling conflicts, then AT&T's conduit relocation crew was reassigned to emergency restoration work after a major storm in southeastern Wisconsin. The cascading delays forced the city to maintain the road closure through winter and into a second construction season. Downtown businesses filed formal complaints with the city council, and several restaurants reported 30-40% revenue declines during the extended closure. The city established a business impact mitigation fund using $500K of the project's contingency.

projects.name: Springfield IL Sixth Street Fiber Installation Gas Strike
projects.description: A fiber optic installation crew struck an Ameren Illinois gas main on Sixth Street in Springfield, forcing evacuation of a two-block area including the Old State Capitol historic district.
projects.detail: During horizontal directional drilling for a fiber optic installation on Sixth Street in Springfield, the drill struck an Ameren Illinois 6-inch gas distribution main, causing a significant gas leak just two blocks from the Old State Capitol. Emergency responders evacuated businesses and residences within a two-block radius for approximately 4 hours while Ameren crews isolated and repaired the main. The fiber installation contractor had obtained locate marks but the gas main had been moved during a previous road project and records were not updated. The Illinois Commerce Commission investigated the incident and the fiber contractor was fined. The incident temporarily halted all fiber installation work in the Springfield historic district.
projects.timeline: Fiber installation suspended for 2 months pending investigation

projects.name: Toledo I-75 Reconstruction Gas Main Strike
projects.description: A pile driving operation during I-75 reconstruction in Toledo struck a Columbia Gas high-pressure transmission main, forcing evacuation of adjacent neighborhoods and shutting down the interstate for 8 hours.
projects.detail: During reconstruction of the I-75/I-475 interchange in Toledo, a pile driving operation for a new bridge bent struck a 16-inch Columbia Gas high-pressure transmission main that was not at its recorded location. The strike caused an uncontrolled gas release that forced evacuation of approximately 200 homes in adjacent neighborhoods and closure of I-75 in both directions for 8 hours. Columbia Gas dispatch crews required 3 hours to isolate the damaged section. ODOT's contractor, Kokosing Construction, had obtained utility locates but the transmission main had shifted during previous highway construction decades earlier and records were never updated. The incident required redesign of two bridge pier locations.

projects.name: Madison Verona Road Reconstruction Fiber Optic Strike
projects.description: WisDOT's Verona Road reconstruction severed a major TDS Telecom fiber optic trunk line serving Dane County government offices, knocking out 911 dispatch communications for 6 hours.
projects.detail: During excavation for WisDOT's Verona Road (US 18/151) reconstruction project in Madison, a contractor's trenching operation severed a TDS Telecom fiber optic trunk line that served as the primary communications backbone for Dane County government offices, including the 911 dispatch center. The severed fiber caused a 6-hour outage of emergency dispatch communications, requiring activation of backup systems and mutual aid from adjacent counties. The fiber line was installed under a highway crossing permit but its exact location was not accurately reflected in utility locate marks. TDS Telecom's repair took 4 days, during which the county operated on degraded communications. The incident prompted Dane County to invest in redundant communications routing.

projects.name: Moline IL River Drive Reconstruction Water Main Strike
projects.description: A road reconstruction crew in Moline struck a 20-inch water transmission main on River Drive, creating flooding that damaged the basement of the adjacent TaxSlayer Centre arena.
projects.detail: During the reconstruction of River Drive in downtown Moline, part of the Quad Cities riverfront improvement program, a contractor struck a 20-inch water transmission main while installing new storm sewer infrastructure. The water main was at a different elevation than shown on city records, likely due to ground settlement over decades. The rupture sent water surging into the basement mechanical room of the adjacent TaxSlayer Centre (now Vibrant Arena), damaging HVAC equipment and forcing cancellation of two scheduled events. The City of Moline was liable for arena damages. Water service to downtown Moline was reduced to minimum pressure for 16 hours during emergency repairs. The incident cost $1.1M in direct damages, arena claims, and construction rework.
projects.timeline: 5-week delay for water main repair and arena damage remediation

projects.name: Sheboygan WI Erie Avenue Road Project Gas Strike
projects.description: A road reconstruction contractor in Sheboygan struck a WE Energies gas service line on Erie Avenue that had been incorrectly located, causing a gas leak requiring evacuation of a senior living facility.
projects.detail: During the City of Sheboygan's Erie Avenue reconstruction project, a contractor struck a WE Energies gas service line while excavating for a new curb and gutter. The service line was approximately 18 inches from its locate-marked position. The resulting gas leak required evacuation of Pine Haven Christian Home, a senior living facility with 85 residents, many of whom required assisted mobility. The evacuation took 2 hours with assistance from the Sheboygan Fire Department and Red Cross. WE Energies crews repaired the service line within 4 hours, but residents were not permitted to return until the following morning after thorough air quality testing. The incident prompted the city to require hand excavation within 10 feet of all gas services for the remainder of the project, adding labor costs of approximately $580K.

projects.name: Detroit Livernois Avenue Streetscape Utility Delays
projects.delayAbs: 4–6 weeks (completion pushed from Nov 2019 to spring 2020)
projects.description: Detroit's $17M Livernois 'Avenue of Fashion' streetscape was set back four to six weeks by heavy rain and utility issues, pushing completion from fall 2019 into 2020.
projects.detail: The City of Detroit began the $17 million Livernois Streetscape Project between Clarita and Eight Mile in spring 2019, adding wide sidewalks, sidewalk-level bike lanes, lighting, landscaping and underground infrastructure. In October 2019 the city's complete streets deputy director said heavy rains and utility issues had pushed the project back four to six weeks, so it would be finished the next spring instead of November. Businesses along the Avenue of Fashion reported serious losses during the prolonged construction.

projects.name: Toledo Secor Road Resurfacing - Columbia Gas Cuts
projects.description: Columbia Gas cut open Toledo's freshly resurfaced Secor Road at multiple locations within 5 months of completion for service line upgrades, leaving substandard patches on a road that cost $12.7M to resurface.
projects.detail: The City of Toledo, using ODOT funding, completed a $12.7M resurfacing of Secor Road, a major north-south arterial serving the University of Toledo area, in fall 2023. Within 5 months, Columbia Gas of Ohio was making cuts at over a dozen locations for gas service line upgrades as part of its distribution system modernization program. The cuts concentrated in the residential sections near the university, where aging service lines connected to homes along the corridor. Toledo's Department of Public Service stated that Columbia Gas had been contacted during the project planning phase and indicated no work was planned. Columbia Gas attributed the timing to a new risk assessment model that flagged the corridor's service lines for priority replacement. Toledo invoiced Columbia Gas $890K for pavement restoration.
projects.timeline: Paving completed September 2023 → Columbia Gas cuts February 2024

projects.name: Des Moines Southeast Connector
projects.description: A major arterial connector project in southeast Des Moines required extensive plan revisions after encountering undocumented utility lines from a former industrial district, increasing costs by $22M.
projects.detail: The Des Moines Southeast Connector was designed to improve traffic flow between US-65 and SE 14th Street through a formerly industrial area. During final design, subsurface utility investigations revealed extensive undocumented utility infrastructure from the area's industrial past, including abandoned gas lines, active storm sewers not on city records, and a MidAmerican Energy transmission duct bank that conflicted with the planned roadway alignment. The project required three rounds of plan revisions and new utility agreements with MidAmerican Energy and Des Moines Water Works. Construction start was pushed back two years while designs were revised to route the road around critical utility corridors that could not be relocated cost-effectively.

projects.name: K-96/I-235 Interchange Reconstruction (Wichita)
projects.description: KDOT's interchange reconstruction at K-96/I-235 required redesign after discovering conflicting Evergy electrical conduits and City of Wichita water transmission mains running through the planned construction zone.
projects.detail: KDOT's $82M reconstruction of the K-96/I-235 interchange in northwest Wichita encountered conflicts during final design when potholing revealed a 36-inch City of Wichita water transmission main and Evergy underground electrical conduits directly in the path of the proposed bridge pier foundations. The water main served as a critical supply line and could not be shut down without impacting service to approximately 15,000 customers. Plan revisions required shifting bridge pier locations, which in turn required redesigning the ramp geometry. Evergy's conduit relocation required a 9-month lead time for materials procurement, contributing to an 11-month overall delay. The additional costs totaled $14M in design modifications and utility relocation agreements.

projects.name: Lincoln South Beltway (Phase 2 Utility Conflicts)
projects.description: The second phase of Lincoln's South Beltway project hit plan revision needs when the alignment crossed multiple Black Hills Energy gas transmission lines and Lincoln Electric System infrastructure not fully captured in earlier surveys.
projects.detail: The $262M Lincoln South Beltway was one of Nebraska's largest highway projects, creating a new expressway south of the city. Phase 2 construction encountered complications when the alignment crossed Black Hills Energy gas transmission lines at three separate locations, plus Lincoln Electric System underground feeders that were not fully documented in the project's initial utility survey. NDOT had to revise grading plans and bridge approach designs to accommodate gas line protection casings and electrical duct bank relocations. Black Hills Energy required a minimum 200-foot separation between the gas line and any blasting operations, forcing changes to rock excavation methods. The plan revisions added $29M to the project cost and delayed completion by 8 months.

projects.name: Rochester Downtown Waterfront Development Infrastructure
projects.description: Rochester's Destination Medical Center waterfront infrastructure work required plan revisions when extensive RPU utility infrastructure beneath 2nd Street SW conflicted with planned streetscape improvements.
projects.detail: As part of Rochester's Destination Medical Center initiative, the $38M waterfront infrastructure project along the Zumbro River and 2nd Street SW corridor required significant plan revisions. Rochester Public Utilities (RPU) infrastructure including a 69kV underground feeder, steam lines serving Mayo Clinic buildings, and a chilled water loop were found in locations conflicting with the planned streetscape and stormwater management improvements. The steam and chilled water lines were particularly problematic because they required continuous operation for Mayo Clinic facilities. Design teams had to revise the streetscape layout to route around the utility corridor, reducing planned green space by 30%. The revisions added $11M to the project and delayed construction start by 13 months.

projects.name: Council Bluffs I-80/I-29 Interchange Modernization
projects.description: Iowa DOT's interchange modernization at the I-80/I-29 junction required extensive plan revisions after discovering MidAmerican Energy underground facilities and OPPD transmission line conflicts at multiple ramp locations.
projects.detail: Iowa DOT's $250M modernization of the I-80/I-29 interchange in Council Bluffs, one of Iowa's busiest freight corridors, required major plan revisions when subsurface utility investigations identified conflicts at five of the eight planned ramp locations. MidAmerican Energy's underground gas distribution infrastructure and Omaha Public Power District (OPPD) transmission duct banks crossed the project area at locations not accurately reflected in utility records. The interchange's proximity to the Missouri River also meant encountering abandoned infrastructure from earlier flood control projects. Plan revisions required relocating an OPPD 161kV transmission line at a cost of $22M alone, with additional gas relocation and design modification costs of $23M. The 20-month delay was primarily driven by the OPPD transmission relocation permitting and engineering timeline.

projects.name: Topeka US-75 Sardou Bridge Replacement
projects.description: KDOT's bridge replacement on US-75 at Sardou Avenue required plan revisions when Evergy underground electrical vaults and an AT&T fiber trunk line were discovered beneath the bridge approaches.
