projects.detail: KDOT's $20M Sardou Bridge replacement on US-75 in Topeka required plan revisions after potholing revealed Evergy underground electrical distribution vaults and an AT&T long-haul fiber trunk line running directly beneath the north bridge approach. The AT&T fiber line was a critical backbone route carrying data between Kansas City and points west, and could not be disrupted without extensive coordination and a minimum 6-month advance notification to downstream carriers. KDOT had to redesign the bridge approach foundations to avoid the fiber line and relocate the Evergy vaults before bridge demolition could begin. The revisions added $4.8M in costs, and AT&T's notification and coordination requirements added 7 months to the schedule.

projects.name: Omaha West Dodge Road Expressway Widening
projects.description: Nebraska DOT's widening of the West Dodge Road expressway required plan revisions when OPPD underground transmission facilities and Metropolitan Utilities District water mains conflicted with proposed median reconstruction.
projects.detail: NDOT's $120M widening of the West Dodge Road expressway in western Omaha hit significant plan revision requirements when detailed subsurface investigations revealed OPPD 69kV underground transmission cables and Metropolitan Utilities District (MUD) 30-inch water transmission mains running through the median area slated for reconstruction. The OPPD cables served as a primary feed to substations in west Omaha and could not be de-energized without affecting thousands of customers. MUD's water main was part of the system's western supply loop. Plan revisions required redesigning the median to protect utilities in place, adding reinforced concrete encasement around both the electrical cables and water main. Additional temporary traffic control measures during the delicate utility protection work added $18M to the project and extended the timeline by 12 months.

projects.name: Bismarck Expressway (I-94 Business Loop) Modernization
projects.description: NDDOT's modernization of the Bismarck Expressway required plan revisions when Montana-Dakota Utilities gas lines and Bis-Man Transit utility conduits were found in conflict with interchange ramp improvements.
projects.detail: NDDOT's $40M modernization of the Bismarck Expressway (I-94 Business Loop) included intersection improvements at several major crossings. During final design, subsurface utility engineering revealed that Montana-Dakota Utilities (MDU) gas distribution lines crossed the project corridor at locations significantly different from recorded positions, conflicting with four of the six planned intersection reconstructions. Additionally, recently installed fiber conduits for Bis-Man Transit's communication system were in the path of proposed ramp widening. Plan revisions required redesigning intersection geometrics to avoid the most critical gas line conflicts, and MDU required 8 months of lead time to relocate other gas infrastructure. The total cost impact was $9.2M, with 10 months added to the project schedule.

projects.name: Rapid City Omaha Street Reconstruction
projects.description: Rapid City's reconstruction of Omaha Street required plan revisions after discovering conflicting Black Hills Energy gas lines and an abandoned municipal steam distribution system beneath the roadway.
projects.detail: Rapid City's $11M reconstruction of Omaha Street between 5th Street and Mount Rushmore Road required plan revisions when test borings revealed an abandoned steam distribution system from the mid-twentieth century intertwined with active Black Hills Energy gas distribution lines. The steam tunnels had partially collapsed in several locations, creating voids beneath the roadway that had not been detected during earlier geotechnical surveys. Black Hills Energy gas lines had been installed through some of the old steam tunnel routes, complicating removal. Plan revisions required a phased approach: first stabilizing the voids and removing abandoned steam infrastructure, then relocating gas lines before road reconstruction could proceed. The revisions added $3.1M in costs and 8 months to the construction schedule.

projects.name: Cedar Rapids Flood Control System Phase 4 (Czech Village)
projects.description: Cedar Rapids' flood control construction in the Czech Village neighborhood required plan revisions when Alliant Energy underground facilities and abandoned industrial utility corridors conflicted with the flood wall alignment.
projects.detail: Phase 4 of Cedar Rapids' $80M flood control system through the Czech Village neighborhood encountered significant plan revision needs when the flood wall alignment was found to conflict with Alliant Energy underground electrical distribution infrastructure and remnant industrial utility corridors from the neighborhood's meatpacking past. Subsurface investigations revealed large-diameter abandoned cast iron pipes, active Alliant Energy duct banks, and a Linn County rural water supply main all within the proposed flood wall footprint. The flood wall foundation design had to be revised to accommodate or relocate these utilities while maintaining structural integrity against 500-year flood levels. Alliant Energy's duct bank relocation required a 10-month design and construction process. Total plan revision costs reached $16M, with a 14-month delay to the flood control completion date.

projects.name: Grand Island US-30/US-281 Interchange Reconstruction
projects.description: NDOT's interchange reconstruction at US-30/US-281 in Grand Island required plan revisions after discovering Southern Power District underground facilities and a Northwestern Energy gas transmission line in conflict with the new interchange geometry.
projects.detail: NDOT's $35M reconstruction of the US-30/US-281 interchange in Grand Island was designed to improve safety and traffic flow at one of central Nebraska's busiest intersections. Plan revisions were triggered when subsurface utility engineering identified Southern Power District underground electrical distribution lines and a Northwestern Energy 6-inch gas transmission line crossing the project area at locations conflicting with proposed bridge foundations and ramp embankments. The gas transmission line served as a key supply route for the Grand Island area and required a pressure reduction coordination with Northwestern Energy's regional supply network during relocation. Plan revisions added $5.6M in utility relocation and design modification costs, extending the project by 7 months.

projects.name: St. Paul Ford Site Redevelopment Infrastructure
projects.description: Infrastructure development at the former Ford Motor Company assembly plant site in St. Paul was delayed 22 months due to scheduling conflicts between Xcel Energy, Saint Paul Regional Water Services, and CenturyLink for utility installations in the new street grid.
projects.detail: The $71M public infrastructure buildout for the 122-acre former Ford Motor Company assembly plant site in Highland Park required coordinating new utility installations by Xcel Energy (gas and electric), Saint Paul Regional Water Services (water and sewer), and CenturyLink (telecommunications) within a new street grid. Each utility had different crew availability windows, construction season preferences, and inspection requirements that could not be aligned. Xcel Energy could not begin gas installation until electric conduits were complete, but their electric crews were committed to another project through the first construction season. CenturyLink's schedule slipped by 8 months due to fiber material shortages, which blocked road base installation. The cascading scheduling conflicts added $15M in standby costs, winter protection measures, and remobilization charges over a 22-month delay.

projects.name: Iowa City Burlington Street Bridge Rehabilitation
projects.description: Rehabilitation of the Burlington Street Bridge in Iowa City was delayed 11 months when MidAmerican Energy and the University of Iowa could not coordinate schedules for utility relocations attached to the bridge structure.
projects.detail: The City of Iowa City's $16.2M rehabilitation of the Burlington Street Bridge over the Iowa River required relocating utilities attached to the bridge structure, including MidAmerican Energy gas and electric lines and University of Iowa chilled water and steam pipes. MidAmerican Energy scheduled their relocation work for spring, but the University of Iowa could not allow steam system disruptions outside the May-August window when heating demand was lowest. The University's chilled water line, however, was in peak demand during summer months and required a temporary bypass that MidAmerican's crews could not work around. The interlocking schedule constraints between the two entities delayed the project by 11 months and added $4.2M in temporary bypass systems, extended traffic control, and contractor standby costs.

projects.name: Joplin Range Line Road Corridor Improvement
projects.description: Joplin's Range Line Road corridor improvement was delayed 14 months by scheduling conflicts with Liberty Utilities and Empire District Electric for underground utility relocations that could not be coordinated with the road construction sequence.
projects.detail: The City of Joplin's $25.5M Range Line Road corridor improvement project, designed to improve the city's primary commercial arterial, was significantly delayed by utility scheduling conflicts. Liberty Utilities (gas) and Empire District Electric had committed their underground construction crews to tornado recovery infrastructure upgrades in other parts of the Joplin region and could not reallocate resources to the Range Line project. Liberty Utilities required an 8-month delay before crews were available, and Empire District's schedule slipped further when their subcontractor went through a merger. The construction sequencing required gas relocation before electric work could begin, and both had to be complete before road reconstruction. The cascading delays added 14 months to the project timeline and $5.1M in escalation costs and contractor delay claims.

projects.name: Omaha ORBT Bus Rapid Transit Extension (North 30th Street)
projects.description: Metro Transit's ORBT bus rapid transit extension along North 30th Street was delayed 15 months due to scheduling conflicts between OPPD, MUD, and CenturyLink for utility relocations required at station platform locations.
projects.detail: Metro Transit's $49M extension of the ORBT bus rapid transit line along North 30th Street in Omaha required utility relocations at each of the planned station platform locations. OPPD (electric), MUD (water and gas), and CenturyLink (telecommunications) each had different scheduling constraints. OPPD could not schedule their relocation during summer peak load season (June-September), MUD's crews were committed to a major water main replacement in the midtown area, and CenturyLink's contractor was backlogged with fiber expansion projects. The three utilities' schedules had only a two-week overlap window, making sequential construction impossible. Station construction at four locations was delayed while utilities negotiated an acceptable sequencing plan. The 15-month overall delay added $9.3M in costs including extended design team mobilization, contractor standby, and material price escalation.

projects.name: Columbia Missouri Discovery Parkway Extension
projects.description: Columbia's Discovery Parkway extension was delayed 12 months when Ameren Missouri and the Boone County Water District could not align their utility relocation schedules with the city's road construction timeline.
projects.detail: The City of Columbia's $26.1M Discovery Parkway extension through the northeastern growth area required utility relocations by Ameren Missouri (electric and gas), Boone County Regional Sewer District, and CenturyLink. Ameren Missouri's overhead-to-underground conversion at the new roadway crossing points was scheduled to begin in March, but the crew was diverted to storm restoration work in Jefferson City for three months. Boone County Regional Sewer District then needed an additional 6 months to relocate a trunk sewer line, but their timeline conflicted with Ameren's rescheduled work. CenturyLink's fiber installation had to follow both utilities. The cascading delays pushed road construction back a full year, adding $4.7M in escalation and remobilization costs.

projects.name: Kearney 2nd Avenue Corridor Reconstruction
projects.description: Kearney's 2nd Avenue corridor reconstruction was delayed 7 months when Charter Spectrum and Northwestern Energy could not coordinate their underground work schedules with the city's phased construction plan.
projects.detail: The City of Kearney's $12.2M reconstruction of the 2nd Avenue corridor through the commercial district required replacing aging water and sewer infrastructure, with utility relocations by Northwestern Energy (gas) and Charter Spectrum (fiber/cable). The city planned a phased block-by-block approach to minimize business disruption, but Northwestern Energy's gas crew was shared across central Nebraska and could only commit to specific two-week windows that did not align with the city's phasing plan. Charter Spectrum's contractor was backlogged with rural broadband expansion work and could not mobilize for the Kearney project on the planned schedule. The misaligned schedules forced the contractor to skip blocks and return later, reducing efficiency and adding $2.8M in remobilization and extended traffic control costs over a 7-month delay.

projects.name: Grand Forks DeMers Avenue Reconstruction
projects.description: Grand Forks' reconstruction of DeMers Avenue was delayed 11 months when Xcel Energy, Nodak Electric Cooperative, and CenturyLink could not align schedules for relocating utilities that crossed the arterial at multiple points.
projects.detail: The City of Grand Forks' $20M reconstruction of DeMers Avenue, the primary east-west commercial corridor, required utility relocations at 12 crossing points involving Xcel Energy gas lines, Nodak Electric Cooperative underground feeders, and CenturyLink fiber trunk lines. Xcel Energy's gas relocation crew was committed to mandatory pipeline integrity work in the Fargo-Moorhead area through the summer construction season. Nodak Electric's underground crew had a 5-month backlog from storm damage repairs. CenturyLink's schedule was contingent on both Xcel and Nodak completing their work first, as the fiber lines were in the shallowest position and could only be safely relocated after deeper utilities were moved. The 11-month delay added $5.4M in costs, with downtown business owners expressing frustration at the extended construction disruption.

projects.name: Mitchell Main Street Revitalization
projects.description: Mitchell's Main Street revitalization project was delayed 6 months when Northwestern Energy and Venture Communications could not schedule utility relocations to fit the city's compressed summer construction window.
projects.detail: The City of Mitchell's $9M Main Street revitalization project, which included new streetscaping, water main replacement, and ADA improvements, was planned for completion in a single summer construction season to minimize disruption to downtown businesses near the Corn Palace tourist attraction. However, Northwestern Energy's gas line relocation crew was unavailable until July, consuming half the construction season before road work could begin. Venture Communications (local telecom) then needed 6 weeks for fiber relocation that overlapped with Northwestern's work window. The project could not be completed before winter, requiring expensive winterization, demobilization, and spring remobilization. The 6-month delay into a second construction season added $1.8M in costs and forced the city to maintain temporary road surfaces through the winter tourist off-season.

projects.name: Ames South Duff Avenue Utility and Road Improvements
projects.description: Ames' South Duff Avenue improvement project was delayed 10 months by scheduling conflicts between Alliant Energy, Iowa State University utilities, and Mediacom for underground utility relocations.
projects.detail: The City of Ames' $16.3M improvement of South Duff Avenue, the city's commercial spine, required coordinated utility relocations involving Alliant Energy (gas and electric), Iowa State University's campus utility system, and Mediacom Communications. Alliant Energy's underground crew was committed to a gas main replacement mandated by pipeline safety regulators in the Des Moines area. Iowa State University's utility relocation work was constrained to the May-August summer session window when campus utility demand was reduced, but this coincided with Alliant's unavailability. Mediacom's fiber relocation contractor was the same firm hired by Alliant for the Des Moines work. The interlocking scheduling constraints pushed the project 10 months behind schedule, adding $3.9M in escalated material costs and extended construction management fees.

projects.name: Lee's Summit MO-291 Widening (Utility Phase)
projects.description: MoDOT's widening of MO-291 through Lee's Summit was delayed 11 months when Spire Energy and Independence Power & Light could not coordinate gas and electric relocation schedules around the phased road widening plan.
projects.detail: MoDOT's $45M widening of MO-291 from two to four lanes through Lee's Summit required relocating Spire Energy gas distribution lines and Independence Power & Light (IPL) electrical infrastructure at multiple intersections. Spire Energy's relocation crew was committed to the federally mandated cast iron main replacement program in St. Louis and could not schedule the Lee's Summit work within the first construction season. IPL's electrical relocation had to follow the gas work for safety reasons, and IPL's schedule was further complicated by a transformer shortage that delayed their material procurement. MoDOT's road contractor was forced to skip sections where utilities were not relocated, working out of sequence and reducing construction efficiency. The 11-month delay added $7.2M in costs including contractor delay claims and material price escalation.

projects.name: Waterloo East 4th Street Reconstruction
projects.description: Waterloo's East 4th Street reconstruction was delayed 7 months when MidAmerican Energy and Windstream Communications could not coordinate utility work schedules with the city's construction timeline.
projects.detail: The City of Waterloo's $12.6M reconstruction of East 4th Street required replacing century-old water and sewer mains alongside utility relocations by MidAmerican Energy (gas and electric) and Windstream Communications (telecom). MidAmerican Energy's gas relocation was scheduled for spring, but a pipeline integrity inspection mandated by PHMSA diverted their crew to another part of the system for three months. Windstream's telecom relocation depended on MidAmerican completing the gas work first, pushing their schedule into late fall when ground conditions were deteriorating. The city's contractor could not proceed with water main installation until both utilities had cleared the corridor. The 7-month delay added $2.4M in winter shutdown costs, remobilization fees, and extended traffic control.

projects.name: Blue Springs 7 Highway Corridor Improvements
projects.description: Blue Springs' 7 Highway corridor improvements were delayed 8 months when Spire Energy and Independence Water Department utility crews were unavailable during the planned construction window.
projects.detail: The City of Blue Springs' $15M improvement project along the 7 Highway corridor required coordinated utility relocations by Spire Energy (gas), Independence Water Department, and AT&T (fiber). Spire Energy's underground crew in the Kansas City metro area was at full capacity with mandated pipeline replacement projects in Independence and Kansas City proper. The Independence Water Department, which provides water service to Blue Springs, had committed its construction crew to an emergency water main repair and could not schedule the Blue Springs work for 5 months. AT&T's fiber relocation then required 3 additional months due to contractor backlog. The sequential delays pushed road construction 8 months behind schedule, adding $3.3M in escalation costs and extended construction management.

projects.name: Duluth Garfield Avenue Sewer Project Gas Line Strike
projects.description: A sewer replacement project on Garfield Avenue in Duluth struck a Minnesota Energy Resources gas distribution line, forcing evacuation of 30 homes and prompting a review of Duluth's historic utility mapping accuracy.
projects.detail: During deep sewer excavation on Garfield Avenue in Duluth's hillside neighborhood, a contractor struck a Minnesota Energy Resources 4-inch gas distribution line that was approximately 3 feet from its marked location. The steep terrain typical of Duluth's hillside neighborhoods had caused the gas line to shift over decades due to soil creep, a phenomenon not accounted for in utility locate standards. The gas leak forced evacuation of 30 homes on the steep hillside while repair crews worked in challenging terrain to isolate and fix the line. The Minnesota Office of Pipeline Safety investigation noted that Duluth's hillside topography creates unique challenges for utility positioning accuracy over time. The project was delayed 6 weeks for complete utility re-verification, adding $780K in costs. The incident prompted the city to initiate a pilot program for 3D subsurface utility mapping in hillside neighborhoods.

projects.name: Omaha Farnam Street Metropolitan Utilities District Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Metropolitan Utilities District trenched into Omaha's Farnam Street for water main replacement 10 months after the city completed a $7.5M complete street reconstruction of the midtown corridor.
projects.detail: Omaha completed a $7.5M complete street reconstruction of Farnam Street through the midtown corridor in fall 2023, adding protected bike lanes, improved pedestrian crossings, and full-depth pavement replacement. Ten months later, Metropolitan Utilities District (MUD) began trenching into the newly reconstructed street for water main replacement, cutting through bike lanes and travel lanes over a six-block stretch. The Midtown Neighborhood Association and cycling advocacy groups protested the destruction of the new bike lanes, which had taken years of planning and community input. MUD stated that the water main replacement was triggered by a break analysis that identified the Farnam Street main as high-priority after the road project was already in construction. Omaha's Public Works Department acknowledged that their coordination process with MUD had gaps and committed to developing a joint 5-year capital improvement planning process. MUD was required to restore the road and bike lanes to city standards, but engineers estimated a 35% reduction in pavement service life in the cut areas.
projects.timeline: Reconstructed fall 2023, MUD cuts began August 2024

projects.name: SH 288 Toll Lanes (Brazoria County)
projects.description: Toll lane project required extensive plan revisions after undocumented petroleum pipelines were found crossing the corridor at multiple points.
projects.detail: The $800M SH 288 toll lanes project in southern Houston encountered significant delays when subsurface investigations revealed multiple undocumented petroleum transmission lines that conflicted with planned bridge foundations and drainage structures. Engineers had to redesign foundation layouts for three interchange ramps and reroute major stormwater conveyance systems. The pipeline owners disputed relocation responsibility, adding months of negotiation. Final cost reached $862M with the corridor opening over a year behind schedule.

projects.name: US-69/US-75 Muskogee Turnpike Interchange
projects.description: Interchange reconstruction plans revised three times after encountering unmapped water transmission mains and abandoned gas infrastructure from a former industrial site.
projects.detail: ODOT's interchange reconstruction project hit repeated design setbacks when potholing revealed a 30-inch water transmission main and abandoned gas piping from a decommissioned industrial facility not shown on any utility records. Initial plan revisions attempted to bridge over the water main, but structural clearance issues forced a second redesign. The third revision relocated the water main entirely at a cost of $8M, shared between ODOT and the Muskogee City-County Port Authority. The project's total cost grew from $82M to $100M.

projects.name: SH 130 Toll Road Segment 5-6 Rehabilitation
projects.description: Pavement rehabilitation project plans were revised after discovering that original construction had buried fiber optic conduit at non-standard depths throughout the corridor.
projects.detail: When crews began milling pavement on the SH 130 toll road south of Austin, they discovered that fiber optic conduit serving the toll system's communication backbone had been installed at significantly shallower depths than shown on as-built drawings. The rehabilitation plans had to be completely revised to either protect in place or relocate approximately 12 miles of fiber conduit. The rework required coordination with the toll system operator to maintain electronic toll collection during construction, adding complexity and cost to what had been planned as a straightforward resurfacing project.

projects.name: Pine Bluff Downtown Revitalization Infrastructure
projects.description: Downtown infrastructure renewal plans required major revision when century-old brick sewers and abandoned steam utility tunnels were uncovered beneath Main Street.
projects.detail: Pine Bluff's federally-funded downtown revitalization project was designed to replace aging water and sewer lines while reconstructing streets and sidewalks. When excavation began, contractors uncovered an extensive network of brick-arch sewers from the 1890s and remnants of a steam heating distribution system that served downtown buildings in the early 20th century. None of this infrastructure appeared on city records. Engineers had to redesign the entire underground layout, and archeological review was required for the historic structures. The project budget grew from $20M to $27.2M, with FEMA and HUD providing supplemental grants.

projects.name: Shreveport Cross Bayou Redevelopment Infrastructure
projects.description: Plans for the Cross Bayou mixed-use redevelopment's underground infrastructure were revised after discovery of contaminated soil around abandoned industrial utility corridors.
projects.detail: Shreveport's signature Cross Bayou Point redevelopment project required extensive underground infrastructure work including new water, sewer, and electrical distribution. During geotechnical investigations, crews discovered abandoned industrial utility corridors containing petroleum-contaminated soils from a former rail yard. Environmental remediation requirements forced a complete redesign of the underground utility layout, pushing several trunk lines deeper and requiring specialized trench construction. The contaminated soil disposal alone cost $3.8M, and the full infrastructure package grew from $60M to $75M.

projects.name: Stillwater SH-51 Corridor Improvement
projects.description: Corridor improvement plans revised when Oklahoma State University's campus utility tunnel system was found to extend farther under the highway than university records showed.
projects.detail: ODOT's SH-51 corridor improvements through Stillwater required plan revision when exploratory excavation near the Oklahoma State University campus revealed that the university's underground utility tunnel system extended beneath the state highway right-of-way. The tunnels carried steam, chilled water, and electrical distribution serving campus buildings. OSU's facilities records were incomplete regarding the tunnels' southern extent, and their structural condition required careful engineering assessment before any roadway work could proceed above them. Load-bearing analysis and protective measures added $4.8M to the $20M project.

projects.name: Bentonville Downtown Street Reconstruction
projects.description: Downtown street reconstruction plans revised after discovering conflicting utility installations from multiple fiber providers that had been installed without proper permitting records.
projects.detail: Bentonville's downtown street reconstruction project, intended to support the city's rapid growth as Walmart's headquarters city, required plan revision when excavation revealed a tangled web of fiber optic conduit from multiple telecommunications providers. Several installations lacked proper permitting records and were placed at varying depths with no clear separation from water and sewer lines. The city had to commission a complete subsurface utility engineering survey of the entire downtown grid before redesigning the street sections. Three fiber providers disputed relocation costs, and the project budget grew from $19.5M to $25M.

projects.name: Oklahoma City I-240 Reconstruction (South Corridor)
projects.description: I-240 reconstruction plans underwent wholesale revision after OG&E transmission line relocations were found to conflict with new interchange geometry at three locations.
projects.detail: ODOT's reconstruction of the aging I-240 corridor on Oklahoma City's south side faced a major planning setback when detailed utility surveys revealed that OG&E high-voltage transmission lines conflicted with proposed interchange improvements at three separate locations. The transmission towers could not simply be relocated due to grid reliability requirements, forcing engineers to redesign interchange ramp configurations around the existing tower locations. Additionally, an ONG gas transmission line required a $12M relocation. The combined utility conflicts pushed the project from $300M to $342M and delayed the start of mainline construction by 18 months.

projects.name: Laredo World Trade Bridge Expansion
projects.description: International bridge expansion plans revised after CBP security utility conduits and Mexican utility crossings created unforeseen design conflicts.
projects.detail: The expansion of the World Trade International Bridge in Laredo, critical for US-Mexico trade, required plan revisions when subsurface investigations revealed CBP surveillance and communication conduit networks that were classified and not included in initial design surveys. Additionally, Mexican utility infrastructure extending into the US side of the bridge approach created jurisdictional complications. TxDOT had to coordinate with CBP, the General Services Administration, and Mexican federal agencies to resolve the conflicts. The security infrastructure could not be disrupted during relocation, requiring nighttime-only construction for portions of the work. Costs grew from $148M to $176M.

projects.name: Edmond Downtown Streetscape Phase 2
projects.description: Downtown streetscape plans revised after ONG gas lines and an abandoned municipal well casing were discovered directly beneath the planned plaza area.
projects.detail: The City of Edmond's Phase 2 downtown streetscape project was designed to create pedestrian plazas and upgrade infrastructure along Broadway. During pre-construction potholing, crews found an ONG gas distribution main running directly beneath the centerline of the planned central plaza, plus an abandoned municipal well casing with unknown depth. The well casing required environmental assessment before it could be capped, and the gas main relocation required ONG to redesign distribution to maintain service to surrounding businesses. The discovery forced a four-month design pause and $2.9M in additional costs on the $10M project.

projects.name: El Paso Spur 601 Downtown Deck Park
projects.description: Highway deck park project delayed by scheduling conflicts between TxDOT, El Paso Water Utilities, and El Paso Electric for sequential utility relocations.
projects.detail: El Paso's plan to cap a section of Spur 601 with a deck park required coordinated utility relocations from three major providers. El Paso Water Utilities could not begin water main relocation until El Paso Electric completed a transmission line rerouting, which itself was delayed by a scheduling conflict with TxDOT's traffic management plan. Each entity had committed resources to other projects and refused to adjust timelines. The three-way scheduling impasse persisted for nearly a year before the city council intervened with a joint scheduling agreement. The delays added $22M in escalation costs and extended the timeline from 5 years to over 6.5 years.

projects.name: Broken Arrow Elm Place Widening
projects.description: Road widening project delayed by scheduling conflict between ONG and the Broken Arrow Municipal Authority over a shared utility easement.
projects.detail: The City of Broken Arrow's widening of Elm Place was stalled when Oklahoma Natural Gas and the Broken Arrow Municipal Authority discovered they both needed to use the same utility easement for their respective relocations but at different times. ONG scheduled gas main work for spring, but the municipal authority's water line replacement required the same trench space beginning in late winter. Neither entity would yield priority, and the narrow right-of-way precluded simultaneous operations. An eight-month delay ensued while a joint construction agreement was negotiated, adding $2.1M in standby and escalation costs to the $11.7M project.

projects.name: New Orleans Claiborne Avenue Corridor Reconstruction
projects.description: Corridor reconstruction delayed over two years by scheduling conflicts between Entergy New Orleans, the Sewerage & Water Board, and Cox Communications.
projects.detail: The reconstruction of North Claiborne Avenue, a major corridor through several historic New Orleans neighborhoods, suffered cascading scheduling delays. Entergy New Orleans could not begin underground cable relocation until the Sewerage & Water Board completed drainage work, but S&WB's crews were committed to consent decree projects elsewhere in the city. Cox Communications then could not schedule fiber relocation until Entergy's underground work was complete, as both occupied the same duct bank. The three-way scheduling dependency chain extended the utility phase by 26 months. Community groups protested the prolonged construction disruption to businesses along the historic corridor.

projects.name: Tyler Loop 49 Completion (Southeast Segment)
projects.description: Loop completion delayed when Oncor, AEP, and multiple rural water districts could not align relocation schedules for the greenfield corridor.
projects.detail: TxDOT's completion of the Loop 49 southeast segment around Tyler encountered unexpected scheduling challenges despite being a mostly greenfield project. The corridor crossed service territories of both Oncor and AEP, requiring coordination between two electric utilities with different operational calendars. Additionally, three rural water supply districts had transmission mains crossing the corridor at various points, each with limited relocation crew availability. The utilities collectively required 16 additional months beyond the planned utility clearance window, pushing mainline construction into the following fiscal year and adding $14M in delay and escalation costs to the $117M project.

projects.name: Little Rock I-630 Pavement Rehabilitation
projects.description: Pavement rehabilitation delayed when Entergy Arkansas and Central Arkansas Water could not coordinate utility access under the highway during limited nighttime work windows.
projects.detail: ArDOT's rehabilitation of I-630, the east-west expressway bisecting Little Rock, required utility access coordination for work beneath the roadway. Entergy Arkansas needed to inspect and reinforce underground duct banks, and Central Arkansas Water needed to replace valve assemblies on a water main crossing. Both required lane closures on the same segments, but traffic management requirements limited closures to nighttime hours. Entergy and CAW could not agree on alternating night schedules, each insisting on continuous multi-night work blocks. The scheduling impasse extended the utility phase by 13 months, with delay costs and material escalation adding $8.8M to the $55M project.

projects.name: Fort Smith Garrison Avenue Bridge Rehabilitation
projects.description: Historic bridge rehabilitation delayed by scheduling conflicts between OG&E, Arkansas Valley Electric, and the Fort Smith water utility for attached utility relocations.
projects.detail: The rehabilitation of the historic Garrison Avenue Bridge in Fort Smith required temporary relocation of utilities attached to and crossing the bridge over the Arkansas River. OG&E, Arkansas Valley Electric Cooperative, and the city water utility each had infrastructure on the bridge that needed to be moved before structural work could begin. The three utilities could not agree on a sequential schedule that maintained service to the downtown commercial district. OG&E required a 90-day lead time for temporary power rerouting, which conflicted with the water utility's seasonal maintenance window. The 16-month delay added $6.1M to the $30.5M rehabilitation project.

projects.name: Grand Prairie SH 161 Interchange Modification
projects.description: Interchange project delayed when TxDOT, NTTA, Oncor, and Atmos Energy could not coordinate lane closures and utility relocations on the overlapping toll/freeway facility.
projects.detail: The modification of the SH 161/SH 180 interchange in Grand Prairie was complicated by the overlapping jurisdiction of TxDOT and the North Texas Tollway Authority. Utility relocations by Oncor and Atmos Energy required lane closures on both the toll and non-toll facilities, but TxDOT and NTTA had different traffic management requirements and approval timelines. Oncor's relocation work, approved by TxDOT, was rejected by NTTA's traffic operations center, causing a three-month standstill. The multi-agency scheduling conflict added $9.3M and 11 months to the $71.5M project.

projects.name: Fayetteville Razorback Greenway Extension
projects.description: Trail extension contractor struck a gas distribution line during concrete pier drilling for a pedestrian bridge, evacuating adjacent apartment complex.
projects.detail: Construction of the Razorback Greenway trail extension through Fayetteville struck a Black Hills Energy gas distribution main while drilling concrete piers for a new pedestrian bridge. The contractor had called 811 and received locate marks, but the gas line was three feet from its marked position. The gas release forced evacuation of a 200-unit apartment complex for six hours. Black Hills Energy shut down a section of the distribution system while making repairs, leaving 85 homes without gas service for two days. The incident halted trail construction for five months pending a complete utility re-survey. Additional costs of $890K on the $5.9M project were split between the contractor's insurance and Black Hills Energy.

projects.name: Baton Rouge Airline Highway Fiber Optic Cable Strikes
projects.description: Road widening contractor struck fiber optic cables three times in six weeks, severing internet service to major commercial district and triggering a work stoppage.
projects.detail: During LADOTD's widening of Airline Highway through Baton Rouge, the contractor struck fiber optic cables belonging to three different telecommunications providers on three separate occasions within a six-week period. The strikes disrupted internet service to hundreds of businesses along the commercial corridor, including a major hospital campus. Investigation revealed that multiple fiber providers had installed cables at varying depths with inadequate separation, and several installations predated the state's one-call notification system. LADOTD imposed a work stoppage to commission a comprehensive subsurface survey. The cumulative delays and repair costs added $1.9M to the $19M project.

projects.name: Lawton Gore Boulevard Reconstruction Gas Line Strike
projects.description: Road reconstruction contractor struck an ONG gas main, evacuating a shopping center and elementary school within the blast radius zone.
projects.detail: During the City of Lawton's reconstruction of Gore Boulevard, a commercial arterial, a backhoe struck a 6-inch Oklahoma Natural Gas distribution main at a depth of only 14 inches — well above the minimum cover requirement. The uncontrolled gas release triggered evacuation of a nearby shopping center and elementary school, affecting approximately 800 people. ONG's investigation found that previous road construction had reduced the soil cover over the gas main without notification. The discovery prompted ONG to lower the main to proper depth along the entire project corridor, adding four months and $1.1M to the $12M project. The city and ONG disputed responsibility for the shallow cover condition.

projects.name: Corpus Christi SPID/SH 358 Interchange Fiber Cut
projects.description: Interchange reconstruction severed a major AT&T fiber trunk line, disrupting communications to Corpus Christi Naval Air Station and the Port of Corpus Christi.
projects.detail: During TxDOT's reconstruction of the South Padre Island Drive/SH 358 interchange, pile driving for a new bridge bent severed an AT&T fiber trunk line carrying critical communications for both the Corpus Christi Naval Air Station and the Port of Corpus Christi. The fiber line, installed in the 1990s, was documented in AT&T's records but at a depth 5 feet shallower than its actual position, placing it in the pile driving zone. The disruption triggered federal and military emergency communications protocols. AT&T's emergency repair took 72 hours, but the incident prompted a comprehensive fiber survey of the entire interchange footprint. The additional survey work, protective measures, and contractor standby added $3.1M to the $62M project.

projects.name: Port Arthur LNG Facility Access Road Gas Strike
projects.description: Access road construction for an LNG export facility struck an active petroleum pipeline, causing a release that required EPA emergency response.
projects.detail: During construction of an access road serving the Sempra Port Arthur LNG export facility, heavy equipment struck a 10-inch active petroleum pipeline that crossed the construction corridor. The strike caused a release of approximately 2,000 gallons of refined petroleum product into adjacent wetlands, triggering an EPA emergency response under the Clean Water Act. The pipeline was on Sempra's project maps but at a location 15 feet from its actual position. The EPA required a complete environmental assessment and remediation plan before construction could resume. Cleanup costs, fines, contractor standby, and additional utility protection measures added $5.4M to the $30M access road project.

projects.name: Durant US-69/US-75 Intersection Improvement
projects.description: Intersection improvement contractor struck a water transmission main serving the Choctaw Nation's tribal complex, cutting water supply to 2,000 people.
projects.detail: During ODOT's improvement of the US-69/US-75 intersection in Durant, excavation for a new turn lane struck a 16-inch water transmission main serving the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma's tribal headquarters complex and surrounding community. The break caused a loss of water pressure affecting approximately 2,000 tribal members and employees. The Choctaw Nation's emergency management division activated its emergency water distribution plan. The tribal water line had been installed under a federal tribal infrastructure grant and was not recorded in the state's utility mapping system or the Oklahoma One-Call database. The incident required a five-month delay for tribal/state coordination on utility protection, adding $1.4M to the $11.5M project.

projects.name: Shreveport Line Avenue Water Main Strike
projects.description: Road reconstruction struck a 20-inch cast iron water main from 1928, causing a catastrophic break that flooded a hospital parking garage and residential neighborhood.
projects.detail: During the City of Shreveport's reconstruction of Line Avenue, a major north-south corridor, a contractor struck a 20-inch cast iron water main dating to 1928. The brittle pipe shattered, releasing water at enormous pressure that flooded a nearby hospital's underground parking garage to a depth of four feet and inundated a residential neighborhood. The cast iron main was at a different alignment than shown on the city's 1980s-era utility maps, which had never been updated to reflect as-built conditions. Emergency water service was rerouted within 24 hours, but the parking garage required extensive remediation. The four-month delay for main replacement and damage claims added $1.1M to the $10M project.

projects.name: Dallas Klyde Warren Park Expansion Utility Discovery
projects.description: Deck park expansion plans revised when TxDOT utility surveys found significantly more underground infrastructure beneath the Woodall Rodgers Freeway than originally mapped.
projects.detail: The expansion of Dallas's landmark Klyde Warren Park over the Woodall Rodgers Freeway faced major plan revisions when detailed subsurface utility engineering revealed a far denser network of underground infrastructure than anticipated. Dallas Water Utilities, Oncor, Atmos Energy, and AT&T all had facilities that conflicted with the expanded deck structure's support columns. The original park construction in 2012 had documented utility conditions only within its footprint, and the expansion area had never been comprehensively surveyed. Engineers redesigned 12 column foundations and two drainage systems to accommodate the existing utilities. The private fundraising campaign had to be extended by $32M, pushing total costs from $200M to $232M.

projects.name: Houston Wastewater Consent Decree Sewer Rehabilitation (Northeast)
projects.description: EPA consent decree sewer work in northeast Houston delayed 2.5 years by scheduling conflicts between the city, CenterPoint Energy, and AT&T for utility relocations in congested corridors.
projects.detail: Houston's EPA consent decree sewer rehabilitation program in the northeast sector faced severe scheduling conflicts in corridors where CenterPoint Energy gas mains, AT&T fiber trunk lines, and the city's own water infrastructure competed for the same underground space. CenterPoint required advanced notice for gas main relocations that the city's aggressive consent decree schedule could not accommodate. AT&T refused to relocate fiber until CenterPoint completed gas work, creating a dependency chain. The EPA twice threatened additional penalties for schedule slippage. The city hired a dedicated utility coordination manager, but the scheduling backlog added 30 months and $85M in escalation costs to the $700M northeast sector program.

projects.name: Fort Worth Panther Island/Central City Utility Relocation
projects.description: Panther Island flood control and development project required extensive plan revisions after discovering the Trinity River channel shift had moved critical utility crossings from their mapped positions.
projects.detail: Fort Worth's ambitious Panther Island project to reroute the Trinity River and create a mixed-use island district encountered massive utility conflicts. Decades of river channel migration had shifted the actual positions of major water, gas, and electrical transmission crossings from their documented locations. Plans for the three new bridges and bypass channel had to be fundamentally revised to account for the true utility positions. The Tarrant Regional Water District's 54-inch water transmission main crossing was found 40 feet from its mapped location. Oncor's 138kV transmission tower foundations conflicted with the bypass channel alignment. The cascading plan revisions added $120M and three years to the $800M project.

projects.name: Dallas Skillman Street Moratorium Violation (AT&T Fiber)
projects.description: AT&T cut into freshly resurfaced Skillman Street for fiber installation within six months of a $3.2M city resurfacing project, violating Dallas's 5-year moratorium ordinance.
projects.detail: The City of Dallas completed a $3.2M resurfacing of Skillman Street through the Lake Highlands neighborhood in early 2024. Within six months, AT&T's fiber installation contractor cut multiple trenches across the new pavement for fiber optic cable installation. Dallas's street cut moratorium ordinance prohibits cuts to newly paved streets for five years without special permission, which AT&T had not obtained. Residents organized protests after seeing their newly smooth street repeatedly cut and patched. The city issued stop-work orders and fines, but AT&T's contractors had already completed most of the fiber installation before enforcement caught up. The city estimated the pavement cuts reduced the street's useful life by 40%.
projects.timeline: Street resurfaced early 2024, cut within 6 months

projects.name: Oklahoma City NW 23rd Street Moratorium Violation (ONG)
projects.description: Oklahoma Natural Gas cut into NW 23rd Street within one year of MAPS 3 streetscape completion for emergency gas main replacement, then took months to properly restore.
projects.detail: Oklahoma City's MAPS 3 program had invested $4.5M in a complete streetscape renovation of NW 23rd Street through the Paseo Arts District, including decorative pavement, artist-designed crosswalks, and specialty lighting. Within one year of completion, Oklahoma Natural Gas performed emergency gas main replacement that required cutting through the decorative pavement and crosswalks at seven locations. While ONG cited emergency safety needs, city officials noted that the gas main's deteriorated condition had been known before the streetscape project began. ONG's initial patch repairs used standard asphalt rather than matching the decorative pavement. After three months of public pressure, ONG agreed to a $890K restoration using original materials.

projects.name: New Orleans Magazine Street Moratorium Violation (Entergy)
projects.description: Entergy New Orleans cut into recently reconstructed Magazine Street through the Garden District for underground cable upgrades within the moratorium period.
projects.detail: The City of New Orleans completed a $9.2M reconstruction of Magazine Street through the Garden District and Uptown neighborhoods, including new pavement, enhanced streetcar track crossing, and historic-style sidewalks. Entergy New Orleans' contractors cut into the new roadway at 18 locations within the moratorium period for underground distribution cable upgrades. The cuts damaged both the new pavement and several newly installed historic-pattern brick crosswalks. The Garden District Association and the Preservation Resource Center publicly condemned the cuts as destructive to the historic streetscape. The city council demanded Entergy fund full restoration at an estimated cost of $680K, including specialty brick crosswalk reconstruction.

projects.name: Shreveport Youree Drive Moratorium Violation (SWEPCO)
projects.description: SWEPCO cut into recently resurfaced Youree Drive within the moratorium period for underground distribution work, creating uneven surfaces in a high-traffic commercial corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Shreveport's $4.8M resurfacing of Youree Drive, the primary commercial corridor on the city's south side, was completed in early 2024. Southwestern Electric Power Company cut into the new pavement within the moratorium period at multiple locations for underground distribution cable replacement. The cuts created uneven surfaces and rough patches in a corridor that carries heavy commercial traffic including frequent bus service. Shreveport Transit System reported that the rough patches were causing passenger complaints and accelerated wear on bus suspensions. The city assessed $290K in restoration fees and submitted a formal complaint to the Louisiana Public Service Commission regarding SWEPCO's pattern of moratorium non-compliance.
projects.timeline: Resurfaced early 2024, cut within moratorium period

projects.name: I-15 Technology Corridor (Point of the Mountain)
projects.description: Major I-15 widening through Utah's Silicon Slopes corridor required extensive plan revisions after survey crews discovered undocumented fiber optic conduit banks serving tech campuses, forcing redesign of drainage infrastructure.
projects.detail: UDOT's $765M project to add capacity on I-15 between Lehi and Draper encountered significant subsurface utility conflicts during the design-build phase. Survey crews found undocumented fiber optic conduit banks serving adjacent tech campuses that were not reflected in any utility records. The discovery forced complete redesign of the stormwater drainage system and retaining walls along a 3.2-mile segment. Multiple fiber providers including Utopia and CenturyLink had installed conduit without updating state records, creating a tangle of infrastructure that took 9 months of additional engineering to resolve.

projects.name: Mesa Light Rail Extension (Gilbert Road)
projects.description: Valley Metro's Gilbert Road light rail extension in Mesa required major plan revisions after discovering SRP irrigation infrastructure and abandoned mine drainage pipes conflicting with track alignment.
projects.detail: The 1.9-mile eastward extension of the Valley Metro light rail to Gilbert Road encountered extensive subsurface conflicts with Salt River Project irrigation infrastructure dating to the early 1900s. Abandoned mine drainage pipes from historic copper operations were also found crossing the alignment at multiple points. Design revisions required relocating over 2,400 feet of century-old irrigation conduit and rerouting a segment of the track alignment to avoid contaminated soils around the old drainage infrastructure. The changes added $38M to the project cost and pushed the opening date back by 18 months.

projects.name: Missoula Reserve Street Reconstruction
projects.description: MDT's reconstruction of Reserve Street required plan revisions after subsurface investigation revealed NorthWestern Energy gas mains conflicting with planned intersection improvements at three major crossings.
projects.detail: Montana Department of Transportation's $20M reconstruction of Reserve Street, one of Missoula's busiest commercial corridors, required significant plan changes after potholing revealed NorthWestern Energy gas transmission mains at different depths than shown on utility records at the Brooks, South, and 39th Street intersections. The 12-inch high-pressure gas main was found running diagonally rather than parallel to the roadway, conflicting with planned turn lane widening and new signal infrastructure at all three intersections. NorthWestern Energy's relocation work added $4.8M in additional costs and required a complete phasing plan revision to maintain gas service during construction.

projects.name: Fort Collins Vine Drive Corridor
projects.description: Vine Drive widening from Shields to Lemay required redesign after discovering Fort Collins Utilities water transmission mains and abandoned Greeley irrigation laterals conflicting with planned multiuse path alignment.
projects.detail: The City of Fort Collins' $17.7M Vine Drive corridor improvement required plan revisions after subsurface investigation discovered that Fort Collins Utilities water transmission infrastructure and abandoned Greeley-Poudre Irrigation District laterals were in direct conflict with the planned separated multiuse path on the south side of the roadway. The abandoned laterals contained residual water that complicated excavation and required dewatering, while the active water mains needed protection-in-place at a different depth than designed. The revised plans shifted the multiuse path to the north side of Vine Drive for 2,200 feet, requiring additional right-of-way acquisition from three commercial properties.

projects.name: Bozeman North 7th Avenue Reconstruction
projects.description: North 7th Avenue reconstruction in rapidly growing Bozeman required extensive redesign after finding undocumented water, sewer, and telecom infrastructure installed by multiple developers without city records.
projects.detail: Bozeman's rapid growth along the North 7th Avenue commercial corridor meant that multiple developers had installed water, sewer, and telecommunications infrastructure during the 2010s building boom without fully recording as-built locations with the city. The $22.6M reconstruction project discovered at least seven undocumented utility crossings during potholing, including a 10-inch water main serving a major subdivision that was 6 feet from its recorded location. The city was forced to conduct a complete subsurface utility engineering survey along the entire 1.8-mile corridor, adding 12 months and $6.1M to the project while redesigning intersection improvements around actual utility locations.

projects.name: Sheridan Main Street Reconstruction
projects.description: Sheridan's historic Main Street reconstruction required plan revisions after discovering abandoned coal gas infrastructure from the early 1900s intertwined with modern utilities beneath the downtown core.
projects.detail: WYDOT and the City of Sheridan's $10M Main Street reconstruction project encountered abandoned coal gasification infrastructure including clay pipe remnants, tar-sealed vaults, and contaminated soil from Sheridan's early 1900s manufactured gas plant. The historic infrastructure was intertwined with modern water and sewer lines in ways not reflected on any utility maps. Environmental remediation of coal tar residue was required under DEQ oversight before utility work could proceed. The discovery forced redesign of water main replacement segments to avoid contaminated zones, adding $2.1M in remediation and redesign costs and pushing the project completion back 6 months.

projects.name: Flagstaff Route 66 Revitalization
projects.description: Downtown Flagstaff's Route 66 streetscape project required extensive redesign after encountering a maze of vintage utility infrastructure including wooden water mains and abandoned gas lines beneath the historic corridor.
projects.detail: Flagstaff's $30M Route 66 streetscape revitalization project through the downtown historic district ran into severe subsurface challenges when crews discovered wooden water mains from the 1890s, abandoned manufactured gas lines, and hand-laid stone drainage channels not shown on modern utility records. The wooden mains were still partially pressurized and connected to the modern water system through undocumented transitions. APS power conduit was found at depths 3 feet shallower than recorded, conflicting with the planned utility vault locations for streetscape lighting. The project required a complete subsurface utility engineering study, archaeological documentation of historic infrastructure, and redesign of the utility improvement plan, adding 15 months and $8.4M to the project.

projects.name: Pocatello Yellowstone Avenue Rehabilitation
projects.description: Yellowstone Avenue rehabilitation required redesign after discovering that Idaho Power and Intermountain Gas infrastructure conflicted with planned sidewalk and ADA improvements at multiple intersections.
projects.detail: The City of Pocatello's $11.9M Yellowstone Avenue rehabilitation from Center Street to Chubbuck Road encountered subsurface utility conflicts at six of the eight intersections slated for ADA-compliant curb ramp upgrades. Idaho Power conduit and Intermountain Gas mains were found at depths and locations that differed significantly from utility records, making the planned corner reconstructions infeasible without relocation. The gas main at the Oak Street intersection was found only 18 inches below grade, well above the standard 36-inch minimum cover. Redesign of the intersection work and gas main lowering added $1.9M and required coordinating a 5-month gas main relocation program before roadway work could resume.

projects.name: Carson City William Street/US 50 Reconstruction
projects.description: NDOT's US 50 reconstruction through Carson City required plan revisions after conflicting underground utility infrastructure from multiple eras was found concentrated at the Stewart Street intersection.
projects.detail: NDOT's $25.4M reconstruction of William Street (US 50) through Carson City encountered severe utility congestion at the Stewart Street intersection where infrastructure from multiple construction eras converged. A 1940s-era concrete-encased telephone conduit bank, a 1970s storm drain, and modern NV Energy electrical duct bank occupied the same subsurface corridor planned for a new left-turn lane. The telephone conduit bank was significantly larger than shown on records and could not be abandoned without disrupting service to several state government buildings. Redesigning the intersection to accommodate the immovable infrastructure required eliminating the planned dual left-turn lane and adding a signal phase instead, fundamentally changing the traffic operation.

projects.name: Pueblo Dillon Drive Extension
projects.description: Pueblo's Dillon Drive extension required plan revision after discovering a Pueblo Board of Water Works transmission main at an unexpected location, forcing realignment of the new roadway.
projects.detail: The City of Pueblo's $16M Dillon Drive extension project required significant plan revisions after subsurface investigation found a 24-inch Pueblo Board of Water Works transmission main running diagonally through the planned roadway alignment. The main, which serves the city's southern growth area, was found 200 feet west of its recorded location. Relocating the transmission main was deemed impractical due to the cost and service disruption risk, so the roadway alignment was shifted eastward, requiring additional right-of-way acquisition from four properties and redesign of the Vinewood Lane intersection. The alignment change triggered a supplemental environmental assessment that added 8 months to the project timeline.

projects.name: Rio Rancho Unser Boulevard Extension
projects.description: Unser Boulevard extension plans were revised after PNM electric and New Mexico Gas Company infrastructure was found in direct conflict with planned grade separations along the new alignment.
projects.detail: Rio Rancho's $17.8M Unser Boulevard extension south of NM 528 encountered underground utility conflicts when PNM electric duct banks and New Mexico Gas Company high-pressure mains were found in the footprint of planned grade-separated intersections. The PNM infrastructure served the Intel semiconductor facility and could not tolerate extended outages for relocation. New Mexico Gas Company's 8-inch high-pressure main was found 5 feet from its recorded position, directly in the planned bridge pier location. The city was forced to redesign two intersections from grade-separated to at-grade signalized, fundamentally changing the traffic capacity of the corridor and requiring revised traffic modeling and public hearings.

projects.name: Helena Last Chance Gulch Pedestrian Mall Reconstruction
projects.description: Helena's pedestrian mall reconstruction required redesign after discovering gold-mining-era tunnels and undocumented NorthWestern Energy steam infrastructure beneath the historic walking mall.
projects.detail: The City of Helena's $10M Last Chance Gulch pedestrian mall reconstruction uncovered remnants of gold mining tunnels and an undocumented NorthWestern Energy steam distribution system beneath the historic downtown walking mall. The mining tunnels, dating to the 1860s placer gold era, had partially collapsed and created subsurface voids that threatened the structural integrity of planned streetscape improvements. The abandoned steam pipes contained asbestos insulation requiring hazardous materials remediation. Archaeological documentation was required under Montana Antiquities Act before any mining-era infrastructure could be disturbed, adding 7 months of permitting and remediation work before construction could resume.

projects.name: CDOT US 550/US 160 Connection (Farmington to Durango)
projects.description: US 550/160 connection project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between CDOT, La Plata Electric Association, and the Southern Ute Indian Tribe's utility operations on tribal land crossings.
projects.detail: CDOT's $182M US 550/160 connection south of Durango faced 18 months of delays due to scheduling conflicts involving La Plata Electric Association, Atmos Energy, and the Southern Ute Indian Tribe's utility department. Utility relocations crossing tribal land required separate permitting through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, which operated on a different timeline than CDOT's construction schedule. La Plata Electric's substation relocation could not begin until the tribe approved an amended easement, and Atmos Energy's gas main relocation required a seasonal construction window to avoid disrupting heating service during mountain winters. The sequential permitting and seasonal constraints created a cascading delay that added $31M in standby and mobilization costs.

projects.name: Billings Grand Avenue Rehabilitation
projects.description: Grand Avenue rehabilitation in Billings was delayed by scheduling conflicts between MDT's construction window and NorthWestern Energy's gas main replacement timeline, which could not overlap due to crew shortages.
projects.detail: MDT's $16.3M Grand Avenue rehabilitation from 13th Street West to Shiloh Road experienced scheduling conflicts with NorthWestern Energy's planned gas main replacement along the same corridor. NorthWestern Energy committed to completing their gas work before MDT's paving window, but regional crew shortages following demand from the Bakken oil field pushed the utility's timeline back by 5 months. MDT could not begin full-depth reclamation work until the gas mains were replaced, and the delayed start pushed paving into late fall when temperatures were marginal for asphalt placement. The contractor required premium pay for cold-weather paving and additional mobilization costs, adding $2.6M to the project.

projects.name: Casper Center Street Bridge and Utility Relocation
projects.description: Center Street Bridge replacement in Casper was delayed by scheduling conflicts between WYDOT, Pacific Power, and the City's water department, with each entity needing bridge-attached utility access during different seasonal windows.
projects.detail: WYDOT's $19.5M Center Street Bridge replacement over the North Platte River in Casper was delayed 11 months by scheduling conflicts among utilities attached to or crossing near the bridge. Pacific Power's electrical lines, the city's water main, and CenturyLink fiber all crossed the river on or adjacent to the bridge structure. Each utility required removal before demolition and reinstallation on the new bridge, but Pacific Power could only schedule their overhead line work during low-wind months (September-November), while the city's water main bypass required installation before the summer irrigation peak. CenturyLink's fiber relocation was dependent on Pacific Power's line removal. The sequential constraints and seasonal limitations created a scheduling cascade that extended the project nearly a year.

projects.name: Sparks Victorian Avenue Complete Streets
projects.description: Victorian Avenue complete streets project was delayed by scheduling conflicts with NV Energy, TMWA, and AT&T, which could not coordinate overlapping relocations in Sparks' narrow historic downtown corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Sparks' $19.6M Victorian Avenue complete streets project through the historic downtown was delayed 13 months due to scheduling conflicts among NV Energy, Truckee Meadows Water Authority (TMWA), and AT&T. The narrow Victorian-era street grid limited construction to one utility relocation at a time. NV Energy required a 4-month lead time for transformer vault relocation that conflicted with TMWA's water main replacement schedule, which was tied to a federal grant with a fixed expenditure deadline. AT&T's legacy copper-to-fiber conversion was already underway and could not be paused. The city attempted three different phasing plans before finding a workable sequence, but the coordination delays added $4.9M in extended overhead and traffic management costs.

projects.name: Santa Fe Cerrillos Road Reconstruction (Phase 2)
projects.description: Cerrillos Road Phase 2 reconstruction was delayed a year by scheduling conflicts between PNM, New Mexico Gas Company, and CenturyLink, exacerbated by Santa Fe's narrow construction season due to monsoon weather.
projects.detail: The City of Santa Fe's $29.5M Cerrillos Road Phase 2 reconstruction from St. Francis Drive to Rodeo Road was delayed 12 months by overlapping utility relocation schedules. PNM's underground electrical duct bank replacement and New Mexico Gas Company's main replacement both required full road closure along the same segments, but neither utility could adjust their material procurement or crew schedules. Santa Fe's usable construction season is limited by monsoon storms from July through September and by the tourist season restrictions in the historic area. The compressed available construction window meant that when PNM's work slipped by 3 months, it cascaded into a full-year delay as the gas company's window shifted to the following spring.

projects.name: CDOT SH-82 Entrance to Aspen
projects.description: SH-82 improvements at the entrance to Aspen were delayed by scheduling conflicts between CDOT, Holy Cross Energy, and the Aspen Consolidated Sanitation District, with ski season construction restrictions limiting available work windows.
projects.detail: CDOT's $90M SH-82 improvement project at the entrance to Aspen was constrained by the town's strict construction moratorium during ski season (November through April) and major summer events. Holy Cross Energy's overhead-to-underground conversion and the Aspen Consolidated Sanitation District's sewer interceptor upgrade both competed for the same May-October construction window. Holy Cross Energy required 8 months of continuous work for the power conversion, consuming more than one full construction season, while the sanitation district's sewer work needed to be completed before CDOT's roadway reconstruction could begin. The narrow seasonal windows and competing utility schedules added 14 months and $18M in additional costs.

projects.name: Laramie Grand Avenue/US 30 Improvements
projects.description: Grand Avenue improvements in Laramie were delayed by scheduling conflicts between WYDOT, Black Hills Energy, and CenturyLink, with University of Wyoming event schedules further constraining work windows.
projects.detail: WYDOT's $12M Grand Avenue/US 30 improvement project through Laramie was delayed 7 months by scheduling conflicts between Black Hills Energy gas main upgrades and CenturyLink's copper retirement program along the corridor. Both utilities had committed to pre-construction relocations but could not coordinate their crews during the same mobilization period. Additionally, the University of Wyoming required construction pauses during football game weekends and move-in/move-out periods, further constraining the available work windows. The combination of utility scheduling conflicts and university event restrictions meant that only 4 months per year of full construction activity were possible, extending the project well beyond its planned completion.

projects.name: Meridian Ten Mile Road Widening
projects.description: Ten Mile Road widening in rapidly growing Meridian was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Idaho Power, Suez Water, and multiple fiber providers all needing to relocate infrastructure in the same corridor.
projects.detail: The Ada County Highway District's $28.9M Ten Mile Road widening from Franklin to Ustick in Meridian was delayed 10 months by scheduling conflicts among Idaho Power, Suez Water (now Veolia), and three fiber optic providers (Sparklight, Lumen, and TDS Fiber). All utilities needed to relocate infrastructure from the same side of the road to accommodate widening, but coordinating five different utility companies' schedules, each with their own contractor and material procurement timelines, proved impossible within the planned 6-month relocation window. Idaho Power's substation feed relocation was on an 8-month transformer delivery lead time that could not be accelerated. The sequential utility work extended the project by 10 months and generated $5.2M in delay costs.

projects.name: NDOT I-11 Boulder City Bypass Utility Coordination
projects.description: I-11 Boulder City bypass segment experienced 20 months of delays from scheduling conflicts with Bureau of Reclamation water infrastructure and NV Energy power transmission lines serving Hoover Dam operations.
projects.detail: NDOT's $700M I-11 Boulder City bypass encountered significant scheduling conflicts with Bureau of Reclamation water infrastructure and NV Energy high-voltage transmission lines that serve Hoover Dam operations. The Bureau of Reclamation required a minimum 18-month advance notice for any work affecting water conveyance infrastructure, but NDOT's construction schedule assumed a 6-month coordination timeline. NV Energy's 230kV transmission line relocation required Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approval and could only be performed during specific low-demand periods. The combination of federal agency coordination requirements and energy transmission constraints added 20 months and $42M in escalation and delay costs to the project.

projects.name: Great Falls 10th Avenue South Reconstruction
projects.description: 10th Avenue South reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between NorthWestern Energy and the City of Great Falls water department, both competing for the same limited warm-weather construction season.
projects.detail: MDT's $10.7M 10th Avenue South reconstruction in Great Falls was delayed when NorthWestern Energy's gas main replacement schedule conflicted with the city's water main upgrade planned for the same corridor. Great Falls' construction season is limited to May through October due to harsh winter conditions, and both utilities needed full road closure for their respective pipe installations. NorthWestern Energy's gas main contractor was committed to another project in the Billings area until July, consuming half the available construction season. The city's water department could not begin their work until the gas main was complete and tested, pushing their installation into October when weather conditions forced a winter shutdown. The remaining work carried over to the following spring.

projects.name: UDOT SR-201 (21st South) Reconstruction
projects.description: SR-201 reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between UDOT, Dominion Energy, and the Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District, complicated by the need to maintain access to the Salt Lake Valley's largest industrial corridor.
projects.detail: UDOT's $87.6M SR-201 reconstruction from Redwood Road to I-215 was delayed 14 months by scheduling conflicts between Dominion Energy's high-pressure gas transmission main and Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District's 42-inch water supply line, both running parallel to the highway. Dominion Energy required federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration approval for its relocation, which took 9 months longer than anticipated. The Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District could not shut down their transmission main during summer peak demand and restricted work to October through March. The corridor serves as the primary access route to the Salt Lake Valley's western industrial zone, limiting traffic control options and preventing concurrent utility work on both sides of the highway.

projects.name: Gallup US 491 Corridor Improvements
projects.description: US 491 corridor improvements near Gallup were delayed by scheduling conflicts between NMDOT, Navajo Tribal Utility Authority, and Continental Divide Electric Cooperative utility relocations across reservation boundaries.
projects.detail: NMDOT's $25.2M US 491 corridor improvement project near Gallup encountered scheduling conflicts involving Navajo Tribal Utility Authority (NTUA) and Continental Divide Electric Cooperative. NTUA utility relocations on tribal land required separate Bureau of Indian Affairs environmental clearance that operated on a different timeline than NMDOT's construction schedule. Continental Divide Electric Cooperative's overhead-to-underground conversion competed for the same contractor workforce as NTUA's work. Coordination between state, federal, and tribal permitting agencies proved time-consuming, with each entity requiring separate approval processes. The multi-jurisdictional complexity added 11 months and $5.3M to the project.

projects.name: Prescott Gurley Street Bridge Replacement
projects.description: Gurley Street Bridge replacement in Prescott was delayed after construction crews struck a live APS 12kV underground power feed, causing a 3-block power outage in the downtown historic district.
projects.detail: During excavation for the Gurley Street Bridge replacement over Granite Creek, construction crews struck a live Arizona Public Service 12kV underground power feed that was not shown on utility locates. The strike caused a 3-block power outage affecting downtown Prescott businesses for 8 hours and required emergency APS repair crews. Investigation revealed the power feed had been installed during a 1990s downtown revitalization project and was never added to APS's GIS mapping system. The incident triggered a full utility re-survey of the entire project footprint, adding 4 months while APS verified all underground facilities in the area. The city imposed enhanced potholing requirements for the remainder of the project, adding $1.8M in additional utility investigation and repair costs.

projects.name: Coeur d'Alene Government Way Sewer Replacement
projects.description: Sewer line replacement on Government Way was disrupted by two separate utility strikes in one week: an Avista gas main and a Frontier Communications fiber conduit, triggering an OSHA investigation.
projects.detail: The City of Coeur d'Alene's $10M Government Way sewer replacement project experienced two separate utility strikes within a single week. The first strike hit an Avista Utilities gas distribution main during trench excavation, requiring evacuation of a one-block radius and emergency repair. Five days later, a different crew struck a Frontier Communications fiber optic conduit 50 feet from the first incident. Both utilities were marked but at locations that differed from actual positions by 2-3 feet in the congested downtown utility corridor. The dual strikes triggered an OSHA investigation and a project-wide safety stand-down.
