The contractor was required to pothole every utility crossing before mechanical excavation, adding $1.1M in costs and 3 months to the schedule.

projects.name: Elko Idaho Street Reconstruction
projects.description: Idaho Street reconstruction was disrupted when excavation struck a Southwest Gas distribution main serving a residential neighborhood, requiring emergency gas shutoff to 85 homes during December.
projects.detail: During the City of Elko's $6M Idaho Street reconstruction project, excavation for storm drain improvements struck a Southwest Gas distribution main at an intersection where the gas line was 3 feet from its located position. The strike occurred in early December, requiring emergency gas shutoff to 85 homes during near-freezing temperatures. Southwest Gas deployed emergency crews and portable heating units to affected residents while repairs were made over 48 hours. The incident was attributed to the gas main having been relocated during a previous water line project in the 1990s without updating utility records. The contractor halted work for 6 weeks while comprehensive potholing of all remaining gas crossings was completed, adding $480K to the project.

projects.name: Kalispell US 93 Bypass Fiber Optic Cut
projects.description: US 93 bypass construction severed a Lumen Technologies fiber optic trunk serving Flathead Valley hospitals, disrupting electronic health records and telemedicine for 18 hours across the region.
projects.detail: During MDT's $18M US 93 bypass construction near Kalispell, grading operations severed a Lumen Technologies (formerly CenturyLink) fiber optic trunk line that served as the primary data connection for Kalispell Regional Healthcare and Logan Health facilities. The cut disrupted electronic health records, telemedicine services, and laboratory systems for 18 hours across Flathead Valley healthcare facilities. The fiber trunk was buried 2 feet below the planned grade cut elevation and was not shown on utility locates because it ran through an easement on adjacent private property rather than within the highway right-of-way. The incident prompted MDT to require contractors to investigate utility easements on adjacent parcels for all future highway projects. Repair and delay costs totaled $720K.

projects.name: Rock Springs Elk Street Utility Upgrades
projects.description: Utility upgrade work on Elk Street struck a Pacific Power underground electric feed serving the city's water treatment plant, causing a brief treatment disruption and triggering a boil-water advisory.
projects.detail: During the City of Rock Springs' $4.8M Elk Street utility upgrade project, excavation for a new water main struck a Pacific Power underground electric feed that provided backup power to the city's water treatment plant. The strike caused a brief disruption to treatment operations that triggered a precautionary boil-water advisory for 2,400 residents lasting 48 hours. The underground power feed was installed during a 2005 treatment plant expansion but was not recorded on city or utility company maps at the Elk Street location. Pacific Power repaired the feed within 6 hours, but the boil-water advisory required 48 hours of water quality testing before it could be lifted. Additional potholing requirements added $340K to the project.

projects.name: Farmington East Main Street Reconstruction
projects.description: East Main Street reconstruction was disrupted when a trenching machine severed a New Mexico Gas Company 4-inch steel main, causing a gas leak that shut down traffic and nearby businesses for 6 hours.
projects.detail: During the City of Farmington's $9.5M East Main Street reconstruction project, a trenching machine installing new storm drain pipe severed a New Mexico Gas Company 4-inch steel distribution main. The gas leak forced evacuation of nearby businesses and closure of a three-block stretch of East Main Street for 6 hours while emergency repairs were completed. The gas main was 4 feet south of its marked location, likely having been shifted during a previous road project without as-built updates. Investigation found that the original utility locate ticket was 45 days old and had not been refreshed, exceeding New Mexico's 15-working-day validity period. The contractor faced penalties and was required to implement real-time GPS tracking of all excavation relative to utility marks for the remainder of the project.

projects.name: West Valley City 3500 South Gas Strike
projects.description: 3500 South road reconstruction struck a Dominion Energy high-pressure gas transmission main, triggering a large-scale evacuation and bringing state pipeline safety regulators to the site.
projects.detail: During West Valley City's $15M 3500 South road reconstruction project, a backhoe operator struck a Dominion Energy 12-inch high-pressure natural gas transmission main during storm drain installation. The strike caused a large uncontrolled gas release that required evacuation of a 500-foot radius including a strip mall and elementary school. Utah's Division of Pipeline Safety responded to investigate. The transmission main was at the correct horizontal position but 2 feet shallower than shown on Dominion Energy records, placing it within the storm drain excavation zone. The incident resulted in a full project shutdown for 3 weeks while Dominion Energy verified the depth of all transmission facilities along the corridor. Enhanced monitoring and protection-in-place requirements added $1.2M and 3 months to the project.

projects.name: Durango East 2nd Avenue HDD Fiber Strike
projects.description: A horizontal directional drill installing new water service on East 2nd Avenue struck and severed a Brightspeed fiber trunk, disrupting internet service to 2,200 Durango customers for 14 hours.
projects.detail: During the City of Durango's $4.7M East 2nd Avenue water infrastructure replacement, a horizontal directional drilling crew installing new water service lines struck and severed a Brightspeed (formerly Lumen) fiber optic trunk line serving the downtown commercial district. The strike disrupted internet and phone service to approximately 2,200 customers for 14 hours, impacting downtown businesses during peak tourist season. The fiber trunk was installed via HDD during a 2018 project and its as-built location was recorded with only GPS coordinates, not depth, making the locate inaccurate for subsurface crossings. The incident prompted the city to require vacuum excavation verification at all HDD crossing points, adding $380K in additional costs.

projects.name: Sedona SR-179 Roundabout Construction Telecom Cut
projects.description: Roundabout construction on SR-179 severed a Cox Communications fiber trunk serving Sedona's hotel and resort corridor, disrupting reservations and point-of-sale systems during peak tourism season.
projects.detail: During ADOT's $18M SR-179 roundabout construction project at the gateway to Sedona, excavation for the roundabout's central drainage system severed a Cox Communications fiber optic trunk line. The cut disrupted internet, phone, and cable television service to Sedona's primary hotel and resort corridor for 22 hours, impacting reservation systems, point-of-sale terminals, and guest Wi-Fi during the peak fall tourism season when Sedona's red rock scenery draws its highest visitor counts. The fiber trunk was located within the ADOT right-of-way but had not been included in the utility relocation scope because Cox's records showed it outside the construction footprint. Cox's emergency splice repair restored service but temporary service degradation continued for an additional week.

projects.name: Logan Main Street Utility Modernization
projects.description: Main Street utility modernization struck a Dominion Energy gas service line while installing new water infrastructure, causing a gas leak in the Cache Valley commercial district and a 4-hour business evacuation.
projects.detail: During the City of Logan's $9.6M Main Street utility modernization project, installation of new water main fittings struck a Dominion Energy gas service line at a connection point that was not shown on utility locate markings. The service line had been installed as part of a building renovation in 2012 and connected to the main at an angle that placed it outside the standard locate zone. The gas leak required evacuation of businesses in a two-block area of the Cache Valley commercial district for 4 hours. Dominion Energy's investigation found that the service line had been installed by a third-party contractor who did not submit as-built information. The city required comprehensive gas service verification at all building connections along the project corridor, adding $870K in potholing and delay costs.

projects.name: Rexburg Main Street Fiber Strike During Water Project
projects.description: Water main replacement on Rexburg's Main Street severed a Fybercom fiber trunk line serving Brigham Young University-Idaho, disrupting campus internet for 10,000 students during finals week.
projects.detail: During the City of Rexburg's $5.2M Main Street water main replacement, a backhoe operator severed a Fybercom fiber optic trunk line that served as the primary internet connection to Brigham Young University-Idaho. The cut occurred during finals week, disrupting internet access for approximately 10,000 students and forcing the university to extend exam deadlines. Fybercom's fiber was installed in 2017 using a micro-trenching technique that placed the conduit at only 12 inches below grade rather than the standard 36-inch depth. The shallow burial was not reflected on utility records, and the locate marks did not indicate the unusual depth. The university and city jointly funded enhanced utility mapping along Main Street to prevent future incidents.

projects.name: Colorado Springs Platte Avenue Resurfacing / Utility Cuts
projects.description: Colorado Springs' $8.5M Platte Avenue resurfacing was undermined when Colorado Springs Utilities cut into the fresh pavement within 4 months to perform gas line repairs, despite the city's own 5-year moratorium policy.
projects.detail: Colorado Springs completed an $8.5M full-depth resurfacing of Platte Avenue from I-25 to Circle Drive in fall 2022. Within 4 months, Colorado Springs Utilities — the city's own municipal utility — cut into the new pavement at three locations to perform emergency gas line repairs. The city's 5-year paving moratorium policy was supposed to prevent such cuts, but the utility claimed emergency exemptions for aging gas infrastructure. The cuts left visible patches on the recently resurfaced roadway and drew complaints from residents and business owners who had endured months of construction disruption. The incident highlighted the coordination gap between the city's public works and utility departments despite being under the same municipal government.
projects.budget: $8.5M resurfacing → $2.1M in restoration and re-paving costs
projects.timeline: Resurfaced fall 2022 → Cut into by February 2023

projects.name: Boise Fairview Avenue Overlay / Idaho Power Cuts
projects.description: Boise's Fairview Avenue overlay project was compromised when Idaho Power cut into fresh pavement at seven locations within 3 months for underground cable replacement, despite pre-construction coordination meetings.
projects.detail: The Ada County Highway District completed a $6.8M overlay of Fairview Avenue between Cole and Curtis Roads in summer 2023. Idaho Power then cut into the fresh pavement at seven locations within 3 months to replace aging underground cables serving commercial properties. ACHD had held pre-construction coordination meetings with Idaho Power, but the utility claimed the cable replacements were reactive maintenance triggered by subsequent failures, not planned projects that could have been scheduled before the overlay. ACHD estimated the utility cuts reduced the pavement life by 3-5 years at each location. The restoration patches failed to match the new overlay surface, drawing complaints from motorists and business owners. ACHD began exploring a formal moratorium policy similar to those in other Idaho cities.
projects.budget: $6.8M overlay → $1.7M in restoration and accelerated degradation costs
projects.timeline: Completed summer 2023 → Cut into by November 2023

projects.name: Reno South Virginia Street Repaving / NV Energy Cuts
projects.description: Reno's $11M South Virginia Street repaving between Plumb Lane and Mount Rose Street was cut open by NV Energy at five locations within 5 months for transformer vault maintenance it classified as emergency work.
projects.detail: The City of Reno completed an $11M repaving of South Virginia Street, the city's primary north-south commercial corridor, in late 2022. Within 5 months, NV Energy cut into the new pavement at five locations for underground transformer vault maintenance and cable replacement that the utility classified as emergency work exempt from the city's paving moratorium. City engineers disputed the emergency classification, noting that the transformer vaults had been identified for maintenance in NV Energy's own capital plan months before the repaving began. The cuts and patches created uneven ride surfaces on the recently smooth roadway. The incident prompted Reno's city council to introduce an ordinance requiring utilities to certify they have no planned work within 100 feet of any repaving project for the next 3 years.
projects.budget: $11M repaving → $2.8M in restoration and accelerated maintenance costs
projects.timeline: Completed late 2022 → Cut into by April 2023

projects.name: St. George Bluff Street / Dixie Drive Resurfacing / Washington County Fiber
projects.description: St. George's recently completed Bluff Street resurfacing was cut into by Washington County's fiber broadband project within 3 months, with the county and city blaming each other for the coordination failure.
projects.detail: UDOT completed a $7.5M resurfacing of Bluff Street (SR-18) through St. George in summer 2023. Within 3 months, Washington County's municipal broadband fiber project began cutting into the fresh pavement to install conduit along the corridor. UDOT and the City of St. George had coordinated with the county's fiber project during the design phase, but the fiber project timeline slipped by 6 months, missing the coordination window. The county claimed the slippage was due to supply chain delays on fiber conduit materials, while the city argued the county should have notified UDOT to delay the resurfacing. The incident highlighted the difficulty of coordinating utility and road projects across overlapping state, county, and city jurisdictions in one of the fastest-growing metropolitan areas in Utah.
projects.timeline: Resurfaced summer 2023 → Cut into by October 2023

projects.name: Albuquerque Central Avenue Complete Streets / PNM Cuts
projects.description: Albuquerque's Central Avenue complete streets renovation along the former Route 66 was cut into by PNM at eight locations within 4 months for underground cable replacement and transformer vault upgrades.
projects.detail: The City of Albuquerque completed a $28M phase of its Central Avenue complete streets renovation along the historic Route 66 corridor in spring 2023, including new bike lanes, transit improvements, and full-depth pavement reconstruction. Within 4 months, PNM began cutting into the completed work at eight locations along a 1.5-mile segment for underground cable replacement and transformer vault upgrades. PNM's underground infrastructure along Central Avenue was among the oldest in the city, and the utility argued that the failures requiring repair were not foreseeable. The city pointed to PNM's asset management records showing the cables were past their rated service life. Restoration of the decorative crosswalk treatments and bike lane markings was particularly costly. The city council accelerated adoption of a formal utility coordination ordinance with financial penalties.
projects.timeline: Completed spring 2023 → Cut into by August 2023

projects.name: Phoenix Cave Creek Road Repaving / Cox Communications Cuts
projects.description: Phoenix's Cave Creek Road repaving project was compromised when Cox Communications cut into the new pavement at six locations within 4 months for fiber upgrades, claiming they were not notified of the repaving schedule.
projects.detail: The City of Phoenix completed a $12M repaving of Cave Creek Road from Cactus Road to Bell Road in late 2023. Cox Communications then cut into the fresh pavement at six locations within 4 months to install fiber optic upgrades serving new residential developments. Cox claimed they were not adequately notified of the repaving schedule despite the city's 90-day advance notification to all utilities. Phoenix's utility coordination office produced email records showing Cox had been notified three times. The cuts were particularly damaging at intersections where the new pavement tied into recent signal upgrades, requiring partial intersection reconstruction. Phoenix's transportation director cited the incident as evidence for the need for a citywide utility coordination platform with mandatory participation.
projects.timeline: Completed late 2023 → Cut into by March 2024

projects.name: Littleton West Main Street Reconstruction / South Denver Water Cuts
projects.description: Littleton's West Main Street reconstruction through the historic downtown was cut into by South Denver Water within 6 months for a water service connection that the utility claimed was not foreseeable during planning.
projects.detail: The City of Littleton completed a $7.8M reconstruction of West Main Street through its historic downtown district, including decorative brick pavers, new streetscape lighting, and underground utility vault improvements, in spring 2023. Within 6 months, South Denver Water cut through the decorative pavers and new concrete to install a water service connection to a new restaurant that received its building permit after the street reconstruction was completed. The utility argued the service connection was a customer-driven request that could not have been anticipated, but the city noted the restaurant building had been under renovation for over a year before the street work began. Replacing the custom decorative pavers required a 3-month fabrication lead time, leaving a temporary asphalt patch in the historic streetscape.
projects.timeline: Completed spring 2023 → Cut into by October 2023

projects.name: Sandy 10600 South Resurfacing / Dominion Energy Cuts
projects.description: Sandy's 10600 South resurfacing was cut into by Dominion Energy at three locations within 2 months for gas service upgrades related to new commercial development, despite pre-construction coordination.
projects.detail: The City of Sandy completed a $4.2M resurfacing of 10600 South from State Street to 700 East in fall 2023. Within 2 months, Dominion Energy cut into the new pavement at three locations to upgrade gas service connections for a new commercial development at the 10600 South/State Street intersection. The development project had been approved before the resurfacing began, and Dominion Energy's gas service design had been submitted to the city. However, the gas work timeline slipped due to material procurement delays, and rather than coordinating with the resurfacing schedule, Dominion Energy proceeded independently. The city assessed restoration penalties under its moratorium policy, marking one of the first enforcement actions under Sandy's recently strengthened utility coordination ordinance.
projects.budget: $4.2M resurfacing → $950K in restoration and penalty costs
projects.timeline: Completed fall 2023 → Cut into by December 2023

projects.name: Billings Rimrock Road Overlay / MDT-NorthWestern Coordination Failure
projects.description: MDT's Rimrock Road overlay in Billings was cut into by NorthWestern Energy within 3 months for gas main repairs at two locations, highlighting Montana's lack of a formal paving moratorium statute.
projects.detail: MDT completed a $5.6M overlay of Rimrock Road in Billings from 24th Street West to Shiloh Road in fall 2023. NorthWestern Energy cut into the new pavement at two locations within 3 months for gas main repairs that the utility classified as reactive maintenance. MDT's project team had contacted NorthWestern Energy during design, but the utility reported no planned work on the corridor. Montana has no statewide paving moratorium statute, and Billings' municipal code did not address post-paving utility cuts on state highways. NorthWestern Energy's restoration patches were of lower quality than the new overlay surface, creating visible ride-quality differences. The Billings city council began exploring a moratorium ordinance modeled on policies in neighboring states.
projects.timeline: Completed fall 2023 → Cut into by January 2024

projects.name: Henderson Water Street Streetscape / Southwest Gas Cuts
projects.description: Henderson's $15M Water Street district streetscape was cut into by Southwest Gas at four locations within 5 months for main replacement work that had been identified in the utility's capital plan before the streetscape began.
projects.detail: The City of Henderson completed its showcase $15M Water Street district streetscape project in downtown Henderson in summer 2023, featuring decorative pavers, enhanced pedestrian lighting, and public art installations. Within 5 months, Southwest Gas cut into the completed streetscape at four locations for gas main replacement along a two-block segment. Investigation revealed that Southwest Gas had identified the Water Street gas main for replacement in its 2022 capital plan, predating the streetscape project. The utility attributed the scheduling overlap to different internal departments managing capital planning and construction coordination. Henderson's city manager called the situation 'an avoidable failure of basic communication' and imposed full streetscape restoration costs on Southwest Gas including replacement of custom-fabricated decorative pavers.
projects.timeline: Completed summer 2023 → Cut into by December 2023

projects.name: CDOT I-25/Cimarron (US 24) Interchange Reconstruction
projects.description: I-25/Cimarron interchange reconstruction required major plan revisions after discovering extensive unrecorded Colorado Springs Utilities infrastructure including a 30-inch sewer interceptor in the bridge pier footprint.
projects.detail: CDOT's $272M I-25/Cimarron interchange reconstruction in Colorado Springs required extensive plan revisions after subsurface investigation revealed a 30-inch Colorado Springs Utilities sewer interceptor running directly through the footprint of planned bridge piers. The interceptor was not shown on utility records at the correct depth or alignment, and its relocation required temporary bypass pumping and a complex sequencing plan to maintain sewer service to the downtown core during construction. Additional undocumented utilities discovered during potholing included abandoned Colorado Interstate Gas Company pipeline segments and a decommissioned military communication conduit from the former Camp Carson era. The cumulative plan revisions added $68M and 2 years to the project.

projects.name: NDOT US 95 Widening (Las Vegas to Indian Springs)
projects.description: US 95 widening required plan revisions after discovery of unrecorded Nellis Air Force Base utility crossings and a Department of Energy fiber optic line serving the Nevada National Security Site.
projects.detail: NDOT's $127M US 95 widening from the northern Las Vegas valley to Indian Springs required plan revisions when subsurface investigation found unrecorded military utility crossings from Nellis Air Force Base and a Department of Energy fiber optic communications line serving the Nevada National Security Site (formerly the Nevada Test Site). The DOE fiber line was classified infrastructure that required special coordination with the National Nuclear Security Administration. Nellis AFB's utility crossings included water and electrical feeds to remote training areas that were installed under blanket military easements without state notification. Coordinating design changes with multiple federal agencies, each with their own security and review requirements, added 12 months and $19M to the project.

projects.name: Sierra Vista Fry Boulevard Reconstruction
projects.description: Fry Boulevard reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between ADOT, Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative, and Fort Huachuca's utility operations, with military base security protocols limiting coordination.
projects.detail: ADOT's $20M Fry Boulevard reconstruction in Sierra Vista was delayed 9 months by scheduling conflicts involving Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative and the U.S. Army's Fort Huachuca installation. The military base's utility infrastructure extends under Fry Boulevard at several locations, and base security protocols required military-escorted utility relocation work that could only be scheduled through a complex approval process. Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative's overhead-to-underground conversion competed for the same construction season, and the cooperative's limited contractor resources in rural southeastern Arizona meant long lead times for crew availability. The combination of military scheduling constraints and limited contractor availability in the region added 9 months and $3.8M to the project.

projects.name: Layton North Main Street Reconstruction
projects.description: North Main Street reconstruction was disrupted when trenching struck a Dominion Energy abandoned-but-pressurized gas main that was not shown on any utility records, causing a 6-hour gas leak and road closure.
projects.detail: During the City of Layton's $12.2M North Main Street reconstruction project, trenching for new storm drain pipe struck what was supposed to be an abandoned Dominion Energy gas main. However, investigation revealed the main was still pressurized — it had been classified as abandoned in Dominion Energy's records during a 2015 system consolidation but was never actually disconnected from the active distribution system. The strike caused a 6-hour gas leak and road closure that required emergency response from both Layton Fire Department and Dominion Energy's emergency crews. The discovery prompted Dominion Energy to conduct a systemwide audit of abandoned gas mains in Davis County to verify disconnection status. Additional verification requirements added $980K and 2 months to the project.

projects.name: Butte Harrison Avenue Reconstruction
projects.description: Harrison Avenue reconstruction required plan revisions after discovering contaminated mine drainage infrastructure and undocumented NorthWestern Energy steam heating conduits beneath Butte's historic commercial corridor.
projects.detail: MDT's $14M Harrison Avenue reconstruction in Butte encountered severe subsurface challenges related to the city's mining heritage. Abandoned mine drainage infrastructure, including acid mine drainage pipes and timber-framed shafts, was discovered crossing beneath the roadway at depths conflicting with planned utility installations. Contaminated soils surrounding the mining infrastructure required EPA coordination under the Butte-Silver Bow Superfund site protocols. Additionally, undocumented NorthWestern Energy steam heating conduits from Butte's early 20th century district heating system were found still intact beneath the intersection of Harrison and Park Street. The combination of environmental remediation requirements and plan redesign around mining-era infrastructure added $3.5M and 10 months.

projects.name: Pueblo West US 50 Widening Fiber Strike
projects.description: US 50 widening in Pueblo West severed a Comcast fiber trunk during shoulder grading, disrupting cable and internet service to 3,400 customers in the unincorporated community for 16 hours.
projects.detail: During CDOT's $8.5M US 50 widening project through Pueblo West, shoulder grading operations severed a Comcast fiber optic trunk line that was buried at a shallower depth than typical utility burial standards. The cut disrupted cable television, internet, and phone service to approximately 3,400 Comcast customers in the Pueblo West community for 16 hours. Investigation revealed the fiber trunk had been installed using a plow method that achieved only 12-18 inches of cover in the rocky Pueblo West soils, rather than the standard 36-inch burial depth. Comcast's as-built records did not note the shallow burial. CDOT required Comcast to verify and if necessary deepen all fiber infrastructure within the project limits before grading operations could resume.

projects.name: Orem University Parkway / Geneva Road Interchange
projects.description: University Parkway/Geneva Road interchange was delayed by scheduling conflicts between UDOT, Rocky Mountain Power, and the Central Utah Water Conservancy District over a critical irrigation pipeline crossing.
projects.detail: UDOT's $73.5M University Parkway/Geneva Road interchange project in Orem was delayed 14 months by scheduling conflicts centered on a 48-inch Central Utah Water Conservancy District irrigation pipeline crossing beneath the planned interchange. The pipeline could only be relocated during the winter irrigation off-season (November through March), but Rocky Mountain Power's overhead-to-underground conversion for the interchange required the same excavation zones during the same period. Rocky Mountain Power's work was dependent on delivery of custom switchgear with a 10-month manufacturing lead time that could not be shortened. The irrigation district's pipeline relocation and Rocky Mountain Power's electrical conversion could not be sequenced within a single off-season, adding a full year to the utility phase alone. The cascading delays increased project costs by $12.5M.

projects.name: Marana Ina Road Widening
projects.description: Ina Road widening plans were revised after discovering an undocumented Tucson Water aqueduct crossing and Tucson Electric Power underground feeds conflicting with the planned widening footprint.
projects.detail: The Town of Marana's $30.5M Ina Road widening from I-10 to Thornydale Road required plan revisions after potholing discovered a Tucson Water aqueduct crossing at a different location and depth than shown on regional utility records. The 36-inch aqueduct was part of the Central Arizona Project water delivery system and could not be taken out of service for relocation during the summer peak demand period. Additionally, Tucson Electric Power underground feeds serving a large master-planned community were found in the planned widening footprint. The combination of water infrastructure constraints and power relocation requirements forced a complete redesign of the Ina Road/Cortaro Farms Road intersection, converting it from a planned diverging diamond to a conventional signalized intersection to avoid the most critical utility conflicts.

projects.name: Muni Metro Subway Renewal Program
projects.description: SFMTA's subway tunnel rehabilitation required extensive plan revisions after subsurface utility surveys revealed unmapped sewer and electrical conduit conflicts beneath Market Street.
projects.detail: The Muni Metro Subway Renewal Program aimed to modernize aging tunnel infrastructure along the Market Street corridor. During the 30% design phase, subsurface utility engineering surveys discovered extensive unmapped sewer laterals and electrical conduits from the 1906 post-earthquake rebuild era that conflicted with planned track bed lowering and station platform extensions. The design team had to revise foundation plans for three stations and reroute over 4,000 linear feet of combined sewer infrastructure. These revisions added $185 million in utility relocation and redesign costs and pushed the construction start date back by two years, delaying the overall completion from 2028 to 2030.

projects.name: SANDAG Mid-Coast Trolley Blue Line Extension Utility Redesign
projects.description: The Mid-Coast Trolley extension required major plan revisions after encountering 72-inch water transmission mains and fiber optic trunk lines in the UCSD campus segment that were not reflected in original utility records.
projects.detail: SANDAG's 11-mile extension of the Blue Line Trolley into the University City and UCSD campus area hit significant design conflicts when field verification revealed that the San Diego County Water Authority's 72-inch prestressed concrete cylinder pipe ran directly through the planned at-grade alignment near the VA Medical Center station. Additionally, multiple fiber optic trunk lines serving the UCSD campus network were found at shallower depths than recorded. The alignment had to be shifted and two stations redesigned to avoid these critical utilities, adding $68 million in change orders and extending the timeline by 18 months. The project highlighted SANDAG's need for better subsurface utility engineering early in the planning process.

projects.name: Sacramento Arden Way Multimodal Corridor
projects.description: Sacramento's Arden Way corridor project required plan revisions after discovering conflicting SMUD underground electrical feeders and an unrecorded AT&T duct bank beneath the planned median transit lane.
projects.detail: The Arden Way Multimodal Corridor project intended to convert the wide arterial into a complete street with a center-running transit lane between Howe Avenue and Watt Avenue. During the 60% design review, SMUD identified that multiple underground 12kV electrical feeders crossed the corridor at points directly beneath the planned median transitway. Additionally, an unrecorded AT&T duct bank with active fiber was discovered during test borings. Relocating these utilities required redesigning intersection geometry at five locations and shifting the transit alignment, adding $8.5 million in costs and 11 months of delay. The project highlighted gaps in Sacramento's utility mapping database.

projects.name: Portland Division Street Transit Project Utility Redesign
projects.description: TriMet's Division Transit Project required major plan revisions after discovering Portland Water Bureau mains and BES combined sewer infrastructure conflicts along the SE Division Street corridor.
projects.detail: TriMet's Division Transit Project, a 14.5-mile bus rapid transit line along SE Division Street, encountered substantial utility conflicts during final design. Portland Water Bureau mains dating to the 1920s were found at depths shallower than recorded, directly conflicting with station platform foundations at five locations. Additionally, Bureau of Environmental Services combined sewer pipes required protection or relocation at multiple planned queue jump locations. The design revisions required relocating approximately 2,800 linear feet of water main and reinforcing sewer infrastructure at an additional cost of $42 million. These changes pushed the project opening from late 2022 to early 2024 and contributed to the total project cost rising beyond initial estimates.

projects.name: Eugene MovingAhead EmX West Extension
projects.description: Lane Transit District's EmX West extension plans were revised multiple times after discovering EWEB electrical infrastructure and Springfield Utility Board water mains conflicting with the exclusive bus guideway design.
projects.detail: The EmX West extension along West 11th Avenue was planned to extend Bus Rapid Transit service from downtown Eugene toward the western neighborhoods. During preliminary engineering, the Eugene Water and Electric Board identified that high-voltage underground electrical transmission lines serving the industrial corridor directly conflicted with the planned exclusive bus guideway at six locations. Additionally, aging water mains along the corridor were found to be in worse condition than mapped, requiring concurrent replacement rather than simple protection in place. The combined utility conflicts forced three rounds of plan revisions, adding $18 million to the project budget and delaying the environmental review process by two years. LTD ultimately scaled back the guideway design to reduce utility impacts.

projects.name: Seattle Ship Canal Water Quality Project Redesign
projects.description: King County's combined sewer overflow storage tunnel project required plan revisions after encountering Seattle City Light underground vaults and unmapped abandoned industrial infrastructure beneath the Ballard neighborhood.
projects.detail: King County's Ship Canal Water Quality Project, a 2.7-mile deep storage tunnel to capture combined sewer overflows in the Ballard and Wallingford neighborhoods, required significant plan revisions after geotechnical investigations revealed unmapped underground vaults belonging to Seattle City Light and remnants of early 20th-century industrial infrastructure including abandoned fuel storage tanks. The discovery forced relocation of the tunnel boring machine launch shaft from its originally planned site on NW 54th Street to an alternative location, requiring additional property acquisition and redesign of the surface facilities. The plan revisions added $95 million to the project cost and pushed the completion date from 2025 to 2027, with implications for King County's consent decree compliance with the EPA.

projects.name: Tacoma Pacific Avenue Streetscape Utility Revisions
projects.description: Tacoma's Pacific Avenue streetscape redesign required extensive plan revisions after utility investigations found a tangle of Tacoma Power conduit, PSE gas lines, and CenturyLink duct banks beneath the planned street tree planting zones.
projects.detail: The City of Tacoma's Pacific Avenue Streetscape project between South 7th and South 17th Streets aimed to transform the corridor with wider sidewalks, street trees, protected bike lanes, and improved transit stops. During the utility design phase, investigations revealed that Tacoma Power conduit, Puget Sound Energy gas distribution lines, and CenturyLink telecommunications duct banks occupied nearly the entire subsurface beneath the planned tree planting zones on both sides of the avenue. The conflicts required redesigning the street cross-section to use structural soil cells and relocating gas lines at five intersections, adding $7.2 million in costs and delaying construction by 10 months while utility relocation agreements were negotiated with three separate utility owners.

projects.name: Spokane University District Gateway Bridge Utility Conflict
projects.description: The University District Gateway Bridge project required plan revisions after discovering Avista Utilities gas transmission lines and Inland Power electrical conduit in the bridge approach embankment zones.
projects.detail: The City of Spokane's Gateway Bridge project to connect the University District to the downtown core required plan revisions after preliminary engineering uncovered Avista Utilities high-pressure gas transmission lines running through the planned western bridge approach embankment. Inland Power and Light's underground electrical conduit also conflicted with the eastern abutment foundation design. The gas transmission line could not be relocated without a lengthy permitting process through the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission, forcing the bridge abutment to be redesigned with a deeper foundation that would span over the gas line with adequate clearance. The redesign added $15 million in structural costs and utility protection measures, with a 12-month delay for permitting and redesign work.

projects.name: Honolulu Kapalama Canal Bridge Replacement
projects.description: The Kapalama Canal bridge replacements on Nimitz Highway and Dillingham Boulevard required plan revisions after discovering HECO underground electrical feeders and BWS water mains attached to the existing bridge structures.
projects.detail: The Hawaii Department of Transportation's project to replace aging bridges over the Kapalama Canal on both Nimitz Highway and Dillingham Boulevard hit significant design hurdles when utility investigations revealed Hawaiian Electric Company underground feeders and Board of Water Supply water transmission mains that had been attached to or routed through the existing bridge structures. These utilities were not documented in the original bridge plans from the 1960s. Accommodating temporary utility bypasses during bridge demolition and incorporating new utility corridors into the replacement bridge designs required extensive plan revisions. The redesign added $22 million in costs and 18 months of delay, further complicated by the concurrent HART rail construction in the area creating additional coordination requirements.

projects.name: Maui Lahaina Bypass Phase 2 Utility Realignment
projects.description: Phase 2 of the Lahaina Bypass required extensive plan revisions after discovering MECO underground electrical lines and Maui County water system infrastructure conflicting with the planned highway alignment through the hillside corridor.
projects.detail: The Lahaina Bypass Phase 2, designed to provide an alternative route to congested Honoapiilani Highway through West Maui, required plan revisions after subsurface investigations discovered Maui Electric Company underground distribution lines and Maui County Department of Water Supply transmission mains that traversed the planned alignment at multiple points. These utilities served critical hillside residential communities and could not be de-energized during relocation. The revised plans required constructing temporary utility bypasses, installing deeper foundations to span over protected utility corridors, and relocating approximately 3,200 feet of water main. The changes added $35 million to the project cost and delayed construction by two years, compounded by post-2023 wildfire recovery priorities that redirected county engineering resources.

projects.name: Anchorage Northern Lights Boulevard Rehabilitation
projects.description: Anchorage's Northern Lights Boulevard rehabilitation required plan revisions after discovering unmapped ENSTAR gas lines and GCI telecommunications infrastructure at depths shallower than expected beneath the planned utility corridor.
projects.detail: The Municipality of Anchorage's rehabilitation of Northern Lights Boulevard between Minnesota Drive and Seward Highway included full road reconstruction, utility upgrades, and pedestrian improvements. Plan revisions became necessary when potholing revealed ENSTAR Natural Gas Company distribution lines and GCI fiber optic cables at significantly shallower depths than recorded in the municipality's utility database, directly conflicting with the planned storm drain installation. Alaska's freeze-thaw cycles had shifted utility positions over decades, a common problem in permafrost-affected areas. The redesign required lowering storm drains, adding utility protection casings, and relocating 1,800 feet of gas line, adding $14 million in costs and 16 months of delay to the project schedule.

projects.name: Fairbanks Cushman Street Bridge Replacement Utility Revisions
projects.description: The Cushman Street Bridge replacement over the Chena River in Fairbanks required plan revisions after discovering IGU gas lines and GVEA electrical conduit routed through the bridge structure that were not shown on original plans.
projects.detail: The Alaska DOT&PF's project to replace the Cushman Street Bridge over the Chena River required plan revisions after utility investigations found Interior Gas Utility distribution lines and Golden Valley Electric Association electrical conduit that had been installed through the bridge deck and abutments without being recorded in the original bridge construction documents. The discovery was particularly problematic because the utilities needed to remain in service during bridge demolition, requiring construction of temporary utility bridges alongside the work zone. The extreme cold weather conditions in Fairbanks limited the construction season to approximately five months per year, amplifying the impact of any design delays. The revised plans added $9 million in utility accommodation costs and 14 months to the project timeline, spanning an additional construction season.

projects.name: San Jose BART Phase II Berryessa Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: VTA's BART Phase II tunnel segment through downtown San Jose required redesign of station entrances and ventilation shafts after encountering PG&E gas transmission lines and San Jose Water Company infrastructure not shown on utility records.
projects.detail: VTA's BART Silicon Valley Phase II extension includes a 5-mile tunnel beneath downtown San Jose with four underground stations. During advanced utility engineering for the Diridon and Santa Clara station areas, the project team discovered PG&E high-pressure gas transmission mains and San Jose Water Company infrastructure that conflicted with planned station entrance locations and tunnel ventilation shaft sites. The gas transmission lines required a minimum clearance zone that could not be achieved with the original station entrance configurations. VTA was forced to redesign two station entrances and relocate one ventilation shaft, adding $210 million in redesign and utility relocation costs. The revisions contributed to the project's overall cost escalation and pushed the environmental clearance timeline back by 18 months as supplemental impact studies were required.

projects.name: Olympia Capitol Way Urban Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Olympia's Capitol Way corridor improvement project required plan revisions after encountering unmapped LOTT Clean Water Alliance sewer infrastructure and PSE gas service lines beneath the planned rain garden installations.
projects.detail: The City of Olympia planned a $20 million urban corridor improvement of Capitol Way between State Avenue and 4th Avenue, featuring bioretention rain gardens, wider sidewalks, and transit improvements. Utility investigations discovered unmapped LOTT Clean Water Alliance sewer laterals and Puget Sound Energy gas service lines running directly beneath four of the six planned rain garden locations. The sewer infrastructure included combined sewer overflow connections that could not be relocated without triggering environmental permits. The project required redesigning the stormwater management approach, replacing in-ground bioretention with elevated planters and permeable pavement alternatives. The plan revisions added $4.8 million in costs and 10 months of delay while the city coordinated with LOTT and PSE on utility protection measures.

projects.name: Juneau Egan Drive Pavement Reconstruction
projects.description: Alaska DOT's Egan Drive reconstruction in Juneau required plan revisions after utility investigations found AEL&P electrical conduit and ACS fiber optic lines at non-standard depths due to glacial soil movement.
projects.detail: The Alaska Department of Transportation's Egan Drive pavement reconstruction project between the Mendenhall River and Lemon Creek required plan revisions when utility potholing discovered Alaska Electric Light and Power underground conduit and Alaska Communications Systems fiber optic lines at depths significantly different from their recorded positions. Glacial soil conditions and decades of freeze-thaw cycles had shifted the utilities from their original installation depths, a recurring challenge in Southeast Alaska infrastructure projects. The revised plans required deeper excavation in some areas and protective utility casings in others, adding $11 million in costs and a full year to the project as utility relocation had to occur during Juneau's limited dry-weather construction window. The short construction season in Southeast Alaska meant that even modest delays could push work into the following year.

projects.name: LA Metro Westside Purple Line Section 3 Utility Scheduling Conflicts
projects.description: Section 3 of the Purple Line extension to UCLA was repeatedly delayed by scheduling conflicts with LADWP, SoCalGas, and multiple telecommunications utilities that could not coordinate simultaneous relocations in the Westwood corridor.
projects.detail: LA Metro's Purple Line Section 3, extending heavy rail from Century City to the Westwood/VA Hospital station, faced severe scheduling conflicts with utility relocations along Wilshire Boulevard and the Westwood Village area. LADWP required exclusive access periods for relocating high-voltage underground transmission lines, which conflicted with SoCalGas's planned gas main replacement schedule. Multiple telecommunications utilities including AT&T, Spectrum, and Crown Castle each demanded separate work windows for their underground infrastructure. The inability to coordinate simultaneous utility relocations in the narrow Westwood corridor created a cascading series of delays, with each utility's work window pushing back the next. The scheduling conflicts added $320 million in delay-related costs and extended the project completion from 2027 to 2030, further complicated by UCLA's requirement that major disruptions not occur during the academic year.

projects.name: Bend Parkway US-97 Safety Improvements
projects.description: ODOT's Bend Parkway safety improvements were delayed by scheduling conflicts with Pacific Power underground conversion work and the City of Bend's concurrent sewer interceptor replacement that required the same traffic detour routes.
projects.detail: The Oregon Department of Transportation's safety improvement project on the Bend Parkway (US-97) through central Bend was delayed by 18 months due to scheduling conflicts with two concurrent infrastructure projects. Pacific Power's planned underground conversion of overhead lines along 3rd Street, the primary detour route for the Parkway project, conflicted with ODOT's proposed construction phasing. Simultaneously, the City of Bend's sewer interceptor replacement project along the Deschutes River paralleled the Parkway corridor and required the same staging areas. The three agencies could not align their construction schedules, and ODOT was forced to delay its project start until Pacific Power completed the undergrounding work. The delay added $16 million in cost escalation and required renegotiation of the construction contract, with Bend's rapid growth during the delay period adding traffic management complexity to the eventual construction.

projects.name: Medford South Stage Road Widening
projects.description: Medford's South Stage Road widening project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Avista Utilities gas main installation and Medford Water Commission's concurrent pipeline replacement project.
projects.detail: The City of Medford's project to widen South Stage Road between Black Oak Drive and Hillcrest Road encountered scheduling conflicts between Avista Utilities and the Medford Water Commission. Avista had scheduled gas main installation work along the corridor to coincide with the road widening, but the Water Commission's concurrent pipeline replacement required exclusive access to the same trench zone for three months longer than anticipated. The Water Commission could not reschedule because it was under a state Department of Environmental Quality compliance deadline. Medford's contractor was placed on standby for extended periods while the two utilities completed their work in sequence rather than in parallel, adding $4.2 million in standby and remobilization costs and delaying the road widening by 10 months.

projects.name: Sound Transit West Seattle Link Extension Utility Coordination
projects.description: Sound Transit's West Seattle Link extension was delayed by scheduling conflicts with Seattle City Light underground transmission upgrades and SPU water main replacements that each required exclusive work windows in the narrow Delridge corridor.
projects.detail: Sound Transit's West Seattle Link light rail extension encountered severe scheduling conflicts along the Delridge Way corridor. Seattle City Light's underground transmission cable upgrade project and Seattle Public Utilities' planned water main replacement both required exclusive work windows in the same narrow right-of-way. City Light's work involved energized high-voltage cables requiring a 50-foot exclusion zone that prevented any concurrent construction. SPU's water main work required temporary service connections that conflicted with Sound Transit's planned station excavation staging areas. Negotiating a sequenced construction schedule acceptable to all three agencies took over a year, and the resulting phased approach added $280 million in extended construction costs and delayed the project by two years. The conflict contributed to Sound Transit's decision to evaluate alternative alignments for the corridor.

projects.name: WSDOT SR 167 Completion Project Utility Delays
projects.description: WSDOT's SR 167 completion project connecting Tacoma to Puyallup was delayed by scheduling conflicts with PSE gas transmission line relocation and Pierce County sewer force main construction.
projects.detail: The Washington State Department of Transportation's SR 167 Completion Project, a new 7-mile freeway segment between I-5 in Tacoma and SR 167 in Puyallup, faced scheduling conflicts with Puget Sound Energy's gas transmission line relocation along the corridor and Pierce County's sewer force main construction project that paralleled the planned highway alignment. PSE's transmission line work required a separate environmental review timeline that did not align with WSDOT's construction schedule, and Pierce County's sewer project had been funded through a state revolving fund loan with its own compliance deadlines. The inability to sequence the three projects efficiently added $92 million in delay costs and extended the completion date by 18 months, with WSDOT ultimately negotiating a complex construction coordination agreement that still required multiple contractor standby periods.

projects.name: Bellingham Bakerview Road Widening
projects.description: Bellingham's Bakerview Road widening was delayed by scheduling conflicts between PSE electrical undergrounding work, Cascade Natural Gas main replacement, and the city's own stormwater system upgrade.
projects.detail: The City of Bellingham's Bakerview Road widening project between I-5 and the Guide Meridian encountered scheduling conflicts among three utility projects that were planned to coordinate with the road widening but could not align their construction windows. Puget Sound Energy's electrical undergrounding work required de-energizing circuits serving the adjacent Bellis Fair Mall commercial area, which PSE refused to schedule during the holiday shopping season. Cascade Natural Gas's main replacement required cold-weather installation conditions that conflicted with PSE's preferred summer schedule. The city's own stormwater system upgrade depended on both utility projects being complete first. The resulting cascading delays added $3.8 million in costs and pushed the project back eight months, requiring the road widening to span a second construction season.

projects.name: Kapolei Rail Station Area Infrastructure
projects.description: Kapolei's rail station area infrastructure improvements were delayed by scheduling conflicts between HECO underground electrical work, BWS water system upgrades, and Hawaiian Telcom fiber installation that each required exclusive road closures.
projects.detail: The City and County of Honolulu's infrastructure improvements around the Kapolei Skyline rail stations were designed to coordinate road reconstruction, sidewalk installation, and utility upgrades to serve anticipated transit-oriented development. However, Hawaiian Electric Company, the Board of Water Supply, and Hawaiian Telcom each required exclusive road closure periods for their underground work that could not overlap due to safety and operational constraints. HECO's electrical work required de-energized conditions that prevented BWS from operating its cathodic protection systems, and Hawaiian Telcom's fiber installation required completed road subgrade that could not be provided until the other utilities finished. The sequential scheduling added $28 million in costs over the planned concurrent approach, with 20 months of additional construction time that frustrated local businesses and commuters already dealing with rail construction impacts.

projects.name: Anchorage A-C Couplet Reconstruction
projects.description: Anchorage's A Street/C Street couplet reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between ENSTAR gas line upgrades, Chugach Electric underground work, and ACS/GCI telecommunications duct bank installation.
projects.detail: The Municipality of Anchorage's reconstruction of the A Street/C Street one-way couplet through the downtown Midtown corridor was designed to coordinate with scheduled utility upgrades from ENSTAR Natural Gas, Chugach Electric Association, and ACS/GCI telecommunications. However, ENSTAR's gas line upgrade required completed road excavation before installation, Chugach Electric's underground work required ENSTAR's gas lines to be in their final position for safety clearances, and ACS/GCI's duct bank installation required both other utilities to be complete. The strict sequential dependency, combined with Anchorage's five-month construction season, meant that the project could not be completed in the planned two seasons. Each utility demanded its own inspection and testing period between phases. The delay added $18 million in costs and one full year to the project schedule, requiring a third construction season.

projects.name: Vancouver Waterfront Way Extension Utility Conflicts
projects.description: Vancouver's Waterfront Way extension was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Clark Public Utilities electrical relocation, NW Natural gas main installation, and CenturyLink conduit work serving the redeveloping waterfront district.
projects.detail: The City of Vancouver's Waterfront Way extension project to support the redeveloping Columbia Waterfront district was delayed when Clark Public Utilities, NW Natural Gas, and CenturyLink could not coordinate their underground utility installations in the new street corridor. Clark Public Utilities required its electrical conduit placed before the roadway subgrade was complete, but NW Natural's gas main installation required compacted subgrade for proper support. CenturyLink's fiber conduit work was scheduled to coincide with Clark PU's electrical work, but the two utilities' trench zones overlapped. The scheduling conflicts required three separate mobilizations instead of one coordinated installation, adding $7.8 million in costs and 11 months of delay. The Vancouver City Council subsequently adopted a utility coordination ordinance requiring joint trenching for new development infrastructure projects.

projects.name: Kenai Spur Highway Reconstruction Utility Coordination
projects.description: Alaska DOT's Kenai Spur Highway reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between ENSTAR gas line upgrades, Homer Electric Association underground conversion, and City of Kenai water/sewer work that could not be coordinated within the short subarctic construction season.
projects.detail: The Alaska Department of Transportation's reconstruction of the Kenai Spur Highway between Kenai and Soldotna required coordinating utility work with ENSTAR Natural Gas, Homer Electric Association, and the City of Kenai's water and sewer department. Alaska's short construction season (typically May through September) meant all utility work needed to occur in a compressed timeframe. ENSTAR's gas line upgrades required frost-free ground conditions available only in July and August, the same window Homer Electric needed for its overhead-to-underground conversion. The City of Kenai's water and sewer upgrades could only occur after the road base was excavated but before utility installation, creating a bottleneck. The inability to perform concurrent work within the seasonal constraints added a full year to the project and $8.5 million in extended contractor mobilization and winter shutdown costs.

projects.name: Kihei North-South Collector Road Phase 2
projects.description: Maui County's Kihei North-South Collector Road Phase 2 was delayed by scheduling conflicts between MECO underground electrical installation, Maui County water main extension, and private developer utility connections.
projects.detail: Maui County's Kihei North-South Collector Road Phase 2 was intended to provide an alternative to the congested Piilani Highway through South Maui. The project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Maui Electric Company's underground electrical installation, Maui County's water main extension to serve new development areas, and multiple private developers' utility connection work that had been promised coordination with the road project. MECO required its underground installation to occur before road base placement but after trench excavation, while the county's water main work required road base for equipment staging. Private developers' utility connections each required separate county inspection periods that had to be scheduled between the public utility work. The conflicts added $15 million in costs and 18 months of delay, compounding public frustration with Kihei's worsening traffic congestion.

projects.name: Clackamas County Sunrise Corridor Fiber Optic Water Strike
projects.description: Fiber optic conduit installation for the Sunrise Corridor highway project struck a Clackamas River Water District 24-inch transmission main, flooding the construction zone and damaging completed road subgrade.
projects.detail: During fiber optic conduit installation along the Sunrise Corridor (I-205 to US-26 connector) in Clackamas County, a horizontal directional drill struck a Clackamas River Water District 24-inch transmission main at a creek crossing. The transmission main, installed in the 1970s, had settled approximately 4 feet below its as-built elevation due to soil conditions in the alluvial floodplain, placing it directly in the path of the directional bore. The rupture flooded approximately 600 linear feet of completed road subgrade and damaged newly installed storm drainage infrastructure. Emergency repairs to the water main took three weeks, during which approximately 8,000 customers were served by temporary above-ground bypass piping. The total cost of repairs, subgrade reconstruction, and storm drain replacement reached $3.2 million with a five-month delay to the corridor project.

projects.name: Seattle Aurora Avenue Rapid Ride E Line Gas Main Strike
projects.description: Construction crews installing bus rapid transit platforms on Aurora Avenue N struck a PSE gas distribution main, forcing evacuation of Shoreline businesses and delaying the RapidRide E Line improvement project.
projects.detail: During construction of bus rapid transit platform improvements for King County Metro's RapidRide E Line on Aurora Avenue N near N 130th Street, a trenching crew struck a 6-inch Puget Sound Energy gas distribution main that was located 3 feet west of its marked position. The gas release forced evacuation of businesses along a two-block stretch of Aurora Avenue and closure of the arterial for six hours during a weekday morning. PSE emergency crews isolated and repaired the line within four hours, but the incident triggered a comprehensive utility re-survey of the entire Aurora corridor construction zone. The re-survey discovered additional unmapped utilities at four other platform locations, leading to a two-month construction pause and $2.5 million in additional costs for utility verification, line repair, and construction remobilization.

projects.name: Everett Waterfront Redevelopment Water Main Strike
projects.description: Excavation for the Everett waterfront redevelopment struck a 16-inch City of Everett water transmission main and a buried Snohomish PUD electrical conduit, flooding the construction site and damaging completed foundation work.
projects.detail: During foundation excavation for the Everett waterfront mixed-use development, construction crews struck a 16-inch City of Everett water transmission main that had been installed in the 1950s and was not reflected in current utility records. The rupture released water into the excavation pit for approximately two hours before the line could be shut off, flooding the site and damaging completed concrete foundation work. Additionally, a buried Snohomish County PUD electrical conduit was damaged during the emergency response excavation. The water main break affected service to approximately 3,000 customers in the downtown Everett area for 18 hours. Total costs including main repair, foundation reconstruction, electrical conduit replacement, and construction delays reached $3.8 million with a four-month delay to the redevelopment project.

projects.name: Beaverton SW Murray Boulevard Road Improvement Gas Strike
projects.description: Road improvement construction on SW Murray Boulevard in Beaverton struck a NW Natural Gas service line during curb ramp installation, forcing evacuation of a nearby apartment complex.
projects.detail: During ADA curb ramp installation as part of the SW Murray Boulevard road improvement project near SW Allen Boulevard, a concrete saw cut through a NW Natural Gas 2-inch service line that was running at a non-standard depth of only 8 inches below the surface. The gas leak forced immediate evacuation of the adjacent Murray Hill apartment complex, affecting approximately 150 residents. The Tualatin Valley Fire & Rescue department established a perimeter while NW Natural crews isolated and repaired the line over a four-hour period. The incident prompted the City of Beaverton to require vacuum excavation for all curb ramp work within 10 feet of known gas infrastructure, adding $1.5 million to the overall road improvement project budget. Construction was paused for five weeks while the city conducted a safety review and NW Natural re-verified gas line locations along the remaining project corridor.

projects.name: Bremerton Manette Bridge Approach Sewer Strike
projects.description: Construction on the Manette Bridge eastern approach struck a City of Bremerton 18-inch sewer main and a Kitsap PUD water service line, causing a sewage spill into the Port Washington Narrows.
projects.detail: During construction improvements to the eastern approach of the Manette Bridge in Bremerton, excavation equipment struck a City of Bremerton 18-inch sewer main and a Kitsap Public Utility District water service line that were co-located in a utility corridor not accurately shown on project plans. The sewer main rupture released approximately 25,000 gallons of sewage into the Port Washington Narrows before emergency crews could establish bypass pumping, triggering a Washington Department of Ecology investigation and shellfish harvest closure advisory. The water service break affected 400 customers for 12 hours. The city was cited for a Clean Water Act violation despite the incident being caused by inaccurate utility records. Repair and environmental remediation costs totaled $2.1 million with a seven-week construction delay while the city conducted a comprehensive utility survey of the bridge approach corridor.

projects.name: Portland NE Glisan Street Repaving Utility Violations
projects.description: NW Natural Gas and Comcast cut into NE Glisan Street within five months of a $10 million PBOT repaving, with utility restoration failing to meet Portland's street standards.
projects.detail: The Portland Bureau of Transportation completed a $10 million repaving of NE Glisan Street between 28th and 60th Avenues in spring 2024 as part of the Fixing Our Streets program. Within five months, NW Natural Gas performed gas service upgrades for a new apartment building and Comcast installed underground conduit for a commercial fiber installation, both cutting into the new pavement. Portland's utility cut moratorium requires a three-year waiting period after major repaving, but both utilities obtained permits by classifying their work as essential service connections. PBOT inspectors documented that the utility pavement restorations did not meet Portland's T-cut specifications, with patches already showing settlement. The estimated long-term pavement damage was $1.6 million. PBOT subsequently added a requirement that all utility cuts within three years of repaving must include full-lane-width milling and overlay rather than simple trench patches.
projects.timeline: Repaving completed spring 2024; utility cuts began within 5 months

projects.name: Tigard Pacific Highway (99W) Utility Cut Violations
projects.description: PGE, NW Natural, and Frontier Communications made multiple utility cuts into Pacific Highway through downtown Tigard within one year of ODOT's $20 million resurfacing, creating a patchwork surface on the city's main corridor.
projects.detail: ODOT completed a $20 million resurfacing of Pacific Highway (99W) through downtown Tigard in 2023, including intersection improvements and ADA ramp upgrades. Within one year, Portland General Electric, NW Natural Gas, and Frontier Communications made a combined 14 utility cuts into the newly resurfaced corridor for service upgrades, main replacements, and fiber optic installation. The frequency and poor quality of utility patches created what the Tigard city manager described as a 'patchwork quilt' on the city's primary commercial corridor. The estimated pavement damage was $3.2 million, but because Pacific Highway is an ODOT facility, the City of Tigard had limited authority to enforce its own utility cut moratorium. The incident led to Tigard advocating for stronger state-level utility coordination requirements and prompted ODOT to revise its utility permit conditions for recently resurfaced state highways.
projects.timeline: Resurfacing completed 2023; 14 utility cuts within one year

projects.name: Seattle Rainier Avenue S Repaving Utility Cuts
projects.description: Seattle City Light, PSE, and CenturyLink cut into Rainier Avenue S within seven months of SDOT's $22 million repaving, with the Vision Zero safety corridor's new pavement markings and surface treatments compromised.
projects.detail: The Seattle Department of Transportation completed a $22 million repaving and safety improvement of Rainier Avenue S between I-90 and Rainier Beach as part of the Vision Zero initiative in late 2023. The project included new high-friction surface treatments, enhanced crosswalk markings, and transit island installations. Within seven months, Seattle City Light performed underground vault maintenance, Puget Sound Energy replaced gas service lines, and CenturyLink installed fiber conduit, collectively making 11 utility cuts into the new pavement. Several cuts damaged the high-friction surface treatment at crosswalk approaches, undermining the safety improvements that were the project's primary purpose. SDOT estimated the pavement and safety treatment damage at $3.5 million. The Seattle City Council requested an audit of utility cut permit compliance with the city's moratorium provisions, finding that emergency classifications were being used to bypass the three-year waiting period.
projects.timeline: Repaving completed late 2023; utility cuts began within 7 months

projects.name: Olympia 4th Avenue Downtown Repaving Utility Cuts
projects.description: PSE and Lumen (CenturyLink) cut into Olympia's 4th Avenue within four months of a $6 million downtown repaving for utility service connections to new mixed-use developments.
projects.detail: The City of Olympia completed a $6 million repaving and streetscape improvement of 4th Avenue through downtown in spring 2025, including new decorative pavement treatments and pedestrian lighting. Within four months, Puget Sound Energy and Lumen Technologies (formerly CenturyLink) cut into the new pavement for gas service connections and fiber optic installations serving two new mixed-use development projects. The utility cuts damaged decorative pavement treatments that had been installed at premium cost, and the standard utility trench patches did not match the decorative surface. The city estimated $1.1 million in pavement damage and aesthetic degradation, with the downtown business association publicly criticizing the lack of coordination. Olympia's public works director noted that the city's three-year pavement cut moratorium had been waived because the utility connections were deemed necessary for occupied building certificates, exposing a gap between the city's paving investment protection and its development permitting process.
projects.timeline: Repaving completed spring 2025; utility cuts began within 4 months

projects.name: Honolulu Kapiolani Boulevard Repaving Utility Violations
projects.description: HECO and BWS cut into Kapiolani Boulevard within nine months of a $28 million repaving, with the city estimating the utility patches would reduce the pavement's service life by 40%.
projects.detail: The City and County of Honolulu completed a $28 million repaving and complete streets improvement of Kapiolani Boulevard between Keeaumoku Street and Date Street in late 2023, a critical corridor connecting Ala Moana and Kaimuki. Within nine months, Hawaiian Electric Company performed underground cable replacement work and the Board of Water Supply replaced aging water service connections, making 18 utility cuts into the newly paved corridor. The City's Department of Facility Maintenance estimated the utility patches would reduce the pavement's design service life from 15 years to approximately 9 years, representing $5.2 million in accelerated deterioration costs. Honolulu's moratorium ordinance was weaker than mainland cities, lacking financial penalties for violations. The city council subsequently introduced a bill modeled on San Jose's excavation moratorium, requiring utility companies to pay 150% of the pavement restoration cost for cuts made within three years of repaving.
projects.timeline: Repaving completed late 2023; 18 utility cuts within 9 months

projects.name: Kailua Town Center Repaving Utility Violations
projects.description: HECO and Hawaiian Telcom cut into Kailua Road and Kuulei Road within five months of a $9 million town center repaving, damaging new crosswalk treatments and decorative pavement.
projects.detail: The City and County of Honolulu completed a $9 million repaving and streetscape improvement in the Kailua town center, covering Kailua Road and Kuulei Road in early 2024. The project included decorative crosswalks, new pavement markings, and ADA ramp improvements funded through a combination of federal and city funds. Within five months, Hawaiian Electric Company cut into both streets for underground cable work, and Hawaiian Telcom performed fiber conduit installation for a new commercial tenant. The cuts damaged two of the new decorative crosswalks and created uneven surfaces along the freshly improved ADA ramps, requiring the city to file ADA compliance concerns with both utilities. The estimated damage was $1.4 million, and the Kailua Neighborhood Board passed a resolution requesting the city enforce its paving moratorium more aggressively against utility companies operating in recently improved town center areas.
projects.timeline: Repaving completed early 2024; utility cuts began within 5 months

projects.name: Corvallis 9th Street Corridor Repaving Utility Disruption
projects.description: NW Natural and Pacific Power cut into 9th Street within three months of Corvallis's $5 million repaving, with the city citing both utilities for moratorium violations.
projects.detail: The City of Corvallis completed a $5 million repaving and safety improvement of 9th Street (Highway 99W) between Circle Boulevard and Harrison Boulevard in early 2025. Within three months, NW Natural Gas performed a gas service upgrade for a new Oregon State University building and Pacific Power installed underground electrical conduit for a campus expansion project, both cutting into the freshly paved corridor. Corvallis has a three-year moratorium on utility cuts after major repaving projects, and the city cited both utilities for violations. However, both utilities argued their work was necessary to serve OSU facilities that had been approved through the city's own planning process. The estimated pavement damage was $890,000. The incident prompted Corvallis to establish a formal pre-paving utility coordination process requiring the city's planning department to notify public works of upcoming development projects that might generate utility work in recently paved corridors.
projects.timeline: Repaving completed early 2025; utility cuts began within 3 months

projects.name: Federal Way S 320th Street Repaving Utility Violations
projects.description: PSE and Lakehaven Water cut into S 320th Street within eight months of Federal Way's $13 million repaving, with utility patches failing before the first winter freeze-thaw cycle.
projects.detail: The City of Federal Way completed a $13 million repaving and safety improvement of S 320th Street between I-5 and 1st Avenue S in late 2024, a critical east-west arterial serving the city's commercial core. Within eight months, Puget Sound Energy cut into the new pavement for gas service upgrades to a new commercial development and Lakehaven Water and Sewer District performed water main connection work for a mixed-use project. The utility patches began showing settlement and cracking before the first winter freeze-thaw cycle, with the city's public works department documenting that the restoration work did not meet Federal Way's pavement specifications. The estimated accelerated pavement damage was $1.5 million. The city council directed staff to draft an enhanced moratorium ordinance with mandatory full-lane-width restoration requirements and performance bonds for any utility cuts made within three years of major repaving projects.
projects.timeline: Repaving completed late 2024; utility cuts began within 8 months

projects.name: Juneau Egan Drive Reconstruction
projects.description: Road reconstruction plans had to be revised three times after survey crews discovered unmarked water, sewer, and electrical conduits running beneath the corridor that conflicted with the new drainage design.
projects.detail: The Alaska DOT&PF's $50M reconstruction of Egan Drive in Juneau encountered repeated underground utility conflicts beginning in 2021. Initial plans assumed utilities ran along standard alignments, but field investigations found decades-old water mains, sewer lines, and buried electrical conduits in unexpected locations that directly conflicted with the proposed stormwater drainage system. The design team was forced to revise the plans three times, each revision requiring new geotechnical assessments and utility relocation agreements with the City and Borough of Juneau. The delays pushed the project $14 million over the original $50 million budget and extended the timeline by two years.

projects.name: Fairbanks Cushman Street Bridge Utility Relocation
