projects.description: Bridge replacement was delayed 18 months because Golden Heart Utilities and GCI could not align their relocation schedules with the narrow summer construction window in Interior Alaska.
projects.detail: The Cushman Street Bridge replacement over the Chena River in Fairbanks was planned as a 3-year project beginning in 2020. However, coordination between ADOT&PF, Golden Heart Utilities, and GCI proved exceptionally difficult due to Alaska's compressed construction season. Utility companies could not schedule crews during the same May-September windows when bridge work was feasible, creating sequential rather than parallel work phases. Winter shutdowns between utility and bridge work created compounding delays. The project ran $6 million over its $30 million budget, with most overruns attributed to extended mobilization costs and winter protection measures for partially completed utility relocations.

projects.name: Kailua Road Complete Streets Redesign
projects.description: Complete streets plans were overhauled after potholing revealed a dense web of unmapped HECO electrical conduits, telecom lines, and century-old water mains beneath the roadway that conflicted with the proposed bike lane and bus stop infrastructure.
projects.detail: The City and County of Honolulu's $20M Kailua Road Complete Streets project aimed to add protected bike lanes, enhanced bus stops, and improved pedestrian crossings along a 1.5-mile corridor. During the design phase, subsurface utility engineering investigations revealed a far more complex underground environment than anticipated, including unmapped Hawaiian Electric Company conduits, abandoned telecom lines, and water mains dating to the early 1900s. The original plans had to be completely redesigned to route new infrastructure around these conflicts. The Hawaii Board of Water Supply required upgraded connections that were not in the original scope. Costs ballooned to $28M and the project slipped 2.5 years behind schedule.

projects.name: Concord Storrs Street Extension Plan Revision
projects.description: Plans for the Storrs Street extension had to be revised after discovering unmapped gas and water utilities beneath the planned intersection that conflicted with the new roundabout design.
projects.detail: The City of Concord's $10M Storrs Street extension project aimed to improve connectivity between downtown and the Heights neighborhood. During 60% design, subsurface utility engineering found unmapped gas mains and a critical water main directly beneath the planned roundabout footprint. Liberty Utilities and the Concord water system both required extensive relocations that fundamentally altered the intersection geometry. The plan revision process added 14 months to the schedule and $3.5 million to the budget, as the roundabout had to be shifted 40 feet south to avoid the most costly utility conflicts. The project required additional right-of-way acquisition from an adjacent property owner.

projects.name: Nashua Main Street Resurfacing Moratorium Breach
projects.description: Liberty Utilities cut open freshly repaved Main Street just 8 months after a $4M NHDOT resurfacing project to install new gas service connections, prompting city officials to demand a moratorium ordinance.
projects.detail: Main Street in downtown Nashua was resurfaced in a $4M New Hampshire DOT project completed in fall 2022. By summer 2023, Liberty Utilities had opened multiple trenches in the new pavement to install gas service connections for a new mixed-use development. The city had no moratorium ordinance in place, leaving officials without enforcement tools. The Board of Aldermen responded by drafting a 5-year moratorium ordinance modeled on Massachusetts regulations, requiring utilities to coordinate planned work before repaving projects begin. Liberty Utilities argued the development timeline was not finalized when NHDOT solicited utility coordination, but city engineers noted the development permits were already under review.

projects.name: Burlington Pine Street Reconstruction Utility Conflicts
projects.description: The Pine Street corridor reconstruction required a full plan overhaul after discovering conflicting Burlington Electric Department underground conduits and a previously unknown combined sewer that ran diagonally beneath the planned stormwater treatment area.
projects.detail: Burlington's $15M Pine Street reconstruction project was designed to transform a key industrial corridor with new sidewalks, stormwater treatment, and improved roadway. During the 90% design phase, test pits revealed Burlington Electric Department conduits crisscrossing the corridor at unexpected depths, plus a combined sewer overflow pipe running diagonally under the planned bioretention area. The discovery required a complete redesign of the stormwater management system and electrical conduit relocations that Burlington Electric estimated would cost $2.5M alone. Vermont Agency of Transportation had to extend the federal funding obligation deadline. The total project grew from $15M to $20M with an 18-month delay.

projects.name: Montpelier State Street Paving Cut by Green Mountain Power
projects.description: Green Mountain Power cut open recently repaved State Street in Montpelier less than a year after VTrans completed a $2.5M resurfacing to replace underground electrical infrastructure, drawing public backlash.
projects.detail: Vermont Agency of Transportation completed a $2.5M resurfacing of State Street through downtown Montpelier in the fall of 2023, part of a broader effort to improve the capital city's infrastructure after the devastating July 2023 floods. Less than 10 months later, Green Mountain Power began excavating sections of the new pavement to replace aging underground electrical distribution lines. The utility argued the flood damage had accelerated the deterioration of their underground infrastructure beyond what was anticipated. City officials and residents were furious, noting that GMP had been asked about planned work during the VTrans coordination process and had indicated no projects. The incident prompted Vermont legislators to examine whether the state needed a formal paving moratorium statute.

projects.name: Portland Baxter Boulevard Sewer Separation Utility Conflict
projects.description: Portland's combined sewer overflow separation project required plan revisions after encountering dense clusters of CMP electrical conduits and Spectrum fiber lines that were not shown on utility maps.
projects.detail: The City of Portland's $30M Baxter Boulevard sewer separation project, mandated by a federal consent decree to reduce combined sewer overflows into Back Cove, hit significant underground utility conflicts in 2022. Excavation revealed Central Maine Power electrical conduits and Spectrum Communications fiber optic lines in locations that did not match submitted utility maps. The conflicts forced the engineering team to redesign several sewer trunk line alignments, adding expensive trenchless construction methods where open-cut had been planned. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection granted a timeline extension on the consent decree milestones. Total project costs rose to $37M with a 2-year delay.

projects.name: Dover South Governors Avenue Resurfacing Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Delmarva Power cut into freshly repaved South Governors Avenue only 6 months after DelDOT completed a $3.2M resurfacing project to upgrade underground electrical service for a new shopping center.
projects.detail: DelDOT completed a $3.2M resurfacing of South Governors Avenue in Dover in spring 2023, including new curb ramps and signal upgrades. By fall 2023, Delmarva Power had opened trenches in the new pavement to run underground electrical service to a new shopping center development on the corridor. DelDOT's 3-year moratorium policy should have prevented the cut, but Delmarva Power argued the work qualified as an emergency service connection. Dover City Council members publicly disputed the emergency classification, noting the shopping center had been in the planning stages for over two years. The incident highlighted gaps in Delaware's moratorium enforcement mechanisms, as DelDOT acknowledged the utility's restoration bond was insufficient to cover the full cost of pavement degradation.

projects.name: Morgantown Beechurst Avenue Combined Sewer Reconstruction
projects.description: Sewer reconstruction plans were overhauled after discovering unmapped Dominion Energy gas lines and WVU campus steam tunnels beneath the corridor that conflicted with the new combined sewer separation design.
projects.detail: The City of Morgantown's $20M Beechurst Avenue sewer reconstruction project, part of the city's EPA consent order compliance, required a major plan revision in 2023. Subsurface investigations near the West Virginia University campus found unmapped Dominion Energy gas distribution lines and WVU steam tunnel infrastructure that directly conflicted with the new separated sewer alignment. The university's underground utility records were decades out of date, and several gas mains predated Dominion Energy's digital mapping system. Redesigning around these conflicts required deeper excavation and trenchless installation methods that added $6M to the project budget. The WV Department of Environmental Protection granted a 20-month extension on the consent order compliance deadline.

projects.name: Wheeling Main Street Utility-Driven Repaving Waste
projects.description: West Virginia American Water cut open recently repaved Main Street in downtown Wheeling just 11 months after a $5M WVDOH resurfacing to replace a failing water main, wasting most of the new pavement.
projects.detail: The West Virginia Division of Highways completed a $5M resurfacing of Main Street through downtown Wheeling in late 2022. Less than a year later, West Virginia American Water began major excavation to replace a 90-year-old cast iron water main that had experienced multiple breaks. The utility argued the main's failure rate had accelerated unpredictably after the repaving, possibly due to construction vibration. City officials disputed this explanation, noting the water main had a documented history of breaks going back years. Wheeling did not have a paving moratorium ordinance, and the incident prompted the city council to explore adopting one. An estimated $1.5M of the original repaving investment was effectively destroyed.

projects.name: Biloxi Howard Avenue Streetscape Plan Revision
projects.description: Downtown streetscape plans had to be redesigned after finding Mississippi Power underground vaults and unmapped storm drainage from the post-Katrina reconstruction directly beneath the planned pedestrian plaza and street tree zones.
projects.detail: The City of Biloxi's $15M Howard Avenue Streetscape project aimed to enhance the downtown corridor connecting the casino district to the historic core. Design phase subsurface investigations in 2023 revealed Mississippi Power underground electrical vaults and unmapped storm drainage infrastructure installed during the rapid post-Hurricane Katrina reconstruction. Much of the post-Katrina utility work was done under emergency permits with minimal as-built documentation. The conflicts required redesigning the pedestrian plaza, relocating planned street tree wells, and rerouting a new stormwater bioswale. Mississippi Power's relocation costs became a dispute over whether the utility or the city bore responsibility under Mississippi's utility accommodation rules. The project grew from $15M to $19M.

projects.name: Hattiesburg Hardy Street Resurfacing Utility Cut
projects.description: Spire Mississippi gas crews cut open Hardy Street near the University of Southern Mississippi only 4 months after MDOT completed a $2.8M resurfacing to replace a corroded gas main.
projects.detail: The Mississippi Department of Transportation completed a $2.8M resurfacing of Hardy Street through the University of Southern Mississippi corridor in early 2024. Just four months later, Spire Mississippi began excavating the new pavement to replace a corroded gas distribution main that had triggered two leak reports. Spire argued the replacement was an emergency safety measure that could not wait for any moratorium period. MDOT officials pointed out that the gas main's age and condition were known before the repaving project began, and Spire had been contacted during the utility coordination process. The city had no moratorium ordinance, and the incident wasted an estimated $700K of the state's resurfacing investment on the affected blocks.

projects.name: Jackson Capitol Street Water Main Relocation Overrun
projects.description: Capitol Street reconstruction was delayed 3 years because the Jackson water system, already under a federal consent decree for failing infrastructure, could not coordinate water main relocations with the road project's schedule.
projects.detail: MDOT's $30M Capitol Street reconstruction through downtown Jackson was designed as a 3-year project beginning in 2020. However, the City of Jackson's water system -- already under a federal consent decree and dealing with chronic system failures -- could not schedule the water main relocations required before road construction could proceed. The city's water system experienced multiple emergencies during the coordination period, including the February 2021 winter storm crisis and the August 2022 treatment plant failure that left 150,000 residents without water. Each crisis diverted the limited utility crew resources away from the relocation work. The project ballooned to $42M due to extended mobilization costs, price escalation, and the need for temporary water service during the prolonged construction.

projects.name: Rapid City Main Street Square Utility Rework
projects.description: Black Hills Energy cut open recently reconstructed streets around Main Street Square just 9 months after completion to replace gas mains, drawing public criticism for wasting the $3.5M streetscape investment.
projects.detail: The City of Rapid City completed a $3.5M streetscape improvement around Main Street Square in 2023, including decorative pavement, new sidewalks, and improved drainage. Nine months after completion, Black Hills Energy began excavating portions of the newly improved streets to replace aging gas distribution mains in the area. The utility argued the mains had passed their useful life and replacement was a safety priority. City council members noted that Black Hills Energy had been contacted during the design coordination phase and had not flagged any planned work. The cuts damaged approximately $1.1M worth of the new streetscape improvements, including decorative pavement that required specialty materials to restore. The incident prompted the city to strengthen its utility coordination requirements for future capital projects.

projects.name: Lincoln South Beltway Utility Relocation Delays
projects.description: Nebraska's largest-ever highway project was delayed 8 months by utility relocation scheduling conflicts with Black Hills Energy, Windstream, and Lincoln Electric System along the 11-mile corridor.
projects.detail: The $352M Lincoln South Beltway, the largest single highway project in Nebraska DOT history, encountered utility relocation scheduling conflicts along its 11-mile corridor. Black Hills Energy gas lines, Windstream fiber optic cables, and Lincoln Electric System power lines all required relocation before highway construction could proceed in multiple segments. The utilities could not coordinate their relocation schedules to allow sequential access, causing idle periods between utility moves. Nebraska DOT had to resequence construction segments to work around the delayed relocations, adding $18M in changed conditions costs and 8 months to the overall schedule. The project ultimately opened in November 2022, months after the planned spring 2022 completion.

projects.name: Omaha Dodge Street Resurfacing Moratorium Breach
projects.description: OPPD and MUD both cut into freshly repaved Dodge Street within 14 months of a $6M Nebraska DOT resurfacing, with MUD arguing its water main replacement was an emergency repair exempt from the city's coordination policy.
projects.detail: Nebraska DOT completed a $6M resurfacing of a 3-mile section of Dodge Street, Omaha's primary east-west arterial, in summer 2023. Within 14 months, both Omaha Public Power District (OPPD) and Metropolitan Utilities District (MUD) had opened trenches in the new pavement. MUD's excavation for water main replacement was the more extensive, affecting 8 blocks of the resurfaced corridor. MUD classified the work as an emergency due to multiple water main breaks in the aging cast-iron pipes, but city engineers noted the pipes' age and failure history were well-documented before the repaving. The combined utility cuts wasted approximately $2M of the resurfacing investment. The Omaha City Council considered but did not pass a formal moratorium ordinance, instead strengthening the existing utility coordination notification requirements.
projects.timeline: Resurfaced summer 2023, cut by OPPD spring 2024, cut by MUD fall 2024

projects.name: Topeka Kansas Avenue Streetscape Underground Conflicts
projects.description: Streetscape revitalization plans were revised after discovering a complex web of Evergy electrical duct banks and unmapped 1950s-era storm drains beneath the planned tree planting and streetlight zones in downtown Topeka.
projects.detail: The City of Topeka's $15M Kansas Avenue Streetscape project, a centerpiece of the downtown revitalization effort, hit underground conflicts during the design phase. Subsurface utility engineering found Evergy electrical duct banks occupying a much wider underground footprint than shown on available records, plus 1950s-era storm drains that had been abandoned in place but never documented. The conflicts required relocating planned street tree wells, shifting streetlight foundations, and redesigning the stormwater collection system. Evergy's relocation costs and timeline became a negotiation point, as the utility argued many of its conduits served critical downtown circuits. The plan revision added $3.5M and 11 months, with the city ultimately absorbing most of the additional costs to keep the project moving.

projects.name: Great Falls 10th Avenue South Reconstruction Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor reconstruction plans had to be redesigned after discovering unmapped NorthWestern Energy gas lines and century-old water mains in locations that conflicted with the new stormwater and turn lane design.
projects.detail: Montana DOT's $12M 10th Avenue South reconstruction in Great Falls, a key commercial corridor, required plan revisions when utility investigations found NorthWestern Energy gas distribution lines and 100-year-old water mains in unexpected locations. The gas lines were at shallower depths than NorthWestern Energy's records indicated, placing them in direct conflict with the planned stormwater conveyance system. The aged water mains, some dating to the 1920s, were too fragile to remain in place during the heavy excavation required for new turn lanes. The City of Great Falls and MDT negotiated a cost-sharing agreement for the water main replacement, but the additional scope and plan revision process added $3M and 12 months to the project.

projects.name: Billings Rimrock Road Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Rimrock Road widening was delayed 14 months because NorthWestern Energy and the City of Billings water department could not coordinate relocation schedules within Montana's short construction season.
projects.detail: MDT's $25M Rimrock Road widening project in Billings was designed to add turn lanes and improve safety along a high-traffic commercial corridor. The project required relocating NorthWestern Energy gas and electric lines as well as City of Billings water mains. However, the utility companies could not align their crew schedules with each other or with the road contractor's work plan. NorthWestern Energy needed to complete gas relocations before electric work could start in the same trench zone, and the city's water department had committed its limited crew to other capital projects. Montana's short construction season (typically May through October) meant each scheduling slip pushed work to the following year. The delays added $4.5M in escalation costs over a 14-month extension.

projects.name: Cheyenne Central Avenue Reconstruction Utility Discovery
projects.description: Downtown reconstruction plans were revised after discovering unmapped Black Hills Energy gas mains and abandoned military utility conduits from the historic Fort D.A. Russell era beneath the corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Cheyenne's $10M Central Avenue reconstruction project encountered unexpected underground conditions during the design phase. Subsurface investigations revealed Black Hills Energy gas distribution mains in locations that did not match utility records, plus abandoned military utility conduits believed to date from the Fort D.A. Russell era (pre-1930). The historical conduits, while no longer in service, contained materials requiring environmental assessment. Wyoming DEQ required characterization testing before the conduits could be disturbed. The combined plan revision for utility conflicts and environmental clearance added $2.5M to the budget and 10 months to the schedule, with the historical conduit issue being the most time-consuming element.

projects.name: Santa Fe Cerrillos Road Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Major corridor redesign required after discovering PNM electrical conduits, New Mexico Gas Company mains, and unmapped acequia irrigation infrastructure beneath the planned BRT stations and bike lane zones.
projects.detail: The City of Santa Fe's $30M Cerrillos Road corridor improvement project, designed to add bus rapid transit stations, protected bike lanes, and improved pedestrian crossings, hit significant underground conflicts. Subsurface investigations revealed PNM electrical conduits, New Mexico Gas Company distribution mains, and -- most unexpectedly -- remnants of historic acequia irrigation channels that had been buried and forgotten over decades of development. The acequia remnants carried legal significance under New Mexico water law, requiring consultation with the local acequia association before they could be disturbed. PNM's conduit relocations required coordination with transmission system operations during off-peak periods. The combined conflicts forced a comprehensive plan revision that added $9M and 18 months.

projects.name: Las Cruces Main Street Downtown Resurfacing Utility Cut
projects.description: El Paso Electric cut open recently resurfaced Main Street in downtown Las Cruces just 10 months after a $3M NMDOT resurfacing to upgrade underground electrical distribution for a new hotel development.
projects.detail: NMDOT completed a $3M resurfacing of Main Street through downtown Las Cruces in spring 2024. Ten months later, El Paso Electric began excavating the new pavement to upgrade underground electrical distribution capacity to serve a new hotel development. The utility argued the hotel project's electrical load requirements were not finalized until after the resurfacing was completed. City officials countered that the hotel had been in the permitting pipeline for over 18 months and the electrical upgrade should have been anticipated. Las Cruces had no formal paving moratorium ordinance. The utility cuts wasted approximately $900K of the state's resurfacing investment and prompted the city council to begin drafting moratorium legislation modeled on Albuquerque's existing rules.

projects.name: Providence Broad Street Dig-In During Fiber Installation
projects.description: A fiber optic installation contractor struck a 6-inch Narragansett Bay Commission sewer force main on Broad Street, causing a sewage spill and shutting down a $15M road reconstruction project for 6 months.
projects.detail: During the City of Providence's $15M Broad Street reconstruction project in 2023, a subcontractor installing fiber optic conduit struck a 6-inch Narragansett Bay Commission sewer force main. The strike caused a significant sewage spill that required emergency environmental cleanup under RIDEM oversight. The force main was at an unexpected depth and several feet from its documented location. The incident shut down construction on a 4-block section for 6 months while the force main was repaired and environmental remediation was completed. The delays and additional costs totaled $2.1M, including emergency repairs, environmental cleanup, extended traffic control, and contractor standby costs.

projects.name: Lewiston Main Street Bridge Approach Plan Revision
projects.description: Bridge approach plans were revised after discovering 1890s-era textile mill utility conduits and an unmapped CMP duct bank directly beneath the planned approach embankment.
projects.detail: MaineDOT's $10M reconstruction of the Main Street bridge approach in Lewiston, connecting to the Lewiston-Auburn bridge over the Androscoggin River, hit unexpected underground conditions. Subsurface investigations revealed utility conduits dating to the city's 1890s textile mill era, including brick-lined tunnels that once carried steam and process water between mill buildings. A Central Maine Power duct bank was also found in a location not shown on utility records, running perpendicular to the approach alignment. The historical conduits required archaeological assessment under Maine Historic Preservation Commission guidelines before they could be disturbed. The combined plan revision added $2.2M and 8 months to the project.

projects.name: Brattleboro Putney Road Water Main Discovery
projects.description: Road reconstruction plans were revised after discovering an unmapped 12-inch water transmission main and GMP underground cable directly beneath the planned roundabout footprint at the Putney Road/Route 5 intersection.
projects.detail: VTrans' $7.5M Putney Road reconstruction project in Brattleboro, including a new roundabout at the Route 5 intersection, required plan revisions when subsurface investigations found a 12-inch water transmission main and Green Mountain Power underground electrical cable directly beneath the planned roundabout center island. Neither utility was shown on available records at that location. The water main served as a critical transmission link for the Brattleboro water system, meaning it could not simply be abandoned. Relocating both utilities outside the roundabout footprint required additional easements from adjacent property owners. The plan revision added $1.8M and 9 months to the project schedule.

projects.name: Grand Island US-30 Corridor Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor improvement plans were revised after discovering that Black Hills Energy gas infrastructure and Southern Power District electrical conduits occupied locations that conflicted with the planned access management improvements.
projects.detail: NDOT's $20M US-30 corridor improvement project through Grand Island aimed to add center medians, turn lanes, and improved access management along a 2-mile commercial strip. Design-phase subsurface investigations revealed Black Hills Energy gas distribution mains and Southern Power District electrical conduits in locations that directly conflicted with the planned median openings and turn lane construction. Several gas mains ran diagonally across the corridor rather than parallel to it, as shown on available records. The plan revision required redesigning seven intersection approaches and relocating over 3,000 feet of gas main. The changes added $3.8M and 10 months to the project schedule.

projects.name: Overland Park 87th Street Parkway Reconstruction
projects.description: Corridor reconstruction delayed 15 months because Evergy, Kansas Gas Service, and WaterOne could not align their utility relocation schedules with each other or the road construction sequence.
projects.detail: The City of Overland Park's $25M 87th Street Parkway reconstruction project, designed to widen the corridor and improve multimodal access, was stalled by scheduling conflicts among three major utility owners. Evergy needed to relocate overhead-to-underground electrical conversion ahead of road construction, but Kansas Gas Service required access to the same corridor for gas main replacement at the same time. WaterOne's water main relocations had to follow the gas work due to trench sharing requirements. The sequential dependencies, combined with each utility's separate contracting and permitting processes, created a 15-month delay. Construction costs escalated $5M due to material price increases and extended traffic management costs during the prolonged utility phase.

projects.name: Helena Last Chance Gulch Pedestrian Mall Utility Conflict
projects.description: Pedestrian mall renovation plans were redesigned after discovering NorthWestern Energy infrastructure and abandoned mining-era utility tunnels beneath the historic walking mall that conflicted with the new plaza design.
projects.detail: The City of Helena's $10M Last Chance Gulch pedestrian mall renovation, aimed at modernizing the downtown walking mall with new pavers, lighting, and gathering spaces, hit unexpected underground obstacles. Subsurface investigations found NorthWestern Energy electrical and gas infrastructure in locations not matching available records, plus abandoned utility tunnels from Helena's gold mining era. The mining-era tunnels were structurally unsound and posed collapse risks during construction. Montana SHPO required archaeological documentation before the tunnels could be filled, adding regulatory complexity. The plan revision process added $2.8M and 11 months, with the mining tunnel stabilization being the single largest cost addition at $1.2M.

projects.name: Rock Springs Downtown Infrastructure Plan Revision
projects.description: Downtown infrastructure plans were revised after discovering unmapped coal mine drainage tunnels and Rocky Mountain Power conduits beneath the corridor that conflicted with the new sewer separation design.
projects.detail: The City of Rock Springs' $8M downtown infrastructure improvement project, including sewer separation and street reconstruction, encountered unexpected subsurface conditions. Investigations revealed unmapped drainage tunnels from the city's coal mining history, plus Rocky Mountain Power electrical conduits in locations not shown on utility records. The mining tunnels, some dating to the late 1800s, had been repurposed over decades as informal utility corridors, creating a complex web of aging infrastructure. Wyoming DEQ required structural assessment of the tunnels before they could be incorporated into or bypassed by the new sewer system. The discoveries added $2M and 9 months to the project.

projects.name: Newport Thames Street Resurfacing Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Rhode Island Energy cut open freshly repaved Thames Street in Newport's historic waterfront district just 6 months after a $3M RIDOT resurfacing to replace aging gas infrastructure.
projects.detail: RIDOT completed a $3M resurfacing of Thames Street, Newport's iconic waterfront commercial street, in spring 2024. Six months later, Rhode Island Energy began excavating the new pavement to replace aging gas distribution mains in the historic district. The utility cited accelerating corrosion rates in the cast-iron pipes as the driver for the emergency timeline. City officials and business owners were outraged, noting the disruption during the crucial tourism season. The Newport City Council had previously lobbied for the statewide moratorium legislation and cited this incident as further evidence of the need for mandatory utility coordination. An estimated $1M of the resurfacing investment was compromised by the utility cuts.

projects.name: Smyrna Duck Creek Road Widening Utility Conflict
projects.description: Road widening plans revised after discovering Chesapeake Utilities gas mains and Delmarva Power conduits in locations that conflicted with the planned turn lanes and stormwater management system.
projects.detail: DelDOT's $15M Duck Creek Road widening in Smyrna required plan revisions after subsurface utility engineering found Chesapeake Utilities gas mains and Delmarva Power electrical conduits occupying the planned turn lane and stormwater management zones. The gas mains were at shallower depths than documented, placing them within the excavation zone for the new drainage system. Delmarva Power's conduits ran diagonally through what was planned as an open stormwater swale. Relocating both utilities required agreements with two different utility holding companies, each with separate engineering review and permitting processes. The plan revisions added $3.2M and 13 months, with most of the time consumed by the parallel but uncoordinated utility relocation processes.

projects.name: Charleston Kanawha Boulevard Reconstruction Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Boulevard reconstruction delayed 18 months because Appalachian Power, West Virginia American Water, and Suddenlink could not coordinate their relocation schedules for the critical riverfront corridor.
projects.detail: WVDOH's $30M Kanawha Boulevard reconstruction in downtown Charleston, a critical riverfront corridor, was delayed by scheduling conflicts among three major utility owners. Appalachian Power needed to relocate overhead-to-underground electrical lines before the road contractor could begin, but their crew availability conflicted with West Virginia American Water's planned water main replacement in the same trench zone. Suddenlink's fiber optic relocation added a third scheduling dependency. Each utility operated on its own fiscal year and capital planning cycle, making synchronized scheduling nearly impossible. The delays extended the project by 18 months, adding $7M in escalation costs, extended traffic management, and contractor standby charges.

projects.name: Gulfport Highway 49 Median Project Gas Line Strike
projects.description: A median construction crew struck a CenterPoint Energy gas transmission line on Highway 49 that was 4 feet from its marked location, causing a major gas release and evacuations.
projects.detail: During MDOT's $20M Highway 49 median improvement project in Gulfport in 2024, an excavation crew installing median barrier foundations struck a 6-inch CenterPoint Energy gas transmission line. The line was located approximately 4 feet from its marked position, outside the tolerance zone established by Mississippi's one-call system. The strike caused an uncontrolled gas release that required evacuation of nearby businesses and closure of a half-mile stretch of the highway for 8 hours. CenterPoint Energy dispatched emergency crews to isolate and repair the line, temporarily disrupting gas service to 200 customers. The incident halted construction for 5 months while a comprehensive utility re-survey was conducted along the entire project corridor, adding $2.3M to the project budget.

projects.name: Wilmington Riverfront Greenway Utility Discovery
projects.description: Greenway trail plans required revision after discovering abandoned industrial utility conduits and active Artesian Water mains beneath the planned multi-use path alignment along the Christina Riverfront.
projects.detail: The City of Wilmington's $8M Christina Riverfront Greenway project encountered significant subsurface utility conflicts during design. The planned multi-use path alignment crossed through former industrial land where abandoned chemical plant utility conduits and an active Artesian Water transmission main occupied the planned trail corridor. The abandoned conduits contained residual contamination requiring environmental assessment under DNREC oversight. The Artesian Water main could not be relocated without disrupting service to a large section of the city. The trail alignment was redesigned to avoid the most contaminated areas and bridge over the water main, adding $2.5M in structural and environmental costs and 10 months to the schedule.

projects.name: Rutland US Route 7 Corridor Improvement Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor improvement plans were overhauled after finding Vermont Gas Systems mains and GMP underground cables in locations that conflicted with the planned intersection realignment and stormwater system.
projects.detail: VTrans' $20M US Route 7 corridor improvement project through Rutland required a comprehensive plan revision after subsurface utility engineering revealed Vermont Gas Systems distribution mains and Green Mountain Power underground electrical cables in locations conflicting with the planned intersection realignment at multiple cross streets. The gas mains ran through what was designed as a new stormwater detention area, while GMP cables occupied the planned realigned intersection footprint. Both utilities had provided record drawings during the design phase, but field verification showed the as-built conditions differed significantly from the records. The plan revision process required redesigning four intersections and the entire stormwater management approach, adding $4.2M and 14 months.

projects.name: Dover NH Central Avenue Bridge Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Bridge replacement over the Cocheco River was delayed 12 months because Liberty Utilities, Consolidated Communications, and the Dover sewer department could not synchronize their infrastructure relocations.
projects.detail: NHDOT's $15M Central Avenue Bridge replacement over the Cocheco River in Dover was delayed by scheduling conflicts among three utility owners. Liberty Utilities needed to relocate gas mains attached to the existing bridge before demolition, Consolidated Communications had fiber optic cables that required temporary bypass routing, and the Dover sewer department needed to reroute a sewer line that crossed beneath the bridge abutment. Each entity operated on separate permitting and contracting timelines. Liberty Utilities' gas relocation was delayed by a permit dispute with NHDES over river crossing methodology, which cascaded into delays for the other utilities. The 12-month delay added $3M in mobilization, traffic management, and price escalation costs.

projects.name: Keene Winchester Street Resurfacing Utility Cut
projects.description: Liberty Utilities cut open recently resurfaced Winchester Street in Keene just 9 months after a NHDOT resurfacing to upgrade gas service for a new commercial development.
projects.detail: NHDOT completed a $2.2M resurfacing of Winchester Street in Keene in the fall of 2023. Nine months later, Liberty Utilities began excavating the new pavement to upgrade gas service capacity for a new commercial development along the corridor. The utility argued the development's gas load requirements were finalized after the resurfacing was complete. City officials countered that the development had been in the planning stages for over two years and the gas upgrade was foreseeable. Keene had no formal paving moratorium policy, relying instead on an informal coordination process that clearly failed in this case. The utility cuts wasted approximately $750K of the state resurfacing investment, prompting the city council to draft a moratorium ordinance.

projects.name: Manchester South Willow Street Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor reconstruction plans were overhauled after discovering extensive Liberty Utilities gas infrastructure and Consolidated Communications conduits beneath the planned median and access management improvements.
projects.detail: NHDOT's $20M South Willow Street corridor reconstruction in Manchester, designed to improve the city's busiest commercial corridor with new medians, access management, and signal upgrades, required major plan revisions. Subsurface investigations revealed that Liberty Utilities gas distribution mains and Consolidated Communications fiber optic conduits occupied far more of the underground space than records indicated. The gas mains ran through planned median locations at multiple intersections, while telecom conduits formed a dense network beneath planned access management islands. Relocating the gas mains required negotiation with Liberty Utilities over cost responsibility under New Hampshire's utility accommodation rules. The plan revision added $4M and 12 months to the project.

projects.name: Auburn-Lewiston Lisbon Street Paving Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Consolidated Communications cut open freshly repaved Lisbon Street in Auburn just 4 months after MaineDOT completed a $1.8M resurfacing to install fiber optic upgrades.
projects.detail: MaineDOT completed a $1.8M resurfacing of Lisbon Street in Auburn in early 2024 as part of a broader Lewiston-Auburn corridor improvement. Just four months later, Consolidated Communications began excavating the new pavement to install fiber optic upgrades along the corridor. The telecom company argued its fiber upgrade project timeline was driven by federal broadband funding deadlines that were not finalized until after the resurfacing was complete. MaineDOT and Auburn city officials expressed frustration, noting that Consolidated Communications had been contacted during the pre-construction utility coordination process and had not disclosed any planned work. The cuts damaged approximately $650K of the resurfacing investment. Maine does not have a statewide paving moratorium statute.

projects.name: Beckley Robert C. Byrd Drive Reconstruction Delay
projects.description: Road reconstruction delayed 14 months by scheduling conflicts between Appalachian Power, Mountaineer Gas, and the Beckley-Raleigh County water authority for utility relocations.
projects.detail: WVDOH's $15M Robert C. Byrd Drive reconstruction in Beckley was delayed by scheduling conflicts among three utility owners. Appalachian Power needed to relocate overhead-to-underground electrical lines in the corridor, Mountaineer Gas had gas mains requiring replacement, and the Beckley-Raleigh County water authority needed to replace aging water mains. The three utilities could not synchronize their relocation schedules because each had different contractor procurement timelines and regulatory approval processes. Appalachian Power's electrical work required clearances from PJM Interconnection for planned outages, adding another scheduling dependency. The project grew from $15M to $18.5M over a 14-month delay, with most overruns from extended traffic management and material price escalation.

projects.name: Meridian 22nd Avenue Widening Utility Conflict
projects.description: Widening plans revised after discovering Mississippi Power underground vaults and an unmapped 1940s-era military communications conduit from the former NAS Meridian that conflicted with the turn lane design.
projects.detail: MDOT's $15M 22nd Avenue widening project in Meridian required plan revisions when subsurface investigations found Mississippi Power underground electrical vaults and an unmapped military communications conduit from the former Naval Air Station Meridian. The electrical vaults were larger than shown on records and extended into the planned turn lane excavation zone. The military conduit, though no longer in active use, contained fiber optic cables that had been installed by a private carrier using the abandoned conduit as a raceway without proper documentation. Relocating the carrier's fiber required a separate agreement and construction sequence. The combined conflicts added $3.2M and 11 months to the project.

projects.name: Salina Santa Fe Avenue Reconstruction Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor reconstruction plans were revised after discovering Kansas Gas Service mains and Evergy conduits in locations that conflicted with the planned stormwater improvements and ADA-compliant sidewalk design.
projects.detail: The City of Salina's $15M Santa Fe Avenue reconstruction project, designed to modernize the historic corridor with ADA-compliant sidewalks, improved stormwater management, and upgraded traffic signals, required plan revisions. Subsurface utility engineering found Kansas Gas Service distribution mains and Evergy electrical conduits in locations that directly conflicted with the planned stormwater conveyance system and new sidewalk construction zones. The gas mains were at shallower depths than documented, placing them within the excavation zone for ADA curb ramp construction. Evergy's conduits occupied the planned bioretention area. Redesigning around these conflicts while maintaining ADA compliance standards added $2.5M and 9 months to the project.

projects.name: Miles City US-12 Bridge Approach Utility Conflict
projects.description: Bridge approach plans revised after discovering MDU gas mains and abandoned water system infrastructure from the former Fort Keogh military installation beneath the planned approach reconstruction.
projects.detail: MDT's $8M US-12 bridge approach reconstruction near Miles City required plan revisions when subsurface investigations discovered Montana-Dakota Utilities gas distribution mains and abandoned water system infrastructure from the former Fort Keogh military installation. The military infrastructure, dating to the late 1800s, included stone-lined water conduits that were not on any modern records. MDU's gas mains were at different depths than recorded, creating conflicts with the planned drainage improvements. The Montana SHPO required documentation of the Fort Keogh-era infrastructure before it could be removed, adding regulatory time to the project. The combined discoveries added $1.8M and 8 months to the project schedule.

projects.name: Laramie Grand Avenue Fiber Optic Gas Line Strike
projects.description: A fiber optic installation contractor struck a Black Hills Energy gas main on Grand Avenue near the University of Wyoming campus, causing an evacuation and delaying a $5M road improvement project.
projects.detail: During the City of Laramie's $5M Grand Avenue road improvement project near the University of Wyoming campus in 2024, a subcontractor boring fiber optic conduit struck a 4-inch Black Hills Energy gas distribution main. The strike occurred adjacent to student housing, prompting evacuation of approximately 200 residents. The gas main was approximately 2 feet shallower than indicated on utility records, placing it within the boring path. Emergency crews isolated the leak within 45 minutes, but the area remained evacuated for 4 hours. The incident halted construction for 3 months while a comprehensive utility re-survey was conducted in the project area near campus, adding $800K in investigation and standby costs.

projects.name: Bridgeport Congress Street Bridge Rehabilitation
projects.description: Bridge rehabilitation plans required major revision after discovery of unmapped gas transmission mains and fiber conduits beneath the Congress Street approach spans.
projects.detail: The City of Bridgeport initiated the $30M Congress Street Bridge rehabilitation to address structural deficiencies and improve multimodal access. During subsurface investigation, crews discovered two unmapped Eversource gas transmission mains and a Southern Connecticut Telephone fiber conduit bank that conflicted with new foundation piling locations. The redesign required shifting three bridge piers and rerouting a 16-inch gas main, adding $8.2M to the project cost and pushing the completion date from fall 2024 to winter 2025. Local businesses along Congress Street reported significant revenue losses during the extended construction period.

projects.name: Hartford Bushnell Park South Green Infrastructure
projects.description: Green infrastructure project near Bushnell Park required plan revisions when boring for bioswale systems encountered unmarked steam tunnels and electrical ductbanks.
projects.detail: Hartford's $15M green infrastructure project aimed to install bioswales, permeable pavement, and stormwater capture systems along the south edge of Bushnell Park. Test borings revealed an extensive unmarked steam tunnel network from the old Hartford Steam Company and Eversource high-voltage electrical ductbanks serving the Capitol complex. The bioswale locations had to be redesigned to avoid these utilities, requiring shallower installations and additional pumping systems. The $5.4M overrun was covered by reallocating funds from other city projects, delaying those initiatives as well.

projects.name: Philadelphia Girard Avenue Streetcar Track Reconstruction
projects.description: SEPTA streetcar track replacement along Girard Avenue required extensive redesign after conflicting with PGW gas mains and PECO electrical conduits throughout the corridor.
projects.detail: SEPTA's $75M project to reconstruct streetcar tracks along the Route 15 Girard Avenue corridor encountered severe underground utility conflicts. PGW cast-iron gas mains running directly beneath the tracks required simultaneous replacement, and PECO electrical ductbanks serving the Fishtown and Northern Liberties neighborhoods created routing conflicts for new drainage infrastructure. The redesign added $22M in utility relocation costs and extended the project by two full years. SEPTA was forced to continue using diesel buses on the route, frustrating riders and local advocates who had pushed for the streetcar restoration.

projects.name: Wilmington DE Christina Riverfront Promenade Extension
projects.description: Riverfront promenade extension plans were revised after subsurface investigation found abandoned industrial utilities and active Delmarva Power conduits conflicting with the new pathway alignment.
projects.detail: The City of Wilmington's $15M Christina Riverfront Promenade extension was intended to connect the Riverfront district to downtown via a multiuse path along the river. Subsurface utility engineering revealed abandoned petroleum pipelines from former riverfront industrial operations, active Delmarva Power high-voltage conduits, and contaminated soil requiring environmental remediation. The pathway alignment was shifted inland, requiring additional property acquisitions and retaining wall construction. The $4.5M cost increase and 9-month delay pushed the project opening past its targeted summer season, reducing the economic benefit of the first-year tourism impact.

projects.name: Burlington VT Main Street-Battery Street Intersection Redesign
projects.description: Intersection redesign in downtown Burlington required plan revisions when utility potholing discovered Green Mountain Power conduits and Burlington Telecom fiber conflicting with new signal foundations.
projects.detail: Burlington's $8M Main Street-Battery Street intersection redesign aimed to improve pedestrian safety and accommodate the city's growing cycling infrastructure. During utility potholing, crews discovered Green Mountain Power underground conduits and Burlington Telecom fiber trunk lines directly in the path of proposed signal mast foundations and ADA ramp relocations. The redesign required relocating signal equipment to alternative positions and rerouting fiber cables through a more expensive bore-under-road alignment. The $2.8M overrun strained the city's transportation improvement budget, and the 8-month delay pushed completion into Vermont's challenging winter construction season.

projects.name: Baltimore Howard Street Transit Corridor Utility Redesign
projects.description: Transit corridor improvements along Howard Street required extensive redesign after subsurface exploration revealed century-old BGE gas infrastructure, abandoned streetcar conduits, and unmapped combined sewers.
projects.detail: Baltimore's $60M Howard Street transit corridor project aimed to improve bus rapid transit service and pedestrian infrastructure between Penn Station and the Inner Harbor. Subsurface utility exploration uncovered BGE gas mains dating to the early 1900s, abandoned United Railways and Electric Company streetcar power conduits, and a network of unmapped combined sewers beneath the roadway. The utility conflicts required a complete redesign of the transit lane configuration and drainage systems. The $18.5M overrun consumed the project's contingency and required supplemental federal funding, while the 20-month delay pushed completion well past the city's original target for improved transit service.

projects.name: Wheeling WV Market Street Streetscape Utility Redesign
projects.description: Downtown streetscape project in Wheeling required plan revision when test pits revealed Mountaineer Gas mains and AEP electrical conduits conflicting with proposed tree pit and lighting foundation locations.
projects.detail: Wheeling's $8M Market Street downtown streetscape project was designed to revitalize the historic commercial district with new sidewalks, decorative lighting, and street trees. Test pit investigations found Mountaineer Gas distribution mains and AEP underground electrical conduits directly beneath the planned tree pit and lighting foundation locations. The redesign required shifting tree pits to alternative locations and using above-ground transformer cabinets instead of underground vaults, compromising the streetscape aesthetic. The $2.1M cost increase required the city to scale back the project's planned second phase along 12th Street.

projects.name: DC Eastern Avenue NE Combined Sewer Separation
projects.description: Combined sewer separation project along Eastern Avenue NE required redesign when PEPCO conduit banks and Washington Gas mains were found to be significantly mislocated from utility records.
projects.detail: DC Water's $50M Eastern Avenue NE combined sewer separation project was part of the Clean Rivers consent decree program. During design-phase utility investigation, PEPCO high-voltage conduit banks and Washington Gas distribution mains were found to be located 8 to 15 feet from their charted positions in multiple locations along the 1.2-mile corridor. The sewer separation alignment required a complete redesign to avoid the actual utility positions, including additional microtunneling segments to pass beneath the PEPCO conduits. The $11.3M cost increase and 16-month delay impacted the overall consent decree compliance timeline, drawing scrutiny from the EPA.

projects.name: New Haven State Street Downtown Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Downtown corridor redesign on State Street required plan revisions after encountering Southern Connecticut Gas mains and Yale University steam tunnels beneath the roadway.
projects.detail: New Haven's $20M State Street corridor redesign sought to transform the downtown street with wider sidewalks, a protected cycle track, and improved transit stops. During subsurface investigation, crews discovered Southern Connecticut Gas distribution mains that conflicted with proposed bus island foundations, and a Yale University steam tunnel extension that was not documented in city utility records. The redesign required relocating the cycle track to the opposite side of the street and redesigning bus stops to avoid the underground infrastructure. The $4.7M overrun forced the city to defer planned improvements to the adjacent Chapel Street corridor.

projects.name: Hagerstown MD Dual Highway Intersection Reconstruction
projects.description: Dual Highway intersection reconstruction required plan revision after discovering Washington County water authority mains and Antietam Broadband fiber ductbanks conflicting with new turn lane foundations.
projects.detail: MDOT SHA's $15M Dual Highway intersection reconstruction at US 40/MD 65 in Hagerstown was intended to add turn lanes and improve signal timing. Subsurface investigation found Washington County water authority trunk mains and Antietam Broadband fiber ductbanks running diagonally across the intersection, conflicting with proposed turn lane foundations and drainage structures. The redesign required relocating 600 feet of water main and boring new fiber conduit paths beneath the intersection. The $4.8M cost increase and 11-month delay impacted commuters along one of Hagerstown's most congested corridors.

projects.name: Bethlehem PA Fahy Bridge Approach Utility Redesign
projects.description: Fahy Bridge approach reconstruction required plan revision when UGI gas mains and PPL Electric conduits were found to conflict with new retaining wall foundations.
projects.detail: PennDOT's $20M Fahy Bridge approach reconstruction in Bethlehem was designed to improve traffic flow and add ADA-compliant pedestrian facilities connecting South Bethlehem to downtown. Utility investigation revealed UGI gas distribution mains and PPL Electric underground conduits running through the planned retaining wall foundation zones on both approach ramps. The redesign required extending the bridge deck to span over the utility zones rather than resting on new retaining walls, adding $5.3M to the project budget. The 12-month delay forced PennDOT to extend the temporary traffic signal plan, which created congestion backups reaching I-78 during peak hours.

projects.name: Hartford CT I-84 Lowering Project Utility Coordination Stall
projects.description: I-84 highway lowering project was delayed by scheduling conflicts with Eversource, Connecticut Natural Gas, and the Metropolitan District Commission water authority.
projects.detail: ConnDOT's $200M I-84 lowering project through downtown Hartford required relocating utilities from beneath and alongside the existing highway before excavation could begin. Eversource required an 18-month utility relocation window, Connecticut Natural Gas demanded a sequential 12-month window for gas main protection work, and the Metropolitan District Commission needed 8 months for water main relocations. None of the three utilities would agree to concurrent work due to conflicting safety zones and labor agreements. The 22-month scheduling cascade added $35M in extended general conditions, escalation costs, and temporary traffic management, drawing criticism from state legislators who had championed the reconnection project.

projects.name: Stamford CT Transit-Oriented Development Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Transit-oriented development infrastructure near the Stamford Transportation Center was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Eversource, Aquarion Water, and Frontier Communications.
projects.detail: Stamford's $40M transit-oriented development infrastructure project near the transportation center required new water, sewer, and electrical service upgrades to support planned high-density residential and commercial development. Eversource demanded a 10-month exclusive window for substation upgrades and feeder installations, Aquarion Water required 7 months for new water main connections, and Frontier Communications needed 4 months for fiber relocation. The three companies could not agree on overlapping construction zones in the constrained downtown area. The 13-month delay and $8.7M cost increase jeopardized several private development deals that had financing contingent on infrastructure completion dates.

projects.name: Philadelphia Hunting Park Avenue Reconstruction Utility Delay
projects.description: Hunting Park Avenue reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between PGW gas replacement, PWD sewer work, and PECO electrical upgrades that each demanded sequential access.
projects.detail: Philadelphia's $30M Hunting Park Avenue reconstruction was designed to replace deteriorated road pavement, add protected bike lanes, and install new LED streetlighting. PGW required an exclusive 10-month window for cast-iron gas main replacement along the entire 1.5-mile corridor, PWD demanded a sequential 8-month window for sewer main lining, and PECO needed 5 months for underground electrical cable replacement. The three utilities refused to work concurrently due to safety requirements and union jurisdictional rules. The contractor estimated that concurrent work could have saved 12 months, but the utilities' sequential approach added 15 months and $7.4M to the project cost.

projects.name: Wilmington DE Market Street Transit Corridor Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Market Street transit corridor improvements were delayed by scheduling conflicts between Delmarva Power, Artesian Water Company, and Comcast utility relocations.
projects.detail: DART's $20M Market Street transit corridor improvement project in downtown Wilmington required utility relocations to accommodate new bus stops, signal priority equipment, and ADA-compliant sidewalks. Delmarva Power required a 7-month exclusive window for underground cable replacement, Artesian Water Company demanded 5 months for water main upgrades, and Comcast needed 4 months for fiber relocation. The three companies could not agree on concurrent construction in the narrow downtown street. The 12-month delay and $5.1M cost increase from extended traffic management and contractor standby costs were particularly frustrating because the Market Street improvements had been in planning for over a decade.

projects.name: Morgantown WV Beechurst Avenue Phase II Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Phase II of Beechurst Avenue improvements was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Mountaineer Gas, Mon Power, and WVU campus utility coordination.
projects.detail: Morgantown's $10M Beechurst Avenue Phase II improvement project near the WVU campus was stalled by scheduling conflicts between three utility operators. Mountaineer Gas required a 5-month window for gas main protection work, Mon Power needed 4 months for underground electrical cable replacement, and WVU's Facilities Management demanded a separate 3-month window for campus utility connections that could only occur during summer break. The sequential scheduling requirements added 9 months and $2.3M to the project, with the timing constraints around the academic calendar proving particularly difficult to resolve. The delay meant students and businesses along the heavily trafficked corridor endured construction disruption through an additional academic year.

projects.name: Newport RI Broadway Corridor Improvement Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Broadway corridor improvement was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Rhode Island Energy gas work, Newport Water Department pipe replacement, and Cox Communications cable relocation.
projects.detail: Newport's $12M Broadway corridor improvement project aimed to reconstruct the city's main commercial street with new utilities, sidewalks, and streetscaping. Rhode Island Energy required a 5-month exclusive window for gas main protection, Newport Water Department needed 4 months for water main replacement, and Cox Communications demanded 3 months for cable relocation. The constrained corridor width prevented any two utilities from working simultaneously. The 9-month delay pushed the project into the summer tourist season, when the city imposed additional construction hour restrictions that further extended the timeline. The $2.7M cost increase required the city to reduce the scope of planned streetscape amenities.

projects.name: Scranton PA Lackawanna Avenue Phase II Utility Scheduling Standoff
projects.description: Lackawanna Avenue Phase II streetscape was delayed by scheduling conflicts between UGI gas main replacement, PA American Water pipe work, and MetroConnect fiber installation.
projects.detail: Scranton's $15M Lackawanna Avenue Phase II streetscape project in the downtown business district encountered scheduling conflicts with three utility companies. UGI required a 6-month exclusive window for cast-iron gas main replacement, PA American Water needed 5 months for water main work, and MetroConnect demanded 3 months for fiber conduit installation. The narrow downtown street could not accommodate simultaneous utility construction. The 10-month delay and $3.4M cost increase from contractor standby and extended traffic management frustrated downtown business owners who had already endured Phase I construction disruptions.

projects.name: Buffalo NY Niagara Street Complete Streets Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Niagara Street complete streets project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between National Grid, Buffalo Water Authority, and Spectrum cable infrastructure relocations.
projects.detail: Buffalo's $25M Niagara Street complete streets project was designed to add protected bike lanes, improved transit stops, and green infrastructure along the West Side corridor. National Grid required an exclusive 8-month window for gas and electric utility relocation, the Buffalo Water Authority needed 6 months for water main replacement, and Spectrum demanded 4 months for cable and fiber infrastructure relocation. The three organizations could not agree on overlapping construction zones in the corridor. The 13-month delay and $5.8M cost increase from extended contractor general conditions and traffic management pushed the project completion past two construction seasons, with winter weather further complicating the extended timeline.

projects.name: Rochester NY Inner Loop East Phase II Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Inner Loop East highway-to-boulevard conversion Phase II was delayed by scheduling conflicts between RG&E, Monroe County Water Authority, and Frontier Communications utility relocations.
projects.detail: Rochester's $40M Inner Loop East Phase II conversion from a sunken highway to a surface boulevard encountered scheduling conflicts with three major utility operators. Rochester Gas & Electric required a 9-month exclusive window for gas and electric infrastructure relocation from beneath the former highway, Monroe County Water Authority needed 6 months for water main installation in the new boulevard alignment, and Frontier Communications demanded 5 months for fiber relocation. The utilities could not work concurrently in the constrained former highway trench. The 14-month delay and $8.4M cost increase threatened to undermine the private development deals that were contingent on boulevard completion, with several developers citing the delay as grounds for renegotiating their commitments.

projects.name: Bangor ME Union Street Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Union Street reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Bangor Gas Company main replacement and Bangor Water District pipe upgrades.
projects.detail: Bangor's $8M Union Street reconstruction project from downtown to the medical center district was stalled by scheduling conflicts between two utility operators. Bangor Gas Company required a 5-month exclusive window for gas main replacement, and Bangor Water District needed a separate 4-month window for water main upgrades. Neither utility would permit concurrent trenching operations in the relatively narrow street due to trench wall stability concerns. The 8-month delay and $1.8M cost increase from extended contractor general conditions pushed the project past the originally planned single-season construction schedule. Area hospitals reported that the extended construction caused ambulance route disruptions that required costly detour protocols.

projects.name: Bridgeport CT Atlantic Street Overpass Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Atlantic Street railroad overpass reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Eversource, United Illuminating, and Metro-North Railroad utility protection work.
projects.detail: ConnDOT's $30M Atlantic Street railroad overpass reconstruction in Bridgeport was critical for improving traffic flow near the Metro-North station. Eversource required a 7-month exclusive window for gas main relocation, United Illuminating needed 6 months for electrical conduit protection, and Metro-North Railroad demanded separate construction windows that could only occur during weekend track outages. The scheduling constraints created a 13-month cascade, with the railroad's limited work windows proving the most difficult constraint. The $6.5M cost increase from extended general conditions and premium weekend labor rates consumed the project's contingency, and ConnDOT had to seek additional legislative appropriation.

projects.name: Harrisburg PA Front Street Utility Scheduling Cascade
projects.description: Front Street riverfront reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between UGI gas work, Capital Region Water infrastructure, and PPL Electric conduit relocation.
projects.detail: Harrisburg's $15M Front Street riverfront reconstruction was designed to improve the Susquehanna River corridor with new multiuse paths, lighting, and flood-resistant infrastructure. UGI required a 6-month exclusive window for gas main protection, Capital Region Water needed 5 months for water and sewer infrastructure work, and PPL Electric demanded 3 months for underground conduit relocation. The narrow riverfront corridor could not accommodate concurrent utility construction without encroaching on active flood control structures. The 10-month delay and $3.8M cost increase pushed the project past its targeted completion for the city's annual riverfront festival season.

projects.name: Hartford CT Park Street Fiber Installation Gas Strike
projects.description: Fiber optic installation contractor struck a Connecticut Natural Gas main on Park Street, forcing evacuation of the Frog Hollow neighborhood and halting a concurrent road improvement project.
projects.detail: A Frontier Communications fiber installation contractor performing horizontal directional drilling on Park Street in Hartford's Frog Hollow neighborhood struck a Connecticut Natural Gas 6-inch distribution main. The gas release forced evacuation of 150 residents from nearby apartment buildings and shut down an ongoing $6M city road improvement project for four months while the utility conflict was investigated. The gas main was found to be 3 feet from its charted position. The $1.4M in additional costs covered emergency response, gas main repair, enhanced utility locating for the remainder of the fiber route, and extended road project general conditions. Hartford's mayor called for stricter permitting requirements for fiber installation contractors.
projects.timeline: 2025 start → 4 months added to concurrent road project

projects.name: Syracuse NY Erie Boulevard Water Main Strike
projects.description: Road reconstruction contractor struck a 16-inch OCWA water transmission main on Erie Boulevard, creating a sinkhole and flooding the adjacent Inner Harbor development area.
projects.detail: During Syracuse's $10M Erie Boulevard reconstruction project near the Inner Harbor, an excavator struck an Onondaga County Water Authority 16-inch transmission main that was 3 feet shallower than indicated on utility records. The resulting water release created a 15-foot sinkhole and flooded portions of the adjacent Inner Harbor mixed-use development, causing significant property damage. Water service was disrupted for 12 hours to approximately 5,000 customers. The $2.2M cost overrun covered emergency sinkhole stabilization, water main repair, property damage claims, and enhanced subsurface investigation for the remaining project corridor. The incident prompted OCWA to initiate a transmission main mapping verification program.

projects.name: Montpelier VT State Street Bridge Gas Line Strike
projects.description: Bridge approach construction crew struck a Vermont Gas Systems distribution line during excavation for new bridge abutment foundations on State Street.
projects.detail: During Montpelier's $5M State Street bridge replacement project over the North Branch of the Winooski River, an excavation crew struck a Vermont Gas Systems 4-inch distribution line while preparing the foundation for a new bridge abutment. The gas release forced evacuation of the adjacent State Street commercial district and the temporary closure of several state government offices. The gas line had been installed after the original bridge was built and was not shown on the bridge project utility plans. The $980K cost overrun covered emergency response, gas line repair, redesign of the abutment foundation to accommodate the gas line, and additional utility investigation. The 4-month delay pushed the bridge opening past the fall foliage tourism season.

projects.name: West Hartford CT Farmington Avenue Fiber Gas Line Strike
projects.description: Fiber installation contractor struck a Connecticut Natural Gas service line on Farmington Avenue, forcing evacuation of the Blue Back Square shopping district.
projects.detail: A Frontier Communications fiber installation contractor performing trenching along Farmington Avenue in West Hartford struck a Connecticut Natural Gas service line near the Blue Back Square mixed-use development. The gas release forced evacuation of the popular shopping and dining district and several adjacent apartment buildings, displacing approximately 500 people for 4 hours. The gas service line was a lateral connection that was not included in the fiber contractor's utility locate request because it ran perpendicular to the planned fiber route. The $1.2M in costs covered emergency response, gas line repair, business revenue loss claims, and enhanced utility locating requirements for the remaining fiber installation route. The town subsequently required fiber contractors to locate all utilities within 25 feet of any proposed excavation, not just those in the direct path.

projects.name: New Haven CT Orange Street Resurfacing Eversource Gas Cuts
projects.description: Eversource cut into newly resurfaced Orange Street within 5 months to replace gas services, wasting $920K in fresh pavement in the East Rock neighborhood.
projects.detail: Five months after New Haven completed a $3M resurfacing of Orange Street in the East Rock neighborhood, Eversource began cutting into the new pavement to replace gas service lines to residential properties. The utility made 11 separate cuts over a three-block stretch, each leaving a patched section that degraded the smooth riding surface. The city estimated $920K in wasted pavement value. New Haven's Board of Alders introduced an ordinance requiring utilities to pay a premium restoration fee for any cuts made within 3 years of resurfacing. Eversource argued that the gas service replacements were mandated by state pipeline safety regulations and could not be deferred, but the city pointed out that Eversource had been notified of the paving schedule 2 years in advance.
projects.budget: $3M paving investment → $920K wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Resurfaced summer 2024 → Eversource cuts began within 5 months

projects.name: Philadelphia Passyunk Avenue Resurfacing PGW Gas Main Cuts
projects.description: PGW cut open recently resurfaced East Passyunk Avenue to perform cast-iron gas main replacement, wasting $2.1M in new pavement in one of Philadelphia's premier dining corridors.
projects.detail: Within 8 months of Philadelphia completing a $7M resurfacing and streetscape improvement of East Passyunk Avenue, PGW began cutting into the new pavement to replace century-old cast-iron gas mains along the popular restaurant corridor. The utility made 18 separate cuts over a 6-block stretch, destroying new crosswalks, bicycle lane markings, and pavement. The city estimated $2.1M in wasted investment. The East Passyunk Improvement District board publicly criticized PGW for failing to coordinate with the Streets Department despite years of advance notice about the resurfacing project. City Council introduced a resolution requiring PGW to obtain mayoral approval before cutting any street within 5 years of resurfacing. PGW countered that the cast-iron replacement was a state-mandated safety priority that could not be delayed.
projects.budget: $7M paving investment → $2.1M wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Resurfaced 2024 → PGW cuts began within 8 months

projects.name: Baltimore Roland Avenue Repaving BGE Gas Moratorium Violation
projects.description: BGE cut into recently resurfaced Roland Avenue in Roland Park to perform gas main replacement, wasting $1.6M in fresh pavement and drawing a City Council hearing.
projects.detail: Within 6 months of Baltimore completing a $5.5M resurfacing and bicycle facility installation on Roland Avenue through the Roland Park neighborhood, BGE began cutting into the new pavement for gas main replacement. The utility made 12 cuts along the corridor, destroying new bike lane markings and pavement. The city estimated $1.6M in wasted investment. The incident prompted a City Council hearing at which the Department of Transportation testified that BGE had been notified of the paving schedule 18 months in advance but failed to coordinate its gas main replacement timeline. BGE was required to restore the pavement to full DOT specifications and reimburse the city for pavement markings, but residents complained that the restored patches never matched the quality of the original resurfacing.
projects.budget: $5.5M paving investment → $1.6M wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Resurfaced 2024 → BGE cuts began within 6 months

projects.name: Portland ME Congress Street Resurfacing Unitil Gas Cuts
projects.description: Unitil cut into recently resurfaced Congress Street within 3 months to replace gas service lines, wasting $680K in fresh pavement along Portland's main commercial corridor.
projects.detail: Three months after Portland completed a $2.5M resurfacing of Congress Street through the Arts District, Unitil began cutting into the new pavement to replace aging gas service connections to adjacent buildings. The utility made 7 cuts along a 4-block stretch, each creating a patched section that degraded the smooth riding surface. The city estimated $680K in wasted pavement value. Portland's city manager publicly expressed frustration that Unitil had not coordinated with the city's published paving schedule despite receiving formal notification. The city council subsequently passed an ordinance requiring utilities to post a surety bond before performing any work within 5 years of resurfacing, with the bond forfeited if the restoration failed to meet city specifications within 2 years.
projects.budget: $2.5M paving investment → $680K wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Resurfaced fall 2024 → Unitil cuts began within 3 months

projects.name: Pittsburgh PA Butler Street Repaving Peoples Gas Cuts
projects.description: Peoples Gas cut into recently repaved Butler Street in Lawrenceville to perform gas main replacement, wasting $1.2M in fresh pavement along Pittsburgh's trendiest commercial corridor.
projects.detail: Within 5 months of Pittsburgh completing a $4M repaving of Butler Street through the Lawrenceville neighborhood, Peoples Gas began cutting into the new pavement for cast-iron gas main replacement. The utility made 7 cuts along a 5-block stretch of the popular restaurant and boutique corridor, destroying new crosswalk markings and creating uneven pavement surfaces. The city estimated $1.2M in wasted pavement value. The Lawrenceville Corporation business district organization publicly demanded that Peoples Gas restore the pavement to original specifications and coordinate future infrastructure work with the city.
