Pittsburgh's city council introduced an ordinance requiring mandatory pre-paving utility coordination conferences and establishing financial penalties for post-paving utility cuts within 5 years.
projects.budget: $4M paving investment → $1.2M wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Repaved spring 2025 → Peoples Gas cuts began within 5 months

projects.name: Stamford CT Bedford Street Resurfacing Eversource Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Eversource cut into recently resurfaced Bedford Street to replace gas services, wasting $1.5M in fresh pavement in Stamford's downtown transit district.
projects.detail: Within 4 months of Stamford completing a $5M resurfacing of Bedford Street near the Metro-North station, Eversource began cutting into the new pavement to replace gas service lines to adjacent commercial buildings. The utility made 8 cuts along a 4-block stretch of the heavily trafficked downtown street, destroying new crosswalk markings and transit stop pavement. The city estimated $1.5M in wasted pavement value. Stamford's Board of Representatives passed an emergency ordinance increasing utility restoration fees by 250% for any cuts within 3 years of resurfacing and requiring utilities to post a 5-year maintenance bond on all cuts. Eversource argued that the gas service replacements were mandated by federal pipeline safety rules, but the city produced evidence that Eversource had declined to participate in pre-paving utility coordination meetings.
projects.budget: $5M paving investment → $1.5M wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Resurfaced spring 2025 → Eversource cuts began within 4 months

projects.name: Cambridge MA Hampshire Street Repaving Eversource Gas Cuts
projects.description: Eversource cut into recently resurfaced Hampshire Street in Kendall Square to perform gas main replacement, wasting $1.8M in fresh pavement in Cambridge's biotech corridor.
projects.detail: Within 5 months of Cambridge completing a $6M resurfacing and bicycle infrastructure installation on Hampshire Street through the Kendall Square biotech district, Eversource began cutting into the new pavement for gas main replacement. The utility made 10 cuts along a 6-block stretch, destroying protected bike lane delineators, new crosswalks, and pavement. The city estimated $1.8M in wasted investment. Cambridge's city manager issued a formal demand for Eversource to restore all pavement to original specifications and reimburse the city for destroyed bicycle infrastructure. The incident became a rallying point for the Massachusetts Municipal Association's campaign for statewide utility coordination legislation, with Cambridge's public works commissioner testifying before the state legislature about the systemic problem of utility cuts destroying newly paved roads.
projects.budget: $6M paving investment → $1.8M wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Resurfaced 2024 → Eversource cuts began within 5 months

projects.name: Springfield MA State Street Corridor Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: State Street corridor reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Columbia Gas, Springfield Water & Sewer Commission, and Eversource electric infrastructure work.
projects.detail: Springfield's $20M State Street corridor reconstruction was designed to revitalize the downtown-to-Mason Square commercial corridor with new utilities, sidewalks, and bus rapid transit infrastructure. Columbia Gas required an exclusive 7-month window for gas main replacement, Springfield Water & Sewer Commission needed 6 months for combined sewer separation work, and Eversource demanded 4 months for underground electrical cable upgrades. None of the three utilities agreed to concurrent work due to right-of-way constraints in the narrow corridor. The 12-month scheduling cascade added $4.3M in extended general conditions, contractor standby, and traffic management costs, undermining the economic revitalization goals that had driven community support for the project.

projects.name: Middletown CT Main Street Extension Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Main Street extension project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Connecticut Natural Gas, the Middletown Water Department, and Comcast cable relocation.
projects.detail: Middletown's $10M Main Street extension and streetscape project connecting downtown to the Harbor Park area encountered scheduling conflicts with three utility operators. Connecticut Natural Gas required a 5-month exclusive window for gas main protection work, the Middletown Water Department needed 4 months for water main installation, and Comcast demanded 3 months for cable relocation. The narrow construction corridor between Main Street buildings and the Connecticut River embankment prevented concurrent utility work. The 9-month delay and $2.5M cost increase pushed the project past two festival seasons at Harbor Park, reducing the anticipated economic benefit of improved downtown connectivity.

projects.name: Bethlehem PA North Side Revitalization Utility Scheduling Standoff
projects.description: North Side revitalization infrastructure was delayed by scheduling conflicts between UGI gas replacement, Bethlehem Water Authority pipe work, and Service Electric cable relocation.
projects.detail: Bethlehem's $15M North Side revitalization infrastructure project was designed to support redevelopment in the historic Moravian district area with new water, sewer, and streetscape improvements. UGI required an exclusive 6-month window for cast-iron gas main replacement, the Bethlehem Water Authority needed 5 months for water main upgrades, and Service Electric demanded 3 months for cable infrastructure relocation. The historic district's narrow streets and proximity to protected Moravian structures prevented concurrent utility construction. The 10-month delay and $3.1M cost increase frustrated the redevelopment authority, which had timed private development projects to coincide with infrastructure completion. Several developers sought contract extensions, citing the utility-driven delays.

projects.name: Silver Spring MD Colesville Road Sewer Gas Line Strike
projects.description: Sewer upgrade contractor struck a Washington Gas transmission line during excavation on Colesville Road, forcing evacuation of the downtown Silver Spring commercial district.
projects.detail: During WSSC Water's $8M Colesville Road sewer and drainage upgrade project in downtown Silver Spring, an excavation crew struck a Washington Gas 8-inch transmission line that was located 5 feet from its plotted position on utility records. The gas release forced evacuation of the downtown Silver Spring commercial district and required Montgomery County Fire Department hazmat response. Washington Gas emergency crews secured the break within 4 hours, but the area remained closed for an additional 24 hours during air quality monitoring. The $1.6M cost overrun covered emergency response, gas line repair, enhanced subsurface utility engineering for the remaining project corridor, and project redesign to avoid other potentially mislocated Washington Gas infrastructure in the area.

projects.name: Waterbury CT East Main Street Bridge Construction Gas Strike
projects.description: Bridge approach excavation on East Main Street struck a Yankee Gas transmission main, forcing evacuation of the adjacent shopping district and halting the $10M bridge project.
projects.detail: During Waterbury's $10M East Main Street bridge rehabilitation project, an excavation crew preparing the east bridge abutment struck a Yankee Gas (Eversource) 8-inch transmission main that was located 3 feet from its charted position. The gas release forced evacuation of the adjacent Brass Mill Center shopping area and closure of East Main Street for 28 hours. Eversource determined that the gas main had been installed during a 1998 road widening project and the as-built drawings were never incorporated into the utility atlas. The $2.1M cost overrun covered emergency response, gas main repair, comprehensive utility re-survey of both bridge approach areas, and project redesign. The 5-month delay pushed the bridge opening into winter, requiring expensive temporary heating for concrete curing.

projects.name: Somerville MA Broadway Resurfacing Eversource Gas Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Eversource cut into recently resurfaced Broadway to perform gas main replacement, wasting $1.4M in fresh pavement along Somerville's main east-west commercial corridor.
projects.detail: Within 4 months of Somerville completing a $5M resurfacing of Broadway through the Winter Hill and East Somerville neighborhoods, Eversource began cutting into the new pavement to replace aging gas distribution mains. The utility made 9 cuts along a 7-block stretch, destroying new bike lane markings, crosswalks, and fresh asphalt. The city estimated $1.4M in wasted pavement value. Somerville's mayor issued a public statement criticizing Eversource for ignoring the city's advance paving notifications sent 16 months before the resurfacing project. The city subsequently amended its utility cut ordinance to require a 300% surcharge on restoration costs for any cuts within 5 years of resurfacing and mandatory escrow deposits from utilities performing planned infrastructure work near recently paved streets.
projects.budget: $5M paving investment → $1.4M wasted in pavement cuts
projects.timeline: Resurfaced spring 2025 → Eversource cuts began within 4 months

projects.name: Norfolk Light Rail Extension Phase 2
projects.description: Light rail extension required complete redesign after engineers discovered conflicting storm sewer and telecom duct banks beneath proposed alignment.
projects.detail: The Norfolk Light Rail Extension Phase 2 was planned to connect the existing Tide line to Naval Station Norfolk. During the 30% design phase, subsurface utility engineering revealed a dense network of Navy-owned telecom conduits and city storm sewers directly in the rail alignment path. The original plans had relied on outdated utility maps that did not reflect post-2015 installations. Engineers had to redesign the entire track alignment to shift it 12 feet east along three critical blocks, requiring new property easements and revised station locations. The plan revision added $78 million to the project and pushed the completion date from 2027 to 2029.

projects.name: Raleigh Union Station Area Streetscape Redesign
projects.description: Downtown streetscape project required full redesign after ground-penetrating radar revealed abandoned industrial utility vaults beneath the planned pedestrian plaza.
projects.detail: The Raleigh Union Station Area Streetscape project aimed to transform West and Hargett Streets into a pedestrian-friendly corridor connecting the train station to downtown. During pre-construction boring, crews found a network of abandoned industrial steam vaults and legacy petroleum pipelines from a former fueling depot. The discoveries forced a complete redesign of the stormwater management system and utility corridor, as the original plan called for bioswales and tree wells in locations now known to contain contaminated infrastructure. The city had to engage environmental remediation consultants and redesign the entire underground layout, adding $12 million and 18 months to the schedule.

projects.name: Savannah River Street Infrastructure Modernization
projects.description: Historic district infrastructure upgrade stalled when engineers found unmapped 19th-century brick utility tunnels beneath River Street that conflicted with modern sewer installation plans.
projects.detail: Savannah's River Street Infrastructure Modernization aimed to replace aging water and sewer lines beneath the historic cobblestone waterfront. During initial excavation, contractors uncovered a network of unmapped 19th-century brick utility tunnels, some dating to the 1850s, that ran beneath the planned sewer alignment. The historic preservation commission required archaeological documentation before any demolition, and the Georgia SHPO mandated that certain tunnel segments be preserved in place. Engineers had to redesign the sewer routing to weave around the preserved structures, requiring deeper excavation and more complex connections. The $18 million cost increase and two-year delay impacted tourism revenue as portions of River Street remained closed through two peak seasons.

projects.name: Jacksonville Southbank Riverwalk Extension
projects.description: Riverwalk extension plans were revised twice after discovery of JEA high-voltage underground feeders and a decommissioned fuel pipeline beneath the proposed path.
projects.detail: The Jacksonville Southbank Riverwalk Extension was designed to add 1.2 miles of pedestrian and cyclist infrastructure along the St. Johns River. During the 60% design review, JEA flagged that their underground high-voltage feeders serving the Southbank district ran directly beneath the proposed riverwalk alignment. Additionally, a decommissioned petroleum pipeline from a former waterfront terminal was found in a condition requiring environmental remediation before construction could proceed. The project required two full plan revisions to reroute the riverwalk alignment inland by 20 feet in critical sections and to accommodate JEA vault access requirements. The changes added $22 million in costs and pushed completion back 14 months.

projects.name: Knoxville Cumberland Avenue Phase 3 Reconstruction
projects.description: Phase 3 of the Cumberland Avenue corridor improvement required plan revision after KUB discovered their 1960s-era gas transmission main was not where records indicated.
projects.detail: Knoxville's Cumberland Avenue Phase 3 Reconstruction continued the multi-year corridor transformation near the University of Tennessee campus. During potholing verification, Knoxville Utilities Board discovered that a high-pressure gas transmission main installed in the 1960s had been improperly recorded and was actually 8 feet north of its documented position, placing it directly under the proposed bus pullout and bike lane. The discovery forced engineers to revise the entire cross-section design for three blocks, eliminating the planned center median and reconfiguring the stormwater system. KUB determined that relocating the gas main would cost more than redesigning the road, so the project absorbed the $8 million plan revision cost. The 10-month delay impacted the university district during the academic year.

projects.name: Charlottesville West Main Street Complete Streets
projects.description: Complete streets redesign required when underground utility investigation found a tangle of UVA steam tunnels, city water mains, and private fiber optic cables in the planned bioswale corridor.
projects.detail: Charlottesville's West Main Street Complete Streets project was designed to add protected bike lanes, bioswales, and improved pedestrian crossings along the corridor connecting the University of Virginia to downtown. During subsurface utility engineering, investigators found that UVA's steam tunnel network extended further east than institutional records showed, and private fiber optic cables installed by multiple providers occupied the exact zone planned for bioswale installation. The city water main also sat at a depth that conflicted with planned tree well excavations. The redesign shifted bioswales to the north side of the street only, replaced tree wells with above-grade planters in the affected blocks, and required a new fiber relocation agreement with three separate telecommunications providers. The plan revision added $5.2 million and 9 months.

projects.name: Fayetteville NC Murchison Road Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Military base-adjacent road widening plans required revision when Fort Liberty utility easements and a classified communications conduit were found beneath the proposed widening footprint.
projects.detail: The Murchison Road Corridor improvement project in Fayetteville aimed to widen the road from two to four lanes between Bragg Boulevard and Cliffdale Road, adjacent to Fort Liberty. During design, the Army Corps of Engineers identified that military utility easements and a classified fiber optic communications conduit ran beneath the proposed widening area on the west side of the road. The classified nature of the conduit meant it could not be relocated without extensive federal review and security protocols. Engineers had to revise the widening plan to expand exclusively to the east, requiring acquisition of additional private property and the relocation of commercial building frontages. The plan revision added $7.5 million in property acquisition and redesign costs, with a 12-month delay for federal coordination and property negotiations.

projects.name: Augusta GA Riverwatch Parkway Interchange Redesign
projects.description: Highway interchange redesign required after discovering a Georgia Power high-voltage underground feeder and Augusta Utilities trunk sewer that conflicted with proposed bridge pier locations.
projects.detail: The Riverwatch Parkway Interchange project in Augusta aimed to replace a congested at-grade intersection with a grade-separated interchange to improve access to the Augusta National area and downtown riverfront. During the foundation design phase, geotechnical borings revealed a Georgia Power 115kV underground feeder and an Augusta Utilities 48-inch trunk sewer running through the proposed locations for two bridge piers. Relocating the high-voltage feeder required a 14-month lead time for Georgia Power to design and permit an alternate route, while the trunk sewer relocation required temporary bypass pumping that could only occur during dry-weather months. The $31 million cost overrun included utility relocation, redesigned pier foundations, and extended construction management. The 20-month delay pushed the project through two additional construction seasons.

projects.name: Franklin TN Columbia Avenue Streetscape Utility Revision
projects.description: Historic downtown streetscape plans revised when an abandoned manufactured gas plant pipeline and AT&T legacy copper trunk lines were found beneath planned tree well locations.
projects.detail: Franklin's Columbia Avenue Streetscape project was part of the city's downtown beautification initiative, aiming to add street trees, decorative pavers, and improved lighting. Subsurface investigation uncovered an abandoned manufactured gas plant pipeline dating to the early 1900s, which required environmental assessment for potential coal tar contamination. AT&T legacy copper trunk lines, some still partially active serving older buildings, were also found in the planned tree well excavation zone. The Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation required soil sampling along the pipeline corridor before any excavation could proceed, adding 4 months before design could resume. The plan revision eliminated tree wells on the east side of Columbia Avenue and replaced them with above-grade planters, redesigned the lighting conduit pathway, and included environmental monitoring costs. The $4.8 million overrun and 8-month delay dimmed enthusiasm for what had been planned as a quick beautification project.

projects.name: Fredericksburg VA Downtown Sewer Separation Utility Redesign
projects.description: Combined sewer separation project plans revised after encountering Civil War-era brick drainage structures and unmarked Dominion Energy underground lines beneath Princess Anne Street.
projects.detail: Fredericksburg's Downtown Sewer Separation project was mandated by a state consent order to reduce combined sewer overflows to the Rappahannock River. During exploratory excavation beneath Princess Anne Street, crews found Civil War-era brick drainage structures that the Virginia Department of Historic Resources required to be documented and assessed. Additionally, unmarked Dominion Energy underground distribution lines were found crossing the planned sewer alignment at multiple locations. The historic drainage structures required archaeological investigation and, in two locations, were determined eligible for the National Register, requiring preservation in place. The sewer alignment had to be redesigned to avoid the historic structures while also working around the Dominion Energy lines. The $11 million cost increase and 14-month delay reflected the archaeological work, utility redesign, and Dominion Energy relocation costs.

projects.name: Rock Hill SC Knowledge Park Infrastructure Overhaul
projects.description: Knowledge Park development infrastructure plans required full utility corridor redesign when Comporium Communications fiber and York Electric underground feeds were found conflicting with planned road alignments.
projects.detail: Rock Hill's Knowledge Park Infrastructure Overhaul was intended to prepare the former industrial area for mixed-use redevelopment with new roads, water, and sewer infrastructure. The project hit a major snag when subsurface investigation revealed that Comporium Communications fiber optic trunk lines and York Electric Cooperative underground distribution feeds crisscrossed the property in patterns not reflected on any available utility maps. These utilities served critical facilities outside the development area and could not be easily relocated. The plan revision required rerouting two planned internal roads, redesigning intersection spacing, and creating a new utility corridor agreement with both providers. The $5.9 million cost increase included utility relocation contributions and redesign engineering, while the 10-month delay reflected the time needed for multi-party utility negotiations.

projects.name: Decatur AL 6th Avenue Corridor Improvement Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor improvement plans revised after encountering Decatur Utilities underground electric and an abandoned TVA transmission conduit beneath the planned median and turn lane construction zone.
projects.detail: Decatur's 6th Avenue Corridor Improvement project aimed to add a center turn lane, bike lanes, and improved pedestrian crossings along a 1.5-mile commercial corridor. During design, subsurface investigation discovered Decatur Utilities underground electric distribution lines at a depth that conflicted with the planned center turn lane storm drains, and an abandoned TVA transmission conduit that could not be confirmed as fully deenergized without TVA inspection. TVA's inspection process took 3 months, during which all design work in the affected area was paused. Once confirmed abandoned, the conduit still required careful removal due to potential asbestos insulation. Engineers redesigned the stormwater system to use shallower inlets and a modified pipe slope to avoid the DU electric lines. The $3.5 million overrun and 8-month delay exceeded the city's contingency budget, requiring a supplemental appropriation from the city council.

projects.name: I-64/I-264 Interchange Reconstruction (Hampton Roads)
projects.description: Major interchange reconstruction delayed by scheduling conflicts between VDOT, Dominion Energy, and Hampton Roads Sanitation District, each requiring sequential access to the same utility corridor.
projects.detail: The I-64/I-264 Interchange Reconstruction in the Hampton Roads area was one of VDOT's highest-priority projects to reduce congestion in the Virginia Beach-Norfolk corridor. The project required relocation of Dominion Energy transmission lines, Hampton Roads Sanitation District force mains, and Virginia Natural Gas pipelines before highway construction could begin. However, each utility owner required exclusive access to the shared utility corridor for their relocation work, and their construction windows conflicted due to seasonal restrictions, equipment availability, and permit timing. Dominion Energy could only perform transmission work during fall outage windows, HRSD required dry-weather months for force main work, and VNG pipeline relocations required spring scheduling per their safety protocols. The sequential scheduling pushed utility relocations alone to 30 months instead of the planned 12, adding $42 million in escalation costs and delaying highway construction by 2 years.

projects.name: Charlotte Gateway Station District Infrastructure
projects.description: Multimodal station district infrastructure delayed 18 months when Charlotte Water, Duke Energy, and Piedmont Natural Gas could not agree on a sequenced utility relocation schedule.
projects.detail: Charlotte's Gateway Station District Infrastructure project was designed to prepare the area around the planned multimodal transportation hub with new roads, water, sewer, and underground power. The project required Charlotte Water to relocate a 36-inch transmission main, Duke Energy to underground an overhead distribution line, and Piedmont Natural Gas to relocate a regulator station and associated piping. All three utilities claimed they needed the same construction window in 2025 to complete their work, and none could begin until the city completed preliminary grading. Negotiations over scheduling priority consumed 8 months, and the final sequenced schedule placed each utility relocation in series rather than parallel. The $28 million cost increase reflected construction cost escalation during the delay period and premium pricing for accelerated utility work. The 18-month delay jeopardized the timeline for the multimodal station itself, which depended on the infrastructure being in place.

projects.name: Mount Pleasant SC Johnnie Dodds Boulevard Widening
projects.description: Boulevard widening delayed by scheduling conflicts between Berkeley Electric Cooperative, Mount Pleasant Waterworks, and SCE&G, each requiring different construction seasons for their utility relocations.
projects.detail: Mount Pleasant's Johnnie Dodds Boulevard Widening project aimed to expand the heavily congested corridor from US 17 to the Isle of Palms Connector. The project required coordinated utility relocations from Berkeley Electric Cooperative, Mount Pleasant Waterworks, and SCE&G (now Dominion Energy South Carolina). Berkeley Electric could only relocate their underground lines during their fall low-demand period, Mount Pleasant Waterworks needed to complete water main relocations before summer peak demand, and SCE&G's gas line relocation required dry-season conditions. The conflicting seasonal requirements meant each utility had to work in separate windows with the road sitting idle between them. Tourist-season construction restrictions further limited available work days. The scheduling conflicts added $11 million in costs from extended traffic management and contractor standby time, with a 14-month delay pushing the project through two additional construction cycles.

projects.name: Lynchburg VA Downtown Streetscape Utility Scheduling
projects.description: Downtown streetscape improvement delayed by Appalachian Power and Liberty University utility extension schedules conflicting with the city's construction window.
projects.detail: Lynchburg's Downtown Streetscape project along Main Street required coordination with Appalachian Power for underground electric relocations and Liberty University, which was simultaneously extending its campus utilities beneath adjacent streets. Appalachian Power's underground work schedule was dictated by their regional capital planning cycle and could not be adjusted to match the city's preferred spring start date. Liberty University's utility extension project, independently permitted, occupied the same blocks and required the same lane closures during the same period the city needed access. The three-way scheduling conflict resulted in a construction plan where the city could only work on alternating blocks, leaving the corridor in a perpetual state of partial construction. The $4.3 million overrun included premium costs for the fragmented construction approach, and the 11-month delay reflected the time needed to work around two other concurrent but uncoordinated projects.

projects.name: Fort Myers Colonial Boulevard Drainage Improvement
projects.description: Drainage improvement project delayed when LCEC, Lee County Utilities, and FPL scheduling conflicts prevented coordinated utility relocation, each requiring hurricane-season work windows that others refused to accept.
projects.detail: Fort Myers' Colonial Boulevard Drainage Improvement project was designed to address severe flooding along a critical east-west corridor. Lee County Electric Cooperative, Lee County Utilities, and Florida Power & Light all required utility relocations. LCEC needed to relocate underground distribution but only had crew availability during hurricane season (June-November) due to winter peak demand commitments. Lee County Utilities refused to perform water main work during hurricane season due to contamination risk from flooding. FPL could not schedule their relocation until LCEC completed theirs to avoid energizing conflicts. The competing seasonal preferences created a year-long gap in the construction schedule. The $9.5 million overrun included costs from the extended timeline and temporary drainage measures installed to mitigate flooding during the delay. The 13-month delay was directly caused by the inability of three utilities to find a mutually acceptable construction season.

projects.name: Dothan AL Ross Clark Circle Interchange Utility Delay
projects.description: Interchange improvement delayed by competing construction schedules between Dothan Utilities, Southeast Alabama Gas District, and ALDOT's own bridge contractor.
projects.detail: Dothan's Ross Clark Circle Interchange improvement project was designed to add ramp lanes and reconstruct bridge decks at two interchange locations. The project required Dothan Utilities to relocate water and sewer lines, Southeast Alabama Gas District to relocate gas mains, and ALDOT's bridge contractor to perform substructure work. Dothan Utilities committed to a spring 2025 start but was pulled off the project when a water main emergency elsewhere in the system required their full crew. SEAGD then lost their construction window because Dothan Utilities' incomplete work blocked their access. ALDOT's bridge contractor could not begin substructure work until all utilities were clear, resulting in a full construction season lost. The $7.2 million cost increase reflected escalation costs and contractor remobilization charges, with the 12-month delay pushing the project from a planned 2027 completion to 2028.

projects.name: Nashville Dickerson Pike Transit Improvement Delay
projects.description: Transit corridor improvement delayed by scheduling conflicts between Nashville Electric Service, Metro Water, and Piedmont Natural Gas, compounded by NFL stadium construction traffic restrictions.
projects.detail: Nashville's Dickerson Pike Transit Improvement was designed to add dedicated bus lanes and improve pedestrian infrastructure along the north Nashville corridor. The project required Nashville Electric Service to underground overhead lines, Metro Water Services to replace a 60-year-old water main, and Piedmont Natural Gas to relocate gas infrastructure. Scheduling was further complicated by construction traffic restrictions related to the new NFL stadium project in the East Bank area, which limited heavy equipment access to Dickerson Pike during certain hours. NES could not begin undergrounding until their pole removal schedule was confirmed, which depended on telecom companies (AT&T, Comcast) removing their attachments first. Metro Water needed access during NES's scheduled work period, and Piedmont Natural Gas would not begin until ground disturbance from other utilities was complete. The multi-party scheduling failure added $18 million and 17 months to what had been planned as a 40-month project.

projects.name: Wilmington NC Oleander Drive Utility Coordination Delay
projects.description: Road widening delayed when CFPUA, Duke Energy Progress, and Piedmont Natural Gas scheduling conflicts forced sequential utility work that consumed the entire planned construction season.
projects.detail: Wilmington's Oleander Drive widening and modernization project required Cape Fear Public Utility Authority to relocate water and sewer, Duke Energy Progress to underground distribution lines, and Piedmont Natural Gas to relocate gas mains. CFPUA demanded first position in the construction sequence due to their need to maintain service during the tourist season, but their proposed schedule extended through the window Duke Energy had reserved for their work. Duke Energy refused to accept a winter construction window due to increased safety risks from shorter daylight hours, and Piedmont Natural Gas required a minimum 30-day buffer after Duke Energy's work for integrity testing before final road construction could begin. The scheduling impasse required NCDOT intervention and ultimately resulted in a compromise that added $5.6 million in premium scheduling costs and 10 months to the project, as each utility worked in truncated windows with expensive overtime.

projects.name: Durham NC Orange Street Fiber Gas Explosion
projects.description: Fiber optic installation contractor struck a PSNC Energy gas main on Orange Street, causing an explosion that damaged two buildings and triggered a citywide fiber installation moratorium.
projects.detail: During AT&T fiber optic installation along Orange Street in downtown Durham, a directional boring contractor struck a PSNC Energy (now Dominion Energy North Carolina) 4-inch gas main. The resulting gas leak ignited approximately 45 minutes later, causing an explosion that damaged the facades of two commercial buildings and blew out windows in a third. Three workers and two pedestrians were treated for minor injuries. The Durham City Council imposed an immediate moratorium on all fiber installation boring within the city limits pending a safety review. The moratorium lasted 6 months and affected multiple telecommunications providers. The $3.5 million in damages included building repairs, emergency response costs, and the fiber contractor's liability payments. PSNC Energy's records showed the gas main at a depth of 36 inches, but it was found at only 18 inches due to previous road reconstruction that removed surface material without updating utility depth records.

projects.name: Murfreesboro TN Medical Center Parkway Sewer Strike
projects.description: Road widening contractor struck a Consolidated Utility District 24-inch sewer force main during pile driving, causing a sanitary sewer overflow that required TDEC emergency response.
projects.detail: During Murfreesboro's Medical Center Parkway widening project, a pile-driving operation for a retaining wall foundation struck a Consolidated Utility District of Rutherford County 24-inch sewer force main. The impact cracked the force main, causing an estimated 200,000-gallon sanitary sewer overflow that reached a tributary of the West Fork Stones River. The Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation issued an emergency response order and required the utility district to implement bypass pumping while the force main was repaired. Investigation revealed that the force main's as-built drawings showed it 5 feet from the retaining wall alignment, but field verification found it only 2 feet away due to an installation deviation that was never recorded. The $2.2 million cost overrun included emergency environmental cleanup, force main repair, bypass pumping costs, and TDEC fines. The 4-month delay included time for environmental monitoring to confirm the SSO had not caused lasting water quality impacts.

projects.name: Summerville SC Berlin G. Myers Parkway Gas Strike
projects.description: Parkway extension contractor struck a Dominion Energy SC gas main during grading operations, triggering evacuation of a nearby elementary school.
projects.detail: During the Berlin G. Myers Parkway extension project in Summerville, a grading contractor struck a Dominion Energy South Carolina 8-inch gas main while performing cut operations for the new road profile. The leak occurred approximately 400 feet from Rollings Elementary School, triggering an immediate school evacuation of 650 students and staff. Dominion Energy's investigation found that the gas main was accurately located horizontally but was at a depth of 24 inches instead of the 42 inches shown on utility records. The discrepancy was attributed to a 2018 road grading project that had removed 18 inches of existing grade above the gas main without triggering a utility relocation. The $1.7 million cost increase included emergency response, gas main lowering along the entire project corridor, and the contractor's lost productivity. The 4-month delay reflected the construction shutdown, gas main depth verification, and lowering work that had to be completed before grading could resume.

projects.name: Port St. Lucie FL Crosstown Parkway Bridge Gas Strike
projects.description: Bridge approach construction contractor struck a Florida City Gas transmission line during pile driving, requiring emergency shutdown and evacuation of adjacent residential area.
projects.detail: During construction of the Crosstown Parkway bridge approach in Port St. Lucie, a pile-driving contractor struck a Florida City Gas 12-inch transmission line while installing support piles for a retaining wall. The impact damaged the pipe wall, causing a high-pressure gas leak that required emergency shutdown of the transmission line and evacuation of 45 homes in the adjacent Sabal Chase community. Florida City Gas emergency crews isolated the damaged section within 2 hours, but the transmission line shutdown affected gas service to 8,500 customers for 36 hours. The Florida Public Service Commission investigation found that the transmission line's precise location was known but the pile-driving plan had inadequate clearance from the pipe. The contractor's pile template placed one pile only 3 feet from the transmission line, well within the minimum safe distance. The $3.1 million cost increase included emergency repairs, customer relight costs, and revised pile design. The 5-month delay included the FPSC investigation period and redesigned foundation work.

projects.name: Cleveland Innerbelt Bridge Stage 3 Utility Redesign
projects.description: Stage 3 of the Innerbelt Bridge reconstruction required extensive plan revisions after unmapped gas transmission lines were discovered beneath the I-90 corridor approach.
projects.detail: The Ohio Department of Transportation had planned a phased reconstruction of the Innerbelt corridor connecting I-77 and I-90 in downtown Cleveland. During Stage 3, crews discovered a network of Dominion Energy gas transmission lines and abandoned industrial utility conduits not shown on any SUE records. The redesign required shifting bridge pier foundations and rerouting a 36-inch gas main, adding $18.5M to the project budget. Construction was delayed 14 months while engineers developed an alternative foundation plan that avoided the utility corridor.

projects.name: Bloomington Normal Uptown Renewal Underground Conflicts
projects.description: The Uptown Normal renewal project required plan revisions when underground utility surveys revealed conflicting gas, fiber, and water infrastructure beneath the transit hub area.
projects.detail: Bloomington-Normal's ambitious Uptown district renewal around the multimodal transit center encountered significant underground utility conflicts during design. Nicor Gas mains, Frontier fiber conduits, and Town of Normal water lines were found in configurations that directly conflicted with planned streetscape foundations and stormwater bioswales. The project team spent 8 months redesigning the underground utility corridor, relocating a 12-inch gas main and rerouting fiber optic lines. The changes added $3.1M to the originally budgeted cost.

projects.name: Dayton Main Street Corridor Utility Plan Overhaul
projects.description: Dayton's Main Street corridor improvement project required a full utility plan overhaul after finding conflicting DP&L conduits and Miami Conservancy District infrastructure.
projects.detail: The City of Dayton launched a Main Street corridor improvement spanning from the Great Miami River bridge to Brown Street. Early excavation revealed Dayton Power and Light underground electrical conduits running directly through planned median foundations, along with Miami Conservancy District flood control infrastructure that was poorly documented. The utility conflicts required a complete overhaul of the road cross-section design and relocation of high-voltage electrical conduits. The project exceeded its budget by $5.6M, and the 11-month delay disrupted downtown business operations during two consecutive holiday seasons.

projects.name: Dubuque Central Avenue Complete Streets Utility Redesign
projects.description: Dubuque's Central Avenue complete streets project required plan revisions after encountering unmapped combined sewer infrastructure dating to the 1880s.
projects.detail: The City of Dubuque initiated a complete streets transformation of Central Avenue in the historic millwork district. During the design phase, subsurface investigations uncovered a network of brick combined sewer lines from the 1880s that were not reflected in city GIS records. These legacy sewers ran at depths and alignments that conflicted with planned bicycle infrastructure foundations and ADA-compliant sidewalk grades. The redesign required rerouting stormwater management systems and adding new sewer separation infrastructure, increasing costs by $2.3M and extending the timeline by 6 months.

projects.name: Racine Uptown District Infrastructure Utility Conflicts
projects.description: Racine's Uptown district infrastructure project was redesigned after discovering conflicting We Energies gas mains and Racine Water Utility lines beneath Washington Avenue.
projects.detail: The City of Racine began an infrastructure renewal of the Uptown business district along Washington Avenue. Pre-construction utility surveys identified conflicts between We Energies gas distribution mains and Racine Water Utility trunk lines that were not apparent in existing records. The gas mains ran at shallower depths than documented, directly in the path of planned road reconstruction and stormwater improvements. The plan revision required relocating 2,400 feet of gas main and redesigning intersection geometry, adding $1.9M in costs and delaying the project 5 months.

projects.name: South Bend East Bank Village Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: South Bend's East Bank Village development infrastructure required plan revisions after discovering abandoned Studebaker-era industrial utility lines beneath the redevelopment site.
projects.detail: The City of South Bend's East Bank Village project, converting former industrial land along the St. Joseph River into mixed-use development, encountered extensive underground complications. Abandoned utility infrastructure from the Studebaker manufacturing era, including cast-iron steam lines, industrial water mains, and electrical conduits, was found throughout the site. These unmapped facilities conflicted with planned street grids, stormwater systems, and building foundations. The required remediation and utility plan revision added $3.8M and delayed infrastructure completion by 8 months.

projects.name: Springfield IL MacArthur Boulevard Utility Corridor Revision
projects.description: Springfield's MacArthur Boulevard widening project required extensive plan revisions after discovering conflicting CWLP utilities and Ameren gas infrastructure.
projects.detail: The City of Springfield initiated a widening and modernization of MacArthur Boulevard, a major commercial corridor. During the design phase, subsurface utility engineering revealed significant conflicts between City Water Light and Power electric and water infrastructure and Ameren Illinois gas distribution mains. Several utility crossings were at depths and locations that made the original road widening design infeasible. The project required a complete utility corridor revision with staggered relocations, adding $4.8M to the project cost. The 9-month delay pushed construction through two additional winter shutdown periods.

projects.name: Columbus Broad Street Bus Rapid Transit Utility Revision
projects.description: Columbus COTA's LinkUS Broad Street BRT project required major utility plan revisions after discovering conflicts with Columbia Gas transmission lines and city water infrastructure.
projects.detail: The Central Ohio Transit Authority's LinkUS program, featuring bus rapid transit along the West Broad Street corridor, encountered extensive utility conflicts during the 30% design phase. Columbia Gas of Ohio transmission mains and City of Columbus water distribution infrastructure were found in configurations that conflicted with planned dedicated bus lanes, station platforms, and signal priority systems. The required utility relocations and plan revisions added $12.3M to the federally-funded project and delayed the environmental review process by 12 months. The delay also impacted the project's competitiveness for FTA Capital Investment Grant funding.

projects.name: Duluth Superior Street Reconstruction Utility Discovery
projects.description: Duluth's Superior Street reconstruction discovered unmapped Minnesota Power utility vaults and abandoned streetcar infrastructure, requiring major plan revisions.
projects.detail: The City of Duluth began reconstructing Superior Street in the downtown commercial district. Early excavation revealed abandoned Duluth Street Railway Company rail beds, electrical vaults, and conduit banks from the former streetcar system, along with Minnesota Power underground electrical infrastructure not accurately reflected in city records. These discoveries conflicted with planned water main replacements and stormwater separation infrastructure. The project required a comprehensive plan revision to navigate around the unexpected underground conditions, adding $3.5M in costs and 8 months of delay.

projects.name: Fort Wayne Wells Street Corridor Utility Redesign
projects.description: Fort Wayne's Wells Street corridor project required plan revisions after finding conflicting NIPSCO gas infrastructure and abandoned utility conduits from the former GE campus.
projects.detail: The City of Fort Wayne launched a Wells Street corridor improvement project connecting downtown to the Riverfront development area. Subsurface utility engineering uncovered NIPSCO gas transmission mains at incorrect depths and alignments, along with extensive abandoned utility infrastructure from the former General Electric campus that extended beneath the public right-of-way. The discovery required a complete redesign of the utility corridor, including relocation of 3,200 feet of high-pressure gas main. The revisions added $4.1M to the project budget and delayed construction by 9 months.

projects.name: Iowa City Riverside Drive Reconstruction Underground Conflicts
projects.description: Iowa City's Riverside Drive reconstruction required plan revisions when University of Iowa utility tunnels and MidAmerican Energy infrastructure conflicted with road plans.
projects.detail: The City of Iowa City began reconstructing Riverside Drive, a major corridor connecting downtown to the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics area. Similar to other university-adjacent projects, underground investigations revealed University of Iowa steam tunnels, chilled water lines, and telecommunications conduits extending beneath the city right-of-way. Combined with MidAmerican Energy gas and electric infrastructure at undocumented locations, the conflicts required extensive plan revisions. The redesign added $2.9M in costs and 7 months of delay while city, university, and utility engineers developed a coordinated underground plan.

projects.name: Middletown OH Central Avenue Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Middletown's Central Avenue revitalization required plan revisions after discovering abandoned AK Steel utility infrastructure beneath the downtown corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Middletown initiated a Central Avenue revitalization project as part of downtown economic development efforts. During subsurface utility engineering, contractors discovered extensive abandoned utility infrastructure from the former AK Steel (now Cleveland-Cliffs) industrial operations, including decommissioned water mains, steam lines, and electrical conduits. These facilities were not documented in city records and directly conflicted with planned streetscape improvements and water main replacements. The redesign required $1.6M in additional funding and 6 months of delay for utility conflict resolution and abandoned pipe removal.

projects.name: Chicago CTA Blue Line Forest Park Branch Modernization
projects.description: CTA's Blue Line Forest Park branch modernization was delayed 2 years by scheduling conflicts with ComEd, Peoples Gas, and Chicago DOWI utility work.
projects.detail: The Chicago Transit Authority's modernization of the Blue Line Forest Park branch required extensive utility relocations along the Eisenhower Expressway corridor. The project encountered severe scheduling conflicts when ComEd's substation upgrade schedule conflicted with CTA's planned track shutdowns, and Peoples Gas insisted on completing its system modernization work in the same corridor before allowing CTA access. Chicago's Department of Water Infrastructure also required priority for water main replacements under its consent decree obligations. The three-way scheduling deadlock delayed the project by 2 years and added $45M in escalation costs.

projects.name: Milwaukee East-West BRT Utility Scheduling Gridlock
projects.description: Milwaukee County's East-West BRT project along Wisconsin Avenue was delayed 12 months by We Energies gas main replacement scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: Milwaukee County Transit System's East-West BRT project along Wisconsin Avenue from downtown to the regional medical center required extensive utility coordination. We Energies had its own gas main replacement program scheduled for the same corridor but on a different timeline. The utility company's replacement schedule could not be accelerated to match BRT construction phasing, and building BRT infrastructure over aging gas mains that would soon be replaced was deemed unacceptable. The scheduling impasse delayed the project 12 months while a coordinated construction sequence was developed, adding $11.2M in costs.

projects.name: Des Moines MLK Jr. Parkway Extension Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Des Moines' MLK Jr. Parkway extension was delayed 10 months by MidAmerican Energy and Des Moines Water Works scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The City of Des Moines initiated an extension of Martin Luther King Jr. Parkway to improve connectivity on the city's south side. The project required relocation of MidAmerican Energy gas distribution mains and coordination with Des Moines Water Works for a major trunk main crossing. MidAmerican Energy's gas main relocation crews were committed to emergency leak repair programs throughout the region, and Des Moines Water Works required a 9-month notification period for work near its Raccoon River wellfield infrastructure. The scheduling conflicts delayed the project 10 months and added $6.8M in costs.

projects.name: Indianapolis Red Line Phase 2 Utility Coordination Delay
projects.description: IndyGo's Red Line Phase 2 BRT extension was delayed 15 months by Citizens Energy Group and CenterPoint Energy utility scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: IndyGo's Red Line Phase 2 bus rapid transit extension along Meridian Street and College Avenue required extensive utility relocations. Citizens Energy Group's water main replacement program and CenterPoint Energy's gas system modernization work were both scheduled for the same corridor on timelines that conflicted with IndyGo's construction plan. Citizens Energy could not advance its water main work to precede BRT construction, and CenterPoint Energy refused to allow BRT infrastructure installation over gas mains scheduled for near-term replacement. The 15-month delay added $19.5M in escalation and remobilization costs.

projects.name: Rockford US 20 Bypass Interchange Utility Delay
projects.description: IDOT's US 20 bypass interchange reconstruction near Rockford was delayed 11 months by Nicor Gas and ComEd scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The Illinois Department of Transportation's reconstruction of interchanges along the US 20 bypass near Rockford required relocation of Nicor Gas transmission infrastructure and ComEd electrical distribution lines. Nicor Gas indicated its pipeline relocation crews were scheduled for work on the I-39 corridor and could not be redirected for at least 10 months. ComEd's underground electrical relocation also required coordination with a planned substation upgrade that was not yet funded. The combined scheduling conflicts delayed construction 11 months and added $8.3M in costs from contract modifications and inflation adjustments.

projects.name: Springfield MO Glenstone Avenue Widening Utility Delay
projects.description: MoDOT's Glenstone Avenue widening in Springfield was delayed 10 months by Spire Missouri and City Utilities of Springfield scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The Missouri Department of Transportation's widening of Glenstone Avenue, a major north-south commercial corridor in Springfield, required relocation of Spire Missouri gas distribution mains and coordination with City Utilities of Springfield for electric, gas, and water infrastructure. Spire's pipeline relocation crews were committed to system integrity work in the St. Louis metro area and could not be redirected to Springfield. City Utilities also had its own capital improvement schedule that did not align with MoDOT's construction phasing. The 10-month delay added $5.1M in costs from contract modifications and inflation.

projects.name: Decatur IL US 36 Corridor Improvement Utility Delay
projects.description: IDOT's US 36 corridor improvements in Decatur were delayed 7 months by Ameren Illinois and Decatur Sanitary District scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The Illinois Department of Transportation's improvements to the US 36 corridor through Decatur required relocation of Ameren Illinois gas and electric infrastructure and coordination with the Decatur Sanitary District for interceptor sewer protection. Ameren Illinois could not schedule its gas main relocation to precede IDOT's construction start, citing resource constraints from system modernization work in the Springfield and Champaign service areas. The Sanitary District also required a separate construction window for work near its interceptor, creating a scheduling deadlock. The 7-month delay added $3.2M in costs.

projects.name: Kokomo IN Markland Avenue Reconstruction Utility Delay
projects.description: Kokomo's Markland Avenue reconstruction was delayed 6 months by Duke Energy Indiana and Indiana American Water scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The City of Kokomo initiated a reconstruction of Markland Avenue, a key corridor connecting US 31 to the Stellantis transmission plant. The project required relocation of Duke Energy Indiana gas and electric infrastructure and coordination with Indiana American Water for water main replacement. Duke Energy's relocation schedule prioritized its own system reliability investments in the Indianapolis service area. Indiana American Water also had a limited construction window due to its capital improvement program commitments in other Indiana communities. The 6-month delay added $1.6M in costs.

projects.name: Mishawaka IN Main Street Reconstruction Utility Delay
projects.description: Mishawaka's Main Street reconstruction was delayed 7 months by NIPSCO gas relocation and Mishawaka Utilities water main replacement scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The City of Mishawaka initiated a reconstruction of Main Street through the downtown commercial district as part of an economic revitalization effort. The project required NIPSCO gas main relocation and Mishawaka Utilities water main replacement. NIPSCO's gas relocation schedule conflicted with Mishawaka Utilities' water main construction window, as both utilities needed to work in the same trench zone but could not agree on sequencing. NIPSCO prioritized system integrity work in the Gary and Hammond service areas over Mishawaka's project. The 7-month delay added $2.3M in costs and disrupted downtown business operations.

projects.name: Chicago Lincoln Park Fullerton Avenue Repaving Peoples Gas Dig-Up
projects.description: Peoples Gas cut open newly repaved Fullerton Avenue in Lincoln Park just 8 weeks after CDOT completed a $4M resurfacing project, wasting $1.8M in road investment.
projects.detail: The Chicago Department of Transportation completed a $4M resurfacing of Fullerton Avenue through the Lincoln Park neighborhood in late 2024. Just 8 weeks later, Peoples Gas crews began cutting trenches along the freshly paved corridor for its system modernization program, replacing cast iron gas mains. The utility's restoration patches left the road in worse condition than before the CDOT resurfacing. Despite Chicago's paving moratorium ordinance requiring a 5-year wait period, Peoples Gas claimed its work was exempt under emergency provisions related to leak-prone pipe replacement mandated by the Illinois Commerce Commission. The wasted road investment totaled approximately $1.8M.

projects.name: Madison WI Monroe Street Resurfacing MG&E Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Madison Gas & Electric cut into freshly resurfaced Monroe Street near the UW-Madison campus within 5 weeks for gas service replacements.
projects.detail: The City of Madison completed a $2.7M resurfacing of Monroe Street, a heavily trafficked corridor between the University of Wisconsin campus and the Dudgeon-Monroe neighborhood. Just 5 weeks later, Madison Gas & Electric (MG&E) began cutting the road for gas service line replacements to individual buildings along the corridor. Madison's street opening moratorium restricts utility cuts for 5 years after resurfacing. MG&E claimed the gas service replacements were triggered by leak surveys conducted after the resurfacing. The poor coordination wasted approximately $870K in newly placed pavement and disrupted the popular commercial district for 2 additional months.

projects.name: Appleton WI College Avenue Resurfacing WE Energies Moratorium Violation
projects.description: We Energies cut into freshly resurfaced College Avenue in downtown Appleton within 4 months for gas line replacement.
projects.detail: The City of Appleton completed a $2.4M resurfacing and streetscape improvement of College Avenue through the downtown commercial district. Within 4 months, We Energies began cutting the newly paved road for gas line replacements under its system modernization program. Appleton's paving moratorium restricts utility cuts for 5 years after resurfacing. We Energies claimed its pipeline replacement was mandated by the Wisconsin PSC to address aging infrastructure. The cuts damaged decorative pavement treatments and disrupted the downtown commercial district during the busy summer season, with approximately $640K in wasted investment.

projects.name: Waterloo IA Downtown Riverwalk Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Waterloo's downtown riverwalk infrastructure project required plan revisions when unmapped MidAmerican Energy conduits and abandoned Rath Packing plant utility lines were discovered.
projects.detail: The City of Waterloo began construction of a downtown riverwalk and streetscape project along the Cedar River. Subsurface investigations revealed MidAmerican Energy gas and electric conduits at undocumented locations, along with extensive abandoned utility infrastructure from the former Rath Packing Company industrial complex. These unmapped facilities directly conflicted with planned riverwalk foundations, stormwater outfalls, and pedestrian bridge abutments. The redesign required rerouting stormwater systems and reinforcing areas above abandoned industrial voids, adding $2.5M in costs and 7 months of delay.

projects.name: Zanesville OH Linden Avenue Sewer Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Zanesville's Linden Avenue sewer separation was delayed 6 months by Columbia Gas and AEP Ohio scheduling conflicts for utility relocations.
projects.detail: The City of Zanesville initiated a sewer separation project on Linden Avenue as part of its consent decree obligations. The project required Columbia Gas of Ohio to relocate gas mains and AEP Ohio to relocate underground electrical conduits before sewer construction could proceed. Columbia Gas could not schedule its relocation crews within Zanesville's construction window due to commitments on the Columbus pipeline replacement program. AEP Ohio also required a 9-month lead time for conduit relocation that exceeded the project schedule. The 6-month scheduling delay added $1.5M in costs and pushed the city closer to consent decree deadlines.

projects.name: Wichita Kellogg Avenue (US-54) Interchange Redesign
projects.description: Major interchange redesign triggered by unmapped gas transmission lines beneath planned flyover ramp foundations.
projects.detail: The Kellogg Avenue interchange reconstruction at Webb Road required complete plan revisions after geotechnical borings revealed a 16-inch high-pressure gas transmission line and associated cathodic protection infrastructure not shown on any utility maps. The discovery forced KDOT engineers to redesign three of four ramp alignments to maintain required clearances from the pipeline. The redesign added $18.4M to the $131M project budget and pushed the completion date from late 2025 to mid-2027. Businesses along the corridor reported significant revenue losses during the extended construction period.

projects.name: Topeka SW 21st Street Corridor Utility Redesign
projects.description: Storm sewer expansion plans conflicted with an abandoned petroleum pipeline and active fiber trunk line beneath SW 21st Street.
projects.detail: The City of Topeka's $19M SW 21st Street corridor improvement project required a complete storm drainage redesign after initial excavation revealed an abandoned petroleum pipeline running parallel to the planned sewer alignment. Additionally, a Level One fiber optic trunk serving western Topeka was found at a shallower depth than recorded. Engineers had to reroute 2,800 linear feet of storm sewer to avoid both conflicts. The redesign cost $4.2M in additional engineering and construction expenses and delayed the project by nearly a year, frustrating commuters on one of the city's busiest east-west corridors.

projects.name: Dodge City Wyatt Earp Boulevard Reconstruction Plan Revision
projects.description: Historic downtown road reconstruction plans had to be redrawn after discovering a network of abandoned utility vaults beneath the roadbed.
projects.detail: Dodge City's signature Wyatt Earp Boulevard reconstruction encountered unexpected underground complications when contractors discovered a series of abandoned steam utility vaults and clay tile conduits dating to the early 1900s. The vaults were not recorded in any city utility database and conflicted with planned water main and sanitary sewer alignments. The city had to commission a subsurface utility engineering study and redesign both the water and sewer systems around the historic infrastructure. The $2.8M cost increase pushed the $10M project well over budget, and the 8-month delay meant construction spanned an additional tourist season, impacting downtown businesses reliant on Boot Hill visitor traffic.

projects.name: Omaha 72nd Street Corridor Reconstruction Utility Redesign
projects.description: Major arterial reconstruction plans revised after MUD water transmission main and OPPD underground electric conflicted with planned median improvements.
projects.detail: Omaha's 72nd Street corridor reconstruction between Dodge and Pacific Streets required extensive plan revisions when the Metropolitan Utilities District's 30-inch water transmission main and OPPD's underground electrical distribution system were found to conflict with planned raised median installations and left-turn bay extensions. The original plans had relied on utility records that placed the water main 6 feet east of its actual location. Redesigning the median geometry, adjusting intersection layouts, and relocating 3,400 feet of electrical conduit added $12.7M to the $79.5M project. The 14-month delay forced the city to maintain temporary traffic configurations through two full winter seasons.

projects.name: Lincoln Cornhusker Highway (US-6) Widening Plan Revision
projects.description: Highway widening plans required revision after discovering conflicting gas and telecommunications infrastructure beneath the planned additional lanes.
projects.detail: NDOT's Cornhusker Highway widening project between N. 27th Street and I-80 required plan revisions after subsurface investigations revealed Black Hills Energy gas mains and a major Windstream fiber optic backbone occupying the planned right-of-way for the new outside lanes. The fiber optic line served as a critical regional telecommunications trunk, and its relocation required coordination with multiple downstream carriers. The gas main relocation required a temporary service bypass affecting 800 residential customers. Combined redesign and utility relocation costs added $8.5M to the $65M project budget, with 10 months of additional schedule impact.

projects.name: Bismarck Memorial Highway (US-83) Interchange Plan Revision
projects.description: Interstate interchange reconstruction plans revised after unmapped MDU gas transmission infrastructure was discovered beneath the planned ramp alignments.
projects.detail: NDDOT's $54.7M US-83/I-94 interchange reconstruction in Bismarck required major plan revisions after exploratory excavation uncovered a Montana-Dakota Utilities high-pressure gas transmission line running beneath the planned northbound on-ramp alignment. The 12-inch gas line was installed in the 1960s and was not accurately represented in available utility records. Redesigning the ramp geometry to maintain safe clearances from the pipeline required shifting the entire interchange footprint 35 feet east, affecting right-of-way acquisition, drainage patterns, and signal infrastructure. The $9.3M cost increase and year-long delay impacted regional freight traffic patterns during the extended construction phase.

projects.name: Grand Forks Gateway Drive (US-2) Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Commercial corridor plans revised after underground utility survey found intertwined water, gas, and telecom lines beneath planned turn lane extensions.
projects.detail: Grand Forks' $10M Gateway Drive commercial corridor improvement project required plan revisions when a Level B subsurface utility engineering study revealed that water mains, Xcel Energy gas lines, and CenturyLink fiber optic cables were intertwined in a utility corridor directly beneath the planned westbound turn lane extensions. The utilities had been installed over different decades without consistent depth or alignment documentation. The city had to redesign the turn lane geometry, relocate 600 feet of water main, and coordinate a complex fiber optic line protection scheme. The $2.4M cost overrun and 8-month delay prompted calls from the City Council for mandatory SUE investigations on all future road projects.

projects.name: Sioux Falls 26th Street Corridor Plan Revision
projects.description: Major east-west corridor reconstruction plans required revision after discovering conflicting Midco fiber trunk and MidAmerican Energy gas main infrastructure.
projects.detail: Sioux Falls' 26th Street corridor reconstruction between Western Avenue and Sycamore Avenue required extensive plan revisions after pre-construction investigations revealed that a Midco fiber optic trunk line and MidAmerican Energy gas distribution main occupied the same underground corridor where new stormwater piping was planned. The fiber trunk served as a primary backbone for internet service to southeast Sioux Falls, making relocation extremely complex and costly. Engineers had to redesign the stormwater system to use a parallel alignment, adding $5.8M in costs to the $32.2M project. The 10-month delay disrupted traffic on one of the city's most critical commercial corridors.

projects.name: Oklahoma City NW Expressway Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: NW Expressway widening plans required complete revision after encountering unmapped petroleum pipelines and ONG gas transmission lines.
projects.detail: ODOT's $150M NW Expressway widening project between I-44 and Council Road required major plan revisions when subsurface investigations uncovered two unmapped petroleum product pipelines and an Oklahoma Natural Gas transmission line running parallel to the expressway within the planned widening footprint. The petroleum lines were remnants of a mid-century pipeline corridor that predated the expressway's original construction. Federal pipeline safety regulations required minimum clearance distances that made the original widening geometry impossible. Engineers had to redesign the entire cross-section, shifting the median barrier and modifying drainage infrastructure. The $22.5M cost increase and 16-month delay significantly impacted commuter traffic in northwest Oklahoma City.

projects.name: Tulsa 71st Street Corridor Reconstruction Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor reconstruction plans revised after discovering PSO underground electric and abandoned gas infrastructure beneath planned bus pullouts.
projects.detail: The City of Tulsa's $40M 71st Street corridor reconstruction between Lewis Avenue and Yale Avenue required plan revisions after pre-construction potholing revealed Public Service Company of Oklahoma underground primary electric cables and abandoned gas infrastructure directly beneath planned bus pullout bays and ADA-compliant sidewalk extensions. The abandoned gas lines contained residual hydrocarbons requiring environmental assessment and remediation before construction could proceed in those areas. Redesigning the bus facilities, rerouting 1,800 feet of electric conduit, and conducting environmental cleanup added $7.2M to the project budget and 11 months to the schedule. The delay pushed construction into a second fiscal year, requiring additional budget authorization from the City Council.

projects.name: Norman Porter Avenue Sewer Replacement Plan Revision
projects.description: Sewer main replacement plans revised after university utility tunnels conflicted with the planned deep sewer alignment near OU campus.
projects.detail: The City of Norman's $8.1M Porter Avenue sewer main replacement between Boyd Street and Lindsey Street required plan revisions when subsurface investigations encountered University of Oklahoma utility tunnels carrying steam, chilled water, and electrical infrastructure at the same depth as the planned 36-inch sanitary sewer replacement. The university tunnels were not included in city utility databases. Engineers had to redesign the sewer alignment with a deeper profile and employ trenchless installation methods to pass beneath the tunnel system. The $1.7M cost increase covered additional engineering, trenchless construction equipment, and extended traffic control on the corridor adjacent to the OU campus.

projects.name: Fort Smith Garrison Avenue Sewer Utility Conflict Redesign
projects.description: Sewer separation project plans revised after discovering Arkansas Valley Electric cooperative duct banks in direct conflict with planned sewer mains.
projects.detail: Fort Smith's $8.1M Garrison Avenue sewer separation project required plan revisions when potholing revealed that Arkansas Valley Electric Cooperative duct banks and associated transformer vaults occupied the underground corridor designated for new separated storm sewer mains. The electric infrastructure served the downtown commercial district and could not be de-energized for relocation without extensive customer impacts. Engineers redesigned the storm sewer alignment to use a deeper parallel route, requiring more expensive excavation techniques and additional structural protection for the electric infrastructure above. The $2.1M overrun and 7-month delay strained the city's capital improvement budget for the fiscal year.

projects.name: Rogers AR Walnut Street Widening Plan Revision
projects.description: Street widening plans revised after Black Hills Energy gas main and AT&T fiber backbone conflicted with the planned turn lane and sidewalk expansions.
projects.detail: The City of Rogers' $15M Walnut Street widening project between I-49 and Dixieland Road required plan revisions when subsurface utility investigations found a Black Hills Energy 8-inch gas distribution main and an AT&T regional fiber optic backbone cable within the footprint of the planned center turn lane and multiuse path. Both utilities were installed with less cover than required by current standards, and the fiber line served as a critical link for Walmart's corporate campus communications. Redesigning the roadway cross-section to accommodate both utilities without relocation required narrower lanes and a modified path alignment. The $3.3M additional cost covered revised engineering, utility protection measures, and the redesigned path system.

projects.name: Hays KS Vine Street Reconstruction Plan Revision
projects.description: Downtown street reconstruction plans revised after encountering abandoned Midwest Energy gas lines and Fort Hays State University steam conduits.
projects.detail: The City of Hays' $4.9M Vine Street reconstruction between Main Street and Canterbury Drive required plan revisions after test excavations revealed abandoned Midwest Energy gas service lines and Fort Hays State University steam conduits crossing the street at unexpected locations. The university's steam distribution system extended further from campus than recorded, and the abandoned gas lines had not been properly retired from the city's utility atlas. The redesign required rerouting the planned water main replacement around the steam conduits and removing sections of abandoned gas infrastructure. The $890K cost increase was significant for the small western Kansas city's capital budget.

projects.name: Norfolk NE US-275 Bypass Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Bypass highway plans revised after discovering a buried NPPD transmission line and rural water district mains in the planned roadway alignment.
projects.detail: NDOT's $31.3M US-275 bypass improvements north of Norfolk required plan revisions when field investigations discovered a Nebraska Public Power District 69kV underground transmission line and Elkhorn Rural Water District mains running through the planned highway alignment. The NPPD line was a critical feed for a regional substation, and its relocation required complex coordination with the Southwest Power Pool transmission planning process. The rural water mains served agricultural operations that could not tolerate extended service interruptions. The $4.7M cost increase covered utility relocations, redesigned drainage structures, and extended right-of-way acquisition. The 9-month delay pushed the project into the following construction season.

projects.name: Rapid City North Lacrosse Street Reconstruction Plan Revision
projects.description: Street reconstruction plans revised after Black Hills Energy gas infrastructure and unmapped irrigation lines conflicted with new storm sewer alignment.
projects.detail: Rapid City's $10M North Lacrosse Street reconstruction between Omaha Street and Anamosa Street required plan revisions when subsurface utility investigations revealed that Black Hills Energy gas distribution mains and unmapped historic irrigation lines from the city's early agricultural period occupied the planned storm sewer corridor. The irrigation lines, some made of wood-stave pipe, were structurally compromised and posed collapse risks during excavation. Engineers redesigned the storm sewer alignment and developed a phased removal plan for the historic irrigation infrastructure. The $2.1M cost overrun included archaeological documentation required for the historic pipes and the redesigned stormwater system.

projects.name: Muskogee OK Okmulgee Avenue Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Road reconstruction plans revised after ONG gas distribution main conflicted with planned sewer replacement beneath Okmulgee Avenue.
projects.detail: The City of Muskogee's $6.8M Okmulgee Avenue reconstruction between York Street and Callahan Street required plan revisions after subsurface utility engineering found that an Oklahoma Natural Gas 6-inch distribution main ran directly through the planned sanitary sewer replacement alignment. The gas main was installed at a non-standard depth and was in the path of the new sewer for approximately 800 linear feet. Relocating the gas main required ONG to coordinate service interruptions for 340 residential customers, while the revised sewer alignment required deeper excavation and a pump station modification. The $1.3M overrun strained Muskogee's limited infrastructure improvement budget.

projects.name: Hot Springs AR Central Avenue Utility Redesign
projects.description: Historic district streetscape plans required complete utility redesign after discovering thermal spring conduits and unmapped utility infrastructure.
projects.detail: Hot Springs' $15M Central Avenue historic district streetscape project required extensive plan revisions when initial excavation uncovered thermal spring water conduits, abandoned hotel plumbing infrastructure, and unmapped natural gas lines dating to the early 1900s. The thermal spring conduits are considered part of the Hot Springs National Park protected system, requiring National Park Service consultation before any construction could proceed near them. Engineers had to redesign the entire underground utility layout to protect the thermal conduits while accommodating modern water, sewer, and electric infrastructure. The $3.9M cost increase and 10-month delay were compounded by the need for federal environmental review and NPS coordination.

projects.name: Pittsburg KS Broadway Street Reconstruction Plan Revision
projects.description: Downtown street reconstruction plans revised after discovering abandoned mining infrastructure and conflicting utility crossings beneath Broadway.
projects.detail: The City of Pittsburg's $6.1M Broadway Street reconstruction between 4th Street and 12th Street required plan revisions when pre-construction borings encountered abandoned coal mining subsidence voids and associated ground instability, along with utility crossings at unexpected depths. The mining voids, remnants of the region's lead and zinc mining era, were not recorded in city infrastructure databases. Engineers had to redesign the pavement structural section with deep soil stabilization and reroute planned water main alignments around areas of subsidence risk.
