The $1.4M cost overrun for the small southeast Kansas city represented a significant strain on the municipal capital budget.

projects.name: Enid OK Owen K. Garriott Road Widening Plan Revision
projects.description: Road widening plans required revision after unmapped petroleum gathering lines and conflicting ONG infrastructure were found in the expansion corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Enid's $15.3M Owen K. Garriott Road widening project between Van Buren Street and 30th Street required plan revisions after field investigations uncovered unmapped petroleum gathering lines, remnants of Enid's oil production heritage, running beneath the planned widening corridor. Additionally, Oklahoma Natural Gas distribution mains were found at shallower depths than recorded, conflicting with planned curb and gutter grades. The petroleum lines required environmental testing before removal, and ONG relocation required coordination with over 200 customer service connections. The $2.6M cost increase and 8-month delay pushed the project well past its originally announced completion date.

projects.name: Overland Park US-69 Widening Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Highway widening delayed 18 months by scheduling conflicts with Evergy substation upgrades and Johnson County Wastewater utility work.
projects.detail: KDOT's $123.3M US-69 widening project in Overland Park was delayed 18 months by scheduling conflicts between the highway construction timeline and Evergy's planned substation upgrades at the 119th Street interchange. The substation work, which required shutting down underground feeder lines beneath the highway, could not be completed concurrently with road construction due to emergency power routing requirements. Johnson County Wastewater Authority's parallel sewer rehabilitation project in the same corridor further complicated scheduling, as both agencies required exclusive access to the same right-of-way segments. The cascading delays added $14.8M in extended overhead, traffic maintenance, and inflation-driven material cost increases.

projects.name: Wichita Central Avenue Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Downtown road reconstruction delayed by scheduling conflicts with Kansas Gas Service main replacement and AT&T fiber installation programs.
projects.detail: Wichita's $17.9M Central Avenue reconstruction between Douglas Avenue and Kellogg was delayed 10 months by scheduling conflicts between the city's construction timeline and Kansas Gas Service's mandatory gas main replacement program. Kansas Gas Service had an NTSB-mandated schedule for replacing aging cast iron mains on Central Avenue that could not be adjusted to accommodate the city's preferred construction sequencing. Simultaneously, AT&T's fiber-to-the-premises buildout required conduit installation in the same corridor. The three-way scheduling conflict required extensive interagency negotiation and ultimately a complete re-sequencing of the project's construction phases. The added project management, extended traffic control, and material escalation costs totaled $3.4M.

projects.name: Olathe 119th Street Widening Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Street widening delayed by WaterOne pipeline relocation scheduling that conflicted with Johnson County stormwater work.
projects.detail: The City of Olathe's $30M 119th Street widening between Mur-Len Road and Renner Boulevard was delayed 12 months by scheduling conflicts between WaterOne's transmission pipeline relocation and Johnson County Stormwater Management's parallel detention basin construction. WaterOne's 24-inch transmission main could only be relocated during low-demand winter months when system redundancy was available, but the county's stormwater work also required winter construction to avoid spring flooding risks. Neither agency could yield their preferred schedule window without incurring significant additional costs or safety risks. The impasse required the road project to be re-sequenced into three phases instead of two, adding $5.1M in mobilization, traffic control, and extended overhead costs.

projects.name: Omaha L Street Corridor Improvement MUD Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Corridor improvement delayed 14 months by Metropolitan Utilities District water main replacement schedule conflicting with OPPD underground electrical work.
projects.detail: Omaha's $59.3M L Street corridor improvement between 72nd and 84th Streets was delayed 14 months by an irreconcilable scheduling conflict between Metropolitan Utilities District's emergency water main replacement and Omaha Public Power District's underground electrical infrastructure upgrade. MUD discovered critical corrosion in its 30-inch transmission main during the road project's pre-construction phase and required immediate replacement, but OPPD's underground substation feed upgrade in the same corridor was already under contract with a fixed construction window tied to summer peak demand preparation. The two utility agencies could not work concurrently due to safety clearance requirements, forcing the road project into a holding pattern. Extended overhead, re-mobilization, and material escalation added $8.3M to the project cost.

projects.name: Bellevue NE Cornhusker Road Reconstruction Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Road reconstruction delayed by Black Hills Energy gas main upgrade schedule conflicting with city water main replacement timing.
projects.detail: The City of Bellevue's $11M Cornhusker Road reconstruction between Fort Crook Road and Galvin Road was delayed 9 months by a scheduling conflict between Black Hills Energy's gas main upgrade program and the city's planned water main replacement. Black Hills Energy's regional gas main upgrade was tied to a winterization deadline that could not be moved, while the city's water main work required summer construction to avoid frozen ground complications. Both projects required exclusive access to the north side of the roadway corridor, and neither could be conducted in the opposite season without significant additional cost. The resulting sequential construction approach added $2.2M in extended project management and traffic control costs.

projects.name: Minot US-2/US-52 Bypass Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Highway bypass construction delayed by MDU gas pipeline relocation schedule conflicting with NDDOT's flood protection coordination timeline.
projects.detail: NDDOT's $53.1M US-2/US-52 bypass improvement in Minot was delayed 15 months by a scheduling conflict between Montana-Dakota Utilities' gas pipeline relocation and the Souris River Joint Water Resource Board's flood protection construction. The bypass improvement required MDU to relocate a high-pressure gas transmission line, but MDU's relocation schedule conflicted with the flood protection authority's construction window, which had federal funding deadlines tied to post-2011 flood recovery grants. Neither project could yield scheduling priority without jeopardizing funding or safety compliance. The highway project was forced to pause, adding $6.9M in standby costs, extended traffic maintenance, and inflation-driven cost increases across the extended timeline.

projects.name: Dickinson ND 21st Street West Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Street reconstruction delayed by MDU electric line burial schedule conflicting with Southwest Water Authority pipeline work.
projects.detail: Dickinson's $7.5M 21st Street West reconstruction was delayed 8 months by scheduling conflicts between Montana-Dakota Utilities' electric line burial program and the Southwest Water Authority's regional pipeline tie-in work. MDU's overhead-to-underground conversion required a multi-week power outage for the commercial corridor that could only occur during mild weather months, but the Southwest Water Authority's pipeline connection required the same corridor during the same window for pressure testing and disinfection. The construction sequencing conflict was compounded by the short North Dakota construction season, which left minimal flexibility for schedule adjustments. The delays added $1.8M in extended overhead and winter protection costs.

projects.name: Oklahoma City Belle Isle Bridge Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Bridge replacement delayed by ONG gas transmission line relocation scheduling conflicting with OG&E underground electric feeder upgrade.
projects.detail: Oklahoma City's $76M Belle Isle Bridge replacement over the North Canadian River was delayed 14 months by a scheduling conflict between Oklahoma Natural Gas's transmission line relocation and Oklahoma Gas & Electric's underground feeder upgrade for the Belle Isle commercial district. ONG's gas transmission line ran beneath the bridge approach and required relocation before demolition could begin, but ONG's construction crews were committed to a federally mandated pipeline integrity project through the same season. Simultaneously, OG&E's underground feeder work required coordination with the same bridge approach area. The sequential utility work before bridge construction could begin added $11.4M in extended overhead, temporary bridge maintenance, and inflation-escalated material costs.

projects.name: Tulsa Peoria Avenue Reconstruction PSO Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Corridor reconstruction delayed by Public Service Company of Oklahoma underground cable replacement schedule conflicting with Tulsa Authority water main work.
projects.detail: Tulsa's $27.2M Peoria Avenue reconstruction between 21st Street and 41st Street was delayed 11 months by scheduling conflicts between Public Service Company of Oklahoma's underground primary cable replacement and Tulsa Metropolitan Utility Authority's water main replacement. PSO's cable replacement was driven by reliability compliance requirements from the Southwest Power Pool with a fixed completion deadline. The water main replacement required excavation in the same trench corridor, but PSO's energized cable work required exclusive access with safety buffer zones. Negotiating a workable phasing plan took 5 months alone, and the resulting sequential construction added $4.9M in extended traffic control, re-mobilization, and project management costs.

projects.name: Lawton OK Cache Road Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Commercial corridor reconstruction delayed by ONG gas main scheduling conflict with Fort Sill utility coordination requirements.
projects.detail: The City of Lawton's $11M Cache Road reconstruction between Sheridan Road and 38th Street was delayed 9 months by scheduling conflicts between Oklahoma Natural Gas's gas main replacement and required coordination with Fort Sill military installation utility staff. Cache Road serves as a primary corridor between the city and the military installation, and Fort Sill's utility infrastructure crosses the road at multiple points with military-controlled shutoff requirements. ONG's gas main replacement required approval from Fort Sill's Director of Public Works, and the military approval process ran on a timeline incompatible with the city's construction schedule. The delays added $2.3M in extended overhead and traffic management costs for the congested commercial corridor.

projects.name: Fayetteville AR North College Avenue Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Corridor improvement delayed by Ozarks Electric cooperative underground conversion schedule conflicting with Arkansas Western Gas main replacement.
projects.detail: Fayetteville's $25.6M North College Avenue corridor improvement between Township Street and the I-49 interchange was delayed 10 months by scheduling conflicts between Ozarks Electric Cooperative's underground conversion program and Arkansas Western Gas's mandatory main replacement. Ozarks Electric had secured federal rural broadband funding tied to a fixed construction timeline that included burying overhead lines in the corridor, but the underground conversion required excavation in the same corridor where Arkansas Western Gas was replacing aging steel gas mains under a state Public Service Commission order. Neither utility could adjust its schedule without losing funding or regulatory compliance. The road project was held until both utilities completed sequential work, adding $4.1M in costs.

projects.name: Salina KS Crawford Street Water Main Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Water main replacement delayed by Kansas Gas Service main replacement schedule conflicting with city stormwater improvement work.
projects.detail: Salina's $6M Crawford Street water main replacement between Iron Avenue and Pacific Avenue was delayed 6 months by scheduling conflicts between Kansas Gas Service's gas main replacement program and the city's parallel stormwater improvement project. Kansas Gas Service's cast iron replacement program was scheduled for the same construction season as the city's water main work, but the gas utility's contract required completing its work before the city could begin water main excavation due to temporary gas service routing through the same trench area. The stormwater project added further complexity by requiring dewatering operations that could not occur simultaneously with gas main installation. The delays added $1.2M in extended traffic control and project management costs.

projects.name: Kearney NE 2nd Avenue Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Downtown reconstruction delayed by NorthWestern Energy gas schedule conflicting with Charter Communications fiber installation.
projects.detail: Kearney's $6.9M 2nd Avenue reconstruction between Railroad Street and 25th Street was delayed 7 months by scheduling conflicts between NorthWestern Energy's gas main replacement and Charter Communications' fiber-to-the-premises installation program. NorthWestern Energy's gas work was mandated by a Nebraska Public Service Commission compliance order with a fixed deadline, while Charter had secured municipal franchise agreement timelines for its fiber buildout. Both projects required trench work along 2nd Avenue, and simultaneous excavation was prohibited by city right-of-way ordinances. The resulting sequential utility work pushed the road reconstruction start date back 7 months, adding $1.6M in extended traffic control and project management costs.

projects.name: Aberdeen SD 6th Avenue SE Reconstruction Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Street reconstruction delayed by NorthWestern Energy gas service replacement scheduling conflicting with city water main replacement.
projects.detail: Aberdeen's $4.9M 6th Avenue SE reconstruction between Melgaard Road and 15th Street SE was delayed 5 months by scheduling conflicts between NorthWestern Energy's gas service replacement program and the city's water main replacement. NorthWestern Energy's gas service line replacements required individual customer coordination with specific appointment windows that conflicted with the city's planned water main shutdown periods. The limited South Dakota construction season compounded the problem, as both projects needed to be completed before freeze-up in October. The scheduling impasse pushed final completion to the following construction season, adding $940K in winter protection costs and extended project management overhead.

projects.name: Bartlesville OK Adams Boulevard Utility Coordination Delay
projects.description: Boulevard reconstruction delayed by scheduling conflict between Phillips 66 pipeline crossing work and ONG gas distribution replacement.
projects.detail: Bartlesville's $6.1M Adams Boulevard reconstruction was delayed 6 months by a scheduling conflict between Phillips 66's pipeline crossing protection work and Oklahoma Natural Gas's distribution main replacement. Phillips 66's pipeline crossed beneath Adams Boulevard at two locations, and the company's pipeline integrity team required specific seasonal windows for excavation near its facilities due to product demand cycles. ONG's gas main replacement was already under contract with a different seasonal requirement. The unique complication of coordinating with a major petroleum company headquarters city's pipeline infrastructure added layers of corporate approval processes. The delays added $1.1M in extended overhead and traffic management costs.

projects.name: Garden City KS US-50 Business Route Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Business route reconstruction delayed by Black Hills Energy gas main schedule conflicting with Southwest Kansas Groundwater Management District irrigation line work.
projects.detail: KDOT's $9M US-50 Business Route reconstruction through Garden City was delayed 7 months by scheduling conflicts between Black Hills Energy's gas distribution main replacement and the Southwest Kansas Groundwater Management District No. 3's irrigation pipeline maintenance in the highway right-of-way. The irrigation infrastructure, which predated the highway, crossed beneath the road at three locations and required seasonal access tied to the agricultural irrigation cycle. Black Hills Energy's gas work was driven by a Kansas Corporation Commission compliance timeline. Neither entity could adjust its schedule without violating regulatory requirements or disrupting the critical agricultural irrigation season. The delays added $1.8M in costs.

projects.name: Hastings NE Burlington Avenue Reconstruction Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Downtown reconstruction delayed by NorthWestern Energy gas main scheduling conflicting with BNSF Railway underpass utility coordination.
projects.detail: Hastings' $5.9M Burlington Avenue reconstruction near the BNSF Railway underpass was delayed 6 months by scheduling conflicts between NorthWestern Energy's gas distribution main replacement and BNSF Railway's required utility coordination windows for work near the rail underpass. BNSF required 90-day advance notice for any utility work within its right-of-way, and the railroad's approved work windows did not align with NorthWestern Energy's gas main construction schedule. The city found itself caught between two entities with inflexible schedules and no mechanism for joint coordination. The delays added $1.3M in extended traffic detour maintenance, flagging costs for railroad proximity work, and project management overhead.

projects.name: Emporia KS Commercial Street Reconstruction Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Street reconstruction delayed by Kansas Gas Service emergency main replacement interfering with planned Evergy underground electric upgrade.
projects.detail: Emporia's $5M Commercial Street reconstruction was delayed 5 months when Kansas Gas Service declared an emergency gas main replacement in the same corridor where the city had planned construction to begin. The gas utility discovered corrosion in a 6-inch cast iron main during a routine inspection and initiated emergency replacement, preempting the planned road construction. Evergy's underground electric upgrade, already scheduled to coordinate with the road work, had to be pushed back until the gas main was completed. The cascading schedule disruption added $950K in extended traffic control, contractor standby time, and re-mobilization costs for the small Flint Hills city.

projects.name: Hutchinson KS 4th Avenue Gas Line Strike
projects.description: Sewer replacement project struck a Kansas Gas Service distribution main, triggering evacuation of three downtown blocks and a 5-month delay.
projects.detail: A contractor excavating for the City of Hutchinson's $7.5M 4th Avenue sewer replacement project struck a 6-inch Kansas Gas Service distribution main at an intersection where the line was 3 feet shallower than recorded on utility locate markings. The strike triggered a gas leak that forced evacuation of three downtown blocks including a senior living facility. Kansas Gas Service's emergency repair took 4 days, during which the sewer project was shut down pending investigation. The Kansas Corporation Commission investigation found that the one-call locate had been performed with outdated maps. The incident added $1.8M in emergency repair costs, environmental remediation, and extended project timeline overhead across a 5-month delay.

projects.name: Little Rock Cantrell Road Water Main Strike During Widening
projects.description: Road widening struck a 20-inch Central Arkansas Water transmission main, causing widespread service outages and $3.4M in additional costs.
projects.detail: During ARDOT's $24.3M Cantrell Road widening project in west Little Rock, a grading operation struck a 20-inch Central Arkansas Water transmission main that was 5 feet shallower than indicated on utility records. The break caused a massive water release that flooded the construction zone and adjacent residential properties, and disrupted water service to approximately 8,000 customers in west Little Rock for 12 hours. Central Arkansas Water's emergency repair required a 48-hour road closure, and subsequent investigation revealed that the transmission main had been installed with less cover than specified during original construction due to rock conditions. The incident added $3.4M in emergency repairs, property damage claims, revised construction procedures, and extended project overhead across a 6-month delay.

projects.name: Lawrence KS Iowa Street Resurfacing AT&T Fiber Moratorium Violation
projects.description: AT&T cut into newly resurfaced Iowa Street for fiber installation 4 months after the city completed a $2.8M overlay, violating the 5-year moratorium.
projects.detail: The City of Lawrence completed a $2.8M overlay of Iowa Street between 23rd Street and Bob Billings Parkway in summer 2025, only to have AT&T begin cutting into the new pavement in November 2025 for fiber-to-the-premises installation. The city's 5-year paving moratorium ordinance explicitly prohibited non-emergency utility cuts on newly resurfaced streets, and AT&T had been notified of the planned resurfacing a year in advance. AT&T's contractor made 14 separate trench cuts across the newly paved surface before the city issued a stop-work order. The pavement restoration required by the city's moratorium ordinance cost AT&T $320K, but the city argued that even the best patches would reduce the pavement's expected lifespan by 30%. The incident prompted the city to strengthen its moratorium enforcement provisions.
projects.timeline: Resurfaced July 2025; AT&T cuts November 2025; restoration February 2026

projects.name: SH 249 Extension (Grimes County)
projects.description: The Aggie Expressway extension north of Pinehurst hit plan revision delays when unmapped rural water cooperative pipelines and Entergy underground feeds were discovered throughout the corridor.
projects.detail: TxDOT's SH 249 toll road extension through Grimes County was intended to improve access between the Houston metro and Texas A&M. Preliminary designs assumed minimal underground utility presence in the rural corridor. However, the Grimes County Water Supply Corporation had installed extensive unmapped distribution lines, and Entergy Texas had underground electrical feeds serving oil field equipment. Plan revisions were required for over 4 miles of the 12-mile segment, adding $12M in utility relocation costs and delaying construction by 18 months.

projects.name: FM 1431 Widening (Cedar Park to Lago Vista)
projects.description: TxDOT's plan to widen FM 1431 west of Cedar Park required a design overhaul when Pedernales Electric Cooperative underground lines and WCID water mains were found throughout the corridor.
projects.detail: The FM 1431 widening from US 183 to Lago Vista was designed as a four-lane divided highway through the Hill Country west of Austin. At the 30% design stage, subsurface investigations revealed Pedernales Electric Cooperative had buried primary distribution lines along the south side of the corridor, directly conflicting with the widening footprint. Additionally, multiple water control and improvement district mains crossed the alignment at uncharted locations. Plan revisions required relocating over 3 miles of electrical conduit and rerouting water distribution, adding $9M and 11 months to the schedule.

projects.name: SH 71 Corridor Improvement (Bastrop County)
projects.description: Widening SH 71 east of Austin required plan revisions when Bluebonnet Electric Cooperative infrastructure and Aqua Water Supply Corporation mains were discovered in conflict with the new road geometry.
projects.detail: TxDOT planned to widen SH 71 from two lanes to a four-lane divided highway between Bastrop and Smithville to address growing commuter traffic from the Austin metro. The design assumed a clear right-of-way based on outdated as-built records. Field investigations found Bluebonnet Electric Cooperative underground primary lines running along the north shoulder for nearly 2 miles, plus Aqua Water Supply Corporation distribution mains crossing the highway at six unrecorded locations. The utility conflicts required redesigning drainage structures and shifting the centerline alignment, adding $7M in costs and a 10-month delay.

projects.name: US 77 Reconstruction (Victoria to Refugio)
projects.description: TxDOT's US 77 reconstruction south of Victoria required plan changes when multiple petroleum pipeline crossings and unmapped AEP Texas underground distribution were discovered.
projects.detail: The US 77 reconstruction project between Victoria and Refugio was planned as a pavement rehabilitation with intersection improvements. During utility coordination, TxDOT discovered three unmarked petroleum pipeline crossings operated by Enterprise Products Partners and Plains All American. Additionally, AEP Texas had underground distribution lines serving rural pump stations that were not reflected in any utility records. The plan revisions required special pipeline crossing protection structures and rerouting electrical service, adding $6M and delaying the project by 8 months while pipeline integrity assessments were completed.

projects.name: SH 114 Flyover Reconstruction (Southlake/Grapevine)
projects.description: TxDOT's SH 114 flyover interchange redesign near DFW Airport required plan revisions when abandoned petroleum pipelines and Oncor underground transmission lines were discovered beneath proposed column locations.
projects.detail: The SH 114 interchange reconstruction between SH 26 and International Parkway aimed to add direct-connect flyovers to reduce weaving conflicts near DFW Airport. Subsurface utility engineering during the design phase uncovered two abandoned petroleum pipelines from a decommissioned refinery operation, plus an Oncor 138kV underground transmission line that was not in the utility company's GIS database. The abandoned pipelines required environmental assessment and removal, while the Oncor line needed relocation to a new duct bank. These discoveries forced a redesign of four column locations and added $28M to the $215M project with a 16-month delay.

projects.name: US 83 Reconstruction (McAllen to Mission)
projects.description: TxDOT's US 83 expressway reconstruction in the Rio Grande Valley required plan revisions when AEP Texas underground distribution and unmapped irrigation district infrastructure conflicted with the expansion.
projects.detail: The US 83 reconstruction between McAllen and Mission was designed to convert the highway to a limited-access expressway with frontage roads. The project encountered significant plan revision needs when AEP Texas underground primary distribution lines were found throughout the corridor serving dense commercial development. Additionally, the Hidalgo County Irrigation District had concrete-lined canals and underground pipelines crossing the highway at nine locations not shown on any available records. The utility relocations and irrigation structure modifications added $8M and pushed the schedule back 12 months.

projects.name: FM 2818 Reconstruction (College Station)
projects.description: The FM 2818 reconstruction in College Station required plan revisions when City of College Station and Wellborn SUD water mains were found throughout the widening footprint.
projects.detail: TxDOT's FM 2818 reconstruction aimed to widen the heavily traveled corridor from Harvey Mitchell Parkway to SH 40. The College Station area's rapid growth had led to numerous water and sewer installations by both the City of College Station and Wellborn Special Utility District, many of which were poorly documented. Plan revisions were triggered when 14 previously unknown utility crossings were identified during subsurface investigation, including two 16-inch water transmission mains. The redesign required adjusting pavement grades and adding utility tunnels, increasing costs by $6.5M and extending the timeline by 10 months.

projects.name: SH 358 (SPID) Ramp Reconstruction (Corpus Christi)
projects.description: Reconstruction of the SPID interchange ramps at Staples Street required plan revisions when AEP Texas underground transmission and City of Corpus Christi water mains conflicted with new ramp foundations.
projects.detail: The SH 358 (South Padre Island Drive) ramp reconstruction at Staples Street was intended to replace aging interchange ramps and improve traffic flow. During design development, AEP Texas identified a 69kV underground transmission line feeding the Flour Bluff substation that ran directly beneath two planned ramp columns. The City of Corpus Christi also discovered a 24-inch water transmission main that crossed the interchange at a different angle than shown on record drawings. Plan revisions to reroute both utilities and redesign the ramp foundations added $10M and an 11-month delay to the $77M project.

projects.name: East Riverside Drive Reconstruction (Austin)
projects.description: Austin's East Riverside Drive corridor reconstruction required a major plan overhaul when Austin Energy underground distribution, Austin Water trunk mains, and multiple telecom duct banks were found throughout the corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Austin planned a complete reconstruction of East Riverside Drive from I-35 to Pleasant Valley Road, transforming it into a multimodal corridor with protected bike lanes and enhanced transit facilities. The corridor's decades of incremental development had left a tangle of underground infrastructure from Austin Energy, Austin Water, AT&T, Google Fiber, and Grande Communications. Subsurface investigations revealed 23 major utility conflicts with the proposed design. The plan revision required a phased utility relocation strategy, redesigned stormwater management, and a shifted road centerline, adding $14M and 15 months to the schedule.

projects.name: Montana Avenue Widening (El Paso)
projects.description: El Paso's Montana Avenue widening from Lee Trevino to Joe Battle required plan revisions when El Paso Water and El Paso Electric underground infrastructure conflicts were far more extensive than anticipated.
projects.detail: The Montana Avenue widening project in far east El Paso aimed to expand the corridor from four to six lanes through a rapidly developing area. Design plans were based on utility records that proved significantly inaccurate. El Paso Water had installed water distribution mains on both sides of the corridor that were 3-6 feet off from their recorded positions, and El Paso Electric had underground primary distribution lines serving new subdivisions that were not yet in the utility records system. The plan revisions required a complete re-survey, utility relocation design, and roadway cross-section modifications that added $7.5M and 14 months.

projects.name: SH 351 Corridor Improvement (Abilene)
projects.description: TxDOT's SH 351 improvement through Abilene required plan revisions when Abilene utilities had unmapped water and gas infrastructure beneath the planned intersection improvements.
projects.detail: The SH 351 corridor improvement through central Abilene included intersection reconstructions at four major cross streets and a median installation. The City of Abilene's water distribution system included several mains installed in the 1950s that were not accurately reflected in the city's GIS. Atmos Energy also had gas service lines running in non-standard locations. When potholing revealed the full extent of conflicts, TxDOT halted design and initiated plan revisions for all four intersections, adding $4M in utility relocation and redesign costs and 7 months of delay.

projects.name: US 75 Frontage Road Reconstruction (Sherman)
projects.description: The US 75 frontage road reconstruction in Sherman required plan revisions when the Texas Instruments mega-fab water infrastructure and Grayson County utility crossings were found throughout the corridor.
projects.detail: TxDOT's frontage road reconstruction along US 75 through Sherman coincided with the massive infrastructure build-out supporting the Texas Instruments semiconductor fabrication campus. The utility landscape had changed dramatically since the original design, with new high-capacity water and sewer lines installed by the City of Sherman to serve the TI campus. These newly installed mains conflicted with the planned frontage road drainage improvements. Grayson County also had fiber conduit crossings that were installed under emergency permits without proper as-built documentation. Plan revisions to accommodate the changed utility environment added $5.5M and 9 months.

projects.name: Loop 20 Reconstruction (Laredo South)
projects.description: TxDOT's Loop 20 reconstruction in south Laredo required plan revisions when City of Laredo water transmission mains and AEP Texas underground distribution were found in extensive conflict with the expansion design.
projects.detail: The Loop 20 reconstruction project south of IH-35 in Laredo was planned to upgrade the aging roadway and add capacity for the growing international trade corridor. Design teams based their plans on utility records from the City of Laredo and AEP Texas. Field verification revealed that the City's 20-inch water transmission main was 8 feet west of its recorded position, running directly beneath the planned new lanes. AEP Texas underground distribution serving the industrial corridor was also mislocated in their records. Complete plan revisions for the 3-mile segment added $9M and pushed the construction start back 11 months.

projects.name: SH 6 Widening (Bryan/College Station North)
projects.description: The SH 6 widening north of Bryan hit plan revision delays when BTU electric infrastructure and City of Bryan water mains conflicted with the interchange reconstruction design.
projects.detail: TxDOT planned to widen SH 6 from four to six lanes with interchange improvements at multiple cross streets north of Bryan. Bryan Texas Utilities (BTU) had underground high-voltage distribution lines running along the SH 6 corridor that were installed during a 2018 reliability improvement program but never shared with TxDOT. The City of Bryan also had water transmission mains crossing the highway at three locations that were 5-10 feet from recorded positions. The combination of electrical and water conflicts required plan revisions for the interchange foundations and frontage road sections, adding $8.5M and 10 months to the $71M project.

projects.name: SH 360 Interchange Reconstruction (Arlington/Mansfield)
projects.description: TxDOT's SH 360 interchange reconstruction at Sublett Road required a major plan revision when a previously unknown TRA sewer interceptor and multiple petroleum pipelines were discovered at the interchange site.
projects.detail: The SH 360 interchange reconstruction at Sublett Road was designed to replace an at-grade intersection with a grade-separated interchange. During geotechnical borings, the construction team encountered a Trinity River Authority 42-inch reinforced concrete sewer interceptor that was 15 feet shallower than TRA's records indicated. Additionally, two petroleum product pipelines operated by Magellan Midstream were found crossing the site at different angles than recorded. The discoveries required redesigning the interchange embankments, adding a utility bridge for the pipelines, and coordinating with TRA on interceptor protection, adding $18M to the $180M project.

projects.name: US 190 Widening (Copperas Cove to Killeen)
projects.description: TxDOT's US 190 widening between Copperas Cove and Killeen required plan revisions when US Army Fort Cavazos utility crossings and Bell County WCID mains were discovered in the corridor.
projects.detail: The US 190 widening project aimed to expand the highway from four to six lanes between Copperas Cove and Killeen, serving the growing military community near Fort Cavazos (formerly Fort Hood). The Department of Defense had installed underground utility crossings serving base facilities that were classified and not shared during initial coordination. Bell County Water Control and Improvement District also had distribution mains in non-standard locations. Once the military utility information was obtained through proper channels, plan revisions for three interchange locations were required, adding $5M and 9 months to the schedule.

projects.name: SH 45 Southwest Extension (Travis/Hays County)
projects.description: The controversial SH 45 Southwest extension required plan revisions when Hays County and LCRA underground infrastructure, plus environmental mitigation features conflicting with utility relocations, created cascading design changes.
projects.detail: The SH 45 Southwest extension from MoPac to FM 1626 encountered significant plan revision requirements when the Lower Colorado River Authority identified a major raw water pipeline crossing the alignment near Onion Creek. Hays County also had water distribution infrastructure serving new subdivisions that had been installed after the initial design survey. Complicating matters, utility relocation routes conflicted with environmental mitigation areas required by the project's environmental clearance. Redesigning the utility corridors to avoid both infrastructure conflicts and environmental constraints added $16M and 18 months to the $80M project.

projects.name: I-35W Managed Lanes (North Tarrant County)
projects.description: TxDOT's I-35W managed lanes project north of Fort Worth was delayed 20 months by scheduling conflicts with Atmos Energy, Oncor, and the City of Fort Worth, each requiring sequential rather than concurrent utility relocations.
projects.detail: The I-35W managed lanes project from I-30 north to SH 114 required relocating utilities from Atmos Energy, Oncor Electric, the City of Fort Worth water department, and three telecom providers. Each utility company insisted on performing their own relocations using their preferred contractors, but their schedules were mutually incompatible. Atmos Energy required the road to remain open during their gas main relocation, which blocked Oncor from accessing their underground transmission lines. The City of Fort Worth's water main relocation crew could not work concurrently with Atmos due to safety zone requirements. The cascading scheduling conflicts stretched a planned 12-month utility phase into 32 months, adding $42M in delay costs and extended traffic management expenses.

projects.name: US 380 Collin County Bypass
projects.description: The US 380 bypass around McKinney and Prosper experienced 22 months of delays when CoServ Electric, Atmos Energy, and multiple water districts could not coordinate overlapping utility relocation schedules.
projects.detail: TxDOT's US 380 Collin County bypass was designed to route traffic around the rapidly growing McKinney and Prosper areas. The new alignment crossed territory served by CoServ Electric, Atmos Energy, Boliver Water Supply Corporation, and North Collin Water Supply Corporation. Each entity had different fiscal year budgets, seasonal construction windows, and contractor availability constraints. CoServ Electric could only schedule their transmission line relocation during their spring outage window, which conflicted with Atmos Energy's summer construction season. The water districts had limited bonding capacity and could only relocate one major main per year. The scheduling conflicts extended the utility relocation phase by 22 months and added $55M in costs including extended right-of-way maintenance and inflation escalation.

projects.name: North Houston Highway Improvement (I-45 Segment 1)
projects.description: Segment 1 of the I-45 NHHIP project north of downtown Houston faced 24 months of scheduling delays as CenterPoint Energy, the City of Houston, and multiple telecom providers could not align their relocation timelines.
projects.detail: The North Houston Highway Improvement Project's Segment 1 from I-10 north to Beltway 8 required relocating an enormous amount of underground infrastructure. CenterPoint Energy had high-pressure gas transmission lines and underground electric distribution throughout the corridor. The City of Houston Public Works had aging water and sewer mains requiring not just relocation but upgrade. AT&T, Comcast, and multiple fiber providers had extensive duct bank networks. CenterPoint Energy's gas division could not begin work until their electric division completed conduit relocation, and the City of Houston's sewer work had to be sequenced after water main relocation. The telecom companies refused to coordinate schedules with each other due to competitive concerns. The scheduling conflicts added $180M in delay-related costs to the multi-billion dollar project.

projects.name: Loop 336 Widening (Conroe)
projects.description: TxDOT's Loop 336 widening in Conroe was delayed 14 months by scheduling conflicts between Entergy Texas, the San Jacinto River Authority, and the City of Conroe water department.
projects.detail: The Loop 336 widening from I-45 west to SH 105 required utility relocations from Entergy Texas, San Jacinto River Authority, the City of Conroe, and CenterPoint Energy. Entergy Texas had a scheduled maintenance outage window that could not be moved, blocking a 3-month period during which no underground work could occur in their easement. The San Jacinto River Authority could only relocate their 24-inch transmission main during the winter low-demand season. The City of Conroe's water department had committed their utility relocation crew to another project through the spring. The stacking of these scheduling constraints meant that utility relocation that could have been completed in 8 months took 22 months, adding $8M in costs.

projects.name: SH 288 Interchange at CR 56 (Brazoria County)
projects.description: The SH 288 interchange construction at CR 56 was delayed 10 months when CenterPoint Energy and Brazoria County Fresh Water Supply District could not agree on a concurrent relocation schedule.
projects.detail: TxDOT's new interchange at SH 288 and CR 56 required relocating a CenterPoint Energy gas transmission main and Brazoria County FWSD No. 1 water distribution mains. CenterPoint insisted on completing their gas main relocation before any other underground work began, citing safety protocols. The FWSD argued they needed to relocate their water mains first to maintain service during the gas work. Neither party would agree to a concurrent work plan despite TxDOT mediation efforts. The impasse lasted 6 months before a sequential schedule was imposed, with the remaining 4 months consumed by the sequential execution. The delay added $6M in costs to the $50M interchange project.

projects.name: US 83/84 Reconstruction (Abilene South)
projects.description: TxDOT's US 83/84 reconstruction south of Abilene was delayed by scheduling conflicts with AEP Texas and the City of Abilene water department, neither of which could align their work crews with the project timeline.
projects.detail: The US 83/84 pavement reconstruction south of Abilene from Loop 322 to FM 89 required relocating AEP Texas distribution lines and City of Abilene water mains at multiple intersection locations. AEP Texas had committed their regional construction crew to a transmission line project in the San Angelo district through the summer, leaving no resources for the Abilene relocation until fall. The City of Abilene water department was engaged in an EPA-mandated water treatment plant upgrade and could not spare crews for highway utility work until the following spring. The scheduling misalignment delayed the project 8 months and added $3.5M in extended overhead costs.

projects.name: IH-10 Reconstruction (Beaumont to Winnie)
projects.description: The IH-10 reconstruction between Beaumont and Winnie was delayed 18 months by scheduling conflicts with multiple petroleum pipeline operators who could not coordinate simultaneous crossing protections.
projects.detail: The IH-10 reconstruction through Jefferson and Chambers counties crossed an area dense with petroleum and petrochemical pipelines. Enterprise Products Partners, Energy Transfer, and Phillips 66 all had pipelines crossing the highway that required protection or relocation during the reconstruction. Each pipeline operator had different regulatory requirements, inspection schedules, and shutdown windows. Enterprise could only perform pipeline work during their October maintenance turnaround. Energy Transfer required a minimum 6-month lead time for any pipeline modification. Phillips 66's pipeline was under an ongoing integrity management program that precluded concurrent construction activity. The inability to coordinate these schedules added 18 months and $25M to the $350M project.

projects.name: Downtown Amarillo Street Reconstruction (Polk/Tyler Streets)
projects.description: Amarillo's downtown street reconstruction was delayed 9 months when Xcel Energy, Atmos Energy, and AT&T could not coordinate their utility relocation schedules with the city's construction window.
projects.detail: The City of Amarillo planned a comprehensive reconstruction of Polk and Tyler Streets through the downtown core, including new water mains, storm drainage, and streetscape improvements. The project required Xcel Energy to relocate underground electric distribution, Atmos Energy to replace aging gas mains, and AT&T to relocate copper and fiber infrastructure. Xcel Energy's scheduled maintenance season conflicted with the city's preferred summer construction window. Atmos Energy could only schedule their crew during months that overlapped with AT&T's fiber relocation work, and both companies refused to work concurrently in the same trench corridor. The scheduling gridlock extended the project 9 months and added $2.5M in costs.

projects.name: Padre Boulevard Reconstruction (South Padre Island)
projects.description: South Padre Island's main boulevard reconstruction was delayed a full year when the Laguna Madre Water District and AEP Texas could not schedule utility work outside of the tourism high season.
projects.detail: The Town of South Padre Island planned to reconstruct Padre Boulevard from the Queen Isabella Causeway to the convention center with improved drainage and utilities. The Laguna Madre Water District needed to relocate water and sewer mains, and AEP Texas had underground distribution requiring relocation. Both utilities were contractually prohibited from performing disruptive work during the March-August tourism season per agreements with local businesses. The remaining construction window of September through February was constrained by hurricane season (September-November) and winter storms. The effective work window of only 3-4 months per year stretched the utility relocation phase to over two years, adding $4M and 12 months to the overall project.

projects.name: SH 550 New Construction (Brownsville to Port Isabel)
projects.description: TxDOT's new SH 550 corridor between Brownsville and Port Isabel experienced 15 months of delays due to scheduling conflicts with Cameron County Irrigation District and SpaceX-related utility installations.
projects.detail: The SH 550 new construction through Cameron County was designed as a new four-lane divided highway. The corridor crossed Cameron County Irrigation District canals and pipelines at multiple points, plus recently installed underground utilities serving the SpaceX Starbase facility at Boca Chica. The Irrigation District could only perform canal modifications during their November-February low-flow season. SpaceX-related utility providers had restricted work zones around launch-related infrastructure with schedule-dependent access windows. The combination of agricultural water scheduling constraints and space launch scheduling windows created a 15-month delay and $12M in additional costs for the $120M project.

projects.name: SH 130/SH 45 Interchange Improvement (Pflugerville)
projects.description: The SH 130/SH 45 interchange improvement was delayed 10 months when Austin Energy, Oncor, and the Pflugerville MUD could not synchronize their relocation timelines across the jurisdictional boundary.
projects.detail: The interchange of SH 130 and SH 45 straddled the boundary between Austin Energy and Oncor Electric service territories, with the Pflugerville Municipal Utility District providing water and sewer service. Austin Energy followed its own relocation scheduling process tied to the City of Austin's permit system, while Oncor operated under PUC-regulated timelines. The Pflugerville MUD had committed its capital improvement budget to other projects and could not fund the relocation until the next fiscal year. The three-way scheduling conflict between entities operating under different regulatory frameworks delayed the project 10 months and added $7M in costs.

projects.name: Loop 250 Reconstruction (Midland)
projects.description: TxDOT's Loop 250 reconstruction in Midland was delayed 11 months when Oncor Electric and the City of Midland water department could not align schedules, complicated by oil field pipeline crossing requirements.
projects.detail: The Loop 250 reconstruction around Midland's commercial core required coordinating utility relocations with Oncor Electric, the City of Midland, Atmos Energy, and three petroleum pipeline operators with gathering lines crossing the corridor. Oncor's West Texas construction crews were committed to oil field electrification projects and had no availability for roadway utility work for 8 months. The City of Midland water department was simultaneously dealing with a drought emergency that consumed all available crews. The petroleum pipeline operators each had different inspection and modification scheduling requirements. The scheduling conflicts extended the utility phase by 11 months and added $9M to the $60M project.

projects.name: US 290 Reconstruction (Brenham to Chappell Hill)
projects.description: TxDOT's US 290 reconstruction west of Brenham was delayed 8 months by scheduling conflicts with Enterprise Products pipeline shutdowns and Bluebonnet Electric Cooperative's construction season.
projects.detail: The US 290 reconstruction between Brenham and Chappell Hill required coordination with Enterprise Products Partners, which operated multiple NGL pipelines crossing the highway, and Bluebonnet Electric Cooperative, which had underground distribution serving rural customers along the corridor. Enterprise Products could only schedule pipeline modification work during planned plant turnarounds twice per year. Bluebonnet Electric's small construction crew was committed to storm restoration work following severe spring weather and could not be redirected to the highway project. The scheduling conflicts pushed utility relocations back 8 months and added $5M in delay costs to the $50M project.

projects.name: FM 2222 Safety Improvements (Austin West)
projects.description: Austin's FM 2222 safety improvement project was delayed 11 months by scheduling conflicts between Austin Energy, Austin Water, and LCRA, with each entity requiring exclusive access to the narrow Hill Country corridor.
projects.detail: The FM 2222 corridor through the Austin Hill Country required safety improvements including turn lanes, shoulders, and retaining walls. The narrow corridor between limestone bluffs contained Austin Energy underground distribution, Austin Water transmission mains, and a Lower Colorado River Authority raw water pipeline. The physical constraints of the corridor meant only one utility could work at a time. Austin Energy required a 4-month window, Austin Water needed 3 months, and LCRA's pipeline work required 5 months with specialized crews. Each utility's schedule was locked into their annual capital improvement program with different fiscal years (Austin: October, LCRA: January). The sequential scheduling in the constrained corridor added 11 months and $6M.

projects.name: Broadway Street Reconstruction (Galveston)
projects.description: Galveston's Broadway Street reconstruction was delayed 10 months when CenterPoint Energy, the City of Galveston water department, and AT&T could not align schedules around hurricane season and tourist season restrictions.
projects.detail: The City of Galveston planned to reconstruct Broadway Street (SH 87) from 25th Street to 61st Street with new utilities, improved drainage, and complete streetscape upgrades. CenterPoint Energy, the City water department, and AT&T all had infrastructure requiring relocation. The construction window was severely restricted: no work during hurricane season (June-November) per city emergency management policy, and limited disruptive work during the March-May spring break tourism peak. CenterPoint could only schedule crews during their fall maintenance window, which fell during hurricane season. AT&T's fiber team was committed to island-wide 5G deployment. The scheduling impossibility added 10 months and $3.5M to the $21M project.

projects.name: US 69 Reconstruction (Lufkin to Nacogdoches)
projects.description: TxDOT's US 69 reconstruction between Lufkin and Nacogdoches was delayed 7 months by scheduling conflicts with East Texas Electric Cooperative and the Angelina & Neches River Authority.
projects.detail: The US 69 pavement reconstruction between Lufkin and Nacogdoches crossed East Texas Electric Cooperative underground distribution serving timber operations and Angelina & Neches River Authority water infrastructure. ETEC's sole underground construction crew was committed to a new subdivision electrification project in Huntsville and could not be reassigned for 7 months. ANRA's pipeline modification work required low-flow conditions that only occurred during the winter drought season. The overlapping scheduling constraints delayed the project start and added $4M in mobilization and traffic management costs to the $44M project.

projects.name: SH 276 Widening (Rockwall County)
projects.description: TxDOT's SH 276 widening east of Rockwall was delayed 7 months when Oncor and the Greater Texoma Utility Authority could not schedule concurrent utility relocations.
projects.detail: The SH 276 widening from IH-30 east to FM 35 through Rockwall County required Oncor Electric and the Greater Texoma Utility Authority to relocate infrastructure. Oncor had underground distribution lines installed as part of recent subdivision development that conflicted with the widening. GTUA had a 20-inch water transmission main crossing the highway. Oncor's scheduled work window overlapped with GTUA's planned system maintenance shutdown, during which no pipeline work could be performed. GTUA could not reschedule their maintenance without PUC approval, which added months to the coordination process. The 7-month delay added $3M to the $25M project.

projects.name: SH 44 Reconstruction (Alice to Robstown)
projects.description: TxDOT's SH 44 reconstruction was delayed 8 months when multiple petroleum pipeline operators in the Eagle Ford Shale region could not coordinate crossing modifications.
projects.detail: The SH 44 reconstruction from Alice to Robstown crossed the heart of the Eagle Ford Shale production area, with numerous petroleum and natural gas pipelines crossing the highway. Operators including Kinder Morgan, DCP Midstream, and Targa Resources each had different regulatory compliance timelines for pipeline modification work. Kinder Morgan required a 90-day advance notice period. DCP Midstream could only perform modifications during quarterly maintenance windows. Targa Resources was in the middle of a system expansion and could not divert crews. The inability to align pipeline operator schedules delayed the project 8 months and added $3.5M to the $35M reconstruction.

projects.name: Texoma Parkway Reconstruction (Sherman/Denison)
projects.description: The Texoma Parkway reconstruction was delayed 9 months when the City of Sherman, City of Denison, and GTUA could not coordinate their respective utility relocations across the municipal boundary.
projects.detail: TxDOT's Texoma Parkway (US 75 Business) reconstruction from Sherman to Denison required utility work by three separate governmental entities: the City of Sherman water and sewer, the City of Denison water and sewer, and the Greater Texoma Utility Authority. Each city had its own budget cycle, approved contractor list, and permitting requirements. Sherman's utility budget was allocated in October, Denison's in January, and GTUA operated on a July fiscal year. The three entities could not align their funding availability and contractor schedules, requiring TxDOT to negotiate separate utility agreements with staggered timelines. The coordination delays added 9 months and $4M to the $31M project.

projects.name: Georgetown Williams Drive Telecom Conduit Strike
projects.description: A road widening crew on Williams Drive in Georgetown severed a major AT&T fiber conduit bank, knocking out internet and phone service to 12,000 customers including Georgetown Medical Center.
projects.detail: During the Williams Drive widening project west of IH-35, a trenching crew severed an AT&T fiber conduit bank containing 288 fiber strands serving the rapidly growing Sun City and Georgetown Village communities. The cut disrupted internet and phone service to approximately 12,000 customers and, critically, severed the primary data circuit serving Georgetown Medical Center. The hospital reverted to backup communications for 36 hours. AT&T's records showed the conduit bank running along the south side of Williams Drive, but it actually ran diagonally under the planned widening area where it had been installed via bore during a 2016 expansion. The fiber splicing repair took 2 weeks, and the broader impact added $1.3M and 8 weeks to the $22M project.

projects.name: Denton Hickory Creek Road Resurfacing (CoServ Gas Work)
projects.description: CoServ Gas cut into the newly resurfaced Hickory Creek Road in Denton to upgrade gas distribution, violating the city's moratorium just 4 months after the $5.8M resurfacing project.
projects.detail: The City of Denton completed a $5.8M resurfacing of Hickory Creek Road from I-35E to Teasley Lane in December 2024. In April 2025, CoServ Gas began cutting into the new pavement to upgrade gas distribution mains serving the rapidly growing Robson Ranch and Savannah developments. Denton's moratorium ordinance prohibits utility cuts for 3 years after resurfacing, and CoServ had been notified of the project during the design phase. CoServ claimed their gas demand projections had changed due to faster-than-expected subdivision buildout, requiring larger mains. The city was unsympathetic, noting that gas demand growth was foreseeable. The violation damaged 4 blocks of new pavement and added $520K in restoration costs assessed to CoServ.
projects.timeline: Resurfacing completed Dec 2024, cut open Apr 2025

projects.name: League City FM 646 Resurfacing (CenterPoint Energy Fiber Duct)
projects.description: CenterPoint Energy cut into the newly resurfaced FM 646 in League City to install smart grid fiber duct, violating the city's moratorium within 5 months of the $8M resurfacing completion.
projects.detail: The City of League City, in cooperation with TxDOT, completed an $8M resurfacing of FM 646 from I-45 to SH 96 in August 2024. In January 2025, CenterPoint Energy contractors began cutting into the new pavement to install fiber optic communication duct for their Advanced Grid Intelligence and Resilience (AGIR) smart grid program. League City's moratorium ordinance prohibits non-emergency utility cuts for 4 years after resurfacing. CenterPoint argued the smart grid installation was critical infrastructure improvement, not a standard utility installation. The city cited the moratorium and issued stop-work orders after CenterPoint had already cut into 3 blocks. The violation added $560K in restoration costs.
projects.timeline: Resurfacing completed Aug 2024, cut open Jan 2025

projects.name: Baton Rouge Nicholson Drive Corridor Improvement
projects.description: Major corridor improvement near LSU campus required complete plan revision after unmapped water mains and gas lines were discovered beneath Nicholson Drive.
projects.detail: The Nicholson Drive corridor improvement was designed to enhance multimodal access near the LSU campus with new bike lanes, drainage, and road widening. During initial excavation, contractors struck unmapped 12-inch water mains and a 6-inch gas distribution line that predated utility records from the 1940s. The entire project had to be redesigned to route improvements around these legacy utilities, adding $14 million in change orders. Construction that was planned for 2021-2024 extended through 2026, disrupting traffic on a major commuter route.

projects.name: Pensacola Bay Bridge (US-98) Approach Utility Redesign
projects.description: Approach road reconstruction on the Pensacola side of the bay bridge required redesign after subsurface utility engineering revealed conflicting water, sewer, and telecom infrastructure.
projects.detail: The US-98 approach road reconstruction was part of the broader Pensacola Bay Bridge replacement project. Subsurface utility engineering surveys conducted after initial design completion revealed that water mains, a 24-inch sewer force main, and multiple telecom duct banks occupied the same corridor planned for new stormwater drainage. FDOT had to redesign the approach with relocated utility corridors, adding $19 million to the project. The redesign delayed the approach road portion by 18 months, causing extended lane closures on one of the region's most critical hurricane evacuation routes.

projects.name: Tuscaloosa University Boulevard East Widening
projects.description: Widening project east of the University of Alabama campus required plan revision after encountering unmarked steam tunnels and electrical conduits serving the university.
projects.detail: The University Boulevard East widening project aimed to add turning lanes and improve pedestrian crossings near the University of Alabama. During design validation boring, crews discovered unmarked university steam tunnels and high-voltage electrical conduits that extended beneath the public right-of-way. The university's own records were incomplete, requiring weeks of field investigation before plans could be revised. The redesign added $6.2 million for utility relocations and protective measures, delaying the project by 11 months and forcing an additional football season of construction-related traffic chaos.

projects.name: Mobile Brookley Aeroplex Access Road Improvement
projects.description: Access road improvements to the former Brookley Air Force Base required plan revision after uncovering legacy military fuel pipelines and electrical infrastructure.
projects.detail: The Brookley Aeroplex access road improvement was intended to support the growing Airbus manufacturing facility and commercial development at the former military base. Subsurface investigations revealed decommissioned military fuel pipelines, high-voltage electrical conduits, and communication cables that were not in any civilian utility records. Environmental testing of the old fuel lines required remediation protocols, and the road design had to be revised to accommodate both the contamination cleanup and new utility corridors. The $11 million overrun and 16-month delay threatened the timeline for a major aerospace supplier relocation.

projects.name: Tallahassee Monroe Street Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Complete streets redesign of Monroe Street required revision after mapping revealed conflicting utility corridors from three separate providers occupying the planned bus rapid transit lane alignment.
projects.detail: The Monroe Street complete streets project was designed to add dedicated bus lanes, protected bike lanes, and improved pedestrian crossings along Tallahassee's main north-south corridor. Utility mapping revealed that Talquin Electric, the City of Tallahassee water department, and CenturyLink all had major infrastructure in the exact alignment planned for the southbound bus lane. The three-way utility conflict required months of coordination meetings and a complete lane redesign, adding $7.4 million. The 13-month delay pushed construction through two legislative sessions, complicating traffic around the state Capitol.

projects.name: Lake Charles Enterprise Boulevard Extension
projects.description: Boulevard extension plans were revised after subsurface investigation revealed active industrial pipelines serving the Sasol chemical complex that crossed the planned roadway alignment.
projects.detail: The Enterprise Boulevard extension was designed to improve access between I-210 and Lake Charles's growing industrial corridor. During the design phase, subsurface utility engineering discovered active high-pressure industrial pipelines carrying chemical feedstock to the Sasol facility. These pipelines required extensive setbacks that conflicted with the planned roadway. The alignment had to be shifted and several pipeline crossings redesigned with protective encasements, adding $5.1 million and 9 months. The delay impacted the timing of several industrial expansion projects that depended on improved road access.

projects.name: Meridian 22nd Avenue South Infrastructure Overhaul
projects.description: Road reconstruction plans required revision when test boring revealed a disused rail spur foundation and abandoned utility lines from a demolished textile mill.
projects.detail: The 22nd Avenue South infrastructure project in Meridian aimed to reconstruct the road surface, replace aging water mains, and add sidewalks. Test boring encountered concrete foundations from a long-removed rail spur and abandoned cast-iron utility lines from a textile mill demolished in the 1970s. The abandoned lines had to be investigated for hazardous materials before removal, and the road base design was revised to account for the irregular subsurface conditions. The $2.9 million overrun and 7-month delay strained the city's limited infrastructure budget.

projects.name: Orange Beach Canal Road Bridge Replacement
projects.description: Bridge replacement plans required revision after underwater survey revealed submarine utility crossings including a major sewer force main and water supply pipe at the bridge foundation location.
projects.detail: The Canal Road bridge replacement in Orange Beach was designed to replace an aging two-lane bridge with a wider four-lane structure. An underwater survey of the canal crossing revealed a 16-inch sewer force main and a 12-inch water supply pipe attached to the existing bridge structure that were not shown on the original design documents. The new bridge had to be redesigned to temporarily support these utilities during construction and permanently accommodate them in a new utility corridor. The $3.4 million overrun and 8-month delay pushed completion past the start of the 2026 tourist season.

projects.name: Panama City 23rd Street Corridor Reconstruction
projects.description: Post-Hurricane Michael corridor reconstruction required plan revision after discovering that emergency utility repairs had created a tangled subsurface that deviated from all existing records.
projects.detail: The 23rd Street corridor reconstruction was part of Panama City's post-Hurricane Michael recovery effort. When design teams investigated the subsurface, they found that emergency utility repairs performed after the 2018 hurricane had created a chaotic underground environment with water lines crossing gas lines at non-standard angles and depths. None of the emergency repairs had been properly documented. The entire corridor design had to be revised based on new survey data, adding $5.6 million in costs. The 10-month delay further extended the city's slow recovery from one of the most destructive hurricanes to hit the Florida panhandle.

projects.name: Dothan Ross Clark Circle Modernization
projects.description: Traffic circle modernization required plan revision after utility mapping revealed that all four quadrants of the circle contained conflicting underground utility infrastructure from different eras of construction.
projects.detail: The Ross Clark Circle modernization project was designed to upgrade intersections and improve traffic flow around Dothan's main commercial ring road. Utility mapping revealed that each quadrant of the circle contained utility infrastructure installed during different decades, with incompatible depths, materials, and routing. Water mains from the 1950s crossed sewer lines from the 1970s, while gas lines from the 1990s conflicted with fiber optic lines from the 2010s. The design team had to create quadrant-specific plans to address each unique combination of conflicts, adding $3.1 million and 7 months to the project.

projects.name: Prattville McQueen Smith Road Extension
projects.description: Road extension required plan revision after encountering an Alabama Power transmission feeder and buried concrete utility vault at the planned intersection location.
projects.detail: The McQueen Smith Road extension in Prattville was designed to connect a rapidly growing residential area to the commercial corridor. During design-phase boring, engineers discovered an Alabama Power underground transmission feeder and a large buried concrete utility vault at the exact location planned for a new traffic signal intersection. The vault served as a junction point for multiple power distribution lines and could not be relocated without extensive outage planning. The road design was revised to shift the intersection 200 feet south, requiring additional right-of-way purchase and environmental review. The $2.8 million overrun and 6-month delay frustrated developers who had timed housing starts to the road completion.

projects.name: New Orleans Gentilly Boulevard Green Infrastructure
projects.description: FEMA-funded green infrastructure project on Gentilly Boulevard required plan revision after encountering Sewerage & Water Board subsurface drainage infrastructure at depths that conflicted with bioswale and rain garden designs.
projects.detail: The Gentilly Boulevard green infrastructure project was a centerpiece of New Orleans' post-Katrina resilience strategy, designed to use bioswales and rain gardens to reduce stormwater runoff. During design, engineers discovered that the Sewerage & Water Board's subsurface drainage canals and pump station intake pipes occupied the same depth range as the planned bioswale root zones. The root intrusion risk to aging drainage infrastructure required a complete redesign of the green infrastructure system with waterproof root barriers and shallower planting beds. The $8.8 million overrun and 14-month delay reduced the project's effectiveness as a resilience demonstration.

projects.name: Oxford MS Highway 7 South Widening
projects.description: Highway widening plans near the University of Mississippi required revision after discovering unmarked university and municipal utilities crisscrossing beneath the corridor.
projects.detail: The Highway 7 South widening project near Ole Miss was designed to expand the two-lane road to five lanes to handle growing university and commercial traffic. Utility investigation revealed a complex web of unmarked university water, sewer, and communication lines that crossed the highway corridor at multiple points, intermixed with municipal utilities from the city of Oxford. The lack of coordination between university and municipal utility records meant the project design team had to conduct extensive field verification before revising the plans. The $3.6 million overrun and 8-month delay caused additional congestion during football seasons.

projects.name: Lafayette Kaliste Saloom Road Widening Phase 3
projects.description: Phase 3 of road widening required plan revision after discovering that LUS fiber optic trunk lines and Cox Communications cable infrastructure created an impassable utility corridor beneath the planned expansion.
projects.detail: The Kaliste Saloom Road Phase 3 widening in Lafayette was designed to extend the previous widening project southward through a rapidly developing commercial corridor. During utility coordination, engineers discovered that LUS Fiber (the municipal fiber optic utility) and Cox Communications had both installed major trunk infrastructure in the exact corridor needed for the road expansion. The competing fiber networks, installed during Lafayette's contentious municipal broadband deployment, created a dense underground environment that left no room for road foundations. The $7.1 million redesign and 12-month delay highlighted the unintended consequences of the utility installation wars between the municipal and private providers.

projects.name: New Orleans S. Claiborne Avenue Sewer Separation
projects.description: Sewer separation project delayed repeatedly by scheduling conflicts with Entergy New Orleans and the Sewerage & Water Board's own internal capital projects competing for the same corridor.
projects.detail: The S. Claiborne Avenue sewer separation was part of New Orleans' EPA consent decree compliance effort. The project was delayed by more than two years due to scheduling conflicts between Entergy New Orleans, which needed to upgrade its underground power distribution in the same corridor, and the Sewerage & Water Board's own parallel waterline replacement program. Each agency insisted on priority access to the narrow right-of-way, and no interagency coordination framework existed to resolve the disputes. The $22 million overrun came from repeated mobilization/demobilization cycles as crews traded access. The delay drew EPA enforcement attention and threatened additional consent decree penalties.

projects.name: Fort Myers Colonial Boulevard Widening Phase 2
projects.description: Road widening delayed by Lee County Utilities sewer force main replacement schedule conflicting with FDOT's road construction timeline.
projects.detail: The Colonial Boulevard Phase 2 widening in Fort Myers was delayed when Lee County Utilities announced that its aging sewer force main beneath the corridor needed emergency replacement during the same period FDOT planned road construction. Lee County argued the force main was at risk of failure and demanded priority access. FDOT's contractor had already mobilized and begun earthwork when the county shut down the corridor for emergency sewer work. The $10.5 million overrun came from contractor remobilization costs, redesigned road foundations to accommodate the new force main, and extended traffic management. The 14-month delay extended construction through an additional tourist season, frustrating businesses dependent on winter visitors.

projects.name: Starkville MS Highway 12 Widening
projects.description: Highway widening delayed by Mississippi State University's refusal to allow utility work during the fall semester and football season, leaving only narrow construction windows.
projects.detail: The Highway 12 widening near Mississippi State University was impacted by the university's insistence that no disruptive utility relocation work occur during the fall semester or football season, when campus access was critical. This restriction eliminated nearly five months of potential construction time each year. MDOT's contractor could only perform utility relocations during summer months and winter break, creating an inefficient stop-start cycle. The $2.4 million overrun came from the resulting inefficiencies and extended general conditions. The 7-month delay meant the widening took two full construction cycles instead of one.

projects.name: Decatur AL Highway 67 Widening Utility Scheduling
projects.description: Highway widening delayed by a scheduling conflict between Alagasco gas line relocation and Decatur Utilities water main work, with each utility refusing to work simultaneously.
projects.detail: The Highway 67 widening in Decatur required both Alagasco and Decatur Utilities to relocate their infrastructure before road construction could proceed. Alagasco insisted on completing its gas line work before any water main activity began in the same trench zone, citing safety concerns. Decatur Utilities argued it should go first because its water main replacement was more time-consuming. The dispute stretched over months of meetings with ALDOT mediating. The sequential utility work that resulted took twice as long as parallel installation would have, adding $4.6 million in delays and contractor standby costs over 10 months.

projects.name: Auburn AL Opelika Road Widening Utility Scheduling
projects.description: Road widening delayed when Alabama Power and Auburn Water Works scheduled overlapping utility projects in the same corridor, each refusing to yield construction access.
projects.detail: The Opelika Road widening between Auburn and Opelika was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Alabama Power's planned underground power conversion and Auburn Water Works' water main upsizing project. Both utilities scheduled their work to begin simultaneously in the same corridor. Alabama Power argued its project was prioritized by the Alabama Public Service Commission, while Auburn Water Works claimed its water main work was essential for fire protection capacity. ALDOT's road contractor was caught in the middle, unable to begin earthwork until both utility projects were resolved. The 8-month delay and $3.9 million overrun coincided with Auburn University game day traffic, amplifying public frustration.

projects.name: Kissimmee US-192 Corridor Revitalization Utility Delays
projects.description: Corridor revitalization along the tourist district delayed by scheduling conflicts with Toho Water Authority, Duke Energy, and multiple telecom providers all claiming corridor access rights.
projects.detail: The US-192 (Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway) revitalization project through Kissimmee's tourist district was delayed 15 months by a multi-party scheduling conflict. Toho Water Authority needed to replace aging water mains, Duke Energy planned underground power conversion, and three telecom providers (Spectrum, AT&T, and CenturyLink) all had fiber deployment projects in the same corridor. No single agency had authority to prioritize the work, and each utility's contract terms gave them the right to their own construction window. The $13 million overrun came from years of sequential rather than coordinated construction. The prolonged disruption impacted tourist-dependent businesses just miles from Walt Disney World.

projects.name: Mandeville US-190 Widening Utility Coordination
