projects.description: Widening project delayed by St. Tammany Parish Utilities and AT&T both scheduling conflicting utility work along the corridor during DOTD's planned construction window.
projects.detail: The US-190 widening in Mandeville was delayed when St. Tammany Parish Utilities began an uncoordinated sewer line extension in the road corridor just as DOTD's contractor was mobilizing for road construction. AT&T then announced plans for fiber deployment in the same corridor during the same period. DOTD was forced to negotiate a three-way construction schedule, with each party insisting on sequential access. The $4.5 million overrun came from contractor delay claims and extended traffic management costs. The 9-month delay frustrated North Shore commuters who already faced long waits on the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway.

projects.name: Cape Coral Del Prado Boulevard Water Main Strike
projects.description: Road resurfacing contractor struck a Cape Coral Utilities 16-inch water main during milling, flooding the intersection and forcing a boil water notice for surrounding neighborhoods.
projects.detail: During the Del Prado Boulevard resurfacing project, a milling machine struck the top of a Cape Coral Utilities 16-inch water main that had heaved upward due to the sandy soil conditions common in the area. The main was only 14 inches below the surface instead of the design depth of 36 inches. The break flooded the Pine Island Road intersection and forced a boil water notice for approximately 5,000 customers. The flood undermined the road base for 400 feet, requiring complete reconstruction rather than simple resurfacing. The $2.3 million overrun covered water main repair, road reconstruction, and the utility's emergency response costs. The 3-month delay impacted traffic on one of Cape Coral's busiest corridors.

projects.name: CDOT US 36 Express Lanes Utility Redesign (Boulder Turnpike)
projects.description: Managed lanes project between Denver and Boulder required extensive plan revisions after discovering unmapped Xcel Energy gas transmission lines and City of Broomfield water mains beneath the median.
projects.detail: The US 36 Express Lanes project aimed to add tolled managed lanes along the Boulder Turnpike corridor. During design-build phase, contractors discovered unmapped Xcel Energy high-pressure gas transmission lines and City of Broomfield raw water mains that conflicted with proposed barrier placements and drainage structures. The plan revisions required redesigning over 4 miles of median barrier and relocating three major utility crossings. CDOT and the concessionaire disputed responsibility for the $38 million in additional costs, ultimately splitting the overrun. The project was delayed 14 months while revised utility agreements were negotiated.

projects.name: Ogden Junction Intermodal Hub Utility Corridor Revision
projects.description: Multimodal transit hub project in downtown Ogden required full plan revision after potholing revealed conflicting Dominion Energy gas mains and Ogden City sewer trunk lines at depths different from recorded plans.
projects.detail: The Ogden Junction Intermodal Hub was designed to connect FrontRunner commuter rail, UTA bus routes, and a future streetcar line. When subsurface utility engineering began, potholing at 14 of 22 planned foundation locations revealed Dominion Energy gas mains and century-old Ogden City brick sewer trunk lines at depths 4 to 8 feet different from recorded plans. The entire foundation design required revision, with the transit platform shifted 35 feet west. Additional utility relocations cost $4.2 million, and the project fell 11 months behind schedule while new easement agreements were secured from three separate utility owners.

projects.name: Eagle Road / I-84 Interchange Utility Redesign (Ada County)
projects.description: Major interchange reconstruction at one of Idaho's busiest intersections required plan revisions when Idaho Power high-voltage conduits and Suez Water mains were found directly in the path of new ramp foundations.
projects.detail: The Eagle Road/I-84 interchange handles over 100,000 vehicles daily and was being reconstructed to add a diverging diamond configuration. During the 60% design phase, subsurface investigation revealed Idaho Power 69kV conduits and 24-inch Suez Water transmission mains running directly through planned ramp pier locations. The utility conflicts required a complete redesign of the northbound on-ramp alignment and relocation of 1,800 feet of high-voltage conduit. ITD absorbed $12.5 million in additional costs and the project schedule extended 10 months while Idaho Power performed the complex conduit relocation during limited nighttime work windows.

projects.name: Kalispell Bypass US 93 Alternate Route Utility Revision
projects.description: The Kalispell Bypass highway project required significant plan revisions after encountering NorthWestern Energy transmission infrastructure and Flathead Electric Cooperative underground distribution lines along the proposed alignment.
projects.detail: Montana DOT's Kalispell Bypass was designed to route US 93 traffic around the congested downtown core. During final design, the project team discovered that NorthWestern Energy's 100kV transmission lines and Flathead Electric Cooperative underground distribution infrastructure ran along nearly 2 miles of the proposed alignment in locations not shown on available utility records. The conflict required redesigning three interchange ramps and relocating multiple utility corridors. MDT incurred $8.7 million in additional costs and an 18-month delay while utility agreements were renegotiated and environmental clearances for the revised alignment were obtained from federal agencies.

projects.name: Sheridan I-90/Main Street Interchange Utility Redesign
projects.description: The I-90 interchange improvement at Main Street in Sheridan required plan revisions after discovering an abandoned coal mine drainage system and active MDU Resources gas infrastructure conflicting with new bridge pier locations.
projects.detail: WYDOT's interchange reconstruction at I-90 and Main Street in Sheridan aimed to replace aging bridge decks and improve turning movements. Subsurface investigation uncovered an abandoned coal mine drainage system from the early 1900s along with active MDU Resources gas infrastructure that was not accurately mapped. The coal mine drainage conduits ran directly beneath proposed bridge pier footings. Engineers had to revise the pier placement design and reroute 600 feet of active gas main. The $3.1 million overrun and 8-month delay were significant for the modestly-sized project, consuming nearly all of its contingency budget.

projects.name: North Las Vegas Water Reclamation Facility Pipeline Redesign
projects.description: Effluent pipeline expansion for the water reclamation facility required full route redesign when NV Energy underground 230kV transmission cables were discovered along the planned pipeline corridor beneath Craig Road.
projects.detail: The North Las Vegas Water Reclamation Facility pipeline expansion project was designed to carry treated effluent to new reuse sites along Craig Road. During the 90% design phase, NV Energy disclosed the presence of 230kV underground transmission cables that had been installed as part of a regional grid upgrade but not yet reflected in shared utility databases. The cables ran within inches of the planned pipeline corridor for over 1.5 miles. The entire pipeline route required redesign to shift to a parallel alignment, necessitating additional easement acquisition from seven private property owners. The $11 million cost overrun and 13-month delay included property acquisition costs and redesign fees.

projects.name: Provo Lakeview Parkway Bridge Underground Utility Revision
projects.description: Bridge replacement over the Provo River required plan revision when Rocky Mountain Power 46kV underground feeders and a Provo City pressurized irrigation main were discovered in the bridge approach area.
projects.detail: Provo's Lakeview Parkway bridge over the Provo River was scheduled for replacement to handle increased traffic from nearby development. During geotechnical boring for the new bridge abutments, contractors encountered Rocky Mountain Power 46kV underground feeders and a 30-inch Provo City pressurized irrigation main that were not shown on any available utility maps. The underground feeders served critical substations supplying BYU campus power. The bridge approach design required revision to avoid the feeders, with the south abutment shifted 20 feet downstream. The $3.5 million overrun and 6-month delay were attributed to utility relocation design and Rocky Mountain Power's required review process.

projects.name: Twin Falls Blue Lakes Boulevard Corridor Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Corridor improvement project on the city's main commercial strip required plan revision after Intermountain Gas Company mains and Idaho Power conduits were found conflicting with planned median and turning lane modifications.
projects.detail: Twin Falls planned a comprehensive corridor improvement for Blue Lakes Boulevard, the city's primary commercial thoroughfare, including new medians, dedicated turning lanes, and improved stormwater drainage. Utility investigation revealed that Intermountain Gas Company high-pressure mains and Idaho Power underground conduits ran directly beneath the planned median locations at multiple points along the 1.8-mile corridor. The plan revision required eliminating two planned medians and replacing them with painted medians, and shifting the stormwater drainage alignment to avoid the gas infrastructure. The $2.1 million overrun and 8-month delay significantly impacted the small city's limited capital improvement budget.

projects.name: Helena Montana Avenue Water Main Replacement Utility Redesign
projects.description: Water main replacement project on Montana Avenue required redesign when NorthWestern Energy gas infrastructure and an abandoned Montana Power Company steam tunnel system were discovered at the planned excavation depth.
projects.detail: Helena's Montana Avenue water main replacement aimed to replace aging cast iron pipes dating to the 1920s. Pre-construction potholing uncovered NorthWestern Energy gas mains running in parallel at nearly the same depth as the planned new water main, along with remnants of a Montana Power Company steam tunnel system from the city's early district heating era. The steam tunnel remnants had partially collapsed and created voids that required stabilization before any adjacent excavation could proceed. The redesign shifted the new water main alignment and added structural grouting for the abandoned tunnels. The $1.9 million overrun was substantial for a project of this scale, and the 7-month delay disrupted the city's construction season schedule.

projects.name: Prescott Valley Glassford Hill Road Corridor Plan Revision
projects.description: Road widening project along the town's primary north-south corridor required plan revision when APS underground distribution lines and an old Fain Water Company main were found conflicting with widening and intersection improvements.
projects.detail: Prescott Valley's Glassford Hill Road widening aimed to add capacity along the town's busiest corridor. During the design phase, Arizona Public Service underground distribution lines and an abandoned Fain Water Company main from the pre-incorporation era were discovered directly in the widening footprint. The old water main had been abandoned in place when the municipal system was built but never documented. The APS distribution lines served multiple commercial developments and required careful sequencing to relocate without extended power outages. The plan revision redesigned three intersection improvements and shifted the widening to the opposite side of the road at two segments. The $4.6 million overrun and 9-month delay strained the town's transportation budget.

projects.name: Longmont Main Street Complete Streets Utility Corridor Discovery
projects.description: Downtown complete streets project required plan revision when a dense web of Longmont Power and Communications conduits and abandoned United Power underground infrastructure was discovered beneath Main Street.
projects.detail: Longmont's Main Street Complete Streets project aimed to transform the downtown corridor with widened sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and improved transit stops. During subsurface investigation, a dense web of Longmont Power and Communications conduits was discovered at depths far shallower than recorded, along with abandoned United Power underground infrastructure from before the city acquired its own electric utility. The abandoned conduits contained degraded insulation material requiring environmental handling. The plan revision shifted the bike lane configuration, modified three bus stop locations, and redesigned the stormwater drainage system. The $3.9 million overrun and 8-month delay were absorbed by the city's general capital fund.

projects.name: Murray 4500 South TRAX Station Area Utility Revision
projects.description: Station area improvement project near the Murray Central TRAX station required redesign when Dominion Energy gas infrastructure and Murray City Power underground distribution were found blocking planned pedestrian infrastructure.
projects.detail: UTA and Murray City planned improvements around the Murray Central TRAX station to enhance pedestrian access and support transit-oriented development. During design, Dominion Energy gas infrastructure and Murray City Power underground distribution conduits were found blocking planned sidewalk widening, ADA ramp installations, and a new plaza area. Murray City Power's underground distribution was particularly problematic because the utility is city-owned but records had not been updated following a 2015 infrastructure upgrade. The plan revision required relocating power conduits, shifting the station plaza design, and modifying three ADA access points. The $2.6 million overrun and 7-month delay forced the city to phase the project differently than planned.

projects.name: Nampa Garrity Boulevard Widening Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Road widening on Nampa's busiest commercial corridor required plan revision when Idaho Power 138kV underground transmission and Intermountain Gas Company high-pressure mains were found in the widening footprint.
projects.detail: The City of Nampa planned to widen Garrity Boulevard to address severe congestion on the city's primary east-west commercial corridor. During subsurface utility investigation, Idaho Power 138kV underground transmission cables and Intermountain Gas Company 8-inch high-pressure mains were discovered running through the planned widening footprint on the south side of the road. The transmission cables served the entire northwest Nampa load area and could not be de-energized for relocation without extended outages affecting thousands of customers. The plan revision shifted the widening to the north side, requiring acquisition of additional right-of-way from four commercial properties. The $3.3 million overrun and 9-month delay included property acquisition and Idaho Power engineering review costs.

projects.name: Missoula North Reserve Street / I-90 Interchange Plan Revision
projects.description: Interchange reconstruction required plan revision when NorthWestern Energy gas transmission lines and Mountain Water Company mains were discovered conflicting with new ramp and bridge pier locations.
projects.detail: Montana DOT's reconstruction of the North Reserve Street/I-90 interchange in Missoula was prompted by severe congestion at one of the state's busiest interchanges. During the design phase, NorthWestern Energy 12-inch gas transmission lines and Mountain Water Company 24-inch water transmission mains were found directly beneath proposed bridge pier footings and ramp embankments. The gas transmission line served as a critical supply link for western Montana and required a complex relocation involving horizontal directional drilling beneath I-90. The plan revision resulted in a $6.8 million cost overrun and 14-month delay while the gas transmission relocation was designed, permitted, and completed before interchange construction could begin.

projects.name: Flagstaff Milton Road Corridor Improvement Underground Utility Discovery
projects.description: Milton Road corridor improvement through Flagstaff's commercial core required plan revision after APS underground conduits, CenturyLink copper infrastructure, and an unmapped Northern Arizona University steam line were discovered.
projects.detail: Flagstaff's Milton Road corridor improvement aimed to enhance multimodal access along the commercial corridor from I-17 to downtown. Subsurface investigation revealed APS underground conduits, CenturyLink legacy copper infrastructure, and an unmapped Northern Arizona University steam line that extended well beyond the campus boundary. The NAU steam line, installed in the 1970s, had been forgotten after a system conversion but remained pressurized in some sections. The discovery triggered a safety shutdown and environmental review. The plan revision required redesigning the entire southbound curb-to-curb section and shifting planned bus pullouts. The $5.2 million overrun and 10-month delay included emergency steam line decommissioning and APS conduit relocation costs.

projects.name: Kingman Andy Devine Avenue Reconstruction Utility Discovery
projects.description: Historic Route 66 corridor reconstruction required plan revision after UniSource Energy underground distribution and an abandoned ATSF Railway utility tunnel were discovered conflicting with planned road improvements.
projects.detail: Kingman's Andy Devine Avenue reconstruction aimed to revitalize the historic Route 66 corridor through downtown. During pre-construction subsurface investigation, UniSource Energy underground distribution conduits and an abandoned Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway utility tunnel dating to the 1920s were found directly beneath the planned reconstruction zone. The abandoned railway tunnel had partially collapsed in several locations, creating subsurface voids that threatened road stability. The plan revision required structural stabilization of the tunnel, relocation of UniSource conduits, and redesign of the stormwater drainage system. The $1.7 million overrun and 5-month delay were particularly challenging for the small city's limited municipal budget.

projects.name: Farmington East Main Street Utility Corridor Plan Revision
projects.description: Road reconstruction along East Main Street required plan revision after CenturyLink fiber conduit banks and an unmapped abandoned gas gathering line from the San Juan Basin oil field era were discovered during potholing.
projects.detail: Farmington's East Main Street reconstruction aimed to replace deteriorated pavement and upgrade the water distribution system. During pre-construction potholing, CenturyLink fiber conduit banks with 144-count fiber cables and an unmapped abandoned 6-inch gas gathering line from the San Juan Basin oil field era were discovered at depths conflicting with the planned water main alignment. The abandoned gas gathering line required environmental testing for residual hydrocarbons. The plan revision shifted the water main alignment and added protective concrete slabs over the fiber conduit banks at three crossing points. The $1.4 million overrun and 5-month delay were attributed to the environmental testing, utility relocation, and design revision costs.

projects.name: Grand Junction 24 Road / I-70B Intersection Utility Revision
projects.description: Intersection improvement at one of Grand Junction's busiest crossroads required plan revision when Grand Valley Power underground distribution and Xcel Energy gas infrastructure were found in the turning lane expansion area.
projects.detail: CDOT and the City of Grand Junction planned intersection improvements at 24 Road and I-70B to address severe congestion and safety issues. During subsurface utility engineering, Grand Valley Power underground distribution conduits and Xcel Energy gas mains were discovered throughout the planned turning lane expansion and signal infrastructure zone. The utility conflicts were compounded by irrigation ditches operated by the Grand Valley Water Users Association that had been piped underground decades earlier but never accurately mapped. The plan revision redesigned the intersection geometry and relocated three utility corridors. The $2.7 million overrun and 7-month delay required supplemental CDOT funding approval.

projects.name: CDOT SH-9 Green Mountain Reservoir Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Highway reconstruction project along SH-9 near Green Mountain Reservoir was delayed 16 months due to scheduling conflicts between CDOT construction windows and Xcel Energy transmission line relocation timelines.
projects.detail: CDOT's SH-9 reconstruction near Green Mountain Reservoir required Xcel Energy to relocate a 115kV transmission line that served the Silverthorne and Dillon load areas. Xcel's transmission relocation schedule required a 14-month lead time for engineering, permitting, and environmental review that CDOT's construction window did not accommodate. The highway project could not begin until the transmission line was moved, but Xcel prioritized other regional grid upgrades and was unable to accelerate the relocation. CDOT was forced to delay the project by 16 months, losing one full construction season in the high-altitude corridor where work is limited to May through October. The delay added $4.1 million in mobilization, demobilization, and contractor standby costs.

projects.name: UDOT I-15 Interchange at Payson Main Street Utility Delay
projects.description: Interchange reconstruction was delayed a full year because Dominion Energy and UTOPIA fiber both had conflicting relocation schedules that could not align with UDOT's construction phasing.
projects.detail: UDOT's reconstruction of the I-15 interchange at Payson Main Street required coordinated utility relocations from Dominion Energy gas, Rocky Mountain Power, and UTOPIA fiber. Dominion Energy's relocation could only occur during low-demand summer months, but UTOPIA fiber insisted on winter relocation to avoid disrupting service during peak usage. Rocky Mountain Power's schedule was contingent on completing another regional project first. The three-way scheduling conflict meant no window existed where all utilities could be relocated before highway construction began. UDOT was forced to delay the project by 12 months while negotiating a phased relocation plan, adding $5.8 million in escalation and standby costs.

projects.name: Star / Middleton Intersection Improvement Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Intersection improvement at Star Road and SH-44 was delayed when Idaho Power and Intermountain Gas Company had conflicting relocation windows that could not be reconciled with ITD's construction season.
projects.detail: The Idaho Transportation Department planned intersection improvements at Star Road and SH-44 to serve the rapidly growing Star and Middleton communities. Idaho Power required a spring relocation window to avoid peak summer load conditions, while Intermountain Gas Company could only perform relocations during summer when ground conditions were favorable for pipe installation. ITD's construction phasing required both relocations complete before pavement work could begin in fall. The conflicting windows meant one full construction season was lost, and the project was delayed 10 months. The $1.9 million overrun included contractor delay claims and re-mobilization costs. Local residents expressed frustration at traffic congestion during the extended construction period.

projects.name: Billings South Billings Boulevard Utility Coordination Delay
projects.description: Corridor improvement was delayed 9 months when NorthWestern Energy, CenturyLink, and Charter Communications all had conflicting relocation schedules that could not align with the city's construction timeline.
projects.detail: The City of Billings planned South Billings Boulevard corridor improvements including road widening, new sidewalks, and stormwater drainage. Three major utilities needed relocation: NorthWestern Energy gas and electric, CenturyLink copper and fiber, and Charter Communications cable. NorthWestern Energy scheduled their gas main relocation for spring, but CenturyLink insisted on completing a separate network upgrade before allowing their facilities to be moved, pushing their availability to fall. Charter Communications required NorthWestern's electric relocation to be complete before their cable could be rerouted. The cascading scheduling dependencies created a 9-month delay, with $2.4 million in additional costs from contractor standby charges, re-mobilization, and material price escalation.

projects.name: Riverton Federal Boulevard Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Downtown road reconstruction was delayed when Black Hills Energy gas main relocation schedule conflicted with the Bureau of Reclamation's irrigation canal maintenance window, blocking simultaneous construction access.
projects.detail: The City of Riverton planned Federal Boulevard reconstruction through the downtown core, requiring Black Hills Energy gas main relocation and work near a Bureau of Reclamation irrigation canal crossing. Black Hills Energy could only perform the gas relocation during summer months, but the Bureau of Reclamation required the canal to be operational during the same period for agricultural water delivery, blocking construction access at the canal crossing. The scheduling conflict forced the project into two separate construction seasons instead of one, adding $1.2 million in contractor mobilization costs and 8 months of delay. The extended construction disrupted downtown businesses during two consecutive summer tourist seasons.

projects.name: Maricopa City Center Infrastructure Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: New city center infrastructure was delayed 11 months when Electrical District No. 3, Global Water, and Southwest Gas could not coordinate relocation schedules for a shared utility corridor beneath Honeycutt Road.
projects.detail: The City of Maricopa's city center infrastructure project required utility relocations along Honeycutt Road to support a new civic center and mixed-use development. Electrical District No. 3, Global Water Resources, and Southwest Gas all had underground facilities in the corridor requiring relocation. ED3 required an 8-month lead time for engineering and permitting of their 69kV underground relocation. Global Water insisted on completing their work first to maintain water service, but ED3's facilities blocked their excavation access. Southwest Gas could not begin until both other utilities cleared the corridor. The sequential dependencies and lack of coordination between the three utilities created an 11-month delay and $3.4 million in additional costs that were passed through to the development budget.

projects.name: Rio Rancho Paseo del Volcan Extension Utility Coordination Failure
projects.description: Highway extension was delayed 14 months when PNM electric, New Mexico Gas Company, and ABCWUA water utility all had conflicting relocation schedules that produced a cascading series of construction halts.
projects.detail: NMDOT's Paseo del Volcan extension in Rio Rancho required coordinated relocation of PNM electric distribution, New Mexico Gas Company mains, and Albuquerque Bernalillo County Water Utility Authority transmission lines. PNM's electric relocation was contingent on completing a substation upgrade at another location, pushing their availability back 8 months. New Mexico Gas Company's crews were committed to a system modernization project in Albuquerque and could not reallocate resources. ABCWUA required PNM's electric relocation to be complete before their water main work could safely proceed. The cascading scheduling failures resulted in 14 months of delay and $4.9 million in additional costs including contractor idle time, re-mobilization, and material escalation charges.

projects.name: CDOT I-25 and SH-7 Interchange Utility Scheduling Delay (Erie/Broomfield)
projects.description: Interchange reconstruction was delayed 13 months because United Power, Xcel Energy, and Town of Erie water utility had irreconcilable relocation schedules, with each utility's work dependent on the others completing first.
projects.detail: CDOT's I-25/SH-7 interchange reconstruction in the rapidly growing Erie/Broomfield area required major utility relocations. United Power's underground 69kV transmission needed an 18-month engineering and construction lead time. Xcel Energy's gas main relocation required United Power's electric to be moved first to maintain safe separation distances. The Town of Erie's water main replacement depended on the gas main being relocated to provide excavation clearance. This three-way dependency chain meant the project could not begin meaningful construction for over a year while United Power completed their work. The 13-month delay added $7.6 million in costs, including contractor standby, re-procurement of expired materials, and construction inflation that hit particularly hard during the 2023-2024 period.

projects.name: Lehi Thanksgiving Point Area Road Network Utility Delay
projects.description: Road network expansion was delayed 10 months when Rocky Mountain Power, Dominion Energy, and UTOPIA fiber could not align their relocation schedules with the city's construction phasing.
projects.detail: The City of Lehi planned road network expansion near the Thanksgiving Point commercial and tech corridor to serve rapidly growing traffic demand. Rocky Mountain Power's underground distribution relocation schedule required a September-to-February window to avoid summer peak loads. Dominion Energy could only relocate gas mains during the May-to-September warm weather window. UTOPIA fiber's relocation was delayed by a regional fiber shortage that pushed their materials delivery out 6 months. The inability to coordinate the three relocation schedules with the city's road construction phasing created a 10-month delay. The $4.5 million overrun included contractor delay claims, re-mobilization costs, and material price increases during the delay period.

projects.name: Great Falls River Drive Rehabilitation NorthWestern Energy Delay
projects.description: River Drive rehabilitation was delayed 9 months when NorthWestern Energy's gas main relocation schedule conflicted with seasonal Missouri River flood stage restrictions that limited construction access.
projects.detail: Great Falls planned River Drive rehabilitation along the Missouri River corridor to address deteriorated pavement and failing stormwater infrastructure. NorthWestern Energy's gas main relocation could only occur during summer months when ground conditions allowed trenching. However, the Montana Department of Natural Resources restricted construction within the river floodplain during the spring and early summer high-water period. The overlapping restrictions left only a narrow August-September window for gas main work, which was insufficient for the scope of relocation needed. The project was forced to spread across two construction seasons, adding $1.8 million in costs and 9 months of delay. Local businesses along River Drive endured two years of construction disruption instead of the planned one.

projects.name: Rock Springs Gateway Boulevard Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Commercial corridor improvement was delayed 7 months when Black Hills Energy and Pacific Power had conflicting utility relocation schedules that could not fit within Rock Springs' short construction season.
projects.detail: The City of Rock Springs planned Gateway Boulevard corridor improvements to support growing commercial development. Black Hills Energy gas main relocation required a warm-weather window from June to September, while Pacific Power's underground distribution relocation was scheduled for the same period due to crew availability constraints. Both utilities needed to occupy the same trench corridor, making simultaneous work impossible. Rock Springs' high-altitude location limits the construction season to roughly May through October, leaving no room for sequential relocation within a single year. The project was delayed 7 months into the following construction season, adding $1.3 million in costs. City officials criticized the lack of utility coordination mechanisms available to small Wyoming municipalities.

projects.name: Henderson Horizon Ridge Parkway Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Parkway widening was delayed 11 months when NV Energy, Southwest Gas, and Cox Communications had overlapping but incompatible relocation schedules for facilities in the widening corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Henderson's Horizon Ridge Parkway widening project required relocating NV Energy underground distribution, Southwest Gas mains, and Cox Communications fiber. NV Energy could not de-energize their circuits during the summer cooling season when the Las Vegas valley's electric demand peaks. Southwest Gas required NV Energy's electric relocation to be complete before safely excavating near their mains. Cox Communications was in the middle of a network upgrade and refused to relocate aging copper facilities, insisting on waiting until their fiber conversion was complete. The triple scheduling conflict created an 11-month delay and $3.7 million in additional costs. Henderson city council passed a utility coordination ordinance in response to prevent similar conflicts on future projects.

projects.name: Durango Main Avenue Streetscape Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Downtown streetscape project was delayed 10 months when LPEA electric cooperative, Atmos Energy gas, and CenturyLink could not coordinate their underground utility relocation schedules within Durango's limited construction season.
projects.detail: Durango's Main Avenue Streetscape project aimed to revitalize the downtown corridor with improved pedestrian infrastructure, decorative paving, and undergrounded utilities. La Plata Electric Association cooperative, Atmos Energy gas, and CenturyLink all had facilities requiring relocation in the narrow downtown right-of-way. LPEA's electric undergrounding schedule conflicted with their annual summer maintenance program. Atmos Energy gas main relocation was limited to warm-weather months. CenturyLink refused to begin work until both other utilities had completed their relocations. Durango's construction season is limited by high-altitude winter conditions to roughly May through October, and the tourist season further restricted work hours. The cascading scheduling conflicts created a 10-month delay and $2.9 million overrun that required the city to seek a supplemental appropriation.

projects.name: Tooele Main Street UDOT Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Main Street reconstruction was delayed 8 months when Dominion Energy, Rocky Mountain Power, and Tooele City water utility could not coordinate their underground facility relocation schedules.
projects.detail: UDOT's Main Street (SR-36) reconstruction through Tooele required coordinated utility relocations for Dominion Energy gas, Rocky Mountain Power underground distribution, and Tooele City water mains. Dominion Energy's relocation schedule was delayed by their system-wide pipeline integrity testing program that consumed available crews. Rocky Mountain Power scheduled their work during a low-load fall window. Tooele City's water main replacement depended on Rocky Mountain Power clearing the corridor first. The sequential dependencies and Dominion's resource constraints created an 8-month delay and $2.2 million in additional costs. UDOT's project manager noted that the delay cost more than the utility relocations themselves, a common pattern in rural Utah transportation projects.

projects.name: Carson City South Carson Street Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Downtown corridor improvement was delayed 9 months when NV Energy, Southwest Gas, and AT&T had conflicting underground utility schedules that sequentially blocked road construction progress.
projects.detail: Carson City planned South Carson Street corridor improvements including road reconstruction, new sidewalks, and stormwater upgrades. NV Energy, Southwest Gas, and AT&T all had underground facilities requiring relocation. NV Energy scheduled their work for fall to avoid summer peak demand restrictions. Southwest Gas required NV Energy's electric to be relocated first. AT&T's fiber relocation was contingent on Southwest Gas completing their work because the AT&T conduit ran directly above the gas main. The cascading dependencies created a 9-month delay that pushed the project through two construction seasons. The $2.1 million overrun included contractor standby charges and material escalation costs that consumed the project's entire contingency allocation.

projects.name: West Jordan 7800 South Water Main Strike During Road Project
projects.description: Road reconstruction on 7800 South struck a Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District 30-inch transmission main, flooding the construction zone and requiring emergency repair and road base reconstruction.
projects.detail: During road reconstruction on 7800 South in West Jordan, an excavator struck a Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District 30-inch water transmission main at a location 6 feet from its mapped position. The strike released an estimated 2 million gallons of water before the line could be isolated, flooding the construction zone to a depth of 3 feet and washing out 400 feet of newly placed road base material. Emergency repair of the transmission main took 5 days, during which 12,000 customers were on restricted water usage. The incident added $1.2 million to the project cost for main repair, road base reconstruction, and environmental remediation of sediment that entered a nearby storm drain. The project was delayed 4 months while the road base was rebuilt and compacted.

projects.name: Bozeman West Babcock Street Water Main Strike (Building Construction)
projects.description: Building foundation excavation on West Babcock Street struck a City of Bozeman 16-inch water main that was 8 feet from its mapped location, flooding the excavation pit and damaging adjacent property.
projects.detail: During foundation excavation for a new mixed-use building on West Babcock Street in Bozeman, a trackhoe struck a City of Bozeman 16-inch water main that was located 8 feet from its position on city utility maps. The strike released high-pressure water that flooded the 20-foot-deep excavation pit within minutes, undermining the shoring system and causing partial collapse of the pit walls. Water also flooded the basement of an adjacent commercial building, causing significant property damage. The city's water department repaired the main within 3 days, but the excavation pit required complete re-excavation and new shoring installation. Total additional costs reached $900,000 including main repair, property damage claims, re-excavation, and new shoring. The project was delayed 3 months.

projects.name: Mesquite Nevada I-15 Widening NV Energy Cable Strike
projects.description: I-15 widening project struck an NV Energy underground 69kV transmission cable, causing a power outage to the entire Mesquite service area and requiring 2 weeks of emergency repair work.
projects.detail: During I-15 widening construction near Mesquite, a drilling rig struck an NV Energy underground 69kV transmission cable that served as the primary power feed for the Mesquite area. The strike caused a complete power outage to approximately 15,000 customers for 8 hours, with partial service restoration taking 3 days and full restoration requiring 2 weeks of emergency splice and cable repair. NDOT's contractor had obtained utility locates, but the cable had been installed during a previous highway project and its as-built location was 12 feet from the recorded position. The incident added $2.1 million to the project cost and caused a 4-month delay while NV Energy installed protective concrete barriers around the repaired cable section and the construction approach was revised to avoid further conflicts.

projects.name: Whitefish US 93 Road Project NorthWestern Energy Gas Strike
projects.description: US 93 road improvement project struck a NorthWestern Energy 6-inch gas main near Whitefish's commercial district, causing evacuation of downtown businesses and a 5-hour gas service outage.
projects.detail: During US 93 road improvement construction near Whitefish's downtown commercial district, excavation equipment struck a NorthWestern Energy 6-inch gas distribution main. The strike occurred near the intersection with 2nd Street, triggering evacuation of nearby restaurants, shops, and a hotel for approximately 5 hours while NorthWestern crews isolated and repaired the damaged main. The Montana PSC investigation found the gas main was 4 feet from its recorded position, likely due to the road having been widened in the 1990s without updating utility records. The $800,000 in costs included gas main repair, emergency response, business interruption claims from downtown merchants, and road surface restoration. MDT suspended work for 3 months to re-survey all utilities in the project corridor.

projects.name: Post Falls Seltice Way Sewer Project Avista Gas Strike
projects.description: Sewer line installation on Seltice Way struck an Avista Utilities 6-inch gas main, causing evacuation of a hotel and restaurant complex for 4 hours.
projects.detail: During sewer line installation on Seltice Way in Post Falls, excavation struck an Avista Utilities 6-inch gas distribution main that was 3 feet from its marked location. The gas release forced evacuation of a hotel and restaurant complex with over 200 occupants for approximately 4 hours while Avista crews isolated and repaired the line. The Idaho PUC investigation found that the Seltice Way corridor had undergone multiple road improvement projects over the decades that had shifted utility alignments without corresponding record updates. The $500,000 in costs included gas main repair, emergency response, business interruption claims, and supplemental utility locating for the remaining sewer project. The project was delayed 2 months while a comprehensive utility re-survey was performed.

projects.name: Alamogordo White Sands Boulevard Fiber Gas Strike
projects.description: Fiber optic installation on White Sands Boulevard struck a New Mexico Gas Company 4-inch main, triggering evacuation of a fast-food restaurant and gas station for 3 hours.
projects.detail: During fiber optic boring along White Sands Boulevard in Alamogordo, a contractor struck a New Mexico Gas Company 4-inch gas distribution main near a busy commercial intersection. The gas release triggered immediate evacuation of a fast-food restaurant and an adjacent gas station, with approximately 50 people displaced for 3 hours while New Mexico Gas Company crews repaired the line. The NMPRC investigation found that the fiber contractor's bore path had drifted from the approved alignment due to rocky subsurface conditions, bringing the drill head into contact with the gas main. The $400,000 in costs included gas main repair, emergency response, business interruption, and road surface restoration. The fiber installation in Alamogordo was halted for 2 months while the contractor demonstrated improved boring accuracy protocols.

projects.name: St. George River Road Resurfacing Dixie Power Trench Cuts
projects.description: Dixie Power cut into newly resurfaced River Road within 6 months of a $5.2 million overlay project to install underground distribution for a new subdivision, violating the city's 3-year moratorium.
projects.detail: The City of St. George completed a $5.2 million overlay of River Road, a key north-south corridor. Within 6 months, Dixie Power cut into the new pavement at 8 locations to install underground electrical distribution serving a new residential subdivision. The city's 3-year paving moratorium ordinance should have prevented the cuts, but Dixie Power argued they had a franchise agreement that superseded the moratorium. The city estimated that the 8 trench cuts caused $900,000 in pavement damage and reduced the expected pavement life by 5 years. The dispute led to litigation between the city and Dixie Power over franchise agreement interpretation. St. George city council subsequently amended the moratorium ordinance to explicitly state that franchise agreements do not override paving protection periods.

projects.name: Boise Ustick Road Resurfacing Idaho Power Underground Cuts
projects.description: Idaho Power performed underground distribution upgrades on newly resurfaced Ustick Road just 5 months after an $8 million overlay, making 12 trench cuts that degraded the new pavement.
projects.detail: The Ada County Highway District completed an $8 million resurfacing of Ustick Road in Boise, a major east-west arterial. Five months later, Idaho Power began cutting into the new pavement at 12 locations to perform underground distribution upgrades serving new development along the corridor. ACHD's 5-year paving moratorium should have prevented the cuts, but Idaho Power's construction schedule had not been coordinated with ACHD's paving program. The 12 trench cuts caused an estimated $1.1 million in pavement degradation and created uneven ride quality along the newly smooth road. ACHD's commissioners expressed frustration at the ongoing coordination failures between the highway district and utility companies, noting that similar incidents had occurred on multiple ACHD roads. The district strengthened its utility coordination requirements in response.

projects.name: Laramie 3rd Street Resurfacing Black Hills Energy Gas Cuts
projects.description: Black Hills Energy cut into newly resurfaced 3rd Street within 7 months of a $2.8 million overlay to perform gas service line replacements, undermining the city's pavement investment.
projects.detail: The City of Laramie completed a $2.8 million overlay of 3rd Street through the downtown and university district. Seven months later, Black Hills Energy began cutting into the new pavement at 6 locations to replace aging gas service lines connecting to commercial buildings. The city did not have a formal paving moratorium ordinance at the time, relying instead on informal coordination with utility companies. The 6 trench cuts caused an estimated $300,000 in pavement damage and created visible patches on the newly smooth road surface. The incident prompted the Laramie city council to draft a formal paving moratorium ordinance requiring utility companies to coordinate their work with the city's paving schedule and providing financial penalties for unauthorized cuts within 5 years of resurfacing.

projects.name: Idaho Falls Woodruff Avenue Resurfacing Intermountain Gas Cuts
projects.description: Intermountain Gas Company cut into newly resurfaced Woodruff Avenue at 5 locations within 6 months of a $3.1 million overlay to repair corroded gas service connections.
projects.detail: The City of Idaho Falls completed a $3.1 million overlay of Woodruff Avenue, a key commercial corridor. Six months later, Intermountain Gas Company began cutting into the new pavement at 5 locations to repair corroded gas service connections identified during a routine system inspection. The city's paving moratorium ordinance restricted utility cuts for 3 years, but Intermountain Gas argued the corrosion repairs were safety-critical and could not wait. The 5 trench cuts caused an estimated $400,000 in pavement damage and created visible patches on the new road surface. The Idaho Falls city council was frustrated that Intermountain Gas had not performed the inspections before the overlay project, which would have allowed coordination. The city subsequently required utilities to perform pre-paving inspections of their facilities in any corridor scheduled for resurfacing.

projects.name: Eagle Road Resurfacing Intermountain Gas Service Cuts (Meridian)
projects.description: Intermountain Gas Company cut into newly resurfaced Eagle Road at 4 locations within 5 months of a $2.8 million ACHD overlay to install new gas service connections for a commercial development.
projects.detail: The Ada County Highway District completed a $2.8 million overlay of Eagle Road through the City of Eagle. Five months later, Intermountain Gas Company began cutting into the new pavement at 4 locations to install gas service connections for a new commercial development. ACHD's utility coordination process should have identified the planned gas work before the overlay, but the commercial development approval came after the overlay contract was awarded. The 4 trench cuts caused an estimated $500,000 in pavement damage. ACHD and the City of Eagle criticized the lack of a unified development-tracking system that could flag utility work triggered by new development approvals. The incident led ACHD to implement a real-time notification system linking building permit approvals to the highway district's paving schedule.

projects.name: Helena Prospect Avenue Overlay NorthWestern Energy Cuts
projects.description: NorthWestern Energy cut into newly overlaid Prospect Avenue within 3 months of a $1.6 million resurfacing to perform gas main valve replacement, undermining the city's limited paving budget.
projects.detail: The City of Helena completed a $1.6 million overlay of Prospect Avenue, a key residential and commercial corridor. Just 3 months later, NorthWestern Energy cut into the new pavement at 3 locations to perform gas main valve replacements identified during a system safety audit. Helena did not have a formal paving moratorium ordinance, and NorthWestern's work proceeded without city coordination. The 3 trench cuts caused an estimated $200,000 in pavement damage. For a city with Helena's limited street maintenance budget, the loss was significant, representing approximately 3% of the annual paving budget destroyed within weeks of placement. The incident, combined with a similar event on Montana Avenue earlier in the year, prompted Helena to adopt a formal paving moratorium ordinance modeled on Missoula's.

projects.name: Sheridan Coffeen Avenue Resurfacing MDU Resources Gas Cuts
projects.description: MDU Resources cut into newly resurfaced Coffeen Avenue at 3 locations within 4 months of a $1.8 million overlay to repair a leaking gas main connection.
projects.detail: The City of Sheridan completed a $1.8 million overlay of Coffeen Avenue, a key commercial corridor on the city's south side. Four months later, MDU Resources cut into the new pavement at 3 locations to repair a leaking gas main connection. While MDU argued the leak repair was an emergency, the city contended that the leak had been reported before the overlay project and should have been repaired during the coordinated utility window offered before paving began. The 3 trench cuts caused an estimated $200,000 in pavement damage. Sheridan's city council used the incident to strengthen the informal utility coordination process, requiring utilities to sign a certification that all known maintenance needs in a paving corridor had been addressed before the overlay contract was executed.

projects.name: Henderson Stephanie Street Resurfacing Southwest Gas Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Southwest Gas cut into newly resurfaced Stephanie Street at 7 locations within 6 months of a $5.1 million overlay to perform gas main pressure testing and valve installations.
projects.detail: The City of Henderson completed a $5.1 million overlay of Stephanie Street. Within 6 months, Southwest Gas cut into the new pavement at 7 locations to perform gas main pressure testing and install new isolation valves as part of a system integrity program. Henderson's 5-year paving moratorium ordinance should have prevented the cuts, but Southwest Gas argued that the pressure testing was mandated by PHMSA regulations and could not be deferred. The 7 trench cuts caused an estimated $900,000 in pavement damage. The city imposed moratorium violation fines and required Southwest Gas to pay for full-lane-width resurfacing at each cut location. The incident prompted Henderson to add a clause to its moratorium ordinance requiring utilities to submit all federally mandated maintenance schedules to the city at least 2 years in advance of any planned paving work.

projects.name: Butte Montana Street Reconstruction NorthWestern Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Downtown road reconstruction was delayed 8 months when NorthWestern Energy gas relocation conflicted with the city's water main replacement schedule, and both projects competed for the same narrow right-of-way.
projects.detail: The City of Butte planned Montana Street reconstruction through the Uptown Historic District, requiring simultaneous water main replacement and NorthWestern Energy gas main relocation. NorthWestern's gas crew availability was limited to a summer window, but the city's water department required the gas to be moved first before trenching for the new water main. NorthWestern delayed their start by 3 months due to crew commitments in Helena, pushing the water main work into the following construction season. The narrow historic district right-of-way could not accommodate simultaneous operations. The 8-month delay added $1.5 million in contractor standby, re-mobilization, and material escalation costs. Butte-Silver Bow County commissioners expressed frustration at the lack of utility scheduling tools available to small Montana communities.

projects.name: Sierra Vista Fry Boulevard Utility Scheduling Coordination Failure
projects.description: Corridor improvement was delayed 9 months when APS, Southwest Gas, and CenturyLink could not coordinate relocation schedules, with each utility requiring the previous one to complete work first.
projects.detail: The City of Sierra Vista planned Fry Boulevard corridor improvements along the city's primary commercial corridor. APS underground distribution, Southwest Gas mains, and CenturyLink fiber all required relocation. APS required a fall window to avoid summer peak demand. Southwest Gas needed APS to complete work first for safety clearance, pushing their schedule to winter. CenturyLink required both APS and Southwest Gas to finish before relocating their fiber conduit, pushing their work to the following spring. The sequential dependency chain created a 9-month delay that was particularly frustrating because all three utilities had been notified of the project 18 months in advance but failed to develop a coordinated schedule. The $2.5 million overrun included contractor standby costs, material price increases, and traffic management during the extended construction.

projects.name: LA Metro Sepulveda Transit Corridor Plan Utility Redesign
projects.description: Preliminary engineering for the Sepulveda Pass transit corridor discovered dense clusters of DWP water trunk lines and SoCalGas high-pressure mains requiring tunnel alignment revisions.
projects.detail: LA Metro's Sepulveda Transit Corridor connecting the San Fernando Valley to the Westside encountered massive utility conflicts during preliminary engineering. The proposed tunnel alignment intersected with three LADWP high-capacity water trunk lines and a SoCalGas 30-inch transmission main beneath Sepulveda Boulevard. Full tunnel profile redesign was required, pushing the alignment 40 feet deeper in two sections and adding a new ventilation shaft location. The utility coordination phase alone consumed 18 months of schedule.

projects.name: Anaheim Canyon Metrolink Station Expansion Redesign
projects.description: Expansion of the Anaheim Canyon Metrolink station required plan revisions after discovering SCE underground transmission vaults and an unreported storm drain collector directly beneath the planned parking structure foundation.
projects.detail: The OCTA-funded expansion of Anaheim Canyon station encountered conflicts during geotechnical boring when crews hit an unreported SCE 66kV underground transmission vault and a City of Anaheim 48-inch storm drain collector not shown on any utility atlas. The parking structure footprint had to be relocated, and the platform extension required redesign to avoid SCE infrastructure. Plan revision added $18M to the $40M project and delayed completion by 18 months while SCE completed protective casing work.

projects.name: San Diego Downtown Waterfront Park Phase II Utility Redesign
projects.description: Phase II of the County Waterfront Park expansion required utility corridor redesign after discovering SDG&E legacy gas lines and city sewer infrastructure conflicting with the planned underground cistern system.
projects.detail: San Diego County's Waterfront Park Phase II expansion hit underground conflicts during early excavation. An SDG&E 12-inch gas distribution main and two city sewer trunk lines running through the planned underground cistern footprint were not shown on record drawings. The cistern had to be split into two smaller units on either side of the utility corridor, requiring complete hydraulic redesign. This added $15M to the $60M budget and delayed the parks opening by one year.

projects.name: Riverside Downtown Main Street Modernization Plan Revision
projects.description: Riverside's Main Street modernization encountered unmapped Southern California Edison underground conduits and century-old brick storm drains requiring complete utility plan revision.
projects.detail: The City of Riverside's downtown Main Street modernization project discovered during potholing that unmapped SCE underground conduits crisscrossed the corridor at multiple points, conflicting with planned bioswale installations and ADA-compliant curb ramps. Additionally, crews found brick-lined storm drains from the early 1900s that were structurally compromised and not on city records. The utility conflicts forced a complete redesign of the stormwater management system and street cross-section, adding $12M to the $40M project.

projects.name: Oakland Hegenberger Road Gateway Improvement Utility Redesign
projects.description: Oakland's Hegenberger Road gateway improvement required redesign after EBMUD water mains and PG&E gas lines were found in conflict with the planned median bus corridor and landscaping.
projects.detail: The City of Oakland's Hegenberger Road gateway improvement project, connecting the Coliseum BART station to Oakland Airport, ran into subsurface conflicts during design validation. EBMUD 24-inch water transmission mains and PG&E gas distribution lines were found directly beneath the planned center-running bus lane median. The median had to be narrowed and shifted, requiring redesign of four signalized intersections and relocation of 1,200 feet of water main. The changes added $14M to the $50M project budget.

projects.name: Irvine Great Park Neighborhood Utility Infrastructure Redesign
projects.description: Great Park neighborhood infrastructure required plan revision when former Marine Corps Air Station utility lines, abandoned fuel pipelines, and legacy electrical conduits were found throughout the development zone.
projects.detail: The Irvine Great Park neighborhood development, built on the former MCAS El Toro site, encountered extensive undocumented military utility infrastructure during grading. Abandoned aviation fuel pipelines, military electrical conduits, and deteriorated concrete-encased water mains from the 1940s were found across the planned residential infrastructure corridor. The developer and City of Irvine had to redesign the entire utility backbone for the neighborhood, adding $45M to the $250M infrastructure budget and delaying home construction starts by two years.

projects.name: SF MUNI Geary Boulevard BRT Phase 2 Utility Redesign
projects.description: Phase 2 of the Geary BRT project was delayed by scheduling conflicts with PG&E, SFPUC, and Recology for utility relocations along the densely packed Geary Boulevard utility corridor.
projects.detail: SFMTA's Geary Boulevard BRT Phase 2 from Masonic to 34th Avenue required coordination with PG&E gas and electric, SFPUC water and sewer, and Recology waste infrastructure. Each utility company had conflicting maintenance and capital schedules that prevented simultaneous work. PG&E insisted on completing gas main replacement before SFPUC could relocate water mains, but PG&E's schedule slipped by 18 months due to its own systemwide gas safety program priorities. The cascading delays added $340M to the $1.55B project.

projects.name: San Diego MTS Mid-Coast Trolley Extension Utility Schedule Conflicts
projects.description: The Mid-Coast Trolley extension to UC San Diego was delayed by scheduling conflicts with SDG&E and City of San Diego utilities, particularly along the Genesee Avenue section.
projects.detail: SANDAG's Mid-Coast Trolley Blue Line extension to the University Community experienced significant scheduling conflicts along the Genesee Avenue section. SDG&E refused to begin gas main relocation until its annual maintenance shutdown window, which conflicted with the City of San Diego's planned sewer rehabilitation in the same corridor. Construction crews sat idle for months while the two agencies negotiated sequencing. The scheduling conflicts contributed $78M in delay costs to the $2.17B project.

projects.name: San Jose Capitol Expressway Light Rail Extension Utility Conflicts
projects.description: VTA's Capitol Expressway light rail extension was delayed by scheduling conflicts between PG&E, San Jose Water Company, and Santa Clara Valley Water District over utility relocation sequencing.
projects.detail: VTA's Capitol Expressway light rail extension faced a scheduling logjam when PG&E, San Jose Water Company, and Santa Clara Valley Water District could not agree on relocation sequencing. PG&E demanded that water lines move first to reduce risk to its gas infrastructure, but SJWC could not mobilize crews until the following fiscal year. Valley Water's aqueduct crossing required a six-month environmental review window that expired before PG&E cleared the corridor. The scheduling conflicts added $65M and two years to the $360M project.

projects.name: LA Metro East San Fernando Valley Transit Corridor SCE Scheduling Delay
projects.description: The East San Fernando Valley transit corridor was delayed by scheduling conflicts between SCE and LADWP over high-voltage transmission line relocation along Van Nuys Boulevard.
projects.detail: LA Metro's East San Fernando Valley Light Rail Transit project along Van Nuys Boulevard was stalled by a jurisdictional scheduling conflict between SCE and LADWP. Both utilities had underground infrastructure requiring relocation, but each demanded the other move first due to safety clearance requirements. LADWP's fiscal year capital budget cycle further constrained its ability to begin work on Metro's preferred timeline. The two-utility standoff consumed 30 months and added $320M to the $3.2B project.

projects.name: Oceanside Coast Highway Complete Streets Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Oceanside's Coast Highway complete streets project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between SDG&E and the City of Oceanside's water department over utility work in the coastal corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Oceanside's Coast Highway complete streets project was stalled by scheduling conflicts between SDG&E and the city's own water department. SDG&E required exclusive access to the corridor during gas main replacement for safety reasons, preventing concurrent water line work. The city's water department had a narrow construction window to avoid impacting summer tourist season water demand. The scheduling conflict pushed water work to the following year, adding $9M and 12 months to the $41M project.

projects.name: Maui North-South Collector Road Phase 3 Utility Redesign
projects.description: MECO high-voltage transmission lines and KIUC fiber conduits beneath the Phase 3 corridor required a ground-up utility redesign for the Kihei collector road extension.
projects.detail: Phase 3 of Maui's long-delayed North-South Collector Road in Kihei hit a major snag when subsurface investigation revealed that Maui Electric Company high-voltage transmission lines and Hawaiian Telcom fiber conduits occupied much of the planned roadway corridor. The original design assumed utilities could be shifted laterally, but rocky volcanic substrate made horizontal relocation impractical. Engineers redesigned the road profile to accommodate deeper utility trenches and added a new utility corridor on the makai side. The redesign added $11M to the $61M project and pushed the opening from 2025 to 2027.

projects.name: Anchorage Seward Highway to Glenn Highway Interchange Plan Revision
projects.description: The Seward-Glenn Highway interchange redesign in Anchorage required rerouting ENSTAR gas transmission and Chugach Electric lines buried in permafrost-affected soils.
projects.detail: Alaska DOT's $230M interchange reconstruction connecting the Seward and Glenn Highways was forced into a major plan revision when subsurface surveys revealed ENSTAR Natural Gas transmission mains and Chugach Electric underground feeders embedded in thaw-unstable permafrost soils. The original plan called for open-cut utility relocation, but engineers determined that thawing the permafrost corridor would destabilize adjacent building foundations. A new plan using horizontal directional drilling through stable bedrock added $28M and required a complete redesign of the interchange's southern approach. Completion slipped from 2026 to 2028.

projects.name: Tacoma Hilltop Neighborhood Complete Streets Utility Revision
projects.description: A Tacoma complete streets project in the Hilltop neighborhood required plan revisions after discovering unmapped military-era utility tunnels beneath MLK Jr Way.
projects.detail: Tacoma's $15M Hilltop Complete Streets project aimed to add protected bike lanes, new sidewalks, and ADA-compliant curb ramps along MLK Jr Way. During utility verification in 2024, crews discovered a network of unmapped concrete utility tunnels dating to the World War II era, likely associated with nearby Fort Steilacoom supply routes. These tunnels contained active PSE gas lines that had been threaded through the old military infrastructure. The entire street cross-section had to be redesigned to avoid disturbing the tunnel network, adding $3.5M in costs and an 8-month delay.

projects.name: Hilo Waianuenue Avenue Water and Sewer Upgrade Plan Revision
projects.description: Hilo's Waianuenue Avenue utility upgrade required a full redesign after encountering lava tube voids and uncharted HELCO electrical conduits.
projects.detail: Hawaii County's $20M water and sewer replacement project along Waianuenue Avenue in downtown Hilo was redesigned after subsurface investigations revealed lava tube voids intersecting the planned sewer alignment and uncharted HELCO (Hawaii Electric Light Company) high-voltage conduits running diagonally across the road corridor. The lava tubes made traditional open trench construction infeasible for a 400-foot section, requiring a switch to micro-tunneling methods. Combined with HELCO conduit relocation, the redesign added $5.8M and pushed completion from March 2025 to May 2026.

projects.name: Fairbanks Johansen Expressway Widening Utility Redesign
projects.description: The Johansen Expressway widening in Fairbanks required extensive plan revisions when Golden Valley Electric and Interior Gas Utility lines were found closer to the surface than mapped.
projects.detail: Alaska DOT's $58M Johansen Expressway widening project was designed to add a third lane in each direction through Fairbanks' commercial corridor. Preconstruction surveys in 2023 revealed that Golden Valley Electric Association transmission lines and Interior Gas Utility mains had shifted upward due to decades of frost heave, placing them within inches of the planned excavation grade. The new design required a deeper road profile and extensive utility protection measures, including thermal insulation systems to prevent further frost-related utility migration. The changes added $9.4M and 18 months to the schedule.

projects.name: Kodiak Near Island Bridge Replacement Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Kodiak's Near Island Bridge replacement project required a utility plan revision after discovering submarine cables and water lines attached to the existing bridge were in worse condition than assessed.
projects.detail: The Borough of Kodiak's $12.5M Near Island Bridge replacement project was designed with a temporary utility bypass for the submarine water main and Kodiak Electric Association cables attached to the old bridge. When divers inspected the existing utility attachments, they found severe corrosion on the water main brackets and degraded cable sheathing that made temporary relocation far more complex than planned. A new plan required installing permanent submarine utility conduits before bridge demolition could begin, adding $3.1M in costs and 10 months to the project timeline.

projects.name: Vancouver Waterfront Gateway Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Vancouver's waterfront gateway road project required a utility corridor redesign when Clark Public Utilities and NW Natural discovered conflicts between their respective underground facilities.
projects.detail: The City of Vancouver's $36M Waterfront Gateway road and infrastructure project was stalled during the design phase when Clark Public Utilities and NW Natural Gas conducted a joint utility review and discovered their underground facilities were far more intertwined than records indicated. A 1990s-era trenchless installation had placed NW Natural gas mains directly above Clark PUD electrical conduits in violation of separation requirements. The entire 1,800-foot utility corridor had to be redesigned with new separation standards, adding $6.2M and pushing the project opening from late 2025 to early 2027.

projects.name: Honolulu Ala Moana Boulevard Complete Streets Redesign
projects.description: The Ala Moana Boulevard complete streets redesign in Honolulu was derailed by discovery of HECO underground transmission lines and BWS water mains in direct conflict with the planned protected bike lanes.
projects.detail: Honolulu's $70M Ala Moana Boulevard Complete Streets project aimed to add protected bike lanes, wider sidewalks, and transit improvements along the iconic corridor. Subsurface utility engineering revealed that Hawaiian Electric Company underground transmission conduits and Board of Water Supply trunk mains occupied the exact footprint planned for the mauka-side protected bike lane. Relocating these facilities required coordination with both utilities plus the Navy (due to proximity to Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam infrastructure), adding $14M and 16 months. The redesign shifted the bike lane to the makai side, requiring additional right-of-way acquisition.

projects.name: Kapolei Farrington Highway Realignment Plan Revision
projects.description: The Farrington Highway realignment in Kapolei discovered a military fiber optic backbone and unrecorded Navy water mains, forcing a complete corridor redesign.
projects.detail: Hawaii DOT's $57M Farrington Highway realignment project through the rapidly growing Kapolei area was forced into a major plan revision when utility surveys encountered a Department of Defense fiber optic communications backbone and unrecorded Navy water mains dating to the Pearl Harbor supply corridor era. Military utility records had never been shared with civilian agencies. Relocating the DoD fiber required security clearances and a separate federal environmental review, adding $8.5M in costs and 14 months to the schedule. The realignment had to be shifted 30 feet south to avoid the most sensitive military infrastructure.

projects.name: Bellingham Meridian Street Complete Streets Plan Revision
projects.description: Bellingham's Meridian Street complete streets project required redesign after finding Cascade Natural Gas and PSE facilities co-located in a single trench violating separation codes.
projects.detail: The City of Bellingham's $12M Meridian Street Complete Streets project aimed to add bike lanes, pedestrian improvements, and stormwater infrastructure. During the 60% design phase, potholing revealed Cascade Natural Gas mains and Puget Sound Energy electrical conduits sharing a trench with only 6 inches of separation, violating the 36-inch code requirement. Both utilities disputed responsibility for the original installation. The redesign required establishing separated utility corridors and relocating approximately 1,100 linear feet of gas main, adding $2.1M and 6 months to the project. A joint utility agreement was eventually reached to share relocation costs.

projects.name: Astoria Bridge Approach Waterfront Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Astoria's waterfront bridge approach reconstruction was redesigned after encountering abandoned cannery-era pilings interlaced with active water and sewer lines.
projects.detail: The City of Astoria's $8M bridge approach reconstruction at the Columbia River waterfront hit unexpected complications when crews discovered that 1920s-era cannery pilings were structurally entangled with active city water mains and sewer lines. The wooden pilings had essentially become structural supports for the utility pipes over decades of soil settlement. Removing the pilings without first supporting the utilities was impossible. Engineers redesigned the approach to install new utility supports before piling removal, adding $1.9M and 8 months. Historical preservation advocates also required documentation of the cannery remains.

projects.name: Eugene West 11th Avenue Transit Corridor Utility Redesign
projects.description: Eugene's West 11th Avenue transit corridor project required a utility redesign after discovering EWEB underground electrical vaults in direct conflict with planned bus rapid transit station foundations.
projects.detail: Lane Transit District's $33M West 11th Avenue transit corridor improvement for the EmX BRT system was redesigned when preconstruction surveys found that Eugene Water & Electric Board underground electrical vaults and duct banks occupied the exact locations planned for three BRT station platforms. EWEB's 1970s-era underground infrastructure had been mapped at a lower resolution than modern SUE standards require. Relocating three major vault installations required EWEB to reroute power to hundreds of commercial customers during construction, adding $5.3M and a full year to the project. Several businesses filed claims for power interruption losses.

projects.name: Olympia Pacific Avenue SE Stormwater Upgrade Plan Revision
projects.description: Olympia's Pacific Avenue SE stormwater upgrade was redesigned after encountering state government campus utility lines running beneath the city right-of-way without recorded easements.
projects.detail: The City of Olympia's $8M Pacific Avenue SE stormwater upgrade project was intended to address chronic flooding near the state capitol campus. During design, engineers discovered that Washington State Department of Enterprise Services had utility conduits for the capitol campus running beneath the city's right-of-way with no recorded easement or as-built documentation. The state refused to allow city construction within 10 feet of their facilities without a new interagency agreement. Negotiating the agreement and redesigning the stormwater system to avoid state utilities added $1.6M and 5 months to the project.

projects.name: Kenmore Burke-Gilman Trail Extension Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Kenmore's Burke-Gilman Trail extension required a plan revision when PSE gas transmission lines were found running directly beneath the planned multi-use path alignment.
projects.detail: The City of Kenmore's $8M Burke-Gilman Trail extension project was redesigned after Puget Sound Energy identified a 12-inch gas transmission main running directly beneath the planned trail alignment for approximately 2,000 feet. PSE's pipeline safety requirements mandated a 25-foot setback from the transmission main for any new construction involving excavation. The trail alignment had to be shifted to the opposite side of the railroad right-of-way, requiring new retaining walls along a steep slope and an additional at-grade crossing. The revision added $1.8M and 7 months to the project.

projects.name: Nome Front Street Coastal Resilience Utility Redesign
projects.description: Nome's Front Street coastal resilience project required a utility redesign when gold mining-era water and sewer infrastructure was found in far worse condition than assessed.
projects.detail: The City of Nome's $25M Front Street coastal resilience project aimed to protect the downtown waterfront from increasingly severe Bering Sea storms. Engineers discovered that underground utilities dating to the early 1900s gold rush era were in such deteriorated condition that any construction vibration would likely cause catastrophic failures. Water mains made of wooden stave pipe and sewer lines of hand-laid stone were still active. The project was redesigned to include full utility replacement before the coastal protection work could begin, adding $4.7M and 15 months. The remote location and short construction season (May-September) compounded the delay.

projects.name: Springfield Oregon Main Street Gateway Utility Revision
projects.description: Springfield's Main Street gateway project was revised after SUB electrical conduits and Springfield Utility Board fiber were found conflicting with planned gateway monument foundations.
projects.detail: The City of Springfield's $12M Main Street Gateway project was designed to create a grand entrance to the downtown district with monument signs, landscaping, and road realignment. During the 90% design review, Springfield Utility Board identified conflicts between their electrical conduit bank, fiber optic network, and the planned gateway monument foundations. The monument structures required 8-foot-deep foundations that would encroach on SUB's underground facilities. Redesigning the monuments as surface-mounted structures and relocating 600 feet of fiber conduit added $2.3M and 6 months.

projects.name: Sitka Lincoln Street Bridge Utility Plan Revision
projects.description: Sitka's Lincoln Street bridge replacement over the Indian River was revised when the water main suspended beneath the bridge was found to be the sole supply for hospital and Coast Guard facilities.
projects.detail: The City and Borough of Sitka's $10M Lincoln Street bridge replacement over the Indian River was redesigned when engineers determined the 10-inch water main suspended beneath the existing bridge was the sole water supply for Sitka Community Hospital and the nearby Coast Guard Air Station.
