The original plan assumed a 6-week water service interruption during bridge demolition, but neither the hospital nor the Coast Guard could tolerate any interruption. A temporary above-ground bypass water main with freeze protection (essential in Sitka's climate) had to be designed and installed, adding $1.5M and 8 months.

projects.name: Longview Industrial Way Railroad Underpass Utility Revision
projects.description: Longview's Industrial Way railroad underpass project was revised when BNSF utility conduits and Cowlitz PUD facilities were found interleaved beneath the railroad right-of-way.
projects.detail: The City of Longview's $16M Industrial Way railroad underpass project was intended to eliminate a dangerous at-grade crossing. During the final design phase, BNSF Railway and Cowlitz County PUD revealed utility conflicts that neither had previously disclosed: BNSF signal cables, fiber optic communications, and Cowlitz PUD electrical feeders were interleaved in a shared utility corridor beneath the tracks. Separating these utilities required a new jacking and boring plan that could maintain railroad operations throughout construction. The revision added $3.4M and 10 months, and required BNSF approval at every stage.

projects.name: WSDOT SR 522 Corridor Improvements Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: PSE and Northshore Utility District could not coordinate their relocation schedules for the SR 522 corridor improvements, leaving WSDOT unable to proceed with road construction.
projects.detail: WSDOT's $120M SR 522 corridor improvement project through Bothell was delayed by 18 months due to irreconcilable scheduling conflicts between Puget Sound Energy and the Northshore Utility District. PSE needed to relocate gas and electric facilities first, but their crews were committed to other mandated relocation projects through 2025. Northshore Utility District's water main relocation could not begin until PSE finished, creating a cascading delay. WSDOT's construction contractor filed a $5M delay claim, and the total project overrun reached $12M. The dispute highlighted the lack of a statewide utility coordination mandate in Washington.

projects.name: Portland SE Division Street BRT Utility Scheduling Delays
projects.description: TriMet's Division Street BRT project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between PGE, NW Natural, and the Portland Water Bureau, each insisting the other relocate first.
projects.detail: TriMet's $95M Division Transit Project along SE Division Street was hampered by a three-way scheduling conflict between Portland General Electric, NW Natural Gas, and the Portland Water Bureau. Each utility insisted their relocation had to follow the other's work, creating a circular dependency. PGE refused to move electrical conduits until NW Natural relocated gas mains; NW Natural would not begin until the Water Bureau moved water lines; and the Water Bureau would not start until PGE cleared the electrical facilities. The stalemate required intervention from the Oregon PUC and added $8.4M in costs and 14 months of delay. TriMet ultimately paid for expedited relocations to break the deadlock.

projects.name: Honolulu Kamehameha Highway Widening Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: HDOT's Kamehameha Highway widening was stalled for nearly two years by scheduling conflicts between HECO, Hawaiian Telcom, and the Navy's Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam utility office.
projects.detail: Hawaii DOT's $80M Kamehameha Highway widening project through Pearl City was paralyzed by scheduling conflicts between three entities that each controlled underground utilities beneath the corridor. Hawaiian Electric Company could only perform relocations during planned outage windows that occurred quarterly; Hawaiian Telcom had a crew shortage and could not schedule work for 14 months; and the Navy's Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam utility office required a 12-month federal review before any work near military infrastructure could be approved. The cumulative scheduling conflicts added $15M and 20 months. HDOT eventually hired a dedicated utility coordinator to manage the three-party schedule.

projects.name: Anchorage Tudor Road Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Delays
projects.description: Anchorage's Tudor Road reconstruction lost two construction seasons to scheduling conflicts between ENSTAR gas, Chugach Electric, and AWWU, each constrained by Alaska's short building window.
projects.detail: The Municipality of Anchorage's $60M Tudor Road reconstruction project was devastated by scheduling conflicts unique to Alaska's short May-October construction season. ENSTAR Natural Gas could only relocate mains during the summer when ground was thawed; Chugach Electric Association was committed to a wildfire-related emergency rebuild during the 2024 season; and Anchorage Water and Wastewater Utility required 8 weeks of continuous warm weather for pipe curing. With only five usable months per year and three utilities competing for the same window, the project lost two full construction seasons. The $7.8M overrun included contractor standby costs and materials escalation.

projects.name: Spokane Division Street Corridor Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Spokane's Division Street corridor project was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Avista Utilities and Inland Empire Paper Company's private industrial water line.
projects.detail: The City of Spokane's $30M Division Street corridor improvement project was stalled when Avista Utilities and Inland Empire Paper Company could not agree on a schedule for relocating their respective underground facilities. Avista's gas and electric lines needed to be moved before the Paper Company's private industrial water supply line could be rerouted, but Avista was committed to a rate-case-mandated infrastructure replacement program that consumed their crew capacity. The Paper Company threatened legal action if their water supply was interrupted during production season. Resolution required a city-brokered agreement and $4.5M in additional costs over 11 months.

projects.name: Corvallis NW 9th Street Utility Coordination Delays
projects.description: Corvallis's NW 9th Street reconstruction was delayed when Pacific Power and Comcast could not coordinate utility relocation schedules with the city's stormwater work.
projects.detail: The City of Corvallis's $8M NW 9th Street reconstruction project was designed to upgrade stormwater infrastructure, replace aging water mains, and resurface the road. Pacific Power needed to relocate overhead-to-underground electrical service, but their schedule conflicted with Comcast's planned fiber upgrade in the same corridor. Neither utility would begin work while the other was in the right-of-way, and both required access to the same trench space. The 7-month delay cost the city $1.4M in contractor standby fees and materials price escalation. The city council subsequently passed an ordinance requiring joint utility trenching for future projects.

projects.name: Maui Lahaina Bypass Route Utility Scheduling Delays
projects.description: The Lahaina Bypass route utility relocation was delayed by scheduling conflicts between MECO, Maui County water, and post-wildfire emergency infrastructure competing for the same utility crews.
projects.detail: Hawaii DOT's $130M Lahaina Bypass road project, already critically important after the 2023 wildfires, was further delayed when utility scheduling conflicts consumed two and a half years. MECO's utility crews were diverted to wildfire recovery restoration, leaving no capacity for bypass road relocations. Maui County's water department was simultaneously rebuilding the fire-destroyed water distribution system and could not schedule bypass road water main installations. The competition for limited utility crews on Maui, where specialized labor must be brought from Oahu, inflated costs by $22M. Federal disaster recovery funds were redirected to cover part of the overrun.

projects.name: Juneau Glacier Highway Rehabilitation Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Alaska DOT's Glacier Highway rehabilitation near Juneau was delayed by scheduling conflicts with AEL&P and Alaska Communications, both limited to summer-only work windows.
projects.detail: Alaska DOT's $40M Glacier Highway rehabilitation project between Juneau and Auke Bay was delayed 16 months by scheduling conflicts between Alaska Electric Light & Power and Alaska Communications Systems. Both utilities could only perform underground work during the May-September window when ground conditions permitted excavation. AEL&P's hydroelectric infrastructure maintenance schedule consumed their summer 2024 crew capacity, while Alaska Communications had committed to a federal broadband grant project requiring simultaneous fiber installation elsewhere in Southeast Alaska. The sequential delays cost $5.6M in mobilization and standby charges for the road contractor.

projects.name: Yakima West Nob Hill Boulevard Widening Utility Delay
projects.description: Yakima's Nob Hill Boulevard widening was delayed when Pacific Power and Cascade Natural Gas scheduling conflicts with irrigaton district infrastructure left no clear work window.
projects.detail: The City of Yakima's $20M West Nob Hill Boulevard widening project was caught in a three-way scheduling conflict between Pacific Power, Cascade Natural Gas, and the Yakima-Tieton Irrigation District. The irrigation district's underground pressurized canals could only be worked on during the November-March off-season, but Pacific Power could not schedule crews during winter months due to storm response commitments. Cascade Natural Gas required Pacific Power to relocate first due to safety separation requirements. The resulting 9-month delay added $2.7M in costs, primarily from contractor standby fees and construction material price inflation.

projects.name: Kona Queen Kaahumanu Highway Widening Schedule Conflict
projects.description: Hawaii DOT's Queen Kaahumanu Highway widening was delayed by scheduling conflicts between HELCO, DHHL water infrastructure, and resort developers competing for utility contractor crews.
projects.detail: Hawaii DOT's $120M Queen Kaahumanu Highway widening on the Big Island's Kona coast was severely delayed by competing demands on utility infrastructure crews. Hawaii Electric Light Company was simultaneously upgrading substations for new solar farms; the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands was installing water infrastructure for a major homestead development; and several resort developers were building utility connections on the same corridor. With only two qualified utility contractors on the Big Island, scheduling conflicts stretched the utility relocation phase from 18 months to over three years. The $18M overrun included contractor mobilization costs and asphalt price escalation.

projects.name: Palmer-Wasilla Highway Water Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: The Palmer-Wasilla Highway widening was delayed when Matanuska Electric Association and the Mat-Su Borough water utility could not align their construction schedules within Alaska's short season.
projects.detail: Alaska DOT's $56M Palmer-Wasilla Highway widening was delayed by 14 months due to scheduling conflicts between Matanuska Electric Association and the Matanuska-Susitna Borough water utility. MEA's underground electrical relocation required a 10-week window of frost-free conditions, but the Borough's water utility had already reserved the same May-July 2024 period for emergency water main repairs elsewhere in the system. When MEA's work slipped to August-October, early freeze conditions in late September halted work mid-relocation. The project lost the entire 2024 season and had to resume in May 2025, adding $6.3M in costs.

projects.name: Walla Walla Isaacs Avenue Reconstruction Utility Scheduling
projects.description: Walla Walla's Isaacs Avenue reconstruction was delayed when Pacific Power and Cascade Natural Gas could not align schedules due to competing wildfire hardening programs.
projects.detail: The City of Walla Walla's $8M Isaacs Avenue reconstruction project was delayed 5 months by scheduling conflicts between Pacific Power and Cascade Natural Gas. Both utilities had been ordered by state regulators to prioritize wildfire hardening programs in eastern Washington, which consumed their crew capacity through summer 2025. The road project's utility relocation was repeatedly bumped from the schedule as wildfire-related work took priority. The $1.1M overrun covered contractor delay claims and the cost of maintaining temporary traffic controls for an extended period.

projects.name: Kauai Kapaa Bypass Road Utility Scheduling Impasse
projects.description: The Kapaa Bypass Road extension on Kauai was stalled by scheduling conflicts between KIUC, the Department of Water, and a private agricultural irrigation cooperative.
projects.detail: Hawaii DOT's $58M Kapaa Bypass Road extension was stalled for 19 months by a three-way scheduling conflict. Kauai Island Utility Cooperative needed to relocate underground power lines but could only schedule outages during periods of low tourist demand. The County Department of Water's crews were committed to a federal consent decree project. And the Kapaa Irrigation Cooperative, which controlled plantation-era agricultural water lines crossing the corridor, could not agree on relocation terms for their private infrastructure. The impasse required legislative intervention and $9.3M in additional costs, including compensation to the irrigation cooperative for easement acquisition.

projects.name: Albany Ellsworth Street Bridge Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Albany's Ellsworth Street Bridge replacement over the Calapooia River was delayed when Pacific Power and the city's own water division could not coordinate shutdown schedules.
projects.detail: The City of Albany's $10M Ellsworth Street Bridge replacement over the Calapooia River was delayed 7 months due to scheduling conflicts between Pacific Power and Albany's own Public Works water division. Pacific Power needed to relocate aerial-to-underground electrical conversion during a planned system outage in September 2025, but the water division had scheduled its annual main flushing program for the same period, which would have pressurized pipes near the electrical work zone. Neither schedule could flex, and the bridge contractor sat idle while the city resolved an internal scheduling conflict with an external utility. The $1.7M overrun embarrassed city officials.

projects.name: Kenai Peninsula Sterling Highway Utility Scheduling Delays
projects.description: Alaska DOT's Sterling Highway realignment near Cooper Landing lost two full construction seasons due to Homer Electric Association and GCI fiber scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: Alaska DOT's $175M Sterling Highway realignment near Cooper Landing, one of Alaska's most critical road projects, was delayed two full years by utility scheduling conflicts. Homer Electric Association could only perform line relocation during the brief June-September window, but GCI's fiber optic installation crew (the sole qualified team in the Kenai Peninsula) was committed to a federal rural broadband project during the same period. With only one viable work season per year and competing federal mandates, each utility pushed the other's schedule by a full year. The $16M overrun included equipment storage costs through two Alaskan winters and contract escalation clauses.

projects.name: Lihue Kuhio Highway Utility Scheduling Bottleneck
projects.description: Kauai's Kuhio Highway improvement was delayed by scheduling conflicts among KIUC, Charter Communications, and the county water department, all needing the same contractor.
projects.detail: Hawaii DOT's $48M Kuhio Highway improvement in Lihue was delayed 15 months by a scheduling bottleneck: the only qualified underground utility contractor on Kauai was simultaneously needed by KIUC for electrical relocation, Charter Communications for fiber installation, and the County of Kauai Department of Water for main replacement. Each entity had scheduled their work assuming exclusive access to the contractor during overlapping periods. The contractor could only serve one client at a time, creating sequential delays that rippled through the highway project. The $6.8M overrun included premium costs to fly in a mainland utility crew for one phase of work.

projects.name: Marysville State Avenue Corridor Utility Coordination Failure
projects.description: Marysville's State Avenue corridor project lost 9 months when Snohomish County PUD and Cascade Natural Gas disputed which utility bore the obligation to relocate first.
projects.detail: The City of Marysville's $20M State Avenue corridor improvement project was delayed 9 months by a dispute between Snohomish County PUD and Cascade Natural Gas over which utility was obligated to relocate first. Both utilities cited franchise agreement clauses placing the other's relocation as a precondition. The city's franchise agreements with each utility had been written decades apart and contained contradictory priority provisions. Legal review consumed 4 months before a mediated resolution was reached, followed by 5 months of actual utility relocation. The $3.3M overrun included legal fees, contractor delay claims, and extended traffic management.

projects.name: Seattle Rainier Avenue S Fiber Strike and Gas Main Rupture
projects.description: A contractor boring for new stormwater infrastructure on Rainier Avenue S struck a PSE gas main and severed a CenturyLink fiber trunk line, causing a 6-block evacuation and service outage.
projects.detail: During the City of Seattle's Rainier Avenue S stormwater improvement project in 2025, a horizontal directional drilling crew struck a 6-inch Puget Sound Energy gas main at 4 feet below grade and simultaneously severed a CenturyLink fiber optic trunk line. The gas rupture forced evacuation of a 6-block commercial corridor for 8 hours, including a busy Vietnamese restaurant district. The fiber cut disrupted internet service to approximately 3,000 customers for 36 hours. Investigation revealed that the utility locate marks were 4 feet off from actual pipe position due to a GIS database error dating to a 2018 system migration. The incident added $2.8M in emergency repairs, utility restoration, and business interruption claims.
projects.timeline: Project delayed 4 months for safety review and re-survey

projects.name: Portland NE Sandy Boulevard Water Main Strike During Road Work
projects.description: A road reconstruction crew on NE Sandy Boulevard struck a 16-inch Portland Water Bureau main, flooding the Hollywood district and shutting down a transit hub.
projects.detail: During PBOT's NE Sandy Boulevard road reconstruction project in the Hollywood district, an excavator struck a 16-inch Portland Water Bureau transmission main in March 2025. The strike caused a geyser that flooded the TriMet Hollywood Transit Center and nearby businesses, sending approximately 2 million gallons of water into the street before crews could shut the valve. The transit center was closed for 5 days and three businesses suffered water damage totaling $400K. The water main had been installed in 1952 and was 3 feet shallower than shown on utility records due to decades of road resurfacing that had raised the street grade. The project was delayed 3 months for main repair and utility re-verification.

projects.name: Fairbanks Airport Way Water Main Strike During Widening
projects.description: Alaska DOT's Airport Way widening project struck a Golden Heart Utilities water main, creating a massive ice sheet on the road during September freeze conditions.
projects.detail: During Alaska DOT's Airport Way widening project in Fairbanks in September 2024, an excavator struck a 12-inch Golden Heart Utilities water transmission main. The broken main released water that, due to sub-freezing temperatures, immediately began forming a massive ice sheet across all lanes of Airport Way. The ice sheet grew to cover approximately 800 feet of roadway before the main was shut off, causing a 14-vehicle accident chain that injured 6 people. Cleanup required industrial ice-melting equipment and took 4 days. The unique Alaskan challenge of water main strikes in freezing conditions added complexity to the repair. Total costs reached $2.1M including emergency response, main repair, road damage, and accident-related claims.

projects.name: Kennewick Columbia Center Boulevard Gas Line Strike
projects.description: A road widening project on Columbia Center Boulevard struck a Cascade Natural Gas main, forcing evacuation of the Columbia Center Mall parking structure.
projects.detail: During the City of Kennewick's Columbia Center Boulevard widening project in 2024, a grading crew's equipment struck a 6-inch Cascade Natural Gas distribution main near the entrance to Columbia Center Mall. The gas leak forced evacuation of the mall's multi-level parking structure and nearby retail stores, affecting approximately 2,000 shoppers during a holiday weekend. Gas service to the mall was interrupted for 18 hours while Cascade Natural Gas completed emergency repairs. The strike occurred in an area where previous road improvements had altered the surface grade, leaving the gas main only 14 inches below the current road surface instead of the standard 36 inches. The incident cost $1.1M and delayed the project 7 weeks.

projects.name: Honolulu King Street Repaving HECO Underground Work Violation
projects.description: Hawaiian Electric cut open newly repaved King Street in downtown Honolulu just 3 months after a $8M complete streets project, destroying new crosswalks and bus pads.
projects.detail: Hawaiian Electric Company cut into South King Street in downtown Honolulu just 3 months after the city completed an $8M complete streets project that included new concrete bus pads, decorative crosswalks, and ADA-compliant curb ramps. HECO claimed the cuts were necessary for underground cable replacement that had not been coordinated with the city's project schedule despite 2 years of advance notice. The cuts destroyed 6 new bus pads and 4 decorative crosswalks. HECO's patch restoration was widely criticized for using mismatched concrete. The $2.4M damage estimate included replacing the destroyed infrastructure to match the original design. The incident prompted the Honolulu City Council to consider a utility coordination ordinance modeled on San Jose's approach.

projects.name: Anchorage Spenard Road Repaving ENSTAR Moratorium Violation
projects.description: ENSTAR Natural Gas cut into freshly repaved Spenard Road 5 months after the municipality completed a $5M road rehabilitation, destroying new pavement and sidewalks.
projects.detail: ENSTAR Natural Gas cut into Spenard Road in Anchorage just 5 months after the Municipality of Anchorage completed a $5M road rehabilitation project that included new pavement, sidewalks, and pedestrian lighting. ENSTAR claimed the work was needed for a gas main upgrade to serve new commercial development along the corridor. The cuts destroyed approximately 600 linear feet of new sidewalk and left asphalt patches in the fresh pavement. The municipality estimated $980K in damage, noting that Anchorage's short summer construction season meant the repairs could not be properly completed until the following year, leaving patched surfaces through an entire winter freeze-thaw cycle that further degraded the road.

projects.name: Hillsboro Tualatin Valley Highway Repaving Comcast Moratorium Violation
projects.description: Comcast cut into Tualatin Valley Highway 9 months after ODOT completed a $7M resurfacing, destroying new bike lane striping and ADA ramps.
projects.detail: Comcast cut into Tualatin Valley Highway through Hillsboro just 9 months after ODOT completed a $7M resurfacing project that included new bike lane striping, ADA-compliant curb ramps, and signal loop detectors. Comcast was upgrading fiber optic trunk lines for their business service division. The cuts destroyed 1,500 feet of new bike lane striping, damaged 4 ADA ramps, and severed signal detection loops at two intersections, causing traffic signal malfunctions for 3 days. ODOT's damage assessment reached $1.1M, which included replacing signal detection equipment and full-depth pavement restoration. The incident prompted ODOT to propose legislation strengthening Oregon's moratorium enforcement provisions.

projects.name: Issaquah Front Street Streetscape Utility Cut Violation
projects.description: CenturyLink cut into Issaquah's newly completed Front Street streetscape 5 months after a $3M historic district renovation, damaging heritage brick pavement.
projects.detail: CenturyLink (Lumen Technologies) cut into Front Street in Issaquah's historic downtown district just 5 months after the city completed a $3M streetscape renovation featuring heritage brick pavement, period-style lighting, and custom tree grates. CenturyLink was upgrading underground conduit for fiber service to nearby businesses. The cuts destroyed 450 square feet of hand-laid heritage brick pavement that had been specially sourced from a historic brick manufacturer. CenturyLink's restoration with standard asphalt was immediately rejected by the city, which demanded matching brick restoration at an estimated cost of $650K. The Issaquah Historic Commission cited the incident as evidence that utilities routinely disregard historic preservation requirements.

projects.name: Wenatchee North Wenatchee Avenue Corridor Utility Redesign
projects.description: Wenatchee's North Wenatchee Avenue corridor project required a utility redesign after discovering Chelan County PUD and Cascade Natural Gas facilities in an undocumented shared trench.
projects.detail: The City of Wenatchee's $13M North Wenatchee Avenue corridor improvement project was forced into a plan revision when potholing revealed that Chelan County PUD electrical conduits and Cascade Natural Gas mains shared an undocumented joint trench beneath the planned road widening footprint. The shared trench violated utility separation codes and neither utility had records of the arrangement, which likely dated to 1960s-era construction. Disentangling the utilities required creating two separate utility corridors, adding $2.6M in redesign and relocation costs and 8 months of delay. The project also discovered an abandoned apple packing plant's private water line still connected to the city system.

projects.name: Kirkland Totem Lake Boulevard Utility Scheduling Stall
projects.description: Kirkland's Totem Lake Boulevard reconstruction lost 10 months to scheduling conflicts between PSE, Northshore Utility District, and a Microsoft campus expansion contractor.
projects.detail: The City of Kirkland's $40M Totem Lake Boulevard reconstruction was delayed by a three-way scheduling conflict between Puget Sound Energy, the Northshore Utility District, and a private contractor performing utility work for Microsoft's adjacent campus expansion. PSE and Northshore could not agree on relocation sequencing, and Microsoft's contractor had reserved the only qualified horizontal directional drilling crew in the Eastside region for their campus project through fall 2025. With no available drilling crews, the city's contractor sat idle for 10 months. The $4.8M overrun covered contractor standby costs and temporary traffic management through the extended construction zone.

projects.name: Hood River Cascade Avenue Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Hood River's Cascade Avenue reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts between Pacific Power, Hood River Electric Cooperative, and the irrigation district.
projects.detail: The City of Hood River's $8M Cascade Avenue reconstruction project was delayed 6 months when Pacific Power, Hood River Electric Cooperative, and the Farmers Irrigation District could not coordinate utility relocation schedules. The irrigation district's pressurized lines could only be modified during the November-March off-season, but Pacific Power's crew was allocated to a wildfire hardening project during the same winter period. Hood River Electric Cooperative would not begin their relocation until both other utilities had completed their work. The cascading scheduling conflicts added $1.3M to the project, primarily in contractor standby fees and construction material price escalation during the 6-month idle period.

projects.name: Kodiak Rezanof Drive Reconstruction MEA Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Kodiak's Rezanof Drive reconstruction lost a full construction season when Kodiak Electric Association and the city water department could not align work windows.
projects.detail: The Borough of Kodiak's $12M Rezanof Drive reconstruction was delayed a full year when Kodiak Electric Association and the city's water department could not coordinate their underground work schedules. KEA's sole underground crew was committed to repairing storm-damaged infrastructure through summer 2025, while the water department's pipe replacement required KEA to de-energize cables first. Kodiak's remote island location meant no mainland utility crews could be economically brought in for the short work season. The project lost the entire 2025 construction season and had to wait until May 2026 to resume. The $1.8M overrun included equipment winterization, re-mobilization, and materials storage on the island.

projects.name: Ketchikan Tongass Avenue Fiber Installation Water Main Strike
projects.description: A broadband fiber boring crew on Tongass Avenue struck a KPU water main, flooding the parking lot of Ketchikan General Hospital.
projects.detail: During a GCI broadband fiber installation along Tongass Avenue in Ketchikan in 2025, a horizontal directional drilling crew struck a 10-inch Ketchikan Public Utilities water main near Ketchikan General Hospital. The pressurized break flooded the hospital parking lot and sent water into the hospital's lower-level mechanical room before KPU could isolate the break. The hospital was forced to reroute ambulances to the emergency entrance for 8 hours while the parking lot was cleared. The water main was a ductile iron pipe installed in the 1980s that had settled 18 inches from its mapped position in the rainforest-saturated soil. The $390K cost included emergency water main repair, hospital cleanup, and a 3-week fiber project halt.

projects.name: Concord I-93 Exit 15-S Diverging Diamond Interchange
projects.description: Redesign required when subsurface utility mapping revealed unmapped sewer and telecom conduits crossing the planned interchange footprint.
projects.detail: The I-93 Exit 15-S diverging diamond interchange project in Concord was designed to improve traffic flow near the hospital district. During early excavation, crews discovered unmapped sewer lines and telecom conduits that were not reflected in existing utility records. NHDOT had to halt work and commission a full subsurface utility engineering survey, leading to a revised design that shifted the diamond geometry by 15 feet. The redesign added $4.2 million to the $30 million project and pushed completion back by nearly a year.

projects.name: Bennington VT Route 7/Route 9 Intersection Reconstruction
projects.description: Intersection reconstruction plans required a complete overhaul after survey discovered intertwined water mains and gas service lines from multiple eras.
projects.detail: The Route 7/Route 9 intersection in Bennington, a key junction for southern Vermont traffic, was slated for modernization with new turn lanes and signal upgrades. Pre-construction boring revealed a tangle of water mains dating from the 1920s through the 1990s intermixed with active gas service lines that were not accurately mapped. VTrans had to redesign the entire underground utility corridor before surface work could proceed, adding $2.8 million to the $14.7 million project and delaying completion by eight months.

projects.name: Saco ME Route 1 Corridor Widening
projects.description: Route 1 widening required plan revisions after discovering undocumented fiber optic and gas infrastructure beneath the shoulders.
projects.detail: MaineDOT initiated a widening of Route 1 through Saco to add center turn lanes and improve pedestrian facilities in the commercial corridor. Early excavation uncovered fiber optic trunk lines and gas distribution mains that were not shown on any utility maps provided during the design phase. Engineers had to redesign the roadway cross-section to accommodate the existing utilities, adding retaining walls and shifting storm drainage. The revisions added $3.5 million to the original $22 million budget and pushed substantial completion back by nearly a year.

projects.name: Milford DE Route 113 Bypass Utility Relocation Redesign
projects.description: Bypass construction required significant plan revision when a high-pressure gas transmission line was found offset from its recorded location by 40 feet.
projects.detail: DelDOT's Route 113 bypass project in Milford was designed to relieve congestion through the downtown commercial area. During pre-construction verification, a high-pressure gas transmission line operated by Eastern Shore Natural Gas was discovered 40 feet from its mapped position, directly in the path of the new interchange ramps. The utility relocation required a complete redesign of the interchange geometry and coordination with FERC-regulated pipeline safety protocols. The changes added $5.1 million to the $42.5 million project and delayed construction by over a year.

projects.name: Bowling Green KY US-231 Connector Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: US-231 connector project in Bowling Green required a utility corridor redesign after unmapped telecommunications and water infrastructure was found at the interchange site.
projects.detail: The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet initiated a US-231 connector improvement to address growing traffic demands near the Bowling Green commercial district. During design validation, subsurface utility engineering revealed a cluster of unmapped AT&T fiber trunk lines, water distribution mains, and a decommissioned but still pressurized gas service line at the planned interchange location. The discovery forced a redesign of the interchange grading plan and the addition of a utility bridge structure. The changes added $3.7 million to the $24.5 million project and pushed completion back by a full year.

projects.name: Meridian MS Highway 39 North Widening
projects.description: Highway 39 widening through Meridian required a plan revision when survey found a major water transmission main and telecom conduit bank conflicting with the new lanes.
projects.detail: MDOT planned to widen Highway 39 North through the growing commercial corridor in Meridian from two to four lanes with a center turn lane. Subsurface investigation discovered a 24-inch water transmission main and a bank of telecom conduits running diagonally beneath the planned new southbound lanes. The water main served the entire northeast quadrant of the city and could not be easily relocated. Engineers redesigned the lane geometry to avoid the main and added a utility easement, increasing the project cost by $2.6 million over the $15.3 million budget and delaying work by ten months.

projects.name: Devils Lake ND Highway 2 Flood Protection Infrastructure
projects.description: Flood protection road raising on Highway 2 required redesign when underground utility conflicts were far more extensive than pre-construction surveys indicated.
projects.detail: The Highway 2 flood protection project in Devils Lake involved raising the road grade and adding flood barriers to protect the city from rising lake levels. Pre-construction surveys significantly underestimated the density of underground utilities beneath the highway, including water mains, sewer force mains, gas distribution lines, and telecommunications conduits that all needed to be raised or relocated with the road. NDDOT had to commission a comprehensive subsurface utility engineering study and revise the road-raising plan to accommodate sequential utility relocations. The revisions added $4.8 million to the $36.8 million project and delayed completion by over a year.

projects.name: Huron SD Dakota Avenue Reconstruction
projects.description: Dakota Avenue reconstruction in Huron required plan revisions after century-old clay tile sewer mains were discovered at depths different from city records.
projects.detail: The City of Huron undertook a reconstruction of Dakota Avenue, the main commercial corridor, to replace aging pavement and improve stormwater drainage. Excavation revealed century-old clay tile sewer mains at depths significantly different from what city utility records indicated, along with abandoned water service lines that still held residual pressure. The discovery required a revised excavation plan and additional shoring to protect the fragile sewer infrastructure during road reconstruction. The changes added $1.4 million to the $6.3 million project and delayed work by six months.

projects.name: McCook NE US-6/US-34 Intersection Reconstruction
projects.description: Intersection reconstruction required redesign after discovering an unmapped high-pressure natural gas line beneath the planned roundabout center.
projects.detail: NDOR planned a modern roundabout at the US-6/US-34 intersection in McCook to improve safety and traffic flow. During design-phase boring, an unmapped high-pressure natural gas transmission line was discovered running directly beneath the center of the proposed roundabout. The line was operated by a regional pipeline company and required a minimum clearance that the roundabout design could not provide. Engineers had to shift the entire roundabout footprint 25 feet to the northeast, requiring additional right-of-way acquisition and utility easement negotiations. The revisions added $1.8 million to the $9 million project.

projects.name: Dodge City KS Wyatt Earp Boulevard Reconstruction
projects.description: Boulevard reconstruction in Dodge City required redesign when multiple layers of uncharted utility infrastructure from different eras were found beneath the roadway.
projects.detail: Dodge City initiated a full reconstruction of Wyatt Earp Boulevard, the primary east-west commercial corridor, to replace deteriorating pavement and upgrade drainage. Excavation revealed multiple layers of utility infrastructure from different construction eras, including cast iron water mains from the 1930s, asbestos cement pipe from the 1960s, and fiber optic conduit from the 2000s, none of which matched available utility records. KDOT and city engineers had to redesign the underground utility corridor to safely separate and protect each utility system before surface reconstruction could proceed. The revisions added $2.1 million to the $13 million project.

projects.name: Kalispell MT US-2 West Corridor Widening
projects.description: US-2 corridor widening required plan changes after discovering irrigation canal infrastructure and fiber optic trunk lines conflicting with the new lane alignments.
projects.detail: MDT planned to widen US-2 west of Kalispell from two lanes to four to handle growing traffic from the Glacier Park tourism corridor. Design-phase subsurface investigation revealed an active irrigation canal infrastructure with pressurized laterals and fiber optic trunk lines that were not reflected in MDT utility databases. The irrigation district's infrastructure predated the highway and had senior water rights, requiring MDT to redesign the widening to accommodate the canal system in place. The changes added $3.2 million to the $23 million project and pushed completion back nine months.

projects.name: Rawlins WY Interstate 80 Business Loop Reconstruction
projects.description: I-80 business loop reconstruction required plan revisions when an oil pipeline spur line was discovered beneath the planned reconstruction zone.
projects.detail: WYDOT initiated reconstruction of the I-80 business loop through Rawlins to address severe pavement deterioration and drainage issues. During pre-construction investigation, an oil pipeline spur line dating from the energy boom era was discovered running beneath the roadway at a depth that conflicted with the planned storm drain installation. The pipeline was still connected to regional infrastructure and required environmental assessment before it could be relocated or abandoned in place. WYDOT revised the storm drainage design to route around the pipeline, adding $1.6 million to the $8.9 million project.

projects.name: Taos NM Paseo del Pueblo Norte Streetscape
projects.description: Streetscape redesign needed after discovering acequia irrigation channels and unmapped gas lines beneath the historic Taos commercial corridor.
projects.detail: The Town of Taos launched a streetscape improvement project on Paseo del Pueblo Norte to enhance pedestrian facilities and upgrade aging water infrastructure in the historic commercial district. Excavation uncovered active acequia irrigation channels that were protected under New Mexico water law, along with unmapped natural gas distribution lines. The acequia channels, some dating to the Spanish colonial era, had legal protections that required the town to redesign the streetscape to avoid any disruption to the historic water system. The revisions added $2.4 million to the $12 million project and delayed completion by nearly a year.

projects.name: Wahiawa HI Kamehameha Highway Improvements
projects.description: Highway improvements required plan revisions when military-era utility infrastructure from the nearby Schofield Barracks was discovered conflicting with the road alignment.
projects.detail: HDOT planned improvements to Kamehameha Highway through Wahiawa to address congestion and safety concerns in the corridor between Schofield Barracks and Wheeler Army Airfield. Subsurface investigation revealed military-era utility infrastructure including communications conduits, water mains, and abandoned fuel transfer lines that extended well beyond the known military installation boundaries. Coordination with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers was required to determine which lines were active and which could be abandoned, adding significant time to the design process. The revisions added $6.3 million to the $39.4 million project and delayed construction by over a year.

projects.name: Kodiak AK Mill Bay Road Rehabilitation
projects.description: Road rehabilitation plans required revision after unmapped military communications cables and water mains from the WWII-era Coast Guard base were found beneath the roadway.
projects.detail: The Alaska DOT initiated rehabilitation of Mill Bay Road in Kodiak to address severe frost heave damage and drainage deficiencies. During excavation, crews discovered unmapped military communications cables and water mains dating from the World War II era Coast Guard installation. Some cables were still in active use by the Coast Guard, requiring coordination with federal authorities before any relocation could occur. AKDOT had to redesign the drainage system and pavement structure to work around the military infrastructure, adding $2.9 million to the $12.6 million project and extending the timeline by ten months.

projects.name: Elkins WV Corridor H Connector Road Utility Redesign
projects.description: Connector road from Corridor H to downtown Elkins required plan revisions when abandoned mine drainage infrastructure and active gas lines were discovered at the interchange site.
projects.detail: The WV Division of Highways planned a connector road from the Corridor H (Appalachian Development Highway) terminus to downtown Elkins to improve regional access. During design verification, engineers discovered abandoned mine drainage infrastructure, including acid mine drainage treatment pipes and settling basins, along with active Mountaineer Gas distribution lines at the planned interchange site. The mine drainage system was under DEP environmental monitoring and could not be disturbed without remediation. Engineers redesigned the interchange to avoid the mine drainage infrastructure, adding $3.1 million to the $20.7 million project.

projects.name: Paducah KY US-60 Bridge Approach Reconstruction
projects.description: Bridge approach reconstruction required revised plans after a cluster of previously unmapped TVA transmission conduits and water mains were found at the interchange site.
projects.detail: KYTC planned a reconstruction of the US-60 bridge approach and interchange near downtown Paducah to improve safety and accommodate heavier traffic loads. Subsurface investigation discovered a cluster of TVA-era transmission conduits, city water mains, and telecommunications lines that were unmapped or incorrectly located in utility databases. The TVA conduits carried critical regional transmission infrastructure and required extensive coordination with federal authorities for any relocation. Engineers redesigned the bridge approach to span over the utility cluster rather than excavate through it, adding $4.5 million to the $34.6 million project.

projects.name: Tupelo MS Main Street Utility Corridor Modernization
projects.description: Main Street modernization required plan revisions after discovery of TVA-era electrical conduits and abandoned gas infrastructure complicating the utility corridor design.
projects.detail: The City of Tupelo launched a Main Street utility corridor modernization to replace aging water and sewer lines and add modern telecommunications conduit in the downtown area. Excavation revealed TVA-era electrical conduits that were still in active service along with abandoned gas infrastructure that required environmental assessment before removal. The active TVA conduits could not be relocated without a lengthy federal coordination process, forcing city engineers to redesign the new utility corridor to thread around the existing infrastructure. The changes added $1.7 million to the $8.9 million project and delayed work by nine months.

projects.name: Nome AK Front Street Seawall and Road Reconstruction
projects.description: Seawall and road reconstruction required extensive plan revisions after gold-dredge era pipes and Cold War military utility infrastructure were discovered beneath Front Street.
projects.detail: AKDOT initiated a combined seawall replacement and road reconstruction project on Front Street in Nome to address chronic storm damage and coastal erosion. During excavation, crews encountered gold-dredge era pipes, Cold War military utility infrastructure from the nearby former Air Force facility, and active water and sewer lines at depths substantially different from available records. The permafrost conditions made utility relocation particularly complex and expensive. The design team had to develop a revised foundation plan that accommodated the discovered infrastructure while maintaining seawall structural integrity, adding $5.7 million to the $31.6 million project.

projects.name: Hilo HI Bayfront Highway Stormwater Improvement
projects.description: Stormwater improvement plans on Bayfront Highway required revision when plantation-era drainage infrastructure was found to conflict with modern utility conduits.
projects.detail: The County of Hawaii initiated a stormwater improvement project along Bayfront Highway in Hilo to address chronic flooding during heavy rains. Subsurface investigation revealed extensive plantation-era drainage infrastructure, including hand-built stone culverts and cast iron pipes, that was intermixed with modern utility conduits installed by HELCO and Hawaiian Telcom. The historic drainage features were structurally integrated with the roadbed foundation, making removal impractical. Engineers redesigned the stormwater system to incorporate the historic drainage features where possible and route new infrastructure around utility conflicts, adding $3.4 million to the $22.7 million project.

projects.name: Berlin NH Route 16 Gateway Improvement
projects.description: Gateway improvement project required plan revisions when century-old paper mill utility infrastructure was discovered beneath the Route 16 corridor.
projects.detail: NHDOT planned gateway improvements on Route 16 entering Berlin from the south, including new sidewalks, lighting, and drainage. Excavation uncovered century-old utility infrastructure from the former Brown Company paper mill operations, including industrial water lines, steam pipe remnants, and electrical conduits that were not shown on any modern utility maps. Some of the abandoned industrial pipes contained residual contaminants requiring environmental assessment. The design had to be revised to avoid disturbing the contaminated pipes and route new utilities around the historic infrastructure, adding $1.5 million to the $7.1 million project.

projects.name: Claremont NH Pleasant Street Bridge Replacement
projects.description: Bridge replacement was delayed when Liberty Utilities could not coordinate gas main relocation within the construction window due to winter moratorium scheduling conflicts.
projects.detail: The Pleasant Street Bridge in Claremont required replacement due to structural deficiency. NHDOT scheduled construction to begin in spring, but Liberty Utilities informed the state that the gas main attached to the bridge could not be relocated until the following fall due to their own winter moratorium on excavation work and competing projects in the region. The scheduling conflict meant the bridge demolition could not proceed as planned, forcing NHDOT to rephase the project around the utility company's availability. The delay added $1.2 million in standby costs and inflation to the $10.8 million project and pushed completion back nine months.

projects.name: Barre VT North Main Street Reconstruction
projects.description: Street reconstruction was delayed by scheduling conflicts with Green Mountain Power and the city water department, both claiming priority for underground work in the same corridor.
projects.detail: Barre planned a full reconstruction of North Main Street including new water lines, drainage, and pavement. Green Mountain Power needed the same construction window to upgrade underground electrical conduits, and the city water department insisted on completing their water main replacement before any road work. Neither utility could adjust their schedules due to workforce and equipment commitments elsewhere. VTrans had to mediate a phased approach that extended the project across an additional construction season, adding $1.8 million in mobilization and traffic management costs to the $12 million project and delaying completion by eleven months.

projects.name: Bluefield WV Princeton Avenue Infrastructure Overhaul
projects.description: Infrastructure overhaul delayed over a year by scheduling conflicts between Appalachian Power, Mountaineer Gas, and the city water department competing for the same construction corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Bluefield planned a comprehensive infrastructure overhaul of Princeton Avenue to replace water mains, upgrade storm drains, and repave the roadway. Appalachian Power, Mountaineer Gas, and the city water department all needed underground access in the corridor but could not coordinate schedules. Appalachian Power's underground cable replacement was scheduled during the only window available for water main work, while Mountaineer Gas insisted on completing their gas main replacement before any other utility excavation occurred. The three-way scheduling impasse required multiple rounds of mediation and ultimately delayed the project by over a year, adding $1.9 million to the $11.2 million project.

projects.name: Somerset KY US-27 South Corridor Widening
projects.description: Corridor widening delayed by scheduling conflicts with Kentucky Utilities, AT&T, and the local water district over underground utility relocation sequencing.
projects.detail: KYTC planned a widening of US-27 South through Somerset to add capacity in the growing commercial corridor near Lake Cumberland. Kentucky Utilities, AT&T, and the Southeastern Water Association all needed to relocate underground infrastructure before road widening could proceed, but each utility demanded that their relocation be completed before the others began work. Kentucky Utilities cited OSHA clearance requirements, AT&T cited fiber optic service continuity needs, and the water district cited pressure maintenance concerns. The sequential approach demanded by each utility extended the utility relocation phase by fourteen months, adding $3.2 million to the $26.8 million project.

projects.name: Starkville MS Highway 12 West Corridor Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Highway 12 corridor improvements delayed by scheduling conflicts between Mississippi State University utility expansion and MDOT road construction timelines.
projects.detail: MDOT planned improvements to Highway 12 West near the Mississippi State University campus, including turn lanes, sidewalks, and drainage upgrades. MSU was simultaneously expanding campus utility infrastructure including chilled water loops and telecommunications conduits that crossed the highway corridor. The university's academic calendar constrained their construction windows, which did not align with MDOT's planned road construction schedule. Neither party could adjust without significant cost implications, leading to a ten-month delay while a compromise phasing plan was developed. The scheduling conflict added $1.5 million to the $9.4 million project.

projects.name: Valley City ND Main Street Flood Mitigation Utility Delay
projects.description: Flood mitigation road improvements delayed when MDU Resources and Otter Tail Power could not coordinate their underground utility relocations within the project schedule.
projects.detail: Valley City planned Main Street flood mitigation improvements including road raising, new storm drains, and flood barriers as part of an ongoing flood protection program. Montana-Dakota Utilities (MDU) and Otter Tail Power Company both needed to relocate underground infrastructure but could not coordinate their schedules. MDU insisted on completing gas main relocation before Otter Tail's electrical conduit work to avoid safety conflicts, but MDU's crews were committed to projects in Bismarck through the prime construction season. The sequential scheduling requirement and crew unavailability delayed road construction by eleven months, adding $2.7 million to the $19.3 million project.

projects.name: Lewistown MT Main Street Reconstruction Utility Scheduling
projects.description: Main Street reconstruction delayed by scheduling conflict between NorthWestern Energy and the city water department over underground work in the historic commercial district.
projects.detail: The City of Lewistown planned a reconstruction of Main Street through the historic downtown area, including new water lines, storm drainage, and pavement. NorthWestern Energy needed to replace aging gas distribution mains in the same corridor but could not align their construction schedule with the city's short summer construction season. NorthWestern's crews were committed to higher-priority projects in Billings and Great Falls, leaving Lewistown without gas utility coordination during the optimal construction window. The delay pushed road construction into the following year, adding $1.4 million to the $7.8 million project and extending the timeline by eight months.

projects.name: Riverton WY Federal Boulevard Utility Coordination Delay
projects.description: Federal Boulevard improvements delayed by scheduling conflicts between Wind River Reservation utility authority and WYDOT over underground infrastructure work sequencing.
projects.detail: WYDOT planned improvements to Federal Boulevard in Riverton, which borders the Wind River Indian Reservation. The project required coordination with the reservation's utility authority for underground infrastructure that crossed the city-reservation boundary. Scheduling conflicts arose because the tribal utility authority operated on a different fiscal year and project approval cycle than WYDOT, and their underground crew availability did not coincide with WYDOT's construction window. Additional federal Bureau of Indian Affairs coordination requirements further complicated the scheduling. The delays added $1.7 million to the $11.3 million project and extended the timeline by ten months.

projects.name: Silver City NM Highway 180 East Utility Scheduling Failure
projects.description: Highway improvement delayed over ten months when New Mexico Gas Company and Freeport-McMoRan mining utilities could not coordinate underground relocations with NMDOT construction.
projects.detail: NMDOT planned improvements to Highway 180 East near Silver City, including shoulder widening and drainage upgrades in the corridor serving the Freeport-McMoRan copper mining operations. New Mexico Gas Company needed to relocate a gas distribution main, and Freeport-McMoRan had private industrial utility lines crossing the highway right-of-way that also needed relocation. Neither entity could coordinate their underground work schedules with NMDOT's construction timeline. The mining company's utility work was constrained by production schedules, while New Mexico Gas Company cited competing projects in the Albuquerque metro area. The coordination failure delayed the project by eleven months, adding $2.2 million to the $16.9 million project.

projects.name: Kapolei HI Farrington Highway Widening Utility Delay
projects.description: Highway widening delayed over a year by scheduling conflicts between HECO underground cable relocation, Navy water main work, and HART rail utility coordination in the same corridor.
projects.detail: HDOT planned a widening of Farrington Highway through Kapolei to address severe congestion in Oahu's growing 'second city' district. Hawaiian Electric Company (HECO) needed to relocate underground cables, the Navy's Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam had water main infrastructure crossing the corridor, and the Honolulu Authority for Rapid Transportation (HART) was performing rail-related utility work in adjacent areas that affected the same utility connections. The three-way scheduling conflict was compounded by military base access restrictions and HART's own construction delays. The coordination failure delayed road construction by sixteen months and added $7.8 million to the $55.7 million project.

projects.name: Palmer AK Glenn Highway Interchange Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Interchange improvement delayed a full year when Matanuska Electric Association and Enstar Natural Gas could not coordinate underground relocations within the short Alaska construction season.
projects.detail: AKDOT planned an interchange improvement on the Glenn Highway in Palmer to address growing traffic from the Mat-Su Valley residential boom. Matanuska Electric Association (MEA) and Enstar Natural Gas both needed to relocate underground infrastructure but could not coordinate their work within the short Alaskan construction season. MEA's underground crew was committed to wildfire recovery work in the Talkeetna area, and Enstar's gas main relocation required ground conditions that were only suitable for a narrow window in summer. The lost construction season pushed the project back a full year, adding $3.6 million in delay costs and inflation to the $24 million project.

projects.name: Covington KY Madison Avenue Streetscape Utility Scheduling
projects.description: Downtown streetscape project delayed by scheduling conflicts between Duke Energy, Northern Kentucky Water District, and Cincinnati Bell underground work in the same corridor.
projects.detail: The City of Covington planned a Madison Avenue streetscape improvement in the downtown core to enhance pedestrian facilities and upgrade aging infrastructure. Duke Energy Kentucky, Northern Kentucky Water District, and Cincinnati Bell all needed to perform underground work in the corridor but could not coordinate their schedules. Duke Energy cited a regional transformer upgrade that required their underground crews, while the water district was constrained by a consent decree timeline for lead service line replacements. Cincinnati Bell's fiber optic installation schedule conflicted with both other utilities' timelines. The coordination failure delayed road construction by ten months, adding $2.5 million to the $15.6 million project.

projects.name: Augusta ME Western Avenue Bridge Utility Strike
projects.description: Bridge reconstruction crew severed a high-voltage Versant Power underground feeder cable, causing a widespread power outage and six-month project delay.
projects.detail: During bridge approach reconstruction on Western Avenue in Augusta, a pile driving crew severed a high-voltage underground feeder cable operated by Versant Power (formerly Emera Maine). The cable was feeding the state government complex and its disruption caused a widespread power outage affecting state offices and nearby businesses. The cable had been incorrectly mapped as running along the opposite side of the road from its actual location. The severing required emergency cable repair, environmental remediation of cable insulation fluid, and a complete re-survey of all underground utilities in the bridge approach area. The incident added $1.3 million to the $11.8 million project and delayed completion by six months.

projects.name: Georgetown DE Route 9 Water Main Strike
projects.description: Road improvement crew struck a water transmission main feeding the Sussex County government complex, flooding the excavation site and delaying the project three months.
projects.detail: During Route 9 road improvement work in Georgetown, an excavation crew struck a 16-inch water transmission main that served the Sussex County government complex. The strike flooded the excavation site and caused a water pressure loss that affected the county courthouse, administrative offices, and detention center. The water main was located eight feet from its marked position due to an error in the utility locate survey. Emergency repairs required road closure for a week and extensive dewatering of the excavation zone. The incident added $480,000 to the $4.8 million road improvement project and delayed work by three months while the utility locate records were corrected for the remainder of the corridor.

projects.name: Jamestown ND Highway 281 Bridge Construction Pipeline Strike
projects.description: Bridge construction crew struck a petroleum product pipeline during approach grading, triggering an environmental cleanup and eight-month construction halt.
projects.detail: During Highway 281 bridge approach grading near Jamestown, construction equipment struck a petroleum product pipeline that was buried at a shallower depth than indicated in pipeline location records. The strike caused a release of refined petroleum product that required emergency environmental response from the ND Department of Environmental Quality. The pipeline was operated by a regional petroleum transport company and had been installed decades earlier when the road was at a different grade. Environmental cleanup and pipeline repair required an eight-month construction halt, during which the bridge approach area was treated as a contaminated site. The incident added $1.8 million to the $13.9 million bridge project.

projects.name: Ewa Beach HI Fort Weaver Road Water Main Strike
projects.description: Road improvement crew struck a Board of Water Supply transmission main on Fort Weaver Road, flooding a residential neighborhood and delaying the project seven months.
projects.detail: During Fort Weaver Road improvement construction in Ewa Beach, a grading crew struck a 20-inch Honolulu Board of Water Supply transmission main that was located outside its mapped position. The strike caused massive water release that flooded an adjacent residential neighborhood, damaging several homes and vehicles. The transmission main served the entire Ewa Beach community and its disruption required emergency water service from tanker trucks for 48 hours. The Board of Water Supply filed a claim against the contractor, and the resulting investigation and repair work delayed the $11.5 million road improvement project by seven months, adding $1.5 million in repair, remediation, and standby costs.

projects.name: Soldotna AK Kenai Spur Highway Electric Line Strike
projects.description: Highway reconstruction crew struck a Homer Electric Association buried feeder line, causing a power outage to the commercial district and a five-month construction delay.
projects.detail: During Kenai Spur Highway reconstruction in Soldotna, a drilling crew struck a buried Homer Electric Association (HEA) feeder line while installing foundation piles for a new traffic signal. The strike caused a power outage that affected the Sterling Highway commercial district, including the Soldotna hospital's transfer switch. HEA's feeder line was mapped as being ten feet from its actual location due to an error in the original as-built survey from the 1980s. The incident required emergency electrical repair, signal foundation redesign, and a complete re-survey of underground utilities along the remaining project corridor. The strike added $940,000 to the $6.7 million project and delayed construction by five months.

projects.name: Corbin KY US-25W Reconstruction Telecom Cable Strike
projects.description: Road reconstruction crew severed a Windstream fiber trunk line serving the regional hospital and 911 dispatch center, causing a four-month project delay.
projects.detail: During US-25W reconstruction through Corbin, an excavation crew severed a Windstream fiber optic trunk line that served Baptist Health Corbin hospital and the local 911 dispatch center. The fiber line was not accurately located during the utility marking process, with the actual cable running four feet from its marked position. The severing disrupted emergency communications for several hours until Windstream could splice the fiber. The incident triggered an investigation by the Kentucky Public Service Commission and required mandatory hand-digging protocols for the remainder of the project, adding $630,000 to the $5.7 million reconstruction project and delaying work by four months.

projects.name: Ketchikan AK Tongass Avenue Utility Corridor Redesign
projects.description: Tongass Avenue road improvement required plan revision after discovering unmapped timber-era water infrastructure and Alaska Power & Telephone conduits beneath the roadway.
projects.detail: AKDOT planned road improvements on Tongass Avenue in Ketchikan, the primary commercial corridor for the island community. Subsurface investigation revealed unmapped water infrastructure from the former pulp mill era along with Alaska Power & Telephone underground conduits that were not reflected in utility databases. The timber-era pipes were structurally compromised and could not support road construction equipment loads without reinforcement. Engineers redesigned the road foundation and utility corridor to bridge over the fragile historic infrastructure, adding $3.8 million to the $22.4 million project and delaying completion by a year.

projects.name: Presque Isle ME Aroostook Avenue Utility Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Road reconstruction delayed by scheduling conflict between Versant Power and Maine Water Company over underground infrastructure work in the short northern Maine construction season.
projects.detail: MaineDOT planned reconstruction of Aroostook Avenue in Presque Isle to address pavement failure and drainage issues. Versant Power and Maine Water Company both needed to perform underground work in the corridor but could not coordinate within the short northern Maine construction season, which runs roughly from late May through early October. Versant Power's underground crew was committed to storm recovery work in the Bangor area, and Maine Water Company could not begin water main replacement until Versant's electrical work was complete for safety reasons. The scheduling conflict delayed road construction by eight months and added $1.4 million to the $8.7 million project.

projects.name: Murray KY 12th Street Reconstruction Scheduling Conflict
projects.description: Road reconstruction delayed by scheduling conflict between Murray Electric System, Murray State University utilities, and the city sewer department.
projects.detail: The City of Murray planned reconstruction of 12th Street, the primary commercial corridor near Murray State University. Murray Electric System, Murray State University's campus utilities division, and the city sewer department all needed to perform underground work in the corridor. Murray State's utilities work was constrained by the academic calendar and could only occur during summer break, which conflicted with Murray Electric's planned transformer vault installation. The city sewer department required access before either other utility but could not begin until a university research project occupying the right-of-way was completed. The three-way scheduling conflict delayed the project by seven months, adding $1.1 million to the $7.8 million project.

projects.name: Wahpeton ND Dakota Avenue Reconstruction Utility Scheduling Delay
projects.description: Avenue reconstruction delayed six months by scheduling conflict between Otter Tail Power Company and the city water department over underground utility work sequencing.
projects.detail: The City of Wahpeton planned reconstruction of Dakota Avenue, the main commercial street in the border community. Otter Tail Power Company needed to upgrade underground electrical infrastructure in the corridor, and the city water department needed to replace aging water mains. The two projects required sequential construction in the same trench zone, but Otter Tail's crew availability did not align with the city's construction season. The power company's underground crews were committed to a transmission upgrade project in Fergus Falls, Minnesota, delaying their Wahpeton work past the optimal construction window. The scheduling conflict added $890,000 to the $5.9 million project.

projects.name: Keene NH Winchester Street Gas Main Strike During Fiber Installation
projects.description: Fiber optic contractor struck a Liberty Utilities gas main during boring on Winchester Street, forcing commercial district evacuation and halting the road project for four months.
projects.detail: A fiber optic installation contractor performing horizontal directional drilling on Winchester Street in Keene struck a Liberty Utilities gas distribution main. The bore path deviated from its planned trajectory due to rocky subsurface conditions and intersected the gas main. The strike caused a gas leak that required evacuation of nearby commercial buildings and Liberty Utilities emergency response. The contractor was working under a permit associated with the city's ongoing road improvement project. The incident halted the road project for four months while all utility locates were re-verified and boring protocols were revised, adding $550,000 to the $5 million project.

projects.name: Middlebury VT Court Street Extension Water Main Strike
projects.description: Sewer installation crew struck a water main on Court Street, flooding the construction zone near Middlebury College and delaying the project three months.
projects.detail: During sewer line installation on Court Street Extension near Middlebury College, a trenching crew struck a 10-inch water main that served the college campus area. The main was located five feet from its marked position due to a survey error in the original utility locate. The strike flooded the construction zone and disrupted water service to portions of the Middlebury College campus for over 24 hours. The incident required emergency main repair, construction zone dewatering, and a full re-survey of underground utilities in the project corridor. The strike added $480,000 to the $4 million sewer project and delayed work by three months.

projects.name: Clarksburg WV Main Street Bridge Utility Strike
projects.description: Bridge approach reconstruction crew struck both a gas line and a water main in the same excavation, causing dual emergencies and a five-month project halt.
projects.detail: During Main Street bridge approach reconstruction in Clarksburg, an excavation crew struck both a Mountaineer Gas distribution line and a city water main in the same trench cut. The dual strike caused simultaneous gas and water emergencies, with the water flow washing gas toward storm drains and creating an explosion hazard. Emergency response required evacuation of the downtown business district and coordinated shutdown of both utilities. The gas line and water main were both located at positions different from their utility markings due to historical road realignment that was never reflected in utility records. The dual-strike incident added $870,000 to the $6.7 million bridge project and halted construction for five months.

projects.name: Juneau AK Egan Drive Gas Line Strike During Drainage Work
projects.description: Drainage improvement crew struck an ENSTAR Natural Gas distribution main on Egan Drive, forcing evacuation of the Mendenhall Valley commercial area and a six-month delay.
projects.detail: During drainage improvement work on Egan Drive in Juneau, a construction crew struck an ENSTAR Natural Gas distribution main while installing new storm drain pipe. The gas main was at its marked horizontal position but at a depth significantly shallower than indicated in utility records, within the excavation zone for the new storm drain. The strike caused a gas leak that required evacuation of businesses in the Mendenhall Valley commercial area and ENSTAR emergency response. The incident occurred in September, and the resulting delay pushed remaining construction into the Southeast Alaska winter, effectively adding a full construction season. The strike added $1.1 million to the $7.8 million project.

projects.name: Floresville Fiber/Gas Explosion
projects.description: Fiber optic contractor struck a CenterPoint Energy gas main due to incorrect utility markings, triggering a house explosion that destroyed one home and damaged 13 properties.
projects.detail: On July 16, 2024, C4 Unlimited was installing telecommunications conduit for Rise Broadband near H Street and 9th Street in Floresville when the crew hit a gas main. A contract locator had incorrectly marked the location of the 2-inch plastic main. While CenterPoint was attempting to isolate the leak, the home at 1605 H St. exploded, destroying the residence and damaging neighboring properties. Total property damage reached $517,016. A second gas line rupture by the same crew occurred two days later.

projects.name: Twinsburg Township Fiber/Gas Explosion
projects.description: A Windstream/Kinetic fiber contractor struck a gas line due to inaccurate third-party utility markings, causing an explosion that destroyed 3 homes and damaged 36 others.
projects.detail: On June 25, 2026, a subcontractor for Windstream's Kinetic Fiber Internet struck an Enbridge Gas Ohio natural gas line while installing fiber optic cable on Hiram Lane in The Woodlands subdivision. The resulting explosion destroyed three homes and damaged approximately 36 others. Miraculously, only minor injuries were reported. Five Northeast Ohio cities — Twinsburg, Hudson, Green, Stow, and Kent — imposed immediate moratoriums on directional drilling operations.

projects.name: Independence Google Fiber Explosion
projects.description: Google Fiber installation crew struck a gas line causing gas to accumulate in a nearby unoccupied home, which then exploded and was destroyed.
projects.detail: On August 26, 2024, a company installing Google Fiber hit a gas line near East Fair Street and South Pearl Street in Independence. Gas accumulated in the basement of a nearby home and eventually exploded, destroying the residence. No injuries were reported as residents were not home. Firefighters rescued two dogs from the scene. Residents within a two-block radius were evacuated while Spire checked gas levels. This was the second fiber-related gas explosion in the Kansas City metro area within a week.

projects.name: Woodstock Gas Explosion (Cross-Bore)
projects.description: Gas main installed through a pre-existing sewer line in 2017 was struck during sewer service work, causing an explosion that damaged 20 buildings and displaced 22 residents.
projects.detail: On October 9, 2023, VISU Sewer of Illinois was performing sewer service work at Tryon Street and Lincoln Avenue in Woodstock when they encountered a gas main that NPL Construction had run through a pre-existing sanitary line during a 2017 Nicor Gas installation. The resulting explosion leveled one home, rendered two additional homes structurally uninhabitable, and damaged a total of 20 buildings. State Farm filed a lawsuit in March 2025 seeking $959,170 in claims.

projects.name: Lexington MO Fiber Boring Fatality
projects.description: Fiber optic drilling crew struck an unmarked gas main; failure to evacuate nearby homes for nearly four hours led to a fatal explosion killing a 5-year-old child.
projects.detail: On April 9, 2025, Alfra Construction was drilling to install fiber optic line for Sellenriek Construction when they struck an unmarked section of a capped underground gas main operated by Liberty Utilities. The crew reported the strike and called 911 at 4 p.m., but for nearly four hours no evacuation was ordered for nearby homes. At 7:42 p.m., the gas exploded, destroying one residence, killing 5-year-old Alistair Lamb and critically injuring his father and sister. NTSB investigation confirmed the gas main was left unmarked.

projects.name: Sheboygan County Pipeline Rupture
projects.description: Spectrum cable contractor struck a 10-inch high-pressure TC Energy gas main, causing an explosion that injured four people and forced evacuation of 60 homes.
projects.detail: On November 14, 2025, an excavation crew working for a Spectrum contractor struck a 10-inch TC Energy natural gas main on Trio Lane in the Town of Mitchell, west of Cascade. The rupture caused an explosion that injured four people and rendered two homes uninhabitable. Approximately 60 homes were evacuated, requiring response from 17 fire departments. The high-pressure nature of the line (600-800 PSI) made this incident particularly dangerous.
projects.budget: Cable installation → $2M+ estimated property and infrastructure damage

projects.name: Oswego Gas Main Fire
projects.description: Construction crew ruptured a Nicor gas main during road work, igniting an 8-hour fire that destroyed two pieces of heavy equipment and shut down Wolf Road.
projects.detail: On June 6, 2025, construction workers on Wolf Road near Fifth Street in Oswego ruptured a Nicor Gas main, igniting a fire that burned for approximately eight hours. Two pieces of construction equipment were destroyed. Wolf Road was closed in both directions between Secretariat Lane and Roth Road. Multiple agencies responded including Oswego Fire, NICOR, OSHA, EPA, and the Illinois Commerce Commission.
projects.budget: $2.5M road project → $2.9M with damage and delays
